About this text

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines (Sanskrit: Āryāṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitā; Tibetan: Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa brgyad stong pa) is one of the foundational scriptures of the Mahāyāna. It is a sūtra that presents the bodhisattva path through the perfection of wisdom, the understanding of the emptiness of all phenomena, and describes how bodhisattvas should practice, what they should realize, and how this wisdom relates to the other perfections. It opens in the traditional manner, with the Buddha teaching at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak before a great assembly of arhats. The text is Toh 12 in the Kangyur, belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā class of sūtras, and it is widely regarded as the oldest and most central of the Perfection of Wisdom scriptures, standing as the basis from which many longer and shorter versions were developed.

Translation

In the language of India: Ārya-aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā. In the language of Tibet: The Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. First volume.

Homage to all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, and to all the noble hearers and solitary buddhas.

Thus did I hear at one time. The Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha, on the mountain called the Vulture Peak, together with a great community of monks, twelve hundred and fifty monks. All of them were arhats, with defilements exhausted, free from affliction, masters of their minds, their minds fully liberated and their wisdom fully liberated, of noble lineage, great elephants. They had done what was to be done, accomplished their task, laid down their burden, attained their own aim, and utterly exhausted the fetters that bind to existence. Through perfect knowing their minds were completely freed, and they had reached the far shore of supreme mastery over all mind. All of them were of this kind, with the exception of one person, namely the venerable Ānanda.

Then the Blessed One addressed the elder, the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, taking as your subject the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the great beings, speak with confident eloquence, so that the bodhisattvas, the great beings, will come to go forth definitively in the perfection of wisdom.

Then the venerable Śāriputra thought: Will the venerable Subhūti, through the power of his own eloquent wisdom, generating it by himself and empowering it, teach the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the great beings? Or is it through the power of the Buddha?

Then, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Subhūti knew in his mind this very thought in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra, and said to the venerable Śāriputra: Venerable Śāriputra, whatever the Blessed One's hearers speak, teach, explain, expound, clarify, and thoroughly clarify, all of it should be understood as the power of the Tathāgata, the supreme person. Why is that? When they train in the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, they realize the nature of reality directly and hold it. Having directly realized and grasped that nature of reality, whatever they declare, teach, explain, expound, clarify, and thoroughly clarify, all of it is in no way contrary to the nature of reality. Venerable Śāriputra, sons of good family such as these, who explain the nature of reality in this way without contradicting it, are also in accord with the causes of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.

Then, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, you have declared: Subhūti, taking as your subject the perfection of wisdom of the bodhisattvas, the great beings, speak with confident eloquence, so that the bodhisattvas, the great beings, will come to go forth definitively in the perfection of wisdom. Blessed One, when one says "bodhisattva, bodhisattva," what is this word "bodhisattva," Blessed One, a designation for? Blessed One, I do not truly see, as an actual phenomenon, any dharma that is called "bodhisattva."

Blessed One, that dharma called the perfection of wisdom, too, I do not truly see as an actual phenomenon. Blessed One, I neither apprehend nor find, nor truly see, either a bodhisattva or the dharma of a bodhisattva; and the perfection of wisdom, too, I neither apprehend nor find nor truly see. Since this is so, which bodhisattva is to be instructed and taught in which perfection of wisdom?

And yet, Blessed One, if, when this is spoken, taught, and explained, the bodhisattva, the great being, is not discouraged in mind, not utterly disheartened, not timid, and does not become faint-hearted; if the mind does not turn back from this, is not broken, and does not retreat; if one is not terrified, not utterly afraid, and does not come to be possessed of fear, then this itself is how the bodhisattva, the great being, is to be taught in the perfection of wisdom. This itself is to be recognized as the perfection of wisdom of that bodhisattva, that great being. This itself is the instruction in the perfection of wisdom. If one abides in this way, that very thing is the instruction and the teaching of this bodhisattva.

Blessed One, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, who practices the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, should train in such a way that he does not become conceited even about this awakening mind. Why is that? Because that mind is no mind; the intrinsic nature of mind is luminosity.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: Venerable Subhūti, does that mind which is no mind exist?

When he had said this, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Śāriputra: Venerable Śāriputra, with respect to that very state of no-mind, is there existence or non-existence in it? Can either be found or apprehended?

Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, that is not so.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, if in that no-mind neither existence nor non-existence is present or apprehended, then, venerable Śāriputra, how could your challenge, when you asked, "Does that mind which is no mind exist?", be reasonable?

When he had said this, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: Venerable Subhūti, then what is that very no-mind?

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, that no-mind is changeless and free of conceptual thought.

Then the venerable Śāriputra gave his approval to the venerable Subhūti, saying "Excellent!": Venerable Subhūti, excellent, excellent! Just as the Blessed One declared you to be supreme among those who abide in freedom from affliction, so you teach well.

Therefore, too, the bodhisattva, the great being, should be understood as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And it should be understood that the bodhisattva, the great being, is never separated from the perfection of wisdom.

One who wishes to train in the stage of the hearers, too, should listen to this very perfection of wisdom, take it up, hold it, recite it, thoroughly understand it, and study it aloud. One should train in this very perfection of wisdom and apply oneself to it in practice.

One who wishes to train in the stage of the solitary buddhas, too, should listen to this very perfection of wisdom, take it up, hold it, recite it, thoroughly understand it, and study it aloud. One should train in this very perfection of wisdom and apply oneself to it in practice.

One who wishes to train in the stage of the bodhisattvas, too, should listen to this very perfection of wisdom, take it up, hold it, recite it, thoroughly understand it, and study it aloud. Endowed with skillful means, one should apply oneself in practice to this very perfection of wisdom, in order to attain all the qualities of a bodhisattva. Why is this so? Because all the qualities of a bodhisattva in which the bodhisattva, the great being, should train and apply himself in practice are taught extensively in this very perfection of wisdom.

One who wishes to train in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, too, should listen to this very perfection of wisdom, take it up, hold it, recite it, thoroughly understand it, and study it aloud. Endowed with skillful means, one should apply oneself in practice to this very perfection of wisdom, in order to attain all the qualities of a buddha. Why is this so? Because all the qualities of a buddha in which the bodhisattva, the great being, should train and apply himself in practice are taught extensively in this very perfection of wisdom.

Then the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One with these words: Blessed One, this very name "bodhisattva" I do not find, I do not apprehend, I do not perceive in truth. The perfection of wisdom, too, I do not find, I do not apprehend, I do not perceive in truth. Blessed One, if I neither find nor apprehend nor perceive in truth this name "bodhisattva," and likewise neither find nor apprehend nor perceive in truth the perfection of wisdom, then what bodhisattva am I to counsel and instruct, and in what perfection of wisdom? Blessed One, since I neither find nor apprehend nor perceive in truth any real entity, to apply and designate the mere name, "bodhisattva," as I do, is a hindrance weighing upon my heart.

Yet, Blessed One, that name too is neither abiding nor not abiding, and it is neither separate from abiding nor not separate from abiding. Why is that? Because that name does not exist. Thus that name neither abides nor does not abide, and it is neither separate from abiding nor not separate from abiding.

Blessed One, when the perfection of wisdom, so profound, is explained, taught, and expounded in this way, the mind of the bodhisattva, the great being, does not become stiff, does not become dejected, does not become anxious, does not become timid. His mind does not turn back or recoil from it. He is not alarmed and not terrified, and does not become possessed by dread. Such a bodhisattva, a great being, who has faith through lofty intention, should be understood as not separated from the perfection of wisdom. He abides on the stage of the irreversible bodhisattva, and he abides well in the manner of not abiding.

Blessed One, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, who practices the perfection of wisdom and cultivates the perfection of wisdom, does not abide in form. Likewise he does not abide in feeling, nor in perception, nor in formations, nor in consciousness. Why is that?

If he were to abide in form, he would be engaging in the mental construction of form, and would not be practicing the perfection of wisdom. Likewise, if he were to abide in feeling, perception, and formations, and if he were to abide in consciousness, he would be engaging in the mental construction of consciousness, and would not be practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Why is that? If he engages in mental construction, he does not take hold of the perfection of wisdom, he does not apply himself in yoga to the perfection of wisdom, and he does not bring the perfection of wisdom to completion. And if the perfection of wisdom is not brought to completion, then by grasping what is not to be grasped, he will not emerge into omniscience.

Why is that? Because in the perfection of wisdom there is no grasping of form. Likewise, in the perfection of wisdom there is no grasping of feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. That which is the absence of grasping at form is not form. Likewise, that which is feeling, that which is perception, and that which is formations, and that which is the absence of grasping at consciousness, is not consciousness. And the perfection of wisdom itself is likewise not grasped.

In just this way, the bodhisattva, the great being, should practice this perfection of wisdom. This is the absorption of the bodhisattva, the great being, called the absence of grasping at all phenomena. It is vast, pioneered by the immeasurable, definitive, and not shared with any of the hearers or solitary buddhas.

Omniscience itself is also not grasped; it is not grasped as a sign. If it were grasped as a sign, then the one who wanders in the cycle of existence would not have faith in it. But the one who wanders in the cycle of existence, having devotion to this wisdom of omniscience, follows it with faith, and enters by way of a wisdom directed to a single purpose. Having entered, he does not grasp at form. Likewise he does not grasp at feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.

Regarding this, that knowing does not rightly perceive joy or bliss. That knowing does not rightly perceive itself as belonging to inner form. It does not rightly perceive itself as belonging to outer form. It does not rightly perceive itself as belonging to form both inner and outer. It does not rightly perceive itself as something other than form. Likewise, that knowing does not belong to inner feeling, perception, or formations. It does not rightly perceive itself as belonging to inner consciousness. It does not rightly perceive itself as belonging to outer consciousness. It does not rightly perceive itself as belonging to consciousness both inner and outer. It does not rightly perceive itself as something other than consciousness.

By this manner of expression, the one who wanders in the cycle of existence has devotion. He follows this wisdom of omniscience everywhere with faith, taking the nature of reality as his authority, and this is what is called devotion. By him no phenomenon whatsoever is grasped. No phenomenon that is to be grasped or to be relinquished is apprehended at all. And he does not even entertain pride in having reached nirvāṇa.

Blessed One, this too should be known as the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva, a great being: such a one does not fully grasp form. In the same way, such a one does not fully grasp feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. And such a one does not pass fully into nirvāṇa midway, before having perfected the ten powers of the Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata, and the eighteen unmixed qualities of a buddha. Therefore, Blessed One, this too should be known as the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva, a great being.

Blessed One, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the perfection of wisdom and meditates on the perfection of wisdom, should examine and reflect with certainty in this way: What is this perfection of wisdom? Whose is this perfection of wisdom? Is it that which is the absence of any phenomenon, that which is not apprehended, that is the perfection of wisdom? If one examines in this way and reflects with certainty in this way, and is not obstructed, not discouraged, not embarrassed, not faint-hearted; if one's mind does not turn back, is not broken and does not recoil; if one does not tremble, is not terrified, and does not come to be possessed of terror, then that bodhisattva, that great being, should be known as one who is not separated from the perfection of wisdom.

Then the venerable Śāriputra spoke these words to the venerable Subhūti: Venerable Subhūti, when form itself is devoid of the essential nature of form; and likewise, when feeling itself, perception itself, and formations themselves, and likewise consciousness itself, are devoid of the essential nature of consciousness; when the perfection of wisdom itself is devoid of the essential nature of the perfection of wisdom; when omniscience itself is devoid of the essential nature of omniscience, then why should a bodhisattva, a great being, be known as one who is not separated from the perfection of wisdom?

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to the venerable Śāriputra: Venerable Śāriputra, it is just so. It is just so. Śāriputra, form itself is devoid of the essential nature of form. In the same way, feeling itself, perception itself, formations themselves, and consciousness itself, venerable Śāriputra, are devoid of the essential nature of consciousness. Venerable Śāriputra, the perfection of wisdom itself is devoid of the essential nature of the perfection of wisdom. Venerable Śāriputra, omniscience itself is devoid of the essential nature of omniscience. The perfection of wisdom is also devoid of the defining characteristic of the perfection of wisdom. The defining characteristic is also devoid of the essential nature of a defining characteristic. The basis of the characteristic is also devoid of the essential nature of the basis of the characteristic. The essential nature is also devoid of the defining characteristic of an essential nature.

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Subhūti: Venerable Subhūti, will whatever bodhisattva, great being, comes to train in this surely emerge into omniscience? The venerable Subhūti replied: Venerable Śāriputra, it is just so. It is just so. Whatever bodhisattva, great being, comes to train in this will surely emerge into omniscience. Why is that?

Venerable Śāriputra, all phenomena are without any definitive emergence, and they are unborn. Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way comes close to omniscience. And as he comes ever closer to omniscience, so too, in order to bring beings to full maturity, his body and mind become fully purified, his marks become fully purified, and the buddha-field becomes fully purified, and he also comes close to the buddhas. Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom in this way is close to omniscience.

Furthermore, the venerable Subhūti spoke as follows with reference to the bodhisattva, the great being. If he practices in form, he practices in signs. If he practices in the sign of form, he practices in signs. If he practices thinking, "Form is a sign," he practices in signs. If he practices in the arising of form, he practices in signs. If he practices in the cessation of form, he practices in signs. If he practices in the destruction of form, he practices in signs. If he practices thinking, "Form is empty," he practices in signs. If he practices thinking, "I am practicing," he practices in signs. If he practices thinking, "I am a bodhisattva," he practices in signs. If he thinks, "I am a bodhisattva," he practices in that very fixation on an object.

In the same way, if he practices in feeling, in perception, in the formations, or in consciousness, he practices in signs. If he practices in the sign of consciousness, he practices in signs. If he practices thinking, "Consciousness is a sign," he practices in signs. If he practices in the arising of consciousness, he practices in signs. If he practices in the cessation of consciousness, he practices in signs. If he practices in the destruction of consciousness, he practices in signs. If he practices thinking, "Consciousness is empty," he practices in signs. If he practices thinking, "I am practicing," he practices in signs. If he practices thinking, "I am a bodhisattva," he practices in signs. If he thinks, "I am a bodhisattva," he practices in that very fixation on an object.

And if it occurs to him, "Whoever practices in this way practices the Perfection of Wisdom; this is cultivating the Perfection of Wisdom," then he is practicing in signs themselves. This bodhisattva should be recognized as lacking skillful means.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Subhūti: Venerable Subhūti, how then does a bodhisattva, a great being, practice so as to practice the Perfection of Wisdom? When he had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to the venerable Śāriputra: Venerable Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva, a great being, does not practice in form, does not practice in the sign of form, does not practice thinking, "Form is a sign," does not practice in the arising of form, does not practice in the cessation of form, does not practice in the destruction of form, does not practice thinking, "Form is empty," does not practice thinking, "I am practicing," does not practice thinking, "I am a bodhisattva," and does not practice in fixation on an object thinking, "I am a bodhisattva"; and likewise, if he does not practice in feeling, nor in perception, nor in the formations, if he does not practice in consciousness, does not practice in the sign of consciousness, does not practice thinking, "Consciousness is a sign," does not practice in the arising of consciousness,

does not practice in the cessation of consciousness, does not practice in the destruction of consciousness, does not practice thinking, "Consciousness is empty." He does not practice thinking, "I am practicing." He does not practice thinking, "I am a bodhisattva," and does not practice in fixation on an object thinking, "I am a bodhisattva." Moreover, he does not think, "One who practices in this way is practicing in the Perfection of Wisdom; this is cultivating the Perfection of Wisdom."

A great bodhisattva who practices in this way is practicing in the Perfection of Wisdom. Yet even while practicing, he does not fully conceive, "I am practicing." He does not fully conceive, "I am not practicing." He does not fully conceive, "I practice, and yet I do not practice," nor "I neither practice nor do not practice." He does not fully conceive, "It should be practiced," nor "It should not be practiced," nor "It both should and should not be practiced," nor "It is neither what should be practiced nor what should not be practiced." Why is this so? Because all phenomena are neither fully realized nor grasped.

This is called the meditative absorption of the great bodhisattva, "the absence of any grasping at all phenomena." It is fixed in its certainty with the Vast One placed before it, and it is not shared in common with any of the hearers and solitary buddhas. The great bodhisattva who abides in this meditative absorption will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Then, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Elder Subhūti spoke thus: Blessed One, that great bodhisattva who abides in this meditative absorption is one who has been prophesied by the Tathāgatas of the past, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Yet I do not see that meditative absorption at all, not even in any way that is correct. Nor do I give rise to pride about the absorption, thinking, "I am in equipoise," or "I enter into the absorption," or "I am settled in the absorption," or "I have entered the absorption." For one such as that, there is not, in any way, in every respect, anything at all.

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Subhūti: Venerable Subhūti, are you able to teach that meditative absorption by which a great bodhisattva abides, and through which the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, prophesy his unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?

Subhūti replied: Venerable Śāriputra, I am not. Why is that? Because that son of good family does not know that meditative absorption, does not know it truly.

The venerable Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, do you say "does not know, does not truly know"?

The venerable Subhūti replied: Venerable Śāriputra, I do say "does not know, does not truly know." Why? Because that meditative absorption does not exist, he does not know and does not truly know. And that meditative absorption too is not known and not truly known.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti, "Excellent!" and continued: Subhūti, in whatever way you teach, through the power of the Tathāgata, through the eloquence given by the Tathāgata and through the Tathāgata's blessing, it is excellent, Subhūti, excellent! Subhūti, it is so, it is just so.

A bodhisattva, a great being, should train in just this way. Why is that? Because when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, he trains in the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, is he training in the Perfection of Wisdom?

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Śāriputra: Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, he is training in the Perfection of Wisdom.

When this had been said, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, in what phenomena does he train?

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Śāriputra: Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way does not train in any phenomenon at all. Why is that? Śāriputra, those phenomena do not exist in the way that ordinary, foolish beings, untaught, are fixated upon them.

The venerable Śāriputra said: Blessed One, then how do they exist?

The Blessed One said: Śāriputra, they truly exist just as they do not exist, and because they do not exist in that way, they are called ignorance. Ordinary, foolish beings who are untaught become fixated on them, and they impute that all phenomena exist where they do not. Having imputed them, they cling to the two extremes, and so they do not know and do not see those phenomena. Therefore, although those things do not exist, they conceptualize about all phenomena. Having imputed, they become fixated on the two extremes. Resting on the basis of that fixation, in the focusing of the mind, they conceptualize about past phenomena, they conceptualize about future phenomena, and they conceptualize about present phenomena. Having imputed in this way, they become fixated on name and form. They impute all phenomena that do not exist. Because they impute all those non-existent phenomena, they do not know and do not see the true path as it really is. Because they do not know and do not see the true path as it really is, they do not emerge definitively from the three realms and do not penetrate the true limit, and for that reason they are counted among those called fools. They have no faith in the true Dharma.

Moreover, Śāriputra, bodhisattvas, great beings, do not become fixated on any phenomenon at all.

When he had said this, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, is he training in omniscience?

The Blessed One said: Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, he trains in omniscience. Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, he trains in all phenomena. Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, he will be training in omniscience, he will draw near to omniscience, and he will definitively emerge into omniscience.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, if someone were to ask, "Will this illusory person train in omniscience, or draw near to omniscience, or definitively emerge into omniscience?" — if one were thus to inquire, Blessed One, how should it be taught to him?

When he had said this,

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, in this matter I shall question you, and you should answer as best you can. Subhūti said, "Excellent, Blessed One," and listened to the Blessed One, who spoke as follows.

Subhūti, what do you think? Is the illusory person different from form? And likewise, is the illusory person different from feeling, or from perception, or from the formations? Subhūti, what do you think? Is the illusory person different from consciousness?

Subhūti replied: Blessed One, it is not so. The illusory person is not different from form. Blessed One, form itself is illusion, and illusion itself is form. In the same way, Blessed One, the illusory person is not different from feeling, nor from perception, nor from the formations. Feeling, perception, and the formations themselves are illusion, and illusion itself is feeling, perception, and the formations. Blessed One, the illusory person is not different from consciousness. Consciousness itself is illusion, and illusion itself is consciousness.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding these five aggregates of clinging, is there the perception, the full knowing, the conscious awareness, and the conventional designation "bodhisattva"?

When he had said this, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in the Perfection of Wisdom will train in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening just like an illusory person. Why is that? Blessed One, because these five aggregates of clinging themselves are to be understood as the illusory person. Why is that? Blessed One, because the Blessed One has taught that form is like an illusion, and whatever is form is just the six sense faculties and these five aggregates. Blessed One, the Blessed One has taught that feeling, perception, and the formations are like an illusion, and the Blessed One has also taught that consciousness is like an illusion; and whatever is consciousness is just the six sense faculties and these five aggregates.

Blessed One, when bodhisattvas, great beings, who have newly entered the Great Vehicle hear this teaching, will they not tremble, become thoroughly terrified, and be seized by terror?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, if bodhisattvas, great beings, who have newly entered the Great Vehicle have fallen into the hands of evil friends, they will tremble, become thoroughly terrified, and be seized by terror. Subhūti, if bodhisattvas, great beings, who have newly entered the Great Vehicle have come into the hands of virtuous spiritual friends, they will not tremble, will not be thoroughly terrified, and will not be seized by terror.

When he had said this, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, who then should be recognized as the virtuous spiritual friends of a bodhisattva, a great being?

The Blessed One said: Those who instruct them in the perfections and teach them accordingly, and those who point out to them the works of Māra.

The faults of Māra should be recognized in this way: these are the faults of Māra; these are the works of Māra. You should understand these works of Māra and abandon them. Subhūti, those who speak in this way should be recognized as the virtuous spiritual friends of bodhisattvas, great beings, who have donned the great armor, who have properly entered the Great Vehicle, and who abide properly in the Great Vehicle.

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, you have said that those who speak in this way should be recognized as the virtuous spiritual friends of bodhisattvas, great beings, who have donned the great armor and have properly entered and abide in the Great Vehicle. Blessed One, concerning what you call a bodhisattva, a great being, what is the meaning of the basis for the name "bodhisattva"?

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, the meaning of the basis for "bodhisattva" is that there is no basis. Why is that? Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in non-attachment to all phenomena. Subhūti, it is by being without attachment, for the sake of realizing all phenomena, that a bodhisattva, a great being, will manifestly and completely awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Subhūti, because he seeks awakening, he is called a bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, you have said "bodhisattva, great being." Blessed One, for what reason is one called a bodhisattva, a great being?

The Blessed One said: Because he thinks, "I will become the supreme one among the great mass of beings, the great multitude of beings." For that reason he is called a bodhisattva, a great being.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, I too feel moved to speak on the meaning for which one is called a bodhisattva, a great being. The Blessed One said: Śāriputra, if you know that the time is right, then speak. The venerable Śāriputra said: He thinks, "I will teach the Dharma in order to abandon such great views as the view of a self, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-force, the view of a person, the view of arising, the view of destruction, the view of annihilation, the view of permanence, and the view of the body as one's own." For that reason he is called a bodhisattva, a great being.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, I too feel moved to speak on the meaning for which one is called a bodhisattva, a great being. The Blessed One said: Subhūti, if you know that the time is right, then speak. Subhūti said: Blessed One, as for what is called a bodhisattva, a great being, Blessed One, he does not cling to, and is not seized by, the awakening mind, the omniscient mind, the undefiled mind, the incomparable mind, the mind that is both unequal and equal, the mind that is not shared with any hearers or solitary buddhas. Why is that? Because that omniscient mind is itself undefiled and is not something that can be seized.

That omniscient mind, which is undefiled and not seized, he does not cling to, and he does not seize it. For that reason he is counted as what is called a bodhisattva, a great being.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: Venerable Subhūti, for what reason does he not cling to that mind and not seize it?

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, because there is no mind, he does not cling to that mind and does not seize it.

Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, is there then that mind which is the mindlessness of mind?

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, does that mindlessness exist, or is it nonexistent? Can it be found as existing or as nonexistent?

Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, that is not so.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, if in that mindlessness there is neither existence nor nonexistence, and it cannot be found, then, venerable Śāriputra, how can you say, "Is there that mind which is the mindlessness of mind?"

Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, in just this way you demonstrate what the Blessed One taught as the supreme abiding in freedom from affliction. Excellent!

Then the venerable Pūrṇa, son of Maitrāyaṇī, said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, one who is called a great being, a great being, is a being who has put on great armor, a being who has properly entered the Great Vehicle and properly abides in the Great Vehicle. For that reason he is counted as what is called a great being.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, since it is said, "one who has put on great armor, one who has put on great armor," Blessed One, in what way is a bodhisattva, a great being, one who has put on great armor?

The Blessed One declared: Subhūti, here a bodhisattva, a great being, thinks: "I shall lead immeasurable beings to complete nirvāṇa. I shall lead innumerable beings to complete nirvāṇa." And yet he thinks: "Those beings who have been led to complete nirvāṇa, and the one by whom they are led, do not exist." Thus he leads that many beings to complete nirvāṇa, yet there is no being at all who has been led to complete nirvāṇa, and no one by whom any being has been led to complete nirvāṇa. Why is that? Subhūti, because when one grasps the nature of an illusion, this is the nature of all phenomena.

Subhūti, suppose a skilled magician, or a magician's apprentice, conjured a great crowd of people at a crossroads on a great highway, and having conjured them, made that great crowd vanish. What do you think, Subhūti? In that case, is there anyone who has been killed, or died, or been destroyed, or been made to vanish, or anyone by whom this was done?

Subhūti replied: Blessed One, there is not.

The Blessed One declared: In just the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, leads immeasurable and innumerable beings to complete nirvāṇa, yet there is no being at all who has been led to complete nirvāṇa, or by whom anyone will be led to complete nirvāṇa.

If a bodhisattva, a great being, hearing such a teaching as this, does not tremble, is not frightened, and does not become filled with terror, then, Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva, this great being, has put on the great armor.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, alas! As I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, it should be known, Blessed One, that this bodhisattva, this great being, has put on armor that is no armor at all.

The Blessed One declared: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. This bodhisattva, this great being, should be known as one who has put on armor that is no armor. Why is that? Subhūti, omniscience is not made, not transformed, not fabricated. And those beings for whose sake this armor has been put on are likewise not made, not transformed, not fabricated.

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata. Why is that? Blessed One, form is neither bound nor liberated. In the same way, feeling, perception, and the formations are neither bound nor liberated; and consciousness, Blessed One, is neither bound nor liberated. Blessed One, the suchness of form too is neither bound nor liberated. In the same way, the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, and the suchness of the formations are neither bound nor liberated; and the suchness of consciousness, Blessed One, is neither bound nor liberated.

Then the venerable Pūrṇa, son of Maitrāyaṇī, said this to the venerable Subhūti: Venerable Subhūti, do you say that form is neither bound nor liberated? In the same way, do you say that feeling, perception, and the formations, and consciousness, venerable Subhūti, are neither bound nor liberated? Venerable Subhūti, do you say that the suchness of form too is neither bound nor liberated? In the same way, do you say that the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of the formations, and the suchness of consciousness, venerable Subhūti, are neither bound nor liberated?

Venerable Subhūti, then what is that form which you say is neither bound nor liberated? In the same way, what is that feeling, what is that perception, what are those formations, and what is that consciousness, venerable Subhūti, which you say is neither bound nor liberated? Venerable Subhūti, what is that suchness of form which you say is neither bound nor liberated? In the same way, what is that suchness of feeling, that suchness of perception, those suchnesses of the formations, and what is that suchness of consciousness, venerable Subhūti, which you say is neither bound nor liberated?

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said this to the venerable Pūrṇa, son of Maitrāyaṇī: Venerable Pūrṇa, whatever is the form of an illusory person, that is neither bound nor liberated. In the same way, whatever is the feeling of an illusory person, whatever is the perception of an illusory person, whatever are the formations of an illusory person, and, venerable Pūrṇa, whatever is the consciousness of an illusory person, that is neither bound nor liberated. Venerable Pūrṇa, whatever is the suchness of the form of an illusory person, that is neither bound nor liberated.

In the same way, whatever is the suchness of the feeling of an illusory person, the suchness of the perception, and the suchness of the formations, and, venerable Pūrṇa, whatever is the suchness of the consciousness of an illusory person, that is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because it is not real, it is neither bound nor liberated. Because it is secluded, it is neither bound nor liberated. Because it is unborn, it is neither bound nor liberated. This is the great armor of the bodhisattvas, the great beings, who have put on the great armor, who have fully entered the Great Vehicle and who abide firmly in the Great Vehicle: it is the great armor that is without armor.

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Pūrṇa, son of Maitrāyaṇī, fell silent.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, what is that Great Vehicle by which a bodhisattva, a great being who has put on the great armor, has fully entered the Great Vehicle and comes to abide in the Great Vehicle? How should one understand that one has fully entered that Great Vehicle? From where does one go forth by means of that Great Vehicle? By whom has one fully entered that Great Vehicle? Where does one come to abide by means of that Great Vehicle? And what is it that goes forth by means of that Great Vehicle?

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, this term "Great Vehicle" is a designation for the immeasurable. Subhūti, it is called "immeasurable" because it is without limit.

Subhūti, as for the question, "How should one understand that one has fully entered that Great Vehicle? From where does one go forth by means of that Great Vehicle? By whom has one fully entered it? Where does one come to abide by means of it? What is it that goes forth by means of it?": having fully entered by way of the perfections, one goes forth from the three realms. By that which is not apprehended, one has fully entered, and one comes to abide in omniscience. The bodhisattva, the great being, goes forth. And yet there is no going forth from anywhere, no one by whom one has fully entered, and no place in which one abides. Nevertheless, in the manner of non-abiding, one abides in omniscience. By that Great Vehicle nothing at all is led forth, nor does anyone go forth, nor is there any going forth. Why is that? Because both that which goes forth and that by which one goes forth are nonexistent and unapprehended. Thus, when all phenomena are nonexistent and unapprehended, what phenomenon could go forth by means of what phenomenon?

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, this which is called the Great Vehicle, the Great Vehicle, is spoken of as overpowering the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, and going forth from it. Because it is equal like space, it is the Great Vehicle. Just as in space there is room for immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings, so too, Blessed One, in the Great Vehicle there is room for immeasurable, countless, boundless sentient beings. Blessed One, for this reason this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the great beings. In it no coming is seen, no going is seen, and no abiding is found.

Blessed One, in this Great Vehicle no earlier extreme is observed, no later extreme is observed, and no middle is observed either. Blessed One, that vehicle is equal in the three times. For this reason it is called the Great Vehicle, the Great Vehicle.

Then the Blessed One said "Excellent!" to the Venerable Subhūti. "Subhūti, excellent, excellent! Subhūti, it is just so, it is just so. Thus this is the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the great beings. Those bodhisattvas, great beings, who train in it have attained, are attaining, and will attain omniscience."

Then the Venerable Pūrṇa, son of Maitrāyaṇī, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it seems to me that the Elder Subhūti, empowered by the blessing of the Perfection of Wisdom, intends to expound this Great Vehicle."

Then the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, is it not the case that I am teaching the Great Vehicle in a way that contradicts the Perfection of Wisdom?"

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, that is not so. Subhūti, you are teaching the Great Vehicle in accordance with the Perfection of Wisdom."

When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is through the power of the buddhas. Blessed One, furthermore, a bodhisattva is not fully realized at the earlier extreme, a bodhisattva is not fully realized at the later extreme, and a bodhisattva is not fully realized in the middle. Why is this not fully realized? Because form has no limit, it should be understood that the bodhisattva too has no limit. In the same way, because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness have no limit, it should be understood that the bodhisattva too has no limit. One does not fully realize form as 'bodhisattva,' for this too does not exist and is not observed. In the same way, one does not fully realize feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as 'bodhisattva,' for this too does not exist and is not observed.

"Blessed One, since I thus observe none of the phenomena of a bodhisattva in any way, in any respect, at all, Blessed One, I do not correctly see any phenomenon in which this name 'bodhisattva' exists. I also do not correctly see or observe the Perfection of Wisdom, and I do not correctly see or observe omniscience either. Blessed One, if I do not correctly see or observe any phenomena in any way, in any respect, at all, then what phenomenon, by means of what phenomenon, would I instruct and teach concerning what phenomenon?

"Blessed One, this which is called 'buddha' is merely a name. Blessed One, this which is called 'bodhisattva' is also merely a name. Blessed One, this which is called 'Perfection of Wisdom' is also merely a name. And that name too is not actually established. Blessed One, just as I speak of 'I, I,' yet, Blessed One, the self is not actually established at all, so it is. Thus, since all phenomena have no intrinsic nature, what is the form that cannot be grasped and is not actually established? What are feeling, perception, and formations? What is that consciousness that cannot be grasped and is not actually established?"

Thus, whatever is without intrinsic nature in all those phenomena is not actually established; and whatever is the non-establishment of all phenomena is also not a phenomenon. Therefore, since the Perfection of Wisdom is not actually established, what could be advised or taught regarding what is not actually established? Blessed One, apart from what is not actually established, no phenomena at all can be apprehended, neither the qualities of the buddhas, nor the qualities of the bodhisattvas, nor anyone who practices toward awakening.

Blessed One, when this is spoken, taught, and explained in this way, if the mind of a bodhisattva, a great being, is not stunned, does not sink into despondency, is not alarmed or made timid; if the mind does not turn back or turn away, and is not dismayed, not terrified, and does not become possessed of terror, then this bodhisattva, this great being, is practicing in the Perfection of Wisdom. This bodhisattva, this great being, is meditating on the Perfection of Wisdom. This bodhisattva, this great being, is closely contemplating the Perfection of Wisdom. This bodhisattva, this great being, is reflecting with certainty on the Perfection of Wisdom. This is how it should be understood.

Why is that? Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, closely contemplates these phenomena in the Perfection of Wisdom, at that time he does not closely conceive of form, does not closely grasp form, and does not correctly perceive form as arising or form as ceasing. In the same way, he does not do so with feeling, with perception, or with formations. He does not closely conceive of consciousness, does not closely grasp consciousness, and does not correctly perceive consciousness as arising or consciousness as ceasing.

Why is that? Blessed One, that which is the non-arising of form is not form, and that which is the non-destruction of form is not form. Therefore, the non-arising and what is called form are not two, and cannot be made into two. Likewise, the non-destruction and what is called form are not two, and cannot be made into two. Whatever is called form is included in the category of the non-dual.

In the same way, it is so for feeling, for perception, and for formations. And that which is the non-arising of consciousness is not consciousness, and that which is the non-destruction of consciousness is not consciousness. Therefore, the non-arising and what is called consciousness are not two, and cannot be made into two. Likewise, the non-destruction and what is called consciousness are not two, and cannot be made into two. Whatever is called consciousness is included in the category of the non-dual.

Blessed One, thus, if one closely contemplates all phenomena in every respect in the Perfection of Wisdom, then one does not closely conceive of form, does not closely grasp form, and does not correctly perceive form as arising or form as ceasing. In the same way, it is not so with feeling, not so with perception, not so with formations.

Consciousness one does not closely conceive, consciousness one does not closely grasp, and one does not correctly perceive consciousness as arising or as ceasing. Why is this so? Because, Blessed One, that which is the non-arising of form is not form, and that which is the non-destruction of form is not form. Therefore, the non-arising and what is called form are not two, and cannot be made into two. Likewise, the non-destruction and what is called form are not two, and cannot be made into two. Whatever is called form is included in the category of the non-dual.

In the same way, so it is with feeling, so it is with perception, and so it is with formations. And so it is with consciousness: that which is the non-arising of consciousness is not consciousness, and that which is the non-destruction of consciousness is not consciousness. Therefore, the non-arising and what is called consciousness are not two, and cannot be made into two. Likewise, the non-destruction and what is called consciousness are not two, and cannot be made into two. Whatever is called consciousness is included in the category of the non-dual.

Then the venerable Śāriputra spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows. "Venerable Subhūti, as I understand the meaning of what you have said, in that case the bodhisattva too is without arising. Venerable Subhūti, if the bodhisattva too is without arising, then what is there for the bodhisattva who practices difficult austerities, or who strives to experience whatever sufferings there are for the sake of sentient beings?"

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, I do not wish for bodhisattvas, the great beings, to practice difficult austerities. One who practices with the perception of difficulty does not even become a bodhisattva. Why is this so? Venerable Śāriputra, having given rise to the perception of difficulty, one cannot accomplish the welfare of immeasurable, innumerable sentient beings. Rather, making the perception of ease itself one's basis, the bodhisattva, the great being, gives rise toward all sentient beings to the perception of them as mother, as father, as son, and as daughter. Likewise, having formed these perceptions toward men and women, the bodhisattva, the great being, practices the bodhisattva's conduct.

"Therefore the bodhisattva, the great being, should give rise toward all sentient beings to the perception of them as mother, as father, as son, and as daughter, and even toward them as oneself. He should think: Just as I should be liberated from all suffering, completely, in every respect, entirely, so too all sentient beings should be liberated from all suffering, completely, in every respect, entirely. In this way he should give rise to this perception toward all sentient beings as well, thinking: I shall not abandon any of these sentient beings. I shall liberate all these sentient beings from the immeasurable mass of suffering. Even if my body were cut into a hundred pieces, I would not give rise to even a little harmful intent toward them. In this way the bodhisattva, the great being, should generate the mind."

If a bodhisattva practices in this way, he is not practicing with the perception of hardship, and he does not abide in the perception of hardship.

Venerable Śāriputra, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, should generate the mind thinking: Just as I am altogether non-existent and unapprehendable, completely, in every respect, entirely, so too all phenomena are altogether non-existent and unapprehendable, completely, in every respect, entirely. In this way he should give rise to this perception toward all phenomena, both inner and outer. If a bodhisattva practices in this way, he is not practicing with the perception of hardship, and he does not abide in the perception of hardship.

Venerable Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, when it is said that a bodhisattva is also without arising, is that so?" Subhūti replied: "It is so, Venerable Śāriputra, it is so. The bodhisattva is without arising."

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, is it only the bodhisattva himself who is without arising, or are the qualities of a bodhisattva also without arising?" Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, the qualities of a bodhisattva are also without arising."

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, are only the qualities of a bodhisattva without arising, or is omniscience also without arising?" Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, omniscience is also without arising."

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, is only omniscience without arising, or are the qualities of omniscience also without arising?" Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, the qualities of omniscience are also without arising."

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, are only the qualities of omniscience without arising, or are ordinary beings also without arising?" Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, ordinary beings are also without arising."

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, are only ordinary beings themselves without arising, or are the qualities of ordinary beings also without arising?" Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, the qualities of ordinary beings are also without arising."

When this had been said, the Venerable Śāriputra spoke to the Venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, if the bodhisattva is without arising, and the qualities of a bodhisattva are without arising, and omniscience is without arising, and the qualities of omniscience are without arising, and ordinary beings are without arising, and the qualities of ordinary beings are without arising, then, Venerable Subhūti, does the bodhisattva, the great being, attain omniscience?"

When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti spoke to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, I do not assert that one attains an unarisen phenomenon, nor that one realizes it. Through an unarisen phenomenon, the unarisen would not come to be attained."

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, would the arisen be attained through an unarisen phenomenon, or would the unarisen be attained through an arisen phenomenon?" Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, but is an unarisen phenomenon something that has arisen?"

"But is the unarisen phenomenon itself simply unarisen?"

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, is the very nature of the arisen unarisen, or is the unarisen phenomenon unarisen?"

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, I do not presume to speak of an arisen phenomenon or of an unarisen phenomenon."

Śāriputra said: "Venerable Subhūti, do you not presume even to speak of non-arising?"

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, non-arising itself is what is disputed, and, Venerable Śāriputra, non-arising itself is what appears distinctly, each in its own way. Venerable Śāriputra, non-arising itself is what I dare to speak of, for, Venerable Śāriputra, it is just suchness that appears so very distinctly."

When this had been said, the Venerable Śāriputra spoke to the Venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti should be placed foremost among those who teach the Dharma. Why is that? Because whatever the Elder, the Venerable Subhūti, is asked about, he comes through to a definite answer on precisely that, and he neither stirs from the nature of reality nor contradicts that nature of reality."

When this had been said, the Venerable Subhūti spoke to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, this is the nature of the Blessed One's hearers, who are of a non-abiding nature: whatever they are asked about, they come through to a definite answer on precisely that, and they neither contradict the nature of reality nor transgress it. Why is that? Because all phenomena are non-abiding."

When this had been said, the Venerable Śāriputra spoke to the Venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Venerable Subhūti! What, then, is this perfection of the bodhisattvas, the great beings, that abides in no phenomenon at all?"

Subhūti said: "Venerable Śāriputra, the Perfection of Wisdom itself, because it abides in no vehicle and in no phenomenon whatsoever, is the perfection that abides in no phenomenon at all. Thus, when a bodhisattva, a great being, is taught, shown, and closely instructed in this profound Perfection of Wisdom in this way, and his mind does not sink, does not become dejected, does not become bewildered, and does not turn to something else, you should know that this bodhisattva, this great being, abides in the abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom and is not separated from this attention."

Then the Venerable Śāriputra spoke to the Venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, how is it that a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in the abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom, is not separated from attention? Venerable Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, is not separated from attention, then he would be separated from the abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom. And, Venerable Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, is not separated from abiding in the Perfection of Wisdom, then he would be separated from that attention."

"Venerable Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva, a great being, were indeed not separated from attention and, because of that, were not separated from abiding in the Perfection of Wisdom, then, if that were so, all sentient beings too would be not separated from abiding in the Perfection of Wisdom. Why is this? Because all sentient beings also abide not separated from attention."

When he had spoken thus, the Venerable Subhūti said this to the Venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, excellent, excellent! Yet even you are open to criticism, for the Venerable Śāriputra has taken up this very point and declared it as a correct statement. Why is this? Venerable Śāriputra, because sentient beings have no intrinsic nature, attention should be understood to have no intrinsic nature. Venerable Śāriputra, because sentient beings are without real substance, attention should be understood to be without real substance. Venerable Śāriputra, because sentient beings are secluded, attention should be understood to be secluded. Venerable Śāriputra, because sentient beings are inconceivable, attention should be understood to be inconceivable. Venerable Śāriputra, because sentient beings are not fully and completely awakened, attention should be understood to be not fully and completely awakened. Venerable Śāriputra, because sentient beings are fully awakened to a meaning that is not the real as it is, attention should be understood to be fully awakened to a meaning that is not the real as it is. Venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, a great being, wishes to abide through this attention of such a nature, and through this abiding."

This is the first chapter, called "The Conduct of Omniscience," from the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

At that time, Śakra, the lord of the gods (Indra), together with forty thousand sons of the gods belonging to the class of the Thirty-Three, gathered in that very assembly and sat down. The four guardians of the world, together with twenty thousand sons of the gods of the class of the Four Great Kings, and Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, together with ten thousand sons of the gods of Brahmā's class, and five thousand sons of the gods of the Pure Abodes, also gathered in that very assembly and sat down. And whatever radiance was born from the ripening of the gods' own karma, all of it was outshone by the power of the Buddha, the splendor of the Buddha, and the blessing of the Buddha.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, spoke to the Venerable Elder Subhūti: "Noble Subhūti, these many thousands of sons of the gods gathered and seated in this assembly wish to hear from the noble Subhūti the instruction, the counsel, and the guidance on the Perfection of Wisdom for bodhisattvas, great beings. How should that bodhisattva, that great being, abide in the Perfection of Wisdom? How should he train? How should he practice?"

The Elder Subhūti said: "Kauśika, for that very reason I will give instruction through the power of the Buddha, the splendor of the Buddha, and the blessing of the Buddha. Those sons of the gods who have not yet generated the mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening should generate it. But those who have entered into the certainty of what is right have no opportunity to generate the mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Why is this?"

Because they have set a boundary to the stream of saṃsāra, they will turn through saṃsāra again and again, and they have no opportunity to generate the mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Even so, if they too should generate the mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, one should rejoice in them as well. I do not obstruct their virtue. Rather, among the noble qualities, one should aim above all at those that are most excellent and noble.

Then the Blessed One said to the Elder Subhūti: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! That you inspire joy in the bodhisattvas, the great beings, is excellent indeed, Subhūti."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the Elder Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, we will repay the kindness of the Blessed One; we cannot fail to repay that kindness. Why is this? Blessed One, in the presence of the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas of the past, when the Blessed One was formerly a bodhisattva and practiced the holy life for the sake of awakening, for our sake, those hearers who exhorted and instructed others in the perfections, those hearers, through the Blessed One's practice, brought forth the unsurpassed wisdom. Just so, Blessed One, we too will take up and uphold the bodhisattvas, the great beings, and we will carry them forward; we will fully take them up, and we will fully carry them forward. Why is this? Blessed One, because in this way we take up the bodhisattvas, the great beings, and carry them forward, and fully take them up and fully carry them forward, they will swiftly become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening."

Then the Elder Subhūti said to Śakra, lord of the gods: "Kauśika, therefore listen well, attend carefully, and keep it in mind. I will explain to you how the bodhisattva, the great being, should abide in the Perfection of Wisdom. Kauśika, the bodhisattva, the great being, should abide in the Perfection of Wisdom by abiding in emptiness. Therefore, Kauśika, the bodhisattva, the great being, should become one who puts on the great armor.

He should not abide in form. He should not abide in feeling, nor in perception, nor in formations, nor in consciousness. He should not abide in the eye. He should not abide in forms. He should not abide in eye-consciousness. He should not abide in eye-contact, the coming together of eye, form, and consciousness. He should not abide in the feeling that arises from eye-contact. In the same way, he should not abide in the ear, the nose, the tongue, the body, or the mind. He should not abide in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; nor in ear-consciousness and so on up to mind-consciousness; nor in mind-contact, nor in the feeling that arises from mind-contact.

He should not abide in the earth element. He should not abide in the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, or the consciousness element. He should not abide in the foundations of mindfulness. He should not abide in the right abandonments, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the limbs of awakening, or the path. He should not abide in the fruit of stream-entry."

He should not abide in the fruit of once-returning, nor in the fruit of non-returning, nor in the state of an arhat. He should not abide in the state of a pratyekabuddha. He should not abide in buddhahood.

Thus he should not abide in the thought, "This is form." Thus he should not abide in the thought, "This is feeling," nor "This is perception," nor "These are formations," nor in the thought, "This is consciousness." Thus he should not abide in anything from the eye up to the feeling that arises from mind-contact. Thus he should not abide in anything from the earth element up to the consciousness element. Thus he should not abide in the thought, "These are the foundations of mindfulness." Thus he should not abide in the thought, "These are the right abandonments, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, and the limbs of awakening," nor in the thought, "This is a limb of the path." Thus he should not abide in the thought, "This is the fruit of stream-entry." Thus he should not abide in the thought, "This is the fruit of once-returning," nor "This is the fruit of non-returning," nor in the thought, "This is an arhat." Thus he should not abide in the thought, "This is a pratyekabuddha." Thus he should not abide in the thought, "This is a buddha."

He should not abide in the thought that form is permanent or impermanent. In the same way, he should not abide in the thought that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are permanent or impermanent. He should not abide in the thought that form is blissful or suffering. In the same way, he should not abide in the thought that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are blissful or suffering. He should not abide in the thought that form is empty or not empty. In the same way, he should not abide in the thought that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are empty or not empty. He should not abide in the thought that form is self or selfless. In the same way, he should not abide in the thought that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are self or selfless. He should not abide in the thought that form is agreeable or disagreeable. In the same way, he should not abide in the thought that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are agreeable or disagreeable.

He should not abide through fixing his attention on form as "empty." In the same way, he should not abide through fixing his attention on feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as "empty."

He should not abide in the thought that the fruit of stream-entry is distinguished by the unconditioned. In the same way, he should not abide in the thought that the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the state of an arhat are distinguished by the unconditioned. He should not abide in the thought that the state of a pratyekabuddha is distinguished by the unconditioned. He should not abide in the thought that buddhahood is distinguished by the unconditioned.

He should not abide in the thought, "The stream-enterer is a worthy recipient of offerings." He should not abide in the thought, "The stream-enterer, at most, will take rebirth seven more times." He should not abide in the thought, "The once-returner is a worthy recipient of offerings." He should not abide in the thought, "Because the once-returner has not fully reached the end, he will return to this world once more and then put an end to suffering." He should not abide in the thought, "The non-returner is a worthy recipient of offerings." He should not abide in the thought, "The non-returner will not return to this world, but will fully pass into nirvāṇa right there." He should not abide in the thought, "The arhat is a worthy recipient of offerings." He should not abide in the thought, "This arhat, in this very life, with no remainder of the aggregates left, will pass completely into the realm of nirvāṇa." He should not abide in the thought, "The pratyekabuddha is a worthy recipient of offerings."

He should not abide in the thought, "The pratyekabuddha will pass beyond the level of the hearers, and without attaining the level of a buddha, will pass completely into nirvāṇa." He should not abide in the thought, "The Buddha is a worthy field for giving." He should not abide in the thought, "The Buddha, having passed beyond the level of ordinary beings, the level of the hearers, and the level of the pratyekabuddhas, works for the benefit of immeasurable, innumerable beings. He leads immeasurable, innumerable hundreds of thousands of billions of beings to complete nirvāṇa. He establishes immeasurable, innumerable beings firmly in the paths of the hearers, the pratyekabuddhas, and the perfectly complete buddhas. Abiding on the level of a buddha, he performs the activities of a buddha, and then, in the realm of nirvāṇa without any remainder of the aggregates, he will pass completely into nirvāṇa through the nirvāṇa of a buddha." He should not abide even in this way.

Then the venerable Śāriputra thought: "If one should not abide even in this way, in the thought that the Buddha, having passed beyond the level of ordinary beings, the level of the hearers, and the level of the pratyekabuddhas, works for the benefit of immeasurable, innumerable beings, leads immeasurable, innumerable hundreds of thousands of billions of beings to complete nirvāṇa, establishes them firmly as hearers, pratyekabuddhas, and perfectly complete buddhas, performs the activities of a buddha while abiding on the level of a buddha, and then passes completely into nirvāṇa without remainder, then how should such a bodhisattva abide in this, and how should he train?"

Then, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Subhūti knew the thoughts in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra, and said to him: "Venerable Śāriputra, what do you think? On what do the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha abide?"

The venerable Śāriputra replied: "Venerable Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha does not abide on anything at all. Why is that? The mind of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha is utterly without abiding. It abides neither in the conditioned realm nor in the unconditioned realm, and yet it does not arise from them either."

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Venerable Śāriputra, just so. A bodhisattva, a great being, should abide in exactly this way and train in exactly this way. He should think: 'Just as the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha does not abide on anything, yet is not non-abiding, does not abide in disagreement, yet is not one who fails to abide in agreement, so I too shall abide.' And he should think: 'Just as the Tathāgata abides, so shall I abide, and so shall I train.' And he should think: 'If I abide just as the Tathāgata abides, then I abide knowing through the manner of non-abiding.' In this way he should train. A bodhisattva, a great being, should abide in this way and train in this way. A bodhisattva, a great being, who trains thus abides in this abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom, and is never separated from this attention."

Then, among that assembly, some sons of the gods thought:

"Whatever the yakṣas speak in the yakṣa language, in yakṣa sounds, yakṣa words, yakṣa discourse, and yakṣa expression, that can be understood. But what the Elder Subhūti explains, expounds, teaches, and demonstrates cannot be understood at all."

Then, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Subhūti fully understood in his own mind the very nature of these thoughts in the minds of those sons of the gods, and said to them: "Sons of the gods, what is called 'not understandable, not understandable' is this: in it there is nothing whatsoever that is spoken, and in it there is nothing whatsoever that is heard."

Then those sons of the gods thought: "Ah! This noble Subhūti will make it clear! Ah! This noble Subhūti will make it clear! The noble Subhūti enters more deeply than the deep, more subtly than the subtle, more profoundly than the profound, and so he teaches and explains."

Again, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Subhūti knew in his own mind the thoughts of those sons of the gods, and said to them: "Sons of the gods, therefore, whoever wishes to attain the fruit of stream-entry, and whoever wishes to abide in the fruit of stream-entry, cannot succeed without relying on this patience. In the same way, whoever wishes to attain the fruit of once-returning, and whoever wishes to abide in the fruit of once-returning; whoever wishes to attain the fruit of non-returning, and whoever wishes to abide in the fruit of non-returning; whoever wishes to attain arhatship, and whoever wishes to abide in arhatship; whoever wishes to attain the awakening of a solitary buddha, and whoever wishes to abide in the awakening of a solitary buddha, cannot succeed without relying on this patience. And whoever wishes to attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and whoever wishes to abide in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, cannot succeed without relying on this patience."

Then those sons of the gods thought again: "What kind of nature should we look for in those who listen to the Dharma from this noble Subhūti?" Then, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Subhūti knew in his own mind the thoughts of those sons of the gods, and said to them: "Sons of the gods, those who listen to the Dharma from me should be sought among beings like illusions and magical emanations. Why is that? Because they do not listen, and they do not bring it to realization."

Then those sons of the gods said to the venerable Subhūti: "Noble Subhūti, are those sentient beings only like illusions? Are they not actually illusions?"

When they said this, the venerable Subhūti said to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like illusions. Sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like dreams. Sons of the gods, in this way illusion and sentient beings are not two; they cannot be made two. In this way dream and sentient beings are not two; they cannot be made two. Sons of the gods, all phenomena too are like illusions and like dreams. The stream-enterer is like an illusion, like a dream. The fruit of stream-entry is like an illusion, like a dream. In the same way, the once-returner and the fruit of once-returning, the non-returner and the fruit of non-returning,

The arhat too is like an illusion, like a dream. Arhatship itself is like an illusion, like a dream. The solitary buddha (pratyekabuddha) is like an illusion, like a dream. Solitary buddhahood itself is like an illusion, like a dream. The perfectly complete buddha is like an illusion, like a dream. Perfect buddhahood itself is like an illusion, like a dream.

Then those sons of the gods said to the Venerable Subhūti, "Noble Subhūti, do you say that the perfectly complete buddha is like an illusion, like a dream? Do you say that perfect buddhahood itself is like an illusion, like a dream?"

Subhūti replied, "Sons of the gods, if I speak of nirvāṇa too as like an illusion, like a dream, what need is there to speak of other phenomena?"

The sons of the gods said, "Noble Subhūti, do you say that nirvāṇa too is like an illusion, like a dream?"

The Venerable Subhūti replied, "Sons of the gods, even if there were some phenomenon more excellent than nirvāṇa, I would say that it too is like an illusion, like a dream. Sons of the gods, in this way illusion and this nirvāṇa are not two; they cannot be made two. In this way dream and this nirvāṇa are not two; they cannot be made two."

Then the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Pūrṇa son of Maitrāyaṇī, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, and other great hearers (śrāvakas), together with many thousands of bodhisattvas, said to the Elder Subhūti, "Venerable Subhūti, who will rightly uphold this Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught?"

Then the Venerable Ānanda said to those elders, "Venerable ones, it will be irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, or persons who have attained the perfect view, or arhats whose defilements are exhausted, who will rightly uphold this Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught."

Then the Venerable Subhūti said to those elders, "Venerable ones, no one at all will arise who rightly upholds this Perfection of Wisdom as it has been explained. Why is that? Because in this teaching no phenomenon has been mentioned, no phenomenon has been made manifest, and no phenomenon has been established. Therefore, just as in this teaching no phenomenon has been mentioned, made manifest, or established, so too no one at all will arise who rightly upholds this Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught."

Then Indra, king of the gods (Śakra), thought, "Noble Subhūti has taught this exposition of the Dharma in such a way. For my part too, as an offering, I will conjure up flowers and scatter them over Noble Subhūti." Then at that moment Śakra conjured up flowers and scattered them over the Venerable Subhūti.

Then the Elder, the Venerable Subhūti, in order to respond to Śakra, thought, "These flowers that Śakra, king of the gods, has scattered are flowers I have never seen before, even in the realm of the Thirty-Three Gods. These flowers are conjured."

Thinking, "These flowers scattered by the lord of the gods are not born from trees, creepers, or vines; they are flowers that arose from the mind," then Śakra, lord of the gods, knowing with his own mind the thought in the mind of the Venerable Subhūti, said to him, "Noble Subhūti, these flowers are unborn. Why is that? There is no flower at all that is born of mind, and neither are they born from trees, creepers, or vines."

Then the Venerable Subhūti said to Śakra, lord of the gods, "Kauśika, when you say that these flowers are unborn, that these flowers are not born of mind and are not born from trees, creepers, or vines, then, Kauśika, what is unborn is not a flower."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, thought, "How marvelous! The noble Subhūti's wisdom is profound. He teaches what is designated by names and words, yet he does not contradict it. He makes that very thing clear, and that very thing he sets forth."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the Venerable Subhūti, "Noble Subhūti, so it is, so it is. Noble Subhūti, just as you have set forth, so should bodhisattvas, great beings, train in this."

When he had spoken thus, the Venerable Subhūti said to Śakra, lord of the gods, "Kauśika, so it is, so it is. Thus should bodhisattvas, great beings, train in this. Kauśika, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way does not train for the fruit of stream-entry. He does not train for the fruit of once-returning, does not train for the fruit of non-returning, does not train for arhatship. He does not train for pratyekabuddhahood, and does not train for buddhahood. Yet one who does not train in these stages trains for buddhahood and omniscience. One who trains for buddhahood and omniscience trains in the immeasurable, innumerable qualities of a buddha. One who trains in the immeasurable, innumerable qualities of a buddha does not train for the sake of increasing or diminishing form. Likewise, he does not train for the sake of increasing or diminishing feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.
