Kauśika, the qualities of that son or daughter of good family, even in this very life, I have already described."

When this had been said, Śakra, lord of the gods, spoke to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, whoever, thinking, 'May the lineage of the buddhas not be severed; may the sacred Dharma not vanish,' and wishing the sacred Dharma to endure for a long time, and so that benefit may be accomplished for bodhisattvas, the great beings, without departing from the proper way, writes out this Perfection of Wisdom, places it in a book, and holds it or keeps it, and honors that Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, cloth, parasols, banners, bells, and flags, with rings of lamps all around, and with many kinds of offerings, showing it reverence, regarding it as their teacher, esteeming it, making offerings to it, adorning it with paintings, and attending upon it with respect: I shall guard, protect, and shelter that son or daughter of good family. And what need is there to speak of those who also ask about this Perfection of Wisdom, take it up, hold it, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give the transmission of it, and rehearse it from memory, and who honor it with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, cloth, parasols, banners, bells, and flags, with rings of lamps all around, and with many kinds of offerings, showing it reverence, regarding it as their teacher, esteeming it, making offerings to it, adorning it with paintings, and attending upon it with respect?"

The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika! Furthermore, Kauśika, when that son or daughter of good family recites this Perfection of Wisdom aloud, then and there many hundreds of gods' sons will come. Many thousands of gods' sons, and many hundreds of thousands of gods' sons, will come close in order to hear the Dharma. As those gods' sons listen to the Dharma, they will think, 'Let us support the eloquence of this speaker of the Dharma.' And whenever that speaker of the Dharma wishes to fall silent, even then, through their very reverence for the Dharma, those gods' sons will resolve to support that son or daughter of good family with eloquence, according to the way the speaker is inclined to speak.

"Kauśika, the son or daughter of good family who holds, bears in mind, reads, comprehends fully, recites aloud, teaches, expounds, gives the transmission of, and rehearses from memory this Perfection of Wisdom will in this very life take hold of these further qualities as well.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, when that son or daughter of good family teaches this Perfection of Wisdom, they will not become timid before the assembly, thinking, 'Someone might challenge me, intending to find fault.' Why is that? Because the Perfection of Wisdom guards, protects, and shelters them. One who abides in the Perfection of Wisdom does not perceive, in truth, any fault-finding. One who abides in the Perfection of Wisdom does not perceive, in truth, anyone who finds fault. Nor does such a one perceive, in truth, anyone to be found fault with. And the Perfection of Wisdom itself they do not perceive, in truth. In this way, no challenge whatsoever arises, by any line of argument, against the son or daughter of good family who is held by the Perfection of Wisdom. Nor will that person be possessed of dread, either of others or of self, or of any thorough fear.

"Kauśika, the son or daughter of good family who holds, bears in mind, reads, comprehends fully, recites aloud, teaches, expounds, gives the transmission of, and rehearses from memory this Perfection of Wisdom will in this very life take hold of these further qualities as well.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, such sons and daughters of good family will be dear to their parents, friends, ministers, kinsmen, blood relations, and to ascetics and brahmins. Should opponents arise, they will have the strength and the ability to refute them in accordance with the Dharma, and when others raise objections, they will be able to give a reasoned reply to the objection.

"Kauśika, the son or daughter of good family who holds, bears in mind, reads, comprehends fully, recites aloud, teaches, expounds, gives the transmission of, and rehearses from memory this Perfection of Wisdom will in this very life take hold of these further qualities as well.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, in whatever place that son or daughter of good family writes out this Perfection of Wisdom, places it in book form, and sets it down with offerings made beforehand, Kauśika, among the gods of the class of the Four Great Kings, those gods' sons who have truly set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening will also think of coming to that place.

Those gods' sons too, having come there, will look upon this Perfection of Wisdom set down in book form; they will pay homage to it and bow down to it; they will take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory. Having looked upon it, paid homage, bowed down, taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it, taught it, expounded it, received its transmission and rehearsed it from memory, they will think of returning again.

Kauśika, among the gods of the Thirty-Three, those gods' sons who have truly set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening will also think of coming to that place. Having come there, those gods' sons too will look upon this Perfection of Wisdom set down in book form; they will pay homage to it and bow down to it; they will take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory. Having looked upon it, paid homage, bowed down, taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it, taught it, expounded it, received its transmission and rehearsed it from memory, they will think of returning again.

Kauśika, among the gods of the Free from Strife (the Yāma gods), those gods' sons who have truly set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening will also think of drawing near to that place. Having come there, those gods' sons too will look upon this Perfection of Wisdom set down in book form; they will pay homage to it and bow down to it; they will take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory. Having looked upon it, paid homage, bowed down, taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it, taught it, expounded it, received its transmission and rehearsed it from memory, they will think of returning again.

Kauśika, among the gods of Tuṣita, the Joyous Realm, those gods' sons who have truly set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening will also think of coming to that place. Having come there, those gods' sons too will look upon this Perfection of Wisdom set down in book form; they will pay homage to it and bow down to it; they will take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory. Having looked upon it, paid homage, bowed down, taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it, taught it, expounded it, received its transmission and rehearsed it from memory, they will think of returning again.

Kauśika, among the gods who Delight in Emanation (the Nirmāṇarati gods), those gods' sons who have truly set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening will also think of coming to that place. Having come there, those gods' sons too will look upon this Perfection of Wisdom set down in book form; they will pay homage to it and bow down to it; they will take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory.

Having looked upon it, paid homage, and bowed down; having taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it aloud, taught it, expounded it, given its transmission, and rehearsed it from memory, they will think of returning again.

Kauśika, among the gods who Wield Power over Others' Emanations (the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods), those gods' sons who have truly set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening will also think of coming to that place. Having come there, those gods' sons too will look upon this Perfection of Wisdom set down in book form; they will pay homage to it and bow down to it; they will take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory. Having looked upon it, paid homage, and bowed down; having taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it aloud, taught it, expounded it, given its transmission, and rehearsed it from memory, they will think of returning again.

In the same way, Kauśika, among all the gods who move in the form realm, up to and including the gods' sons of the Brahmā Assembly in the world of Brahmā, those gods' sons who have truly set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening will also think of coming to that place. Having come there, those gods' sons too will look upon this Perfection of Wisdom set down in book form; they will pay homage to it and bow down to it; they will take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory. Having looked upon it, paid homage, and bowed down; having taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it aloud, taught it, expounded it, given its transmission, and rehearsed it from memory, they will think of returning again.

Kauśika, you should not understand this only as it applies to the Brahmā Assembly. Just as with the Brahmā Assembly, so too among the gods who stand before Brahmā, whatever gods' sons there are, the same text is to be supplied as before.

In the same way, it applies to the gods of Great Brahmā, of Limited Radiance, of Immeasurable Radiance, of Clear Light, of Limited Virtue, of Immeasurable Virtue, of Increasing Virtue, of Cloudless, of Merit Increase, of Great Fruit, to the beings without perception, and to the gods of Not Great, Not Afflicted, Fine Appearance, and Perfect Vision. And Kauśika, among the gods of Akaniṣṭha, those gods' sons who have truly set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening will also think of coming to that place. Having come there, those gods' sons too will look upon this Perfection of Wisdom set down in book form; they will pay homage to it and bow down to it; they will take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory. Having looked upon it, paid homage, and bowed down; having taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it aloud, taught it, expounded it, given its transmission, and rehearsed it from memory, they will think of returning again.

Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family should generate the following thought: Toward all those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and non-human beings who dwell in the immeasurable, innumerable world systems of the ten directions,

From this volume, look upon the Perfection of Wisdom, pay homage to it, bow down to it, take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory. Having looked upon it, paid homage, and bowed down; having taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it aloud, taught it, expounded it, given its transmission, and rehearsed it from memory, return once more to your own dwelling. Let this very gift of the Dharma be given to them. This is what that son or daughter of good family should think.

Kauśika, in this regard you might think: "Among the sons of the gods who move in the desire realm and the form realm of this very world system of the four great continents, only those who have properly entered upon unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening will come there." You should not suppose that, Kauśika; it is not to be regarded in that way.

Kauśika, rather, in the world system of the great thousand of the three thousand, all the sons of the gods, however many there are, who move in the desire realm and the form realm and who have properly entered upon unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, will also think of coming there. Having come there, they will look upon this Perfection of Wisdom set down in a volume, pay homage to it, bow down to it, take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory. Having looked upon it, paid homage, and bowed down; having taken hold of it, borne it in mind, read it, comprehended it fully, recited it aloud, taught it, expounded it, given its transmission, and rehearsed it from memory, they will think of returning again.

Moreover, Kauśika, the house, dwelling, and residence of that son or daughter of good family will be thoroughly protected. Except for the ripening of previous karma, no one at all will be able to harm them. Kauśika, this is so because gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-human beings, who are called "the greatly majestic," will think of coming there. Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family will also acquire these qualities in this very life.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, when that son or daughter of good family is there, how should I understand the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans who come there in order to listen to this Perfection of Wisdom, look upon it, pay homage to it, bow down to it, take hold of it, bear it in mind, read it, comprehend it fully, recite it aloud, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and rehearse it from memory?"

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to Śakra, lord of the gods: "Kauśika, if that son or daughter of good family sees great radiances there, then that son or daughter of good family should know: certainly gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans have come and arrived here.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, if that son or daughter of good family smells a fragrance of a non-human kind never smelled before, and becomes delighted by it,"

and having smelled that fragrance, that son or daughter of good family should know: certainly gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans have come and arrived here.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, if that son or daughter of good family becomes careful in conduct and becomes pure in conduct, then through that careful and pure conduct, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans will think of coming there. And whichever gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans have come there, they will be pleased and greatly delighted by that careful and pure conduct, and contentment and mental ease will arise in them.

"Then the gods of little majesty who dwell there will also think of departing from that place. Why is that? Because they cannot bear the splendor, majesty, and dignity of those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans of great majesty. Thus the gods of little majesty think of departing.

"Moreover, Kauśika, just as those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans of great majesty think of coming there constantly, in just that way, that son or daughter of good family will also become one of great faith. Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family will also take hold of these qualities in this very life.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family should not engage in impure or careless conduct in the vicinity of that place of the Dharma's way, for the sake of regarding it as a teacher, showing it reverence, and bringing it to completion.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family will not become bodily weary or mentally weary. He will sleep happily and will go about happily. Even when he falls asleep, he will not see evil dreams; and if he does dream, he will see the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas themselves; he will see stūpas; he will see bodhisattvas; he will see the śrāvakas of the Tathāgata. If he hears sounds, he will hear the very sounds of the perfections. He will hear the teachings of the factors that lead to awakening. He will see the trees of awakening themselves. And at those trees he will see the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, as they attain manifest and complete awakening.

"Likewise, he will see those who have become fully awakened turning the wheel of Dharma. He will see many bodhisattva mahāsattvas who delight in discussing the Perfection of Wisdom, discussing this very Perfection of Wisdom, and he will see them skillfully showing: 'In this way omniscience is to be embraced; in this way the buddha-fields are to be purified.' And he will also hear the great resounding proclamation that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have become fully awakened."

In such and such a direction, in such and such a quarter, in such and such a world-realm, there is a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly awakened buddha named so-and-so. He is surrounded and honored by many śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, by many hundreds of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, by many thousands, by many hundreds of thousands, by many millions, by many hundreds of millions, by many thousands of millions, by many hundreds of thousands of millions, indeed by countless billions of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas, and he is teaching the Dharma before them. Such is the great resounding proclamation of the Buddha that he will also hear.

"Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family will see such dreams as these. He will sleep in comfort and awaken in comfort. Radiance will be established within his body, and he will experience great bodily ease, a lightness and spaciousness of the body. Because of this, a craving for food will not arise in his mind, and his perception of food will diminish.

"Kauśika, it is just as when a monk who practices yoga rises from meditative absorption, and, thoroughly moistened by the mental engagement of that absorption, no strong craving for food arises in him and his perception of food diminishes. In the same way, Kauśika, in that son or daughter of good family no strong craving for food will arise, and his perception of food will diminish.

"Why is that? Kauśika, it is because the more that son or daughter of good family strives in the yoga of meditating on the Perfection of Wisdom, the more non-human beings will think of bringing radiance to his body. Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family will also take hold of these qualities in this very life.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, there is a son or daughter of good family who writes out this Perfection of Wisdom, puts it into book form, and places it with offerings as the foremost act, making offerings to it, but who does not hold it, does not bear it in mind, does not read it, does not fully comprehend it, does not recite it, does not teach it, does not explain it, does not give its transmission, and does not memorize it. Yet, Kauśika, a son or daughter of good family who has faith in this Perfection of Wisdom, who reflects on it, is inclined toward it, and has a serene mind, and who has generated the mind of awakening, produces more merit than that one. With a superior intention, such a person listens to it, holds it, bears it in mind, reads it, comprehends it, recites it, teaches it, explains it, gives its transmission, and memorizes it. He also expounds it extensively and correctly to others, elucidates its meaning, follows its sense with his mind, and examines it thoroughly here with wisdom, according as it is established. He does so with the wish: 'May the lineage of the buddhas not be cut off. May the sacred Dharma not vanish.' Thus he makes the sacred Dharma endure for a long time. And since he is not separated from the proper way, he accomplishes benefit for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. At the very least, he puts it into book form and keeps it or sets it in place.

Such a person should also honor that Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, fragrances, garlands, unguents, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, and flags, with rows of lamps set all around, and with many other kinds of offerings. If he reveres it, venerates it, treats it as his teacher, gives it gifts, makes offerings to it, depicts it in painting, and serves and honors it, then, Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family will thereby generate an exceedingly great store of merit.

Therefore, Kauśika, a son or daughter of good family who wishes to uphold these exceptional qualities in this very life should have faith in this Perfection of Wisdom, examine it closely, and be devoted to it. Having generated the awakening mind with a clear and serene heart, with higher resolve he should listen to it, grasp it, retain it, read it, fully comprehend it, recite it, teach it, explain it closely, receive its transmission, and memorize it. He should also expound it extensively and correctly to others, elucidate its meaning, follow its sense with his mind, and examine it thoroughly here with wisdom, according as it is established. He should do so with the wish: "May the lineage of the buddhas not be cut off. May the sacred Dharma not vanish." Thus he should make the sacred Dharma endure for a long time. And since he is not separated from the proper way, he will accomplish benefit for the bodhisattva mahāsattvas. At the very least, he should put it into book form and keep it or set it in place. He should also bestow it correctly upon those sons and daughters of good family who seek its meaning. He should dedicate the merit: "May I and other virtuous beings never be separated from the great vision of the buddhas' way." To it he should always make offerings of divine flowers, divine incense, divine fragrances, divine garlands, divine unguents, divine powders, divine robes, divine parasols, divine banners, divine bells, and divine flags, with rows of divine lamps set all around, and with many other kinds of offerings. He should revere it, venerate it, treat it as his teacher, give it gifts, make offerings to it, depict it in painting, and serve and honor it.

This is the third chapter of the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, called "Upholding the Immeasurable Qualities of Honoring the Perfection and the Stūpa."

Furthermore, the Blessed One said to Śatakratu (Indra), lord of the gods: "Kauśika, suppose this Jambudvīpa were completely filled with bodies of the Tathāgata, as thick as a mass of clustered grains, and were given to you. And suppose this Perfection of Wisdom were also written out and entrusted to you, and then one were to divide the offering and set before you one of the two portions. Kauśika, which portion would you take?"

Indra replied: "Blessed One, if this Jambudvīpa were filled with bodies of the Tathāgata, as thick as a mass of clustered grains, and were bestowed on me, and if this Perfection of Wisdom were also written out and entrusted to me, and one portion were to be set aside from the two, then, Blessed One, I would take this very Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that? It is for the sake of depicting the Tathāgata's way, for this is the Tathāgata's body of true meaning. Why so? Because the Blessed One has said: 'The buddhas, the blessed ones, are the Dharma body. Monks, do not regard this physical body as the supreme body. Monks, look upon me as fully perfected in the Dharma body.' Since this was taught, the Tathāgata's body should be seen as distinguished by the ultimate limit, namely the Perfection of Wisdom. Yet, Blessed One, I do not lack reverence for those bodies of the Tathāgata."

Blessed One, I do hold those bodies of the Tathāgata in reverence. Yet, Blessed One, it is from this very Perfection of Wisdom that those bodies of the Tathāgata arise and receive offerings. Therefore, Blessed One, when offerings are made to this very Perfection of Wisdom, offerings to those bodies of the Tathāgata are thereby fully accomplished as well. Why is that? Because the bodies of the Tathāgatas have come forth from the Perfection of Wisdom.

Blessed One, it is like this. When I am in the presence of the gods of the Dharma hall, and I sit upon my own divine seat, then the sons of the gods come to attend upon me. And when I am absent, even then the sons of the gods, out of reverence for me, pay homage to that seat of mine, circumambulate it, and then depart again. Why is that? Because they think: "Śakra, the lord of the gods, having sat upon this seat, taught the Dharma to the gods of the Thirty-Three."

In the same way, Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom, renowned as powerful and become the cause and the condition, is what brings about the omniscience of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened Buddha. The bodies of the Tathāgata are the basis of omniscience, but they are not the cause that gives rise to wisdom, nor are they its condition. Thus, Blessed One, the offering made to the body of the Tathāgata arises from the cause that is omniscient wisdom.

Therefore, Blessed One, of those two portions, I take this very Perfection of Wisdom. Blessed One, I am not lacking in reverence for those bodies of the Tathāgata. Indeed, Blessed One, I hold those bodies of the Tathāgata in reverence. Yet the bodies of the Tathāgata receive offerings because they are thoroughly pervaded by the Perfection of Wisdom.

Blessed One, set aside Jambudvīpa filled with bodies of the Tathāgata like a thicket of sugarcane or reeds; set aside the world system of the four great continents so filled; set aside the thousandfold world system so filled; set aside the second, the middle, two-thousandfold world system so filled. Blessed One, suppose this entire great thousandfold world system of the three-thousandfold was filled with bodies of the Tathāgata like a thicket of reeds, and it were set down as one portion; and suppose this Perfection of Wisdom, written out as a book, were set down as the second portion; and suppose someone, offering one portion, said: "Of these two portions, take whichever you wish." Then, Blessed One, I would take this very Perfection of Wisdom.

Blessed One, I am not lacking in reverence for those bodies of the Tathāgata. Indeed, Blessed One, I hold those bodies of the Tathāgata in reverence. Yet the bodies of the Tathāgata also receive offerings because they are thoroughly pervaded by the Perfection of Wisdom. The bodies of the Tathāgata are the basis of omniscient wisdom, and that omniscient wisdom itself issues forth from the Perfection of Wisdom.

Therefore, Blessed One, of those two portions, I take this very Perfection of Wisdom.

Blessed One, it is not that I lack reverence for the body of the Tathāgata. Indeed, Blessed One, I hold those bodies of the Tathāgata in reverence. Yet, Blessed One, those bodies of the Tathāgata are born from this very Perfection of Wisdom, and those bodies of the Tathāgata receive offerings because they are thoroughly infused by the Perfection of Wisdom.

Here ends the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, fifth section.

Blessed One, suppose there were a priceless, precious jewel endowed with qualities of this kind. Wherever it is placed, neither humans nor nonhumans can find an opening to harm that place. Whenever a man or a woman is seized by a nonhuman, then the moment that great precious jewel is brought near, the nonhuman departs from there. If the jewel is placed on a body swollen and tormented by wind disorder, that wind disorder is cut off, ceases to increase, and is pacified. If it is placed on a body made feverish by bile, that bile too is cut off, ceases to increase, and is pacified. If it is placed on one swollen and tormented all over by phlegm, that phlegm too is cut off, ceases to increase, and is pacified. If it is placed on one who suffers from a combined disorder of the humors, that combined disorder too is cut off, ceases to increase, and is pacified. In the pitch darkness of the night it gives light. In hot weather, wherever it is placed, that place becomes cool. In cold weather, wherever it is placed, that place becomes warm. In any place where there are venomous snakes and other tiny creatures, if one holds it and sets it down there, those venomous snakes and tiny creatures go away. Blessed One, if a man or a woman is bitten by a venomous snake and the precious jewel is shown to that person, then the very moment the jewel is seen, the venom is overcome and vanishes. Blessed One, that precious jewel is also endowed with these and other such qualities.

Blessed One, if that precious jewel is placed upon the eyes of those who have a film, or blurred vision, or eye disease, or a cataract, then the very moment it is placed there, those afflictions of the eye are cleared and pacified. Blessed One, that precious jewel is endowed with these and other such qualities.

If it is dropped into water, the water takes on its own color. If it is wrapped in white cloth and dropped into water, the water turns white. In the same way, if it is wrapped or bound in blue, yellow, red, or crimson cloth, or in any of the various kinds of cloth, and dropped into water, the water takes on the very color of each of those cloths. And whatever turbidity there was in that water becomes clear. Blessed One, that precious jewel is endowed with qualities of this kind.

Then the venerable Ānanda said this to Śakra, lord of the gods: "Kauśika, do such precious jewels exist only in the world of the gods, or do those precious jewels exist among the people of Jambudvīpa as well?" Śakra replied:

"Noble Ānanda, those precious jewels exist among the gods. Among the people of Jambudvīpa there are also precious jewels, but they are heavy, small, and coarse, and their qualities are incomplete, for they do not possess such essential qualities. They do not approach even a hundredth part of those jewels of the gods, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-times-a-hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part. They cannot be reckoned by number, shown by comparison or by example, nor can they serve as a basis or come close as a cause. For those precious jewels of the gods are refined and perfectly complete in every aspect of quality. If that precious jewel is placed in any vessel of food or drink, then even after the jewel is taken out, the food and drink is rendered pleasing to the heart. By those very qualities of the precious jewel, a deep and heartfelt delight arises toward that food and drink."

Then, speaking to the Blessed One, Śakra continued: "Blessed One, in the same way, even though the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha has passed into nirvāṇa, the offerings received by the bodies of the Tathāgata are due to the qualities of the Perfection of Wisdom and of omniscient wisdom. These bodies of the Tathāgata have become vessels of omniscient wisdom. And, Blessed One, just as the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who teach the Dharma in all world systems are to be honored because they were born from the Perfection of Wisdom, so too the Dharma teacher who expounds the Dharma is to be honored because he was born from the Perfection of Wisdom.

"Blessed One, just as the son of a king, through the king's power, is revered fearlessly by great multitudes of people, so too that Dharma teacher, through the power of the Dharma body, is honored fearlessly by great multitudes of beings. Just as the Dharma teacher who proclaims the Dharma receives honor, so too the relics of the Tathāgata's body have received honor.

"Blessed One, therefore, to say nothing of a great trichiliocosm, which is filled to the brim with the bodies of the Tathāgata like a bubbling mass, consider this, Blessed One: suppose one placed in one pan of a scale world systems as many as the sand grains of the river Ganges, filled to the brim in this way with the bodies of the Tathāgata, and in the other pan one placed this Perfection of Wisdom, written down in a book. Blessed One, if someone were to offer me the choice, saying, 'Of these two portions, take whichever one you wish,' then of those two portions I would take this very Perfection of Wisdom. Blessed One, it is not that I lack reverence for those bodies of the Tathāgata; I too hold those bodies of the Tathāgata in reverence. But, Blessed One, omniscience has been disclosed from the Perfection of Wisdom, and the offering made to the body of the Tathāgata has arisen from omniscient wisdom. Therefore, Blessed One, if one honors this Perfection of Wisdom, one will have made offerings to the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present."

Blessed One, furthermore, in countless, innumerable world systems there are buddhas, Blessed Ones, who at this very time are present, living and sustained. A son of good family or a daughter of good family who wishes to see those buddhas in the nature of reality should practice this Perfection of Wisdom, should apply themselves to this Perfection of Wisdom, and should meditate on this Perfection of Wisdom.

When Śakra had spoken in this way, the Blessed One said to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Kauśika, so it is, so it is. Kauśika, those Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas who appeared in the past also relied on this very Perfection of Wisdom, and so fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. Kauśika, those Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas who will appear in the future will likewise rely on this very Perfection of Wisdom, and so will attain full awakening to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. Kauśika, those buddhas, Blessed Ones, who at the present time are present, living and sustained, in countless, innumerable world systems have also relied on this very Perfection of Wisdom, and so have fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening. And, Kauśika, I too, the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly complete buddha of this present time, have relied on this very Perfection of Wisdom, and so have fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfectly complete awakening."

When he had spoken in this way, Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom is indeed the great perfection. For the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete buddha, thoroughly knows and rightly sees the mental conduct of all sentient beings."

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, so it is, so it is. Kauśika, if a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom for a long time, then by means of the Perfection of Wisdom he rightly knows and rightly sees the mental conduct of all sentient beings."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, does a bodhisattva, a great being, practice only the Perfection of Wisdom, and not the other perfections?"

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, a bodhisattva, a great being, practices all six perfections. Nevertheless, Kauśika, it is the Perfection of Wisdom of the bodhisattva, the great being, that goes before them all. The giving of gifts, the keeping of moral discipline, the cultivation of patience, the undertaking of diligence, the settling of the mind in meditative concentration, and the discerning of phenomena: it is the Perfection of Wisdom of the bodhisattva, the great being, that goes before each of these."

Kauśika, the six perfections are embraced by skillful means, and they are dedicated through the Perfection of Wisdom and dedicated toward omniscience. Among these there is no distinction, and no separate division is perceived. Kauśika, it is like this. The various trees of Jambudvīpa differ in color, differ in shape, differ in leaves, differ in flowers, differ in fruit, and differ in the richness of their size and abundance. Yet the shadows of those trees show no distinction and no separate division; otherwise they could not be counted simply as "shadow, shadow." In just the same way, Kauśika, the six perfections are embraced by skillful means, dedicated through the Perfection of Wisdom, and dedicated toward omniscience, and among them no distinction and no separate division is perceived.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom possesses great qualities. Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom possesses immeasurable qualities. Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom possesses limitless qualities."

This is the fourth chapter, called "Praise of the Qualities," from the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family has faith in this Perfection of Wisdom, reflects on it and inclines toward it with a clear and confident mind, and has generated the mind of awakening. With a superior intention, such a person listens to it, holds it, retains it, reads it, comprehends it, recites it, teaches it, explains it, gives instruction in it, learns it by heart, and expounds it extensively and correctly to others. Such a person also explains its meaning, reflects on it in mind, and examines it here with the wisdom of one who has truly understood it. Thinking, 'May the lineage of the buddhas not be cut off, and may the sacred Dharma not vanish,' such a person makes the sacred Dharma endure for a long time. Inseparable from this way of practice, such a person brings about benefit for the bodhisattvas, the great beings. Even if only in small part, such a person has it written down in a book, and keeps it or sets it in place. Having heard this teaching, such a person thinks: 'How wonderful! This Perfection of Wisdom is of such great meaning. How wonderful! This Perfection of Wisdom is of such great benefit. How wonderful! This Perfection of Wisdom is of such great effect. How wonderful! This Perfection of Wisdom is of such great ripening. How wonderful! This Perfection of Wisdom possesses so many qualities. I must not abandon this Perfection of Wisdom. I must guard this Perfection of Wisdom. I must keep this Perfection of Wisdom hidden. This Perfection of Wisdom is exceedingly hard to find.' With such deep devotion, that person honors this Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, cloth, parasols, banners, bells, and pennants, and with rows of lamps all around, and with many kinds of offerings. That person reveres it, venerates it as a teacher, esteems it, makes offerings to it, adorns it with painted images, and attends it with respect.

And suppose another person, having even put it into book form, makes offerings to it. Then a son or daughter of good family, for the sake of others, gives, bestows, presents, and freely offers it to those who seek it and request it with eager wish. Blessed One, of these two, the one who has the intention of giving and the one who does not, which of them produces the greater merit? When he had asked this, the Blessed One spoke to Śatakratu, the lord of the gods (Indra): "Kauśika, I ask you this very question here, so answer as best you are able. Kauśika, what do you think? Suppose a son or daughter of good family treats the body of the Tathāgata who has passed into nirvāṇa with honor, serves it and keeps it, honors it, holds it as a teacher, esteems it, makes offerings to it, adorns it with painted images, and attends it with respect. And suppose another son or daughter of good family, thinking, 'If I myself honor the body of the Tathāgata, hold it as a teacher, esteem it, make offerings to it, adorn it with painted images, and attend it with respect, the offerings will be vast,' out of compassion for sentient beings also teaches others extensively and correctly, gives it to them, and spreads it widely. Kauśika, of these two sons or daughters of good family, which produces the greater merit? Does the one who himself makes offerings, and also teaches others extensively and correctly, gives to them, and spreads it widely, produce the greater merit? Or does the one who alone makes offerings to his own self produce much merit?"

Śakra replied: "Blessed One, the son or daughter of good family who thinks, 'If I myself honor the body of the Tathāgata, hold it as a teacher, esteem it, make offerings to it, adorn it with painted images, and attend it with respect, the offerings will be vast,' and who, out of tender compassion for sentient beings, also teaches others extensively and correctly, gives it to them, and spreads it widely, this one, of the two, produces the greater merit."

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, so it is, so it is. Kauśika, suppose a son or daughter of good family writes out this Perfection of Wisdom in this way and puts it into book form, and holds it, bears it in mind, reads it, comprehends it, recites it thoroughly, teaches it, explains it closely, gives its transmission, and memorizes it. And suppose that, for other sons or daughters of good family who seek it and request it with eager wish, he even puts a small part of it into book form, and gives, bestows, presents, and freely offers it. Kauśika, of these two, the son or daughter of good family who takes up the cause of others and who has the intention of giving freely produces, on that basis, the greater merit.

"Moreover, Kauśika, suppose a son or daughter of good family goes to whatever place a son or daughter of good family who is a worthy vessel for this Perfection of Wisdom is staying, and gives this Perfection of Wisdom to them and spreads it among them properly. Kauśika, this son or daughter of good family produces even greater merit than that."

"Moreover, Kauśika, suppose a son or daughter of good family were to establish and settle all the sentient beings there are in Jambudvīpa firmly upon the path of the ten virtuous actions. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son or daughter of good family produce a great deal of merit on that basis?"

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Blessed One, a great deal. Sugata, a great deal."

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, even more merit than that is produced by this son or daughter of good family who takes this Perfection of Wisdom, even a small portion of it, and puts it into book form, and then gives it with a pure intention to a bodhisattva. That bodhisattva is one with faith through faith, with discernment through discernment, with deep confidence through deep confidence, with a serene mind through a serene mind, with excellent and complete higher aspiration through excellent and complete higher aspiration, and one who has generated the awakening mind through generating the awakening mind.

"Further, the giver strives diligently to have that bodhisattva practice even the smallest part of it, such as asking questions about it and reading it. He causes that bodhisattva to take it up, teaches it properly, establishes it properly, praises it properly, and delights that bodhisattva properly. He explains it through words, through indications, and through further indications, and he teaches that bodhisattva its meaning properly. He says to that bodhisattva: 'Child of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas in this way. If you train in this path, practice it, and strive, you will quickly come to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring to discipline, through the unsurpassed exhaustion of the aggregates, the countless realms of sentient beings, that is, through the analysis of the true limit.' By speaking in this way, he purifies that bodhisattva's mind and frees it from doubt.

"Kauśika, this son or daughter of good family, who has such a mind of complete relinquishment, produces even more merit than the former son or daughter of good family.

"Moreover, Kauśika, set aside all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa. By the same reasoning, Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish and settle firmly upon the path of the ten virtuous actions all the sentient beings there are in the world system of the four great continents. And further, Kauśika, set aside all the sentient beings of the four great continents. By the same reasoning, suppose all the sentient beings there are in the world system of the small chiliocosm, the thousandfold world, were so established upon the path of the ten virtuous actions by some son or daughter of good family. And further, Kauśika, set aside all the sentient beings of the thousandfold world. By the same reasoning, suppose all the sentient beings there are in the world system of the middling dichiliocosm, the twice-thousandfold world, were so established by some son or daughter of good family. And further, Kauśika, set aside all the sentient beings of the middling twice-thousandfold world. By the same reasoning, suppose all the sentient beings there are in the world system of the great trichiliocosm, the thousand-thousand-thousandfold world, were so established by some son or daughter of good family. And further, Kauśika, set aside all the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm."

In the same way, Kauśika, suppose all the sentient beings there are in as many world systems of the great trichiliocosm as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were established and set firmly in the ten paths of virtuous action by some son or daughter of good family. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son or daughter of good family produce a great deal of merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Blessed One, a great deal. Sugata, a great deal."

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, even more merit is produced by this son or daughter of good family who does the following. Even if only in a small measure, they have this Perfection of Wisdom written down in a book, and with faith they bring a person of faith to it, with discernment a person of discernment, with devoted conviction a person of devoted conviction, with a clear and serene mind a person of clear and serene mind, with excellent higher intention a person of excellent higher intention, and they give it with higher intention to a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening with the mind of awakening. Even if only in a small measure, they apply themselves without laxity to writing and reading it. With diligence they urge that person to take it up, they teach it correctly, establish the person in it correctly, encourage the person correctly, and bring the person correct delight. They explain it through words, through definitions, through further elaborations, and they teach its meaning correctly. And they speak to that person thus: 'Child of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train and practice this path and make effort, you will swiftly become fully and completely awakened in unsurpassable, perfect awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring about the complete exhaustion of the unmeasurable realms of sentient beings, the unsurpassed discerning of the true limit.' Speaking thus, they purify that person's mind and make it free of doubt. Kauśika, this son or daughter of good family, who possesses a mind of complete renunciation, produces much more merit than the former son or daughter of good family.

Further, Kauśika, suppose all the sentient beings there are in Jambudvīpa were established in the four meditative concentrations by some son or daughter of good family. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son or daughter of good family produce a great deal of merit on that basis?"

Śakra replied: "Blessed One, a great deal. Sugata, a great deal."

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, even more merit is produced by this son or daughter of good family who does the following. Even if only in a small measure, they have this Perfection of Wisdom written down in a book, and with faith they bring a person of faith to it, with discernment a person of discernment, with devoted conviction a person of devoted conviction, with a clear and serene mind a person of clear and serene mind, with excellent higher intention a person of excellent higher intention, and they give it with higher intention to a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening. Even if only in a small measure, they apply themselves without laxity to writing and reading it. With diligence they urge that person to take it up, they teach it correctly, establish the person in it correctly, encourage the person correctly, and bring the person correct delight. They explain it through words, through definitions, through further elaborations, and they teach its meaning correctly. And they speak to that person thus: 'Child of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas.'"

"If you train in this path, practice it, and strive, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring to discipline, in the supreme exhaustion of the aggregates, immeasurable realms of sentient beings, that is, in the thorough discernment of the true limit." Speaking in this way, they purify that person's mind and free it from doubt.

Kauśika, set aside all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa. Kauśika, in just that way, consider all the sentient beings in a world system of four great continents. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish every one of them in the four meditative concentrations. And set aside, Kauśika, all the sentient beings of a world system of four great continents. In the same way, consider all the sentient beings in a "small thousand" world system. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish every one of them in the four meditative concentrations. And set aside, Kauśika, all the sentient beings of the small thousand world system. In the same way, consider all the sentient beings in a "middling second thousand" world system. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish every one of them in the four meditative concentrations. And set aside, Kauśika, all the sentient beings of the middling second thousand world system. In the same way, consider all the sentient beings in a great thousand of thousands, a threefold-thousand world system. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish every one of them in the four meditative concentrations. And set aside, Kauśika, all the sentient beings of that threefold-thousand great-thousand world system. In the same way, consider all the sentient beings in as many threefold-thousand great-thousand world systems as there are grains of sand in the River Gaṅgā. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish every one of them in the four meditative concentrations.

Kauśika, what do you think? Would that son or daughter of good family generate abundant merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Many, Blessed One (the Buddha)! Many, Sugata!"

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, even more abundant is the merit generated by the son or daughter of good family who, even in a small measure, commits this Perfection of Wisdom to writing in a book. With faith they have faith in it. With discernment they discern it. With devotion they are devoted to it. With a clear and joyful mind they delight in it. With excellent and complete higher intention they hold it with excellent higher intention. And they give it with higher intention to a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening. Even if only in a small measure, they apply themselves without laxity to writing and reading it. With diligence they urge that person to take it up, they teach it correctly, establish the person in it correctly, encourage the person correctly, and bring the person correct delight. They explain it through words, through definitions, through further elaborations, and they teach its meaning correctly. And they speak to that person thus: 'Child of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and strive, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.'"

"Having fully awakened, I shall bring to complete discipline the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, through the unsurpassed exhaustion of the aggregates, that is, through the thorough distinction of the true limit." Speaking thus, they purify that person's mind and remove all doubt.

Kauśika, consider further. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings who live in Jambudvīpa in the four immeasurables, and likewise, just as with the immeasurables, in the four formless absorptions and the five higher knowledges, so that they were established in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, and the higher knowledges without exception. Kauśika, what do you think? Would that son or daughter of good family generate a great deal of merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Blessed One, a great deal! Sugata, a great deal!"

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, even more merit than that is generated by the son or daughter of good family who takes up this Perfection of Wisdom, even if only a small portion of it, and commits it to a book. With faith, they are devoted to those who have faith; with careful discernment, to those who discern carefully; with firm conviction, to those who are firmly convinced; with a serene mind, to those whose minds are serene; with an excellent and superior intention, to those whose intention is excellent and superior. They give it, with superior intention, to a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening. Even if it is only a little, they apply themselves without laxity to writing and reading it. With diligence they urge that person to take it up, they teach it correctly, establish the person in it correctly, encourage the person correctly, and bring the person correct delight. They explain it through words, through definitions, through further elaborations, and they teach its meaning correctly. And they speak to that person thus: 'Child of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and strive, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Having fully awakened, you will bring to complete discipline the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, through the unsurpassed exhaustion of the aggregates, that is, through the thorough distinction of the true limit.' Speaking thus, they purify that person's mind and remove all doubt.

Kauśika, let alone the merit produced by establishing all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, and the higher knowledges. Kauśika, in the same way, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings who live in the world system of the four great continents in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, and the higher knowledges. Let alone, Kauśika, the merit produced by that establishing of all the beings of the world system of the four great continents in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, and the higher knowledges. Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings who live in the thousandfold world system, the small chiliocosm, in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, and the higher knowledges, and so on."

Kauśika, let alone the merit produced by establishing all the beings of the world system of the thousandfold world, the small chiliocosm, in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, and the higher knowledges. Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings in the second thousand, the middling world system, in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, and the higher knowledges. Let alone the merit produced by establishing all the beings of that middling world system in them.

Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings who live in the great thousand of the third thousand, the great chiliocosm, in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, and the higher knowledges. Let alone the merit produced by establishing all the beings of that great chiliocosm in them.

Kauśika, in the same way, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings who live in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the river Ganges, each a great chiliocosm, in the meditative concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless absorptions, and the higher knowledges. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?

Indra said: "Blessed One, it would be much. Sugata, it would be much."

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, even so, this son or daughter of good family generates far more merit. Whoever writes this Perfection of Wisdom, even in a small volume, and gives it to a bodhisattva who has generated the awakening mind, one who has faith through faith, discernment through discernment, devotion through devotion, a serene mind through serenity of mind, and an excellent higher intention through excellent higher intention, giving it with a higher intention; and who, even if the person only writes and reads it, undertakes it without laziness, with effort and diligence, and has that person take it up; who teaches it rightly, establishes the person in it rightly, praises it rightly, and gladdens the person rightly; who explains it with words, with detailed expression, and with further indications; who rightly explains its meaning to that person; and who says to that person, 'Son of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and exert yourself, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring immeasurable realms of sentient beings to discipline in the unsurpassed exhaustion of the aggregates, that is, in the discernment of the true limit,' and who thus purifies that person's mind and frees it from doubt.

Kauśika, furthermore, suppose some son or daughter of good family writes this Perfection of Wisdom, reads it himself or herself, and also, having written it, gives it to others as before."

Kauśika, this son or daughter of good family generates far more merit than the previous one.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family who is skilled in the meaning reads this Perfection of Wisdom, and having written it, gives it to others as before, and teaches it to them together with its meaning and its words, and makes it thoroughly clear. Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family generates even far more merit than the former.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, should this Perfection of Wisdom also be taught to those who do not understand it?"

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to Śakra, lord of the gods: "Kauśika, this Perfection of Wisdom should indeed be taught to a son or daughter of good family who does not understand. Why is that? Kauśika, in the future there will appear a semblance of the Perfection of Wisdom. Those sons and daughters of good family who do not understand it, and who wish to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, must not be allowed to hear that semblance of the Perfection of Wisdom and thereby be ruined."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should one recognize, in the future, that what is taught is the semblance of the Perfection of Wisdom, and say, 'This is that semblance'?"

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to Śakra, lord of the gods: "Kauśika, in the future there will be some monks whose bodies are undeveloped, whose moral discipline is undeveloped, whose minds are undeveloped, and whose wisdom is undeveloped. Their wisdom will be corrupt, they will be mute and dull like sheep by nature, and their discernment will be utterly ruined. Thinking, 'We are teaching the Perfection of Wisdom,' they will teach its semblance.

"Kauśika, how will they teach the semblance of the Perfection of Wisdom? They will teach that the destruction of form is the impermanence of form. In the same way, they will teach that the destruction of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is the impermanence of consciousness. They will also expound in this way: 'Whoever searches thus will be practicing the Perfection of Wisdom.' Kauśika, this should be recognized as the semblance of the Perfection of Wisdom.

"Moreover, Kauśika, one does not view the destruction of form as the impermanence of form. In the same way, one does not view the destruction of feeling, perception, and formations as their impermanence, and, Kauśika, one does not view the destruction of consciousness as the impermanence of consciousness. If one sees in this way, one is practicing the semblance of the Perfection of Wisdom.

"Therefore, Kauśika, a son or daughter of good family should teach the meaning of this Perfection of Wisdom. If one teaches the meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom, that son or daughter of good family generates far greater merit.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose someone were to establish all the sentient beings that exist in Jambudvīpa in the fruit of stream-entry. Kauśika, what do you think? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?"

Śakra (Indra), the lord of the gods, replied, "Blessed One, it would be much. Sugata, it would be much."

The Blessed One declared, "Kauśika, even more merit is generated by that son or daughter of good family who writes this Perfection of Wisdom, even in a small measure, into a book; who, with faith, gives it to one who has faith; with discernment, to one who has discernment; with deep conviction, to one who has deep conviction; with a clear and serene mind, to one whose mind is clear and serene; with a superior and perfect intention, to one whose intention is superior and perfect; and who, having generated the mind of awakening, gives it with a superior intention to a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening.

"Even in a small measure, such a person applies themselves to writing and reading it without neglect. With diligence they cause others to hold it. They teach it rightly, establish others in it rightly, praise it rightly, and bring others to rightful delight in it. They explain it through words, through distinct expressions, and through successive indications, and they rightly explain its meaning to them. They say to that person: 'Son of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and make effort, you will quickly become fully awakened in unsurpassable, perfect awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will establish beings, whose realm is immeasurable, in the utter exhaustion of the aggregates, the unsurpassable, that is, in the discernment of the ultimate limit.' In this way they purify that person's mind and free it from doubt, and they say, 'Son of good family, attain precisely those qualities that accord with the Perfection of Wisdom.'

"Kauśika, this son or daughter of good family generates far more merit than the former one. Why is that? Kauśika, because through this teaching the fruit of stream-entry is clearly distinguished.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, leave aside the merit produced by establishing all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the fruit of stream-entry. Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the sentient beings that exist in the world system of the four great continents in the fruit of stream-entry. Leave aside, Kauśika, the merit produced by establishing all the beings of the world system of the four continents in that fruit.

"Kauśika, suppose someone were to establish all the sentient beings that exist in a world system of one thousand, the small chiliocosm, in the fruit of stream-entry. Leave aside, Kauśika, the merit produced by establishing all the beings of the small chiliocosm in that fruit.

"Kauśika, suppose someone were to establish all the sentient beings that exist in the world system of the second thousand, the middle chiliocosm, in the fruit of stream-entry. Leave aside, Kauśika, the merit produced by establishing all the beings of the middle chiliocosm in that fruit.

"Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the sentient beings that exist in the world system of the third thousand, the great thousand, the great chiliocosm, in the fruit of stream-entry."

Kauśika, leave aside the merit produced by establishing all the sentient beings of the world system of the great chiliocosm, the third thousand, in the fruit of stream-entry. Kauśika, suppose that some son or daughter of good family were to establish in the fruit of stream-entry all the sentient beings that exist in as many world systems of the great chiliocosm as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Blessed One, much! Sugata, much!"

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, even more merit is generated by that son or daughter of good family who, having committed this Perfection of Wisdom even to a book, however small, gives it with an exalted intention to a bodhisattva who has the confidence of faith, the discernment of careful reflection, the inclination of deep conviction, a serene mind, and the perfection of an exalted intention, a bodhisattva who has given rise to the awakening mind by means of the awakening mind. And even if it is only a small matter of writing and reading, that person, striving with diligence and with nothing less than full commitment, causes that bodhisattva to grasp it, teaches it correctly, establishes the bodhisattva in it correctly, praises it correctly, and brings correct delight. By means of words, by signs, by distinct characterizations, and by further indications, that person explains its meaning correctly, and says to the bodhisattva: 'Child of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and make an effort, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring to discipline the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, so that the aggregates are completely exhausted, unsurpassed, which is to say, within the discernment of the true limit.' In this way that person purifies the bodhisattva's mind and removes doubt, and says: 'Child of good family, obtain these very dharmas that accord with the Perfection of Wisdom.'

"Kauśika, this person generates far more merit than the former son or daughter of good family. Why is that? Kauśika, because from this the fruit of stream-entry is distinguished.

"Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the sentient beings that exist in Jambudvīpa in the fruit of once-returning. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?"

Śakra replied: "Blessed One, much! Sugata, much!"

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, even more merit is generated by that son or daughter of good family who, having committed this Perfection of Wisdom even to a book, however small, gives it with an exalted intention to a bodhisattva who has the confidence of faith, the discernment of careful reflection, the inclination of deep conviction, a serene mind, and the perfection of an exalted intention, a bodhisattva who has given rise to the awakening mind by means of the awakening mind. And even if it is only a small matter of writing and reading, that person, striving with diligence and with nothing less than full commitment,

Such a person encourages that bodhisattva to take hold of this Perfection of Wisdom, instructs him, establishes him in it, praises him, and fills him with joy. Through words that indicate, that fully indicate, and that follow upon the indication, the person truly explains the meaning of this to him. And the person says to him: "Noble son, come here. Train yourself in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practise it, and make an effort, you will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring to discipline immeasurable realms of sentient beings, until the aggregates are completely exhausted, that is, in the unsurpassed manifestation of the true limit." Speaking in this way, the person purifies that bodhisattva's mind and frees it from doubt. And the person says these words: "Noble son, strive to attain those very qualities that accompany the Perfection of Wisdom."

Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family generates even more merit than the former one. Why is that? Kauśika, from this the fruit of the once-returner is distinguished.

Kauśika, set aside the merit produced by someone who establishes all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the fruit of the once-returner. Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish in the fruit of the once-returner all the sentient beings there are in a world system of the four great continents. And set aside, Kauśika, the merit produced by establishing all the sentient beings of that world system of four continents in the fruit of the once-returner.

Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish in the fruit of the once-returner all the sentient beings there are in a small thousandfold world system. And set aside, Kauśika, the merit produced by establishing all the sentient beings of a small thousandfold world system in that fruit.

Kauśika, suppose someone were to establish in the fruit of the once-returner all the sentient beings there are in a middling twice-thousandfold world system. And set aside, Kauśika, the merit produced by establishing all the sentient beings of a middling twice-thousandfold world system in that fruit.

Kauśika, suppose someone were to establish in the fruit of the once-returner all the sentient beings there are in a great thousandfold world system of three thousand. And set aside, Kauśika, the merit produced by establishing all the sentient beings of a great three-thousandfold world system in that fruit.

Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish in the fruit of the once-returner all the sentient beings there are in as many great three-thousandfold world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Much, Blessed One (the Buddha). Much, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, even more merit than that is generated by this son or daughter of good family."

Suppose someone writes out this Perfection of Wisdom, even in a small book, and then, with faith, gives it to one who has faith; with careful discernment, to one who discerns carefully; with strong devotion, to one of strong devotion; with a serene mind, to one of serene mind; with excellent superior intention, to one who has excellent superior intention; and, having generated the mind of awakening, gives it with superior intention to a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening. And suppose that even for the writing and reading of it, that person does not remain content with mere inclination, but applies himself with diligence and earnest effort. He has others take it up, teaches it properly, sets it forth properly, praises it properly, and brings others to proper delight in it. He explains the meaning of this text by way of words, by designations, by detailed indications, and by following expositions. And he says to that person: "Son of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and strive, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring to maturity immeasurable realms of sentient beings, and you will bring them to the supreme exhaustion of the aggregates, that is, to the discernment of the ultimate limit." In this way he purifies that person's mind and removes doubt, and he says: "Son of good family, you should attain just those qualities that accord with the Perfection of Wisdom."

Kauśika, this son or daughter of good family generates much more merit than the earlier one. Why is that? Kauśika, because from this the fruit of the once-returner is clearly distinguished.

This is the sixth section of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish in the fruit of the non-returner all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?

Śakra replied: "Much, Blessed One. Much, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, even more merit than that is generated by this son or daughter of good family who writes out this Perfection of Wisdom, even in a small book, and then, with faith, gives it to one who has faith; with careful discernment, to one who discerns carefully; with strong devotion, to one of strong devotion; with a serene mind, to one of serene mind; with excellent superior intention, to one who has excellent superior intention; and, having generated the mind of awakening, gives it with superior intention to a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening. Even for the writing and reading of it, he does not remain content with mere inclination, but applies himself with diligence and earnest effort. He has others take it up, teaches it properly, sets it forth properly, praises it properly, and brings others to proper delight in it. He explains its meaning by way of words, by designations, by detailed indications, and by following expositions. And he says to that person: 'Son of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and strive, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.'"

"Having fully awakened, he will also bring to maturity the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, in the unsurpassed exhaustion of the aggregates, that is, in the full distinction of the limit of reality." Saying this, he thus purifies that person's mind and removes his doubt, and says these words: "Son of good family, you should attain precisely those qualities that accompany the Perfection of Wisdom."

Kauśika, such a son or daughter of good family generates far more merit than the former. Why is that? Kauśika, it is because this person fully discerns the fruit of the non-returner.

Kauśika, set aside the merit of establishing all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the fruit of the non-returner. Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the sentient beings of the world-system of the four great continents in the fruit of the non-returner. And set aside, Kauśika, the merit of establishing all the sentient beings of the world-system of the four great continents in that fruit.

Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the sentient beings in a world-system of a thousand worlds, the small chiliocosm, in the fruit of the non-returner. And set aside, Kauśika, the merit of establishing all the sentient beings of that small chiliocosm in that fruit.

Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the sentient beings in the world-system of the middle, twice-thousandfold chiliocosm in the fruit of the non-returner. And set aside, Kauśika, the merit of establishing all the sentient beings of the middle chiliocosm in that fruit.

Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the sentient beings in the world-system of the great thousandfold world-system, the threefold-thousand great chiliocosm, in the fruit of the non-returner. And set aside, Kauśika, the merit of establishing all the sentient beings of the great chiliocosm in that fruit.

Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the sentient beings in as many great chiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā in the fruit of the non-returner. Kauśika, what do you think? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Much, Blessed One. Much, Sugata."

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, a son or daughter of good family who does the following generates even far more merit than that. Having even copied this Perfection of Wisdom in a book, in a small form, he gives it with a lofty intention to a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening: one who has faith through true faith, discernment through thorough discernment, devotion through superior devotion, serene confidence through serene confidence, and who, through the excellence of a lofty intention, has an excellent lofty intention. Or he does not remain content with mere inclination toward even the small act of writing and reading it, but applies himself with diligence, has others take it up, teaches it properly, sets it forth properly, praises it properly, and brings others to proper delight in it."

He explains the meaning of it to him properly, through indication in words, through detailed indication, and through further indication. And he says to him: "Noble son, come here and train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and strive, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring to complete discipline, through the unsurpassed exhaustion of the aggregates, the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, which is to say, through the definitive distinguishing of the true limit." Speaking in this way, he purifies that person's mind and removes his doubt. And if he says these words: "Noble son, may you attain those very qualities that accord with the Perfection of Wisdom," then, Kauśika, this noble son or noble daughter produces far more merit than the former one. Why is that? Kauśika, because from this the fruit of the non-returner is distinguished.
