Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose that some noble son or noble daughter were to establish in arhatship all the beings who live in Jambudvīpa. Kauśika, what do you think? Would that noble son or noble daughter generate much merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Blessed One, much indeed. Sugata, much indeed."

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, even more merit than that is generated by this noble son or noble daughter, who takes this Perfection of Wisdom, even in small measure, and sets it down in a book; and who, to a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening, one who has faith through true faith, discernment through thorough discernment, devotion through superior devotion, serene confidence through serene confidence, and an excellent lofty intention through the excellence of a lofty intention, gives it with a lofty intention. Or he does not remain content with mere inclination toward even the small act of writing and reading it, but applies himself with diligence, has others take it up, teaches it properly, sets it forth properly, praises it properly, and brings others to proper delight in it. He explains the meaning of it to him properly, through indication in words, through detailed indication, and through further indication. And he says to him: 'Noble son, come here and train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and strive, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring to complete discipline, through the unsurpassed exhaustion of the aggregates, the immeasurable realms of sentient beings, which is to say, through the definitive distinguishing of the true limit.' Speaking in this way, he purifies that person's mind and removes his doubt. And if he says these words: 'Noble son, may you attain those very qualities that accord with the Perfection of Wisdom,' then, Kauśika, this noble son or noble daughter produces far more merit than the former one. Why is that? Kauśika, because from this arhatship is distinguished as well.

In this regard, noble son, to whatever extent you train in the Perfection of Wisdom, to that extent you will gradually attain the qualities of a buddha and draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening."

If you train in this training and practice it with effort, you will come to distinguish the fruit of stream-entry. You will come to distinguish the fruit of once-returning. You will come to distinguish the fruit of non-returning. You will come to distinguish arhatship. You will come to distinguish the state of a pratyekabuddha. You will come to distinguish the state of a perfectly complete buddha." In this way he will cause joy to increase.

Kauśika, let alone the merit produced by some noble son or noble daughter who establishes all the beings of Jambudvīpa in arhatship. Suppose, Kauśika, that some noble son or noble daughter were to establish in arhatship all the beings there are in the world-system of the four great continents. And let alone the merit of establishing in arhatship all the beings of the world-system of the four continents. Suppose, Kauśika, that someone were to establish in arhatship all the beings there are in a world-system of a thousand, a small thousand. And let alone the merit of establishing in arhatship all the beings of a small thousandfold world-system. Suppose, Kauśika, that someone were to establish in arhatship all the beings there are in a world-system of the second thousand, the intermediate one. And let alone the merit of establishing in arhatship all the beings of that intermediate world-system. Suppose, Kauśika, that someone were to establish in arhatship all the beings there are in a world-system of the third thousand, the great thousand, the great trichiliocosm. And let alone the merit of establishing in arhatship all the beings of the great trichiliocosm. Suppose, Kauśika, that some noble son or noble daughter were to establish in arhatship all the beings there are in as many great trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that noble son or noble daughter produce much merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Blessed One, much! Sugata, much! Blessed One, that mass of merit is not easily reckoned. Blessed One, that mass of merit cannot easily be counted, nor illustrated by an example, nor shown by a simile, nor taken as a basis, nor made a close approximation."

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, even so, this noble son or noble daughter produces far more merit than that. Namely, one who writes out this Perfection of Wisdom, even if only in a small volume, and with faith gives it to one who has faith, with careful investigation to one who investigates carefully, with eager devotion to one who is eagerly devoted, with a clear and serene mind to one whose mind is clear and serene, with excellent and perfect intention to one of excellent and perfect intention, to a bodhisattva who has generated the awakening mind, with a lofty motivation. Or, even if only in small measure, he takes up writing it and reading it without any laxity, and with diligence causes others to grasp it. He shows it properly, establishes others in it properly, praises it properly, and gladdens others in it properly. He explains it through words, through indications, and through follow-up explanations, and properly expounds its meaning to them.

To such a one he says: "Noble son, come here and train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and strive in it, you will swiftly awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring to maturity the countless realms of sentient beings, through the unsurpassable exhaustion of the aggregates, that is, through the discernment of the true limit." In this way he speaks, purifying that person's mind and removing all doubt. And if he says these words: "Noble son, strive to attain those very qualities that accord with the Perfection of Wisdom," then this very act brings forth far greater merit. Why is that? Kauśika, from this the state of an arhat is discerned.

To him he says: "Noble son, as you train in the Perfection of Wisdom, so, step by step, you will attain the qualities of a buddha and draw near to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. If you train in this, practice it, and strive, you will realize the fruit of the stream-enterer. You will realize the fruit of the once-returner. You will realize the fruit of the non-returner. You will realize the state of an arhat. You will realize the state of a pratyekabuddha. You will realize the state of a perfectly complete buddha." In this way he increases the other's joy.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish all the beings of Jambudvīpa, as many as there are, in the state of a pratyekabuddha. What do you think, Kauśika? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Much, Blessed One, much, Sugata."

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, even more merit than that is generated by the son or daughter of good family who does the following. Even if only in small measure, he puts this Perfection of Wisdom into a book, and gives it, with lofty motivation, to a bodhisattva who has generated the awakening mind: one who has faith, to one who has faith; one who has keen discernment, to one who has keen discernment; one who has deep conviction, to one who has deep conviction; one whose mind is serene, to one whose mind is serene; one with excellent and perfect lofty intention, to one with excellent and perfect lofty intention. Or, even if only in small measure, he takes up writing it and reading it without any laxity, and with diligence causes others to grasp it. He shows it properly, establishes others in it properly, praises it properly, and gladdens others in it properly. He explains it through words, through indications, and through follow-up explanations, and properly expounds its meaning to them.

"To such a one he says: 'Noble son, come here and train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and strive in it, you will swiftly awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And having become fully awakened, you will bring to maturity the countless realms of sentient beings, through the unsurpassable exhaustion of the aggregates, that is, through the discernment of the true limit.' In this way he speaks, purifying that person's mind and removing all doubt. And if he says these words: 'Noble son, strive to attain those very qualities that accord with the Perfection of Wisdom,' then this very act brings forth far greater merit. Why is that? Kauśika, from this the state of a pratyekabuddha is discerned."

To such a one he should say: "Noble son, to the degree that you train in the Perfection of Wisdom, to that very degree you will gradually obtain the qualities of a buddha. You will draw near to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. If you train in this discipline, practice it, and strive, you will come to discern the fruit of a stream-enterer. You will come to discern the fruit of a once-returner. You will come to discern the fruit of a non-returner. You will come to discern the state of an arhat. You will come to discern the state of a pratyekabuddha. You will come to discern the state of a perfectly complete buddha." In this way he should increase that person's joy.

Kauśika, setting aside the merit produced by establishing all the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa in the state of a pratyekabuddha, consider the following. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish in the state of a pratyekabuddha every sentient being in the world-realm of the four great continents. Setting aside even that merit, suppose they were to establish in the state of a pratyekabuddha every sentient being in a world-realm of the small thousandfold system. Setting that aside too, suppose they were to establish in the state of a pratyekabuddha every sentient being in the middling twofold thousand world-realm. Setting that aside as well, suppose they were to establish in the state of a pratyekabuddha every sentient being in the great threefold thousand world-realm.

Now, Kauśika, suppose some son or daughter of good family were to establish in the state of a pratyekabuddha as many sentient beings as there are in world-realms, each a great threefold thousand world-system, as numerous as the grains of sand in the river Ganges. Kauśika, what do you think? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Blessed One, it would be much. Sugata, it would be much."

The Blessed One declared: "Kauśika, even so, a son or daughter of good family who does the following generates far more merit than that. Suppose one commits this Perfection of Wisdom to writing, even in a small volume. Then, with faith toward one who has faith, with careful discernment toward one who discerns carefully, with deep conviction toward one who is deeply convinced, with serene confidence toward one who has serene confidence, with excellent and superior intention toward one whose intention is excellent and superior, one gives it, with superior intention, to a bodhisattva who has generated the awakening mind. Even for so small a matter as writing and reading it, one practices without negligence and with diligence. One causes that person to take it up. One shows it correctly, sets it forth correctly, praises it correctly, and brings correct delight. One expresses it through words, through full characterization, and through further indication. And one explains its meaning correctly to that person."

To that person one says: "Child of good family, come here. Train in this path of the bodhisattvas. If you train in this path, practice it, and make effort, you will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And once you have fully awakened as a buddha, you will bring about the taming, within the unsurpassable exhaustion of the aggregates, of beings whose realms cannot be measured, so that they are distinguished in the true limit." One speaks in this way, thereby purifying that person's mind and removing all doubt. And if one says these words: "Child of good family, strive to attain just those qualities that accompany the Perfection of Wisdom," then this gives rise to far greater merit than the former.

Why is that so? Kauśika, from this very practice one distinguishes the state of a solitary buddha. Child of good family, to whatever degree you come to train in the Perfection of Wisdom, to that degree you will gradually attain the qualities of a buddha and draw near to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. If you train in this training, practice it, and make effort, you will distinguish the fruit of stream-entry. You will distinguish the fruit of once-returning. You will distinguish the fruit of non-returning. You will distinguish the state of an arhat. You will distinguish the state of a solitary buddha. You will distinguish the state of a perfectly complete buddha. In this way one makes that person's joy increase.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose that some son or daughter of good family were to bring all the beings that exist in Jambudvīpa to generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And suppose, Kauśika, that some other son or daughter of good family, having brought all of them to generate that mind, were to write out this Perfection of Wisdom and give it to them. And suppose, Kauśika, that some other son or daughter of good family, thinking, "This one will train in this Perfection of Wisdom and apply himself to it; through this very practice, by meditating on this Perfection of Wisdom, and by its growth, increase, and expansion, he will bring the qualities of a buddha to complete fulfillment," were to entrust this Perfection of Wisdom to an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being. This latter son or daughter of good family generates far greater merit than the former. Why is that so? Because this great being will certainly awaken fully to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening and bring the suffering of beings to an end.

Kauschika, let alone the merit of generating the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening in all the beings of Jambudvīpa. Kauśika, consider rather the case where some son or daughter of good family brings all the beings that exist in the world system of the four great continents to generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And again, Kauśika, set aside even the merit of generating that awakening mind in all the beings of the world system of the four great continents.

Kauśika, consider next a world system of a thousand worlds. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to bring all the beings who dwell there to generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And yet, Kauśika, set aside even the merit of generating the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening in all the beings of that world system of a thousand worlds.

Kauśika, consider a world system of a second thousand, the middle one. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to bring all the beings who dwell there to generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And yet, Kauśika, set aside even the merit of generating that awakening mind in all the beings of that middle world system of a second thousand.

Kauśika, consider a world system of a third thousand, the great thousand of thousands. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to bring all the beings who dwell there to generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And yet, Kauśika, set aside even the merit of generating that awakening mind in all the beings of that great world system of three thousand.

Kauśika, consider now as many great world systems of three thousand as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā. Suppose some son or daughter of good family were to bring all the beings who dwell in them to generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And suppose, Kauśika, that some other son or daughter of good family, having brought all those beings to generate the mind of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, were to write out this Perfection of Wisdom and give it to them. Suppose that person thinks: "They will study this Perfection of Wisdom and practice it in yoga. In this way, through meditating on it intensely, this Perfection of Wisdom will grow, increase, and expand, and so become fully complete." And suppose that person then entrusts this Perfection of Wisdom to a bodhisattva, a great being, who is irreversible from awakening. Then, Kauśika, that son or daughter of good family will generate far greater merit than the former one.

Why is this so? Because this bodhisattva will surely become fully and perfectly awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, and will bring the suffering of beings to an end.

Furthermore, Kauśika, suppose all the beings who exist in Jambudvīpa have become irreversible from unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. And suppose some son or daughter of good family, having had this Perfection of Wisdom written down in a book, gives it to those very beings and entrusts it to them, and teaches it to them with its meaning and with its letters. Kauśika, what do you think? Would that son or daughter of good family generate much merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra) replied: "Blessed One, much! Sugata, much! Blessed One, that mass of merit cannot easily be counted. Blessed One, that mass of merit cannot easily be reckoned, nor easily shown by any example, nor easily made a basis or a cause."

The Blessed One said: "Kauśika, this son or daughter of good family generates even greater merit than that."

Suppose, then, that for those irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, who wish to quickly and fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, someone writes this Perfection of Wisdom down in a book, gives it to them and entrusts it to them, and teaches it to them with its meaning and with its letters, and instructs them in this Perfection of Wisdom and guides them in it. Kauśika, setting aside the merit generated by entrusting this Perfection of Wisdom to all the beings of Jambudvīpa who have become irreversible, consider this.

Kauśika, suppose that all the beings who exist in the world system of the four great continents have become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and that some son or daughter of good family writes this Perfection of Wisdom down in a book, gives it to them and entrusts it to them, and teaches it to them with its meaning and with its letters. Kauśika, set aside even the merit generated by entrusting this Perfection of Wisdom to all the beings of the world system of the four great continents who have become irreversible.

Kauśika, suppose that all the beings who exist in the world system of the small thousandfold realm have become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and that some son or daughter of good family writes this Perfection of Wisdom down in a book, gives it to them and entrusts it to them, and teaches it to them with its meaning and with its letters. Kauśika, set aside even the merit generated by entrusting this Perfection of Wisdom to all the beings of the small thousandfold world system who have become irreversible.

Kauśika, suppose that all the beings who exist in the world system of the middling twofold thousand have become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and that some son or daughter of good family writes this Perfection of Wisdom down in a book, gives it to them and entrusts it to them, and teaches it to them with its meaning and with its letters. Kauśika, set aside even the merit generated by entrusting this Perfection of Wisdom to all the beings of the middling twofold-thousand world system who have become irreversible.

Kauśika, suppose that all the beings who exist in the world system of the great thousand of the three thousand have become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and that some son or daughter of good family writes this Perfection of Wisdom down in a book, gives it to them and entrusts it to them, and teaches it to them with its meaning and with its letters. Kauśika, set aside even the merit generated by entrusting this Perfection of Wisdom to all the beings of the great thousand world system of the three thousand who have become irreversible.

Kauśika, suppose that in world systems as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, each a great thousand of the three thousand, all the beings there are have become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And suppose that some son or daughter of good family writes this Perfection of Wisdom down in a book, gives it to them and entrusts it to them, and teaches it to them with its meaning and with its letters. Kauśika, what do you think? Would that son or daughter of good family generate a great deal of merit on that basis?

Śakra (Indra), the lord of the gods, replied: Blessed One, a great deal! Sugata, a great deal! Blessed One, that mass of merit cannot easily be counted. Blessed One, that mass of merit cannot easily be reckoned, nor shown by example, nor made a basis, nor made a cause.

The Blessed One declared: Kauśika, even more merit than that is generated by the son or daughter of good family who writes this Perfection of Wisdom down in a book and gives it and entrusts it to those bodhisattva great beings who are irreversible and who wish to quickly attain complete awakening in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, who teaches it to them with its meaning and with its letters, and who instructs them in this Perfection of Wisdom and guides them in it.

Then, Kauśika, suppose another bodhisattva great being appears and says: I shall attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening more quickly than these. Kauśika, if a son or daughter of good family instructs and guides in this Perfection of Wisdom that bodhisattva great being, whose higher knowledge is exceedingly swift, then that son or daughter of good family generates even more merit than the former one.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, in whatever way bodhisattva great beings draw near to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, in just that way they should be instructed and guided in the Perfection of Wisdom. By being instructed and guided in the Perfection of Wisdom in just that way, they come close to suchness. When they have come close to suchness, those who make use of their robes, alms food, bedding, seats, medicines for the sick, and requisites accomplish what is to be done, and make that offering bring great fruit and great reward. Therefore that person generates very great merit. Why is that? Blessed One, it is because such is the very nature of the bodhisattva great being who draws near to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, it is excellent, excellent, that you inspire the people who follow the bodhisattva vehicle with joy, that you support them and attend to them. Kauśika, this is what you should do. Any noble hearer (śrāvaka) who wishes to look after all beings should cause bodhisattva great beings to increase their joy in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and should support them and attend to them. That is what is to be done. And why is that?

For the unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening of bodhisattva great beings is born from this. If bodhisattva great beings had not given rise to this awakening mind, those bodhisattva great beings would not train in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, nor would they train in the six perfections. And if they did not train, they would not become fully and completely awakened in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. But it is because bodhisattva great beings train in these six perfections, the training of bodhisattvas, that they give rise to the awakening mind. And for that reason they become fully and completely awakened in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

This is the fifth chapter, called "The Chapter on the Categories of Merit," from the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the bodhisattva great being Maitreya said this to the venerable Subhūti: Noble Subhūti, consider further the basis of meritorious action that is accompanied by rejoicing and dedication on the part of a bodhisattva great being. Of all the bases of meritorious action that arise from the generosity of all beings, all the bases of meritorious action that arise from moral discipline, and all the bases of meritorious action that arise from meditation, this very basis of meritorious action, accompanied by a bodhisattva great being's rejoicing and dedication, is called the supreme, the sublime, the chief, the excellent, the most excellent, the finest, the highest, the unsurpassed. It is called the peerless, the unequaled, and that which equals the unequaled.

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said this to the bodhisattva great being Maitreya: Maitreya, consider a bodhisattva great being who rejoices in the following. In the worlds of the ten directions, which extend everywhere and in all ways, there are world-systems, each a great trichiliocosm, that are immeasurable beyond measure, innumerable beyond number, limitless beyond limit, inconceivable beyond conception, without boundary or end. In each direction, in each of those great trichiliocosm world-systems, in times gone by, there were tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas, immeasurable beyond measure, innumerable beyond number, limitless beyond limit, inconceivable beyond conception, without boundary or end. Their path was cut off and their entry into rebirth was cut off. Elaboration and the leading on to existence were cut off, their tears were exhausted, and their thorns were destroyed. They had set down the burden completely, attained their own aim, and utterly exhausted the bonds to existence. Their minds were thoroughly liberated through right and perfect knowledge, and they had reached the far shore of the sovereign mastery of all minds. These buddhas passed completely beyond sorrow into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates. The bodhisattva rejoices in all of this, from the time when those buddhas first gave rise to the mind of awakening, up to the time when they became fully and completely awakened in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; and up to their passing beyond sorrow into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates; and up to the time when the sacred Dharma had not yet vanished, that is to say,

And likewise, the bodhisattva rejoices in the roots of virtue of all those blessed buddhas in between: the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation; whatever roots of virtue are endowed with the six perfections; the roots of virtue endowed with the perfect qualities of a buddha; the roots of virtue endowed with the perfection of the powers and of fearlessness; and likewise those endowed with the perfection of the higher knowledges, with the perfection of thorough understanding, and with the perfection of aspiration; whatever roots of virtue are endowed with the perfect wisdom of omniscience; whatever benevolent intention they held, whatever great loving-kindness, whatever great compassion; whatever immeasurable, incalculable qualities of a buddha there are; whatever unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening there is, and whatever bliss belongs to that unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; whatever perfection of sovereign mastery over all phenomena there is; the immeasurable, unsurpassable supreme exercise of miraculous power that overpowers everything; and whatever power of the Tathāgata's wisdom there is, knowing things exactly as they are, unobstructed, unattached, unimpeded, without equal, beyond the equal and the unequal, without analogy, immeasurable. He rejoices in whatever power of buddha wisdom there is among the powers, in whatever wisdom and vision of a buddha there is, in whatever perfection of the ten powers there is, in whatever full and supreme realization of the four fearlessnesses there is, and in whatever realization of the Dharma there is through ultimately accomplishing all phenomena.

He rejoices in the turning of the wheel of Dharma; in the holding up of the lamp of Dharma, the beating of the drum of Dharma, the blowing of the conch of Dharma, the proclaiming of the conch of Dharma, the wielding of the sword of Dharma, the sending down of the rain of Dharma, the giving of the sacrificial offering of Dharma; and in the way that, through the gift of Dharma, they fully satisfied and thoroughly nourished all sentient beings.

He rejoices in whatever teachings were taught, and in the roots of virtue of all those who were tamed, trained, inclined, made certain, and turned toward complete awakening through those teachings, whether the Dharma of the buddhas, the Dharma of the solitary buddhas, or the Dharma of the hearers. He rejoices in the roots of virtue endowed with the six perfections of those bodhisattvas, great beings, whom those blessed buddhas prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; in the roots of virtue of all those individuals of the solitary buddha vehicle who were prophesied to the awakening of a solitary buddha; in the bases of meritorious action arising from generosity, those arising from moral discipline, and those arising from meditation, belonging to individuals of the hearer vehicle; in the undefiled roots of virtue of those still in training; in the undefiled roots of virtue of those beyond training; and in the roots of virtue that ordinary beings have produced in regard to those teachings.

Likewise, I rejoice in the bases of meritorious action arising from generosity, from moral discipline, and from meditation, belonging to the fourfold assembly of those buddhas, the Blessed Ones: the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen. I rejoice in all the roots of virtue produced there, in the presence of those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as they taught the Dharma, by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, and by whatever sentient beings have gone to rebirth among animals. I rejoice in the roots of virtue that anyone has produced in regard to the complete passing beyond sorrow of those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and likewise in regard to their having passed beyond sorrow. And I rejoice in all the roots of virtue produced in dependence upon the Buddha, the Blessed One, in dependence upon the Dharma, in dependence upon the Saṅgha, and in dependence upon those individuals who cultivate meditation in their minds.

Gathering all these roots of virtue together without exception and without remainder, adding them up and weighing them, one should rejoice with the supreme rejoicing. One rejoices with a rejoicing that is holy, chief, excellent, most excellent, sublime, supreme, unsurpassed, unexcelled, without equal, beyond compare, and equal to the unequalled. Having rejoiced in this way, one should say aloud: "I dedicate that basis of meritorious action, endowed with this rejoicing, to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. May I accomplish unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening." So one should think and speak.

Now, as for those individuals who follow the bodhisattva vehicle: with what bases, what objects, and what aspects do they dedicate, and give rise to that mind? Do they focus on those bases, those objects, and those aspects just as they have taken them as signs?

When this had been said, the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, spoke thus to the elder, the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, they do not focus on those bases, those objects, and those aspects just as they have taken them as signs."

When this had been said, the elder, the venerable Subhūti, spoke thus to the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya: "If one were to focus on, and take as a sign, what has no basis and no object, how would this not become an inverted perception, an inverted state of mind, and an inverted view? Why is that? In just this way, attachment, though there is no real basis, imagines and thoroughly imputes permanence upon what is impermanent, happiness upon what is suffering, self upon what is selfless, and beauty upon what is unattractive, and so inverted perception, inverted mind, and inverted view arise.

"Furthermore, just as the basis is, just as the object is, and just as the aspect is, so too is awakening, and so too is the mind. If that is so, then all phenomena and all elements are likewise so. And if, just as the basis, the object, and the aspect are, awakening and mind are likewise so, then by means of which bases, which objects, and which aspects would any mind dedicate anything to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?"

Then what basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing is there that one could dedicate to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, said this to the venerable elder Subhūti: "Noble Subhūti, this should not be explained or taught in the presence of bodhisattvas, great beings, who have newly entered the Great Vehicle. Why is that? Whatever faith, joy, devotion, and reverence they may have, all of it would be destroyed. Noble Subhūti, this should be explained and taught in the presence of bodhisattvas, great beings, who are irreversible. And a bodhisattva, a great being, who is sustained by a spiritual friend will not be daunted by this, will not shrink from it, will not be unnerved, and will not be disheartened. His mind will not turn back, will not be crushed and turn back, will not tremble, will not be utterly terrified, and will not come to possess utter terror. In this way, the bodhisattva, the great being, having rejoiced, should dedicate all the bases of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing to omniscience."

This is the seventh volume of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable elder Subhūti said this to the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya: "Maitreya, the mind by which one rejoices and dedicates has itself been exhausted, has ceased, has vanished and been transformed. That being so, what is that mind by which one dedicates to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening? And what is that mind that dedicates the basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening? When two minds do not meet, and that mind cannot by its intrinsic nature dedicate anything either, then how could a mind possibly dedicate a mind?"

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), said this to the venerable elder Subhūti: "Noble Subhūti, if those bodhisattvas, great beings, who are newly entered into the Great Vehicle were to hear this teaching and tremble, be utterly terrified, and come to possess utter terror, that would not be right. Noble Subhūti, then how should a bodhisattva, a great being, dedicate that basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening? In grasping the basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing, and in dedicating the mind accompanied by rejoicing, how does that mind accompanied by rejoicing come to be well grasped and well dedicated?"

Then the venerable elder Subhūti, addressing the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, taking him as his basis, spoke to him.

"Maitreya, here a bodhisattva, a great being, may consider the worlds of the ten directions: the immeasurable, countless world systems, each a great trichiliocosm, that exist in every single direction. In each and every one of those great trichiliocosms there are buddhas, Blessed Ones of the past, who have cut off the path, cut off the entering, cut off proliferation and the leading into existence, who have exhausted their tears, destroyed the thorns, thoroughly laid down the burden, attained their own aim, utterly exhausted the bonds of existence, whose minds are perfectly liberated through right and complete knowledge, who have reached the far shore of mastery over all minds, and who, immeasurable and countless, have passed into nirvāṇa. From the time when those buddhas, those Blessed Ones, first generated the mind of awakening, up to their fully awakening into unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; and up to their passing completely into nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without any remainder of the aggregates; and up to the time before the sacred Dharma had disappeared: whatever roots of virtue those buddhas, those Blessed Ones, had during all that time, together with the perfections; whatever formation of merit and formation of roots of virtue they accomplished; whatever aggregate of moral discipline, aggregate of meditative absorption, aggregate of wisdom, aggregate of liberation, and aggregate of the seeing of the wisdom of liberation those buddhas, those Blessed Ones, possessed; whatever their wish to benefit others, their great loving-kindness, and their great compassion; and whatever immeasurable and countless qualities of a buddha they had.

Further, whatever Dharma those buddhas, those Blessed Ones, taught, and the roots of virtue of those who trained in that Dharma, who had devotion to it, and who abided in it; the roots of virtue, endowed with the six perfections, of those bodhisattvas, great beings, whom those buddhas, those Blessed Ones, prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; the roots of virtue of those individuals of the vehicle of the solitary buddhas whom those buddhas prophesied to their own awakening; the roots of virtue arising from generosity, from moral discipline, and from meditation among individuals of the hearer vehicle; the undefiled roots of virtue of those still in training, and the undefiled roots of virtue of those beyond training; the roots of virtue that ordinary beings have created in relation to that Dharma; the roots of virtue created by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who heard that Dharma and, having heard it, created roots of virtue; the roots of virtue created by sentient beings born as animals who heard that Dharma and, having heard it, created roots of virtue; and the roots of virtue that sentient beings created in relation to those buddhas, those Blessed Ones, as they were passing into nirvāṇa and after they had passed into nirvāṇa.

Having gathered all of these roots of virtue into one, summed them up, measured them, and left nothing out, and having rejoiced in all that is worthy of rejoicing without exception, if he then dedicates that basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, who dedicates it not come to have a distorted perception, not come to have a distorted mind, and not come to have a distorted view?"

When he had spoken thus,

The bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, spoke to the venerable elder Subhūti and said: "Noble Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, does not form the perception of "mind" regarding the mind by which he dedicates, and the mind to which he dedicates. In that case, that bodhisattva, a great being, has dedicated the basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Because he does not truly think of that mind, "This is that mind," a bodhisattva, a great being, does not come to have a distorted perception, does not come to have a distorted mind, and does not come to have a distorted view.

But suppose he knows of the mind by which he dedicates, and the mind to which he dedicates, "That mind is such and such," and he forms the perception of it as mind. Then that bodhisattva, a great being, comes to have a distorted perception, a distorted mind, and a distorted view.

Suppose, then, that a bodhisattva, a great being, knows rightly about the mind by which he dedicates, and thinks in this way: "When that mind is considered, it is exhausted, and what is exhausted is simply exhausted." He knows it as exhausted, and knows that it has ceased, is devoid of any basis, and has changed. And what is exhausted cannot be dedicated. Moreover, the nature of the mind by which he dedicates is just this; the nature of the things by which he dedicates is just this; and the nature of the things to which he dedicates is just this. If he dedicates in this way, it is a right dedication and not a wrong dedication. It is in this way that a bodhisattva, a great being, should dedicate.

Noble Subhūti, furthermore, there is this. A bodhisattva, a great being, should consider the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, and likewise those yet to come, whose paths of rebirth have been cut off, whose entry into new existence has been cut off, whose elaborations have been cut off, and whose pull toward becoming has been cut off, who are immeasurable and innumerable. He should consider the roots of virtue of those Blessed Buddhas, from the time they first generated the mind of awakening, until they become fully and completely awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, until they pass fully into nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates, and until the sacred Dharma comes to an end, and so across all that interval. These are the roots of virtue connected with the perfections of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; their wish to benefit others, their great loving-kindness, and their great compassion; the immeasurable and innumerable qualities of a buddha; the Dharma that those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will teach, the roots of virtue of those who will train in that Dharma, those who will be devoted to it, and those who will abide in it; the roots of virtue connected with the six perfections of those bodhisattvas whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will prophesy to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; and the roots of virtue of those persons of the vehicle of the solitary buddhas whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will prophesy to the awakening of a solitary buddha, and so on.

the roots of virtue of those persons who belong to the vehicle of the hearers, namely the bases of meritorious action that arise from giving, the bases of meritorious action that arise from moral discipline, and the bases of meritorious action that arise from meditation; the undefiled roots of virtue of those still in training, and the undefiled roots of virtue of those beyond training; and the roots of virtue that ordinary beings will generate in regard to that Dharma; and all those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans who will hear that Dharma, and the roots of virtue they will generate having heard it; and the sentient beings born in animal realms who will also hear that Dharma, and the roots of virtue they will generate having heard it; and the roots of virtue that beings will generate in regard to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who pass completely beyond sorrow, and in regard to those who have passed completely beyond sorrow.

Having gathered all of these roots of virtue into one, having totaled and measured them so that nothing is left over, and having rejoiced in what is to be rejoiced in without exception, the bodhisattva, the great being, dedicates that basis of merit, which is endowed with rejoicing, to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. How, then, does such a bodhisattva avoid perverted perception, perverted thought, and perverted view?

If that bodhisattva, the great being, does not perceive as a mind the very mind by which, and toward which, he dedicates, then in this way the bodhisattva, the great being, has dedicated the basis of merit endowed with rejoicing to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. In that the bodhisattva does not apprehend that mind, saying "this is that mind," in just this way he does not fall into perverted perception, perverted thought, or perverted view.

But if he truly knows, "this is that mind, the mind by which and toward which I dedicate," and comes to perceive it as a mind, then the bodhisattva, the great being, falls into perverted perception, perverted thought, and perverted view.

If the bodhisattva, the great being, knows and reflects in this way regarding the mind that dedicates: when I reflect on that mind, it is exhausted; he truly knows that what is exhausted is exhausted, that it has ceased, is separated, and has changed. And so he knows that what is exhausted cannot itself be dedicated. The nature of the mind by which one dedicates is just this; the nature of those phenomena with which one dedicates is just this; and the nature of those phenomena toward which one dedicates is just this. If one dedicates in this way, one dedicates correctly and not incorrectly. In this way the bodhisattva, the great being, should dedicate.

Noble Subhūti, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, considers the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are present now in the immeasurable and innumerable world systems of the great trichiliocosm, who have cut off the path, cut off entry, cut off conceptual elaboration, and cut off the leading into existence, who dwell, live, and sustain themselves, from the moment they first generated the mind of awakening, up until they became fully and perfectly awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and so on.

From then until they pass into nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates, and until the sacred Dharma disappears, throughout that whole span, the bodhisattva takes into account the roots of virtue of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that are endowed with the perfections; the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; their wish to benefit others, their great loving-kindness, their great compassion, and the immeasurable and innumerable qualities of a buddha.

He takes into account whatever Dharma those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have taught, and the roots of virtue of those who train in that Dharma, who have devoted themselves to it, and who abide in it; the roots of virtue endowed with the six perfections of those bodhisattvas, great beings, whom those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening; the roots of virtue of those individuals of the vehicle of the solitary buddhas whom those Buddhas have prophesied to the awakening of a solitary buddha; and the bases of meritorious action arising from generosity, the bases of meritorious action arising from moral discipline, and the bases of meritorious action arising from meditation, of individuals of the vehicle of the hearers.

He takes into account the undefiled roots of virtue of those still in training, and the undefiled roots of virtue of those beyond training; the roots of virtue that ordinary beings have produced with regard to that Dharma; and the roots of virtue produced by those who have heard that Dharma, whether gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans, who heard that Dharma and, having heard it, produced roots of virtue; and the roots of virtue produced by those sentient beings who have been born in animal births, who heard that Dharma and, having heard it, produced roots of virtue.

Further, whatever roots of virtue have been produced in relation to the passing into nirvāṇa and the having passed into nirvāṇa of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, he gathers all of these roots of virtue into one, sums them up, measures them, and leaves nothing out. Having rejoiced in all that is to be rejoiced in, without exception, the bodhisattva, the great being, dedicates that basis of meritorious action, endowed with rejoicing, to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Venerable Subhūti may ask: how does the bodhisattva, the great being, come to have no distorted perception, no distorted thought, and no distorted view?

If that bodhisattva, the great being, does not perceive as a mind that very mind with which he dedicates, then the bodhisattva, the great being, has dedicated the basis of meritorious action endowed with rejoicing to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Because he does not truly know that mind, saying "that mind is this," in just this way the bodhisattva, the great being, has no distorted perception, no distorted thought, and no distorted view.

But suppose that, with regard to the very mind by which he dedicates, he truly knows "that mind is this," and comes to hold it as a mind in his perception. In that case, the bodhisattva, the great being, would have a distorted perception, a distorted thought, and a distorted view.

On the other hand, if the bodhisattva, the great being, regarding the mind by which he dedicates, knows and reflects in this way: "When one examines that mind, it is exhausted, and one truly knows it as exhausted; it is free from cessation, separated from it, and transformed." Knowing it thus, he understands that whatever is exhausted cannot be dedicated. "The nature of reality of the mind by which one dedicates is just this. The nature of reality of those phenomena with which one dedicates is just this. The nature of reality of those phenomena to which one dedicates is also just this." If he dedicates in this way, it is correct dedication, not incorrect dedication. In this way the bodhisattva, the great being, should dedicate.

Noble Subhūti, furthermore, the bodhisattva, the great being, should consider the following. Take the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, of the future, and of the present, immeasurable and innumerable, who have cut off the path, cut off entry, cut off conceptual elaboration, and cut off the leading on to existence. Consider them from the time they first generated the awakening mind, through the time they become, and will become, fully and completely awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, up to their full awakening; then their passing fully beyond sorrow into the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates, and their going to, and being about to go to, final nirvāṇa; and then up to the time when the sacred Dharma has not disappeared, will not disappear, and has not come to disappear.

Of all those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, throughout that span, he should dedicate the roots of virtue of their perfections. He should dedicate the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation of those buddhas, the Blessed Ones. He should dedicate their wish to benefit others, their great loving-kindness, their great compassion, and their immeasurable and innumerable buddha qualities.

He should also dedicate the roots of virtue of those who, through whatever Dharma those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have taught, are teaching, and will teach, have trained, are training, and will train in those teachings; who have faith, are coming to have faith, and are having faith; and who have dwelt, are dwelling, and will dwell in them. He should dedicate all the roots of virtue of those bodhisattvas, great beings, whom those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have prophesied, will prophesy, and are prophesying to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. He should dedicate all the roots of virtue of those persons of the solitary buddha vehicle whom those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have prophesied, will prophesy, and are prophesying to their own awakening.

He should dedicate the roots of virtue of persons of the hearer vehicle: the roots of virtue arising from generosity, those arising from moral discipline, and those arising from meditation. He should dedicate the undefiled roots of virtue of those still in training, and the undefiled roots of virtue of those beyond training.

As for that Dharma, there are ordinary persons who have created, will create, and are creating roots of virtue through it. There are also gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and nonhuman beings who have heard that Dharma, will hear it, and are hearing it, and who, having heard it, have generated, will generate, and are generating roots of virtue. There are, moreover, sentient beings born in animal births who have heard, will hear, and are hearing that sacred Dharma, and who, having heard it, have created, will create, and are creating roots of virtue. And there are beings who have created, will create, and are creating roots of virtue with regard to those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have passed, will pass, and are passing into complete nirvāṇa.

All the roots of virtue of all of these he should gather together into one, sum up, measure, and leave nothing out. Then, with the supreme rejoicing that rejoices in all that is to be rejoiced in, with rejoicing that is sacred, foremost, excellent, supreme, most excellent, lofty, highest, unsurpassed, unequaled, without peer, and equal to the unequaled, having rejoiced in this way, he should dedicate the merit that accompanies such rejoicing, this unsurpassed basis of meritorious action, to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. He should express in words the wish: May this bring about unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Venerable Subhūti asks: How does a bodhisattva, a great being, who does this avoid distorted perception, distorted mind, and distorted view?

The Blessed One answers: Suppose the one who dedicates thinks, "Those phenomena are exhausted, ceased, departed, and changed, so I shall dedicate them in such a way that they will never be exhausted." If he reflects in this way, then the dedication to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening has been made. And suppose he reflects, "By means of a phenomenon one does not dedicate a phenomenon." Then too the dedication to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening has been made. Venerable Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who dedicates in this way does not fall into distorted perception, distorted mind, or distorted view.

Why is this so? Because he has no fixation on that dedication. And suppose he rightly understands, "Mind does not know mind, and a phenomenon does not know a phenomenon." Then too the dedication to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening has been made. This is the unsurpassed dedication of a bodhisattva, a great being.

But if that bodhisattva, that great being, takes the volitional formation of merit to be something he knows, then the dedication to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening has not been made. Why is this so? Because he is fixated on that dedication.

And suppose he thinks, "That volitional formation of merit is itself secluded and peaceful, and that basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing is also secluded and peaceful." If he thinks in this way, then the dedication to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening has been made.

But if he does not know even this, that all conditioning factors are secluded and peaceful, then, in that case, this is the Perfection of Wisdom of that bodhisattva, that great being.

Now consider the roots of virtue of those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have passed into complete nirvāṇa, and the way in which they were dedicated. If he knows that his own root of virtue is just like that, and that what is dedicated is of that same kind, has that same defining mark, belongs to that same category, and has that same intrinsic nature, then the dedication to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening has not been made. Why is this so? Because the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not sanction a dedication made through the mode of signs. What is past is exhausted, ceased, departed, transformed. What is future has not been attained. And in what is present, no abiding is found. What is not found is neither a sign nor an object. If he dwells on it in that way, making it a sign and thinking about it, then the dedication to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening has not been made.

Suppose instead that, being without recollection, he neither makes a sign nor thinks; or that, being without recollection or failing to comprehend, he pays it no attention. Even so, the dedication to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening has not been made. But if he thinks of that sign and yet does not make it a sign, then in this way the bodhisattva, the great being, has dedicated that root of virtue to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Thus the bodhisattva, the great being, should train in this, and this is to be recognized as that bodhisattva's skillful means. This dedication of roots of virtue through skillful means brings one close to omniscience. A bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to train in this skillful means should listen to this very Perfection of Wisdom without interruption. He should take it up, retain it, recite it, thoroughly understand it, study it intensively, teach it, explain it, chant it, memorize it, and inquire into it fully.

Why is this so? Without relying on the Perfection of Wisdom, and without having heard it, one is unable to engage in this work of dedication. Now if someone says, "Even without relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, one can dedicate that basis of meritorious action to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening," he should be told, "Do not say so." Why is this so? Because those very things belonging to the self have ceased, and those conditioning factors too have ceased. They are peaceful, secluded, free from any object of focus. Yet that person makes a sign of what is real, imagines it conceptually, and perceives as real what is not as it truly is. Taking as an object what cannot be apprehended as an object, he performs the dedication. The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not sanction the dedication of his root of virtue to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening in this way. Why is this so? Because whatever signifying, conceptualizing, and objectifying one does regarding the complete nirvāṇa of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is itself that person's great fixation.

The Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly complete buddhas, do not say that a dedication made by one who holds a perception of an object accomplishes a great purpose. Why is this so? Because such a dedication is accompanied by poison and by a thorn.

Consider an example. There is a fine meal that has been poisoned. In its color, smell, taste, and texture it may seem excellent, and yet, because it is accompanied by poison, the wise reject it entirely and do not partake of it. But a childish person, whose wisdom is confused, thinks to enjoy that very meal. When he eats it, he finds pleasure in its color, smell, taste, and texture; but when it is digested, its ripening becomes suffering for him, and on that basis he dies, or suffers pain close to death.

Noble Subhūti, in the same way, there are some who have grasped this teaching wrongly, understood it wrongly, and recited it wrongly. They do not know the meaning of what was well spoken, and do not comprehend the true meaning as it really is. They say: "Child of good family, come here. Take all the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present, in the immeasurable, countless world systems of all the worlds. Begin from their first generation of the mind of awakening. Take their awakening into unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, whether they have awakened, will awaken, or are awakening. Take their complete nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder of the aggregates, whether they have passed, will pass, or are passing, and the time until the sacred Dharma has vanished, will vanish, or is vanishing. Throughout that span, gather together the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation belonging to the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, and to their hearers.

"Likewise gather the roots of virtue that have been planted, will be planted, and are being planted by those bodhisattvas, the great beings, whom those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have prophesied, will prophesy, and are prophesying to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Gather the roots of virtue planted by those persons of the vehicle of the solitary buddhas who have been prophesied, will be prophesied, and are being prophesied to their own awakening. Gather the roots of virtue planted by those persons of the vehicle of the hearers who have been prophesied, will be prophesied, and are being prophesied to the awakening of hearers. And gather the roots of virtue planted there, in the past, future, and present, by ordinary beings.

"Collect all those roots of virtue into one, bring them together, measure them, leave nothing out, and rejoice in them without exception. Then dedicate the basis of merit, which is endowed with rejoicing, to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening." This is how they instruct and advise others.

A dedication made in that way, as a dedication made through the mode of signs, becomes poison itself, just like that poisoned meal. Thus, for one who holds a perception of an object, there is no dedication. Why is this so?

For the perception of an object comes together with poison. Therefore, a person on the path of the bodhisattva vehicle should not train in that way.

Then how should one train? How should one take up the roots of virtue of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present? How, when they are taken up, are they well taken up? How should one dedicate them, and how, when they are dedicated, are they well dedicated to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?

Here, noble son or noble daughter, one who follows the bodhisattva vehicle and wishes not to slander the Tathāgata should rejoice in all those roots of virtue in this way, and dedicate them in this way. One should think: "Just as those Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, know and see that root of virtue with the wisdom of a buddha and the eye of a buddha, and just as they know its type, the class to which it belongs, what it is like, its intrinsic nature, its defining characteristic, and the nature of reality by which it exists, so I rejoice in it. And just as those Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, have approved of how that root of virtue is to be dedicated to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, so I shall rejoice and dedicate."

A bodhisattva, a great being, who rejoices in this way and dedicates in this way does not harm the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Such a one has rejoiced rightly, the root of virtue becomes well dedicated to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, are not slandered. For when one dedicates with superior intention and with deep conviction, that dedication is a dedication without poison. It is a great dedication. It is a dedication of the dharmadhātu. It is complete, and utterly complete.

Furthermore, noble son or noble daughter, one who follows the bodhisattva vehicle should dedicate in the following way. Whatever moral discipline there is, whatever meditative absorption, whatever wisdom, whatever liberation, and whatever seeing of the wisdom of liberation there is, these should be dedicated as not belonging to the desire realm, not belonging to the form realm, and not belonging to the formless realm, and as neither past, nor future, nor present.

Why is this so? Because they do not belong to the three times or the three realms, and so the dedication likewise does not belong to them. The phenomenon to which one dedicates, and the phenomenon of dedication by which one dedicates, are also not included in them. If one rests in conviction in this way and dedicates in this way, then the dedication of that bodhisattva, that great being, is not wasted. It is a dedication that is not included in them, a dedication without poison, a great dedication, a dedication of the dharmadhātu, complete and well and fully complete.

But if one becomes attached to that dedication and makes a sign of it, then it is a mistaken dedication.

Here, if a bodhisattva, a great being, thinks: "The dedication of that root of virtue is just as the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know it and just as they have approved it. By this dedication of the dharmadhātu, it is dedicated to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and so it is well dedicated. In this way I dedicate it" — then this is a right dedication. A dedication made in this way is well dedicated to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Then the Blessed One said "Excellent!" to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, you are doing the work of a teacher, and in teaching the Dharma to bodhisattvas, great beings, you have spoken well. Excellent, Subhūti, excellent! Why is that? Subhūti, this dedication is the dedication of the dharmadhātu of a bodhisattva, a great being.

"In this very nature of reality, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know and see that root of virtue in every respect: what its type is, what category it belongs to, what it is like, what its intrinsic nature is, what its defining characteristic is, and by what nature of reality it exists. Rejoicing in it in just that way, and thinking, 'Just as they have approved, so do I dedicate it,' one gathers a mass of merit. Now suppose that in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the River Ganges, each a great thousand of the third thousand, whatever sentient beings there are, all of them were established and set firmly on the path of the ten virtuous actions by some son or daughter of good family, and that this person produced the merit of that. Compared with that merit, this mass of merit born from the dharmadhātu dedication of a bodhisattva, a great being, is called supreme. It is called excellent, chief, foremost, the best of the best, lofty, the highest, unsurpassed, without anything above it, without equal, and equal to the unequaled.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit produced by all the sentient beings in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges being established in the ten virtuous paths of action. Subhūti, suppose all the sentient beings in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges had attained the four meditative concentrations. Even greater than the merit those beings produce is this mass of merit possessed of the dedication of a bodhisattva, a great being. It is called supreme. It is called excellent, chief, foremost, the best of the best, lofty, the highest, unsurpassed, without anything above it, without equal, and equal to the unequaled.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit of all those sentient beings in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges having perfected the four meditative concentrations. Subhūti, suppose all the sentient beings in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges had attained the four immeasurables, and"

Furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit of all the sentient beings in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, having attained the four immeasurables. Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings, however many there are, in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, had attained the four formless absorptions. And furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit of all the sentient beings in such world systems having attained the four formless absorptions.

Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings, however many there are, in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, had attained the five higher knowledges. And furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit of all those sentient beings having attained the five higher knowledges.

Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings, however many there are, in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, had become stream-enterers. And furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit of all those sentient beings having become stream-enterers.

Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings, however many there are, in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, had become once-returners. And furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit of all those sentient beings having become once-returners.

Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings, however many there are, in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, had become non-returners. And furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit of all those sentient beings having become non-returners.

Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings, however many there are, in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, had become arhats. And furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit of all those sentient beings having become arhats.

Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings, however many there are, in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, had become pratyekabuddhas. And furthermore, Subhūti, set aside the merit of all those sentient beings having become pratyekabuddhas.

Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings, whoever they are, in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, had set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And suppose that each of those bodhisattvas, for all the sentient beings, whoever they are, in yet other world systems, as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm, were to provide robes and alms food,

...with bedding, medicines for the sick, requisites, and every kind of comfort and every means of dwelling in ease, serving them in this way for eons as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, and suppose they gave this gift with a perception that apprehends an object. Taking this as the measure, suppose that each of those bodhisattvas, for each and every one of those sentient beings, were to attend them for eons as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, with Dharma robes, alms food, bedding, medicines for the sick, requisites, and every kind of comfort and every means of dwelling in ease, honoring them, revering them, regarding them as their teachers, esteeming them, making offerings to them, venerating them, and serving them. And suppose that all those bodhisattvas, each in just this way, gave gifts, and in just this way gave to all beings. Subhūti, what do you think? Would those bodhisattvas, on that basis, generate a great deal of merit?

Subhūti replied: Blessed One, a great deal. Sugata, a great deal. Blessed One, it is immeasurable. Sugata, it is immeasurable. Blessed One, the mass of that merit is not even easy to count. Blessed One, that mass of merit is not easy to count, nor to illustrate by example, nor to teach through analogy, nor to treat as a basis or as a cause. Blessed One, if that mass of merit had a form, it would not fit even in world systems as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each a great trichiliocosm.

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to the venerable elder Subhūti: Subhūti, so it is, so it is. Furthermore, Subhūti, a person who is of the Bodhisattva Vehicle, who is embraced by the perfection of wisdom and by skillful means, and who dedicates the roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening through this dedication, which is the dedication of the dharmadhātu, generates a great deal of merit on that account.

Subhūti, compared to this mass of merit born from the dedication of the dharmadhātu, that earlier accumulation of merit arising from the generosity of bodhisattva great beings who hold a perception that apprehends an object does not come to a hundredth part of it. It does not come to a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even the most minute fraction of such an immense number. It cannot be reckoned in number, nor counted, nor illustrated by example, nor treated as a basis, as a cause, or even as a proximate cause. Why is that? Because the generosity of those earlier bodhisattvas, who hold a perception that apprehends an object, though it may be given in great abundance, comes to be counted as great only in the sense of a reckonable number.

Then twenty thousand gods of the class of the Four Great Kings joined their palms, bowed down, and said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, this dedication of all roots of virtue toward omniscience, embraced by the perfection of wisdom and skillful means of the bodhisattva great being, is indeed a great dedication.

Even so much merit arising from the generosity of those bodhisattvas who hold a perception that apprehends an object, even that much is overwhelmed and surpassed.

Then a hundred thousand sons of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three scattered and strewed all over the Blessed One a rain of divine flowers, divine incense, divine fragrances, divine garlands, divine unguents, and divine powders, a rain of divine jewels and a rain of divine garments. With divine parasols, divine banners, divine bells, divine pennants, and many kinds of divine offerings, they honored the Blessed One, revered him, held him supreme, made offerings to him, adorned him, and attended him. Sounding their divine cymbals, they spoke these words: Blessed One, this dedication of the dharmadhātu by the bodhisattva great being is indeed a great dedication. Even that great mass of merit arising from the generosity of those bodhisattvas who hold a perception that apprehends an object is overwhelmed and surpassed. Because it is embraced by the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, this is a great dedication.

In the same way, gods of the other classes also came to the Blessed One. With the finest honoring, the finest veneration, the finest gain, the finest offering, the finest adornment, and the finest attendance, they honored, revered, held supreme, made offerings to, adorned, and attended him, and then they cried out in the same words and echoed them in song. In the same manner, the gods of the Heaven Without Combat, the Joyful Heaven, the Heaven of Delighting in Creation, and the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Creations, the gods of the Brahmā class, the Priests of Brahmā, the Retinue of Brahmā, and the Great Brahmā, the gods of Lesser Light, Immeasurable Light, and Radiant Light, the gods of Lesser Virtue, Immeasurable Virtue, and Increasing Virtue, the gods of Cloudless, Merit-Born, and Great Fruit, the beings without perception, and the gods of Not Great, Not Burning, Fair-Seeming, Well-Seeing, and Akaniṣṭha, all likewise joined their palms and bowed down to the Blessed One, and said this: Blessed One, the dedication of roots of virtue embraced by the perfection of wisdom and skillful means of the bodhisattva great being is wonderful. Even that mass of merit, so vast and so perfectly accomplished, is overwhelmed and surpassed, though those bodhisattvas who hold a perception that apprehends an object have gathered theirs over so long a time.

Then the Blessed One addressed all those sons of the gods, beginning with the sons of the gods of the Pure Abodes: Sons of the gods, leave aside the merit of giving generosity for the sake of all the beings, as many as the sands of the Ganges, in a world system of a trichiliocosm, who have entered perfectly toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening, so that they might attain unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Sons of the gods, by this way of reckoning, suppose that all the beings who dwell in other world systems, as many as the sands of the Ganges, again and again, of a trichiliocosm, were each to make an aspiration for unsurpassed, perfect awakening and to arouse the awakening mind.

Suppose that, in other world systems of a trichiliocosm, as many as the sands of the Ganges, there were beings, and that to all of them one gave robes, alms food, bedding, medicines for the sick, requisites, everything that brings comfort and everything that allows one to dwell in ease. Suppose that each bodhisattva, for as many eons as the sands of the Ganges, remained there giving such gifts. And suppose that all of those who give with a notion of an object were to give in this same way, down to the very last of them. By this way of reckoning, consider all those beings and all those bodhisattvas one by one. Suppose that each bodhisattva, in turn, through the whole sequence of those bodhisattvas, remained for eons as many as the sands of the Ganges, serving all those beings in order with robes, alms food, bedding, medicines for the sick, requisites, everything that brings comfort and everything that allows one to dwell in ease; and suppose that this giving were also done with a notion of an object.

Now suppose that a great bodhisattva, a great being, who is fully held by the Perfection of Wisdom and by skillful means, gathers into one, sums up, and measures completely, without exception, the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the seeing of the wisdom of liberation of all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present, and of those bodhisattvas, solitary buddhas, and persons of the Hearers' Vehicle; and also all the roots of virtue that other beings have planted, are planting, and will plant in them. And suppose that this bodhisattva rejoices in that entire totality with the supreme rejoicing: a rejoicing that is sublime, chief, excellent, most excellent, exalted, supreme, unsurpassed, without anything higher, higher even than the highest, without equal, without peer, matchless, and inconceivable. And suppose that from that rejoicing he fully dedicates the unsurpassed basis of meritorious action, endowed with rejoicing, saying, "May this accomplish unsurpassed, perfect awakening," dedicating it to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Compared with this basis of meritorious action, endowed with rejoicing and dedication, the earlier accumulation of merit of those bodhisattvas who have a notion of an object does not come to a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred ten-millionth part, nor a thousand ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand billionth part.
