It cannot be counted, reckoned, illustrated by an example, shown by analogy, or supported by any basis or cause. Why is that? Because all those bodhisattvas give their gifts with a notion of an object.

This is the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, the eighth volume.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "The Blessed One has said this: all the roots of virtue of all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present, of the bodhisattvas, solitary buddhas, and the whole Saṅgha of Hearers, and of all beings, whether past, future, or present, are to be gathered into one, summed up, and measured completely, without exception."

"You have spoken of rejoicing with a supreme rejoicing that is without remainder, a rejoicing that is holy, chief, excellent, best, most exalted, sublime, unsurpassed, without superior, higher than the highest, without equal, equal to the unequalled, and utterly without peer, a rejoicing that surpasses rejoicing and is beyond thought. Blessed One, to what extent does one become supreme among those who rejoice?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows.

"Subhūti, suppose persons who follow the bodhisattva vehicle do not grasp at phenomena of the past, future, and present. They do not take them as objects of pride, do not form a notion of them, do not apprehend them, do not conceptualize them or imagine them, and do not perceive them as truly existent. Suppose they further consider those phenomena in this way: all phenomena are established through conceptual thought; they are unborn, definitely unborn, without coming and without going. In this, no phenomenon has been born, no phenomenon will come to be born, no phenomenon is born. In this, no phenomenon has ceased, no phenomenon will come to cease, no phenomenon ceases. Having examined those phenomena in this way, they rejoice in accordance with the nature of those phenomena just as it is. Having rejoiced in this way, they dedicate it, in that very same manner, to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. Subhūti, to this extent a bodhisattva, a great being, becomes supreme among those who rejoice.

"Subhūti, compared with this dedication of roots of virtue, the merit arising from the giving of those earlier bodhisattvas, who hold a notion of an object and a view that apprehends an object, does not come to a hundredth part of it. It does not come to a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a part measured by a hundred thousand of the greatest numbers. It cannot be counted, cannot be tallied, cannot be conveyed by any comparison or illustration, and cannot be admitted as a basis or a cause.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a person who follows the bodhisattva vehicle and wishes to rejoice in the generosity of all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present, and wishes to rejoice in their moral discipline, their patience, their diligence, their meditative concentration, and their wisdom, should rejoice in this way. As liberation is, so is generosity. As liberation is, so is moral discipline. As liberation is, so is patience. As liberation is, so is diligence. As liberation is, so is meditative concentration. As liberation is, so is wisdom. As liberation is, so is liberation itself. As liberation is, so is the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation. As liberation is, so is rejoicing. As liberation is, so is the basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing. As liberation is, so is dedication. As liberation is, so are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the solitary buddhas. As liberation is, so are those Hearers of theirs who have passed completely beyond sorrow. As liberation is, so are those phenomena that are past and have ceased. As liberation is, so are those phenomena that are future and have not yet arisen."

As liberation is, so are those phenomena that are present, that have arisen and are abiding. As liberation is, so are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, and their Hearers. As liberation is, so are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the future, and their Hearers. As liberation is, so are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the present, who dwell, live, and sustain themselves in world-systems immeasurable and innumerable, and their Hearers. As liberation is, so are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present. Whatever the nature of reality of these phenomena is, which are thus unbound, unliberated, and unattached, in that I rejoice with unsurpassed rejoicing. Having rejoiced, I dedicate the unsurpassed basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing, by way of not dedicating it to perfect and complete awakening as a thing, but rather as the nature of reality of those phenomena is, in just that way, without shifting and without perishing. This is what is meant by dedication.

Subhūti, this much is the supreme rejoicing of a bodhisattva, a great being.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose that all those sentient beings who exist in other and still other world-systems, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, in a great trichiliocosm, had properly entered upon unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. Having entered upon it, suppose they roused the awakening mind in all the sentient beings of other and still other world-systems, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in a great trichiliocosm. And suppose that each one of all those bodhisattvas, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, should offer gifts to each of those bodhisattvas, serving them with robes, alms food, bedding, medicine for the sick, provisions, and everything that gives comfort and ease, doing so with a perception of objective support (a notion of someone giving, receiving, and something given). And suppose that in this same manner each of them served every one of the others. Set aside that giving, Subhūti, offered with a perception of objective support.

Suppose that all the sentient beings, however many there are in world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in a great trichiliocosm, had properly entered upon unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. Having entered upon it, suppose that for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges they had undertaken and maintained the moral discipline of good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind, with a perception of objective support. And suppose that in this same manner each of those bodhisattvas, for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, undertook and maintained that moral discipline of good conduct of body, speech, and mind, with a perception of objective support. And suppose that all those bodhisattvas maintained their moral discipline in this manner, with a perception of objective support.

Now let there be a bodhisattva, a great being, who is fully embraced by the perfection of wisdom and by skillful means. For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present, that bodhisattva rejoices in their moral discipline, their meditative absorption, their wisdom, their liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation, and in...

the moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation of those solitary buddhas (pratyekabuddhas), and of those hearers (śrāvakas), the moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation. Having gathered together into one, summed up, and measured all those roots of virtue of all beings of the past, future, and present, leaving nothing out, that bodhisattva rejoices in all of it with the supreme rejoicing. With a rejoicing that is excellent, foremost, choice, supreme, exalted, unsurpassed, without any higher, higher than the highest, without equal, unequaled, equal to the unequaled, and inconceivable, the bodhisattva rejoices. And having rejoiced, that bodhisattva dedicates the meritorious basis of action, endowed with rejoicing, to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Subhūti, compared with this meritorious basis of action endowed with rejoicing, the former merit that those bodhisattvas with objective support produced from their moral discipline does not approach even a hundredth part of it. It does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousandth part of a trillion. It does not approach it in number. It cannot be counted, nor illustrated by any example, nor shown by comparison, nor can it bear comparison as a basis or as a cause. Why is that? Because all those bodhisattvas maintain their moral discipline with a perception of objective support.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose that all the beings in as many billion-fold world systems as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were fully set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And having set out, suppose that for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they maintained, with a perception of objective support, the moral discipline of good conduct of body, speech, and mind. Leave that aside. Suppose that all the beings who exist in as many billion-fold world systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were fully set out toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and having set out, remained so for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. And suppose that all the beings in other such world systems, as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, one after another, were to strike and beat each of those bodhisattvas, and shower them with abuse, yet with pride and with a perception of objective support, those bodhisattvas took up and maintained patience. In that same way, suppose that all those bodhisattvas with a perception of objective support took up and maintained patience. By this way of reckoning, suppose that each one of those bodhisattvas, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, were struck, beaten, and abused by all the beings who live in still other world systems, as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, and yet with pride and with a perception of objective support took up and maintained patience. And suppose that all of them, though all were struck, beaten, and abused, likewise took up and maintained patience with pride and with a perception of objective support.

Subhūti, now consider a bodhisattva, a great being, who is embraced by the perfection of wisdom and by skillful means. Such a bodhisattva gathers into one, brings together, and measures, leaving nothing out, all the following: the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation belonging to the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present; the moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation belonging to those solitary buddhas; the same belonging to those hearers; and all the roots of virtue of all sentient beings, past, future, and present. Having left nothing out, the bodhisattva rejoices in all of it with the supreme rejoicing. With a rejoicing that is holy, chief, excellent, supreme, most excellent, unsurpassed, without superior, higher than the highest, unequalled, matching the unmatched, utterly without equal, and inconceivable, the bodhisattva rejoices. And having rejoiced, the bodhisattva fully dedicates to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening the basis of meritorious action that accompanies that rejoicing.

Subhūti, compared with this basis of meritorious action accompanied by rejoicing, the merit produced by those earlier bodhisattvas who held to objective support, merit that comes with patience, does not approach even a hundredth part. It does not approach a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth, nor a ten-millionth, nor a hundred-ten-millionth, nor a thousand-ten-millionth, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth, nor even a hundred-thousandth part of a billion-fold ten-millionth. It cannot be reckoned by number, by count, by simile, by illustration, by comparison, by cause, or by any ground of comparison. Why is that? Because all those bodhisattvas take up and maintain patience with a perception of objective support.

Furthermore, Subhūti, leave aside the case of those bodhisattvas who, struck, beaten, and abused by all the beings of other world systems, as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, each system a great trichiliocosm, took up and maintained patience for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, with pride and with a perception of objective support.

Subhūti, suppose that in a great trichiliocosm world system, as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges, there are beings, however many there may be, and that all of them have entered rightly upon unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Having so entered, suppose that for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges they remain walking and sitting, standing vigilantly, and that for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges they do not grow weary or dull, and are not overcome by torpor or sleep, but take up and maintain diligence with a perception of objective support.

And suppose there is a bodhisattva, a great being, embraced by the perfection of wisdom and skillful means, who gathers together the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation belonging to the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present.

And also the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation belonging to those solitary buddhas; and likewise the aggregate of moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the vision of the wisdom of liberation belonging to those hearers. And all the roots of virtue that sentient beings have produced in the past, the future, and the present, all of these he gathers into one, brings together, and measures, so that nothing is left out. Then, for all that is without remainder, he rejoices with the supreme rejoicing. He rejoices with a rejoicing that is holy, chief, excellent, most excellent, sublime, supreme, unsurpassed, without anything higher, higher than the highest, without equal, matchless, comparable only to the incomparable, utterly without peer, and inconceivable. And having so rejoiced, he fully dedicates the meritorious basis of action that is endowed with that rejoicing to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Subhūti, compared with this meritorious basis of action endowed with rejoicing, the merit produced by the diligence of those earlier bodhisattvas who hold to an objective support does not come to a hundredth part of it. It does not come to a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a part of a hundred thousand times ten billion. It cannot be reckoned by number, nor counted, nor compared by any example, nor shown by simile, nor accepted as a basis or a cause of comparison. Why is that? Because all those bodhisattvas abide having taken up diligence with a perception of objective support.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings, as many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, in a great trichiliocosm world-system were to set out completely toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Having so set out, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they remain standing, walking, and sitting. For as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges they do not grow weary, and are not overcome by torpor or sleep, but abide having taken up diligence with a perception of objective support. Let that be as it may.

Subhūti, suppose all those sentient beings, as many as there are grains of sand in the Ganges in a great trichiliocosm world-system, were to set out completely toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and having so set out, were for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges to rest in the four meditative concentrations with a perception of objective support.

And suppose, further, there is a bodhisattva, a great being, embraced by this perfection of wisdom and by skillful means, who gathers together the aggregate of moral discipline, the aggregate of meditative absorption, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision of the wisdom of liberation belonging to all the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present; and likewise the aggregate of moral discipline, meditative absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the vision of the wisdom of liberation belonging to those solitary buddhas; and the same for those hearers. And all the roots of virtue that sentient beings have produced in the past, the future, and the present, all of these he gathers into one, brings together, and measures, so that nothing is left out; and for all that is without remainder, he rejoices with the supreme rejoicing.

He rejoices with a rejoicing that is holy, chief, excellent, supreme, most exalted, unsurpassed, without superior, higher even than the highest, without equal, equal to the unequalled, matched by none, and inconceivable. Having rejoiced in this way, he fully dedicates the merit that accompanies that rejoicing, the basis of meritorious action, to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Subhūti, compared with this basis of meritorious action that accompanies rejoicing, the earlier merit that a bodhisattva generates from the four meditative concentrations, which still involve an object of focus, does not come near to a hundredth part of it. It does not come near to a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth, nor a ten-millionth, nor a hundred-ten-millionth, nor a thousand-ten-millionth, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth, nor even a hundred-thousand-times-a-billionth part. It cannot be reckoned by number, nor counted, nor conveyed by any simile or demonstrated by any example, nor made the basis or cause of any comparison. Why is this so? Because all those bodhisattvas, holding perceptions that fix upon an object, rest in the meditative concentrations.

This is the sixth chapter, called "Rejoicing and Dedication," from the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom brings to full accomplishment the wisdom of omniscience. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is omniscience itself.

The Blessed One declared: So it is, Śāriputra, so it is, just as you say.

Śāriputra said: Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom makes things clear. Blessed One, I pay homage to the Perfection of Wisdom. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is worthy of homage. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is utterly unstained. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is not stained by any world. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom brings light. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom frees all who dwell in the three realms from the blurring of sight. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom dispels all the darkness of affliction and wrong view. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is what one relies upon. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom makes beings supreme. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom brings the factors that accord with awakening to a good and happy state. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom brings light to sentient beings who wander blind. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom wholly removes all fear and harm and brings light. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom, by holding the five eyes, shows the path to all sentient beings. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is the eye. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom frees beings from delusion, darkness, and the blurring of sight. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom frees beings from the blurring of sight.

Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom does not make any phenomena. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom leads onto the path those sentient beings who have strayed from the path. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is itself omniscience. Blessed One, in order to abandon the afflictions, the habitual tendencies of the cognitive obscurations, and all the links that bind, the Perfection of Wisdom does not cause any phenomena to arise. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom does not bring any phenomena to cessation. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is unborn and unceasing. Blessed One, because of the emptiness of own-characteristic, the Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the great beings. Blessed One, in order to bestow all the precious qualities of the buddhas, the Perfection of Wisdom brings about the ten powers. Blessed One, because it brings about the four fearlessnesses, the Perfection of Wisdom cannot be subdued. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is the protector of sentient beings who have no protector. Blessed One, because nothing abides permanently, the Perfection of Wisdom is the antidote to saṃsāra. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom reveals the essential nature of all phenomena. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is the complete fulfillment of the turning of the wheel of Dharma by the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, which is turned three times in twelve aspects. Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva, a great being, abide in the Perfection of Wisdom? Blessed One, how should one attend to the Perfection of Wisdom in the mind? Blessed One, how should one pay homage to the Perfection of Wisdom?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Śāriputra as follows. Śāriputra, just as the Teacher has taught, so one should abide in the Perfection of Wisdom. Śāriputra, just as the Teacher has taught, so one should attend to the Perfection of Wisdom in the mind. Śāriputra, just as the Teacher has taught, so one should pay homage to the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), thought: Alas, why has the noble Śāriputra asked this? On what ground has the noble Śāriputra asked this? Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the venerable Śāriputra: Noble Śāriputra, why do you ask this? On what ground, noble Śāriputra, do you ask this?

When he had said this, the venerable Śāriputra said to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, consider a bodhisattva, a great being, who is held by the skillful means of the Perfection of Wisdom, and who dedicates to omniscience every meritorious act, every basis of meritorious action, that accompanies rejoicing. Whatever merit is generated from the generosity of all those earlier bodhisattvas who are still caught up in objectifying, whatever arises from their moral discipline, whatever arises from their patience, and whatever arises from their diligence,

It overpowers and surpasses all of that merit, whatever it may be, which arises from meditative concentration and is brought about through deliberate construction. That is why I put this question on this basis.

Kauśika, moreover, it is the Perfection of Wisdom itself that goes before the other five perfections, so that they may enter the path of omniscience. Kauśika, it is like this. Suppose there were a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand blind people, and no one to lead them. They would have no chance of entering the road, and no chance of reaching a village, a town, or a city. In just the same way, Kauśika, generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, when separated from the Perfection of Wisdom, do not earn the name of perfections. They are like the blind, for they have no guide. Since they have no chance even of entering the path of omniscience, how could they ever enter the great city of omniscience, or even see it, let alone attain it?

But, Kauśika, when generosity, moral discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration are embraced by the Perfection of Wisdom, then they gain the name and designation of perfections. Then these five perfections come to possess eyes, so that they may enter the path of omniscience and attain omniscience.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva, a great being, accomplish the Perfection of Wisdom?

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Śāriputra: Śāriputra, one should view form as not being accomplished. In the same way, Śāriputra, one should view feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as not being accomplished. Śāriputra, that which does not construct the five aggregates is called, Śāriputra, accomplishing in the Perfection of Wisdom. Accomplishing in the five aggregates by not constructing in this way is accomplishing in the Perfection of Wisdom; this is what is called accomplishing.

When he had said this, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, when the Perfection of Wisdom is accomplished in this way, what phenomenon does it destroy?

The Blessed One said: Śāriputra, when the Perfection of Wisdom is accomplished in this way, it does not destroy any phenomenon whatsoever. Śāriputra, when no phenomenon is destroyed, then it is counted as what is called the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, does this Perfection of Wisdom not destroy even omniscience?

The Blessed One said: Kauśika, when you ask, "Does this Perfection of Wisdom not destroy even omniscience?", know that it does not destroy it in the way that it is objectified. It does not destroy it in the way that it is named. It does not destroy it in the way that it is constructed.

Śakra said: Blessed One, then in what way does it destroy?

The Blessed One said: Kauśika, it destroys in the way that it does not destroy.

Śakra said:

Śakra said: Blessed One, since by this Perfection of Wisdom no phenomenon is produced and none is stopped, and since all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, this Perfection of Wisdom neither abides nor is it something that abides. It is wonderful!

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, if a bodhisattva, a great being, conceives of things in this way, would he not be making this Perfection of Wisdom distant, accumulating it, and amassing it? Would he not, then, be failing to practice this Perfection of Wisdom?

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, there is a way in which one makes this Perfection of Wisdom distant, accumulates it, and amasses it, and a way in which one fails to practice it. Why is that? Subhūti, when this Perfection of Wisdom is fully illumined, it is not form that is fully illumined. It is not feeling, not perception, not the formations, and it is not consciousness that is fully illumined. The fruit of stream-entry is not fully illumined, the fruit of once-returning is not fully illumined, the fruit of non-returning is not fully illumined. Arhatship is not fully illumined. Pratyekabuddhahood is not fully illumined. Buddhahood is not fully illumined.

The elder Subhūti said: Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is, in this sense, a great perfection.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you have in mind? In what way is this Perfection of Wisdom a great perfection?

The elder Subhūti said: Blessed One, one does not make form great, nor make it small; one does not gather form together, nor scatter it. In the same way with feeling, with perception, with the formations; Blessed One, one does not make consciousness great, nor small; one does not gather consciousness together, nor scatter it. Whatever the powers of the Tathāgatas are, those too one does not make endowed with power, nor make empty, nor gather together, nor scatter. Whatever omniscience is, that too one does not make great, nor small, nor gather together, nor scatter. Why is that? Blessed One, because omniscience itself is neither gathered nor scattered.

Blessed One, if a bodhisattva, a great being, were to think in this way, he would not be practicing the Perfection of Wisdom. How much less, then, would he be practicing it if he thought: "I possess the wisdom of omniscience; thus I shall teach the Dharma to beings; thus I shall bring these beings completely beyond sorrow." Why is that? The thought "I shall bring these beings completely beyond sorrow" is not in accord with the cause of the Perfection of Wisdom, for this very focusing upon beings becomes for him a great object of fixation. Why is that? Because the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as having the nature of beings being without essential nature and without arising.

Because beings are without essential nature, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as without essential nature. Because beings are secluded, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as secluded. Because beings are inconceivable, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as inconceivable. Because beings have the nature of being indestructible, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as having the nature of being indestructible. Because beings cannot be fully awakened to, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as not being fully awakened to. Because beings cannot be fully awakened to as the true meaning, just as it is, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as not being fully awakened to as the true meaning, just as it is. Because beings accomplish the powers perfectly, it should be understood that the powers of the Tathāgata are accomplished perfectly. Blessed One, by this way of explanation, the Perfection of Wisdom is the great perfection.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva, a great being, has faith in this profound Perfection of Wisdom and feels no hesitation, no doubt, and does not fall into bewilderment, then, Blessed One, from where should it be understood that he passed away and was reborn here? Blessed One, how long should it be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, who will follow, realize, and gain insight into the meaning, the nature, the way of the meaning, and the way of the nature of this Perfection of Wisdom, has practiced and kept to discipline in a single-minded way?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Śāriputra as follows: "Śāriputra, it should be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, has served and honored the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and questioned them, and then passed away from other world systems and was reborn here. Why is that? Śāriputra, any bodhisattva, any great being, who has served and honored the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and questioned them, and who passed away from other world systems and was reborn here, listens to the explaining, teaching, demonstrating, and prophesying of this profound Perfection of Wisdom. Having heard this Perfection of Wisdom, he develops the perception of the Teacher with regard to this Perfection of Wisdom. He gives rise to the thought: 'My Teacher has appeared before me; I have seen my Teacher.' He lends his ear and listens respectfully to the explaining, teaching, demonstrating, and prophesying of this Perfection of Wisdom, and he does not interrupt the discourse. Śāriputra, it should be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, is of such a nature that he has practiced and kept to discipline for a long time. Śāriputra, it should be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, is of such a kind that he has served and honored many buddhas."

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, is it also possible to listen to this Perfection of Wisdom, to realize it, to reflect upon it, to give rise to it, or to take hold of it?"

Is it possible to teach or to listen to this Perfection of Wisdom by saying, "This is that Perfection of Wisdom," or "That Perfection of Wisdom is here," or "That Perfection of Wisdom is in such and such a place," or "It is indicated by this form, this sign, this mark"?

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is not so. Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom cannot be taught, listened to, realized, reflected upon, given rise to, or taken hold of as an aggregate, an element, or a sense source. Why is that? Subhūti, because all phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature, because all phenomena are utterly secluded, the Perfection of Wisdom cannot be taught, listened to, realized, reflected upon, given rise to, or taken hold of.

"It should be understood that the Perfection of Wisdom does not exist apart from the aggregates, elements, and sense sources. Why is that? Subhūti, because the aggregates, elements, and sense sources themselves are empty, secluded, and peaceful. Therefore this Perfection of Wisdom and these aggregates, elements, and sense sources are not two; they cannot be made into two. Because of emptiness, seclusion, and peace, there is nothing to be observed. The non-observing of all phenomena is what is called the Perfection of Wisdom. When perception, recognition, designation, and conventional expression no longer arise, then it is called the Perfection of Wisdom."

The venerable Subhūti said: "Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, applies himself in yoga to this profound Perfection of Wisdom, for how long should it be understood that he has practiced and kept to discipline?"

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, since the faculties of bodhisattvas, great beings, differ in degree, I will explain this by distinguishing and prophesying. Subhūti, there are also grounds on which bodhisattvas may see many hundreds of buddhas, many thousands of buddhas, many hundreds of thousands of buddhas, and lead the holy life in their presence, and yet still have no faith or devotion toward this Perfection of Wisdom.

"Why is that? Because in the past, in the presence of those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, when this profound Perfection of Wisdom was being explained, demonstrated, and taught, they showed no respect. Being disrespectful, they did not listen well. Not listening well, they did not serve or honor it. Not serving or honoring it, they did not inquire into it. Not inquiring, they had no real faith. Having no real faith, they drifted away from that assembly. On that basis they performed, accumulated, fully gathered, and amassed karma conducive to being deprived of the Dharma. As a result, even now, when this profound Perfection of Wisdom is being explained, demonstrated, and taught, they are disrespectful and drift away. They have no faith and no devotion, and with body and mind they do not engage in gathering the accumulations.

"Because they do not engage in the accumulations, they do not know, see, comprehend, or realize this Perfection of Wisdom. Thus they come to lack faith in the Perfection of Wisdom. Lacking faith, they do not listen. Not listening, they do not know. Not knowing, they do not see. Not seeing, they do not comprehend. Not comprehending, they perform karma conducive to being deprived of the Dharma; they fully accumulate it, gather it everywhere, and amass it."

"Through the karma they have performed, accumulated, fully accumulated, and amassed, a karma conducive to being deprived of the Dharma, they come to perform a karma conducive to the corruption of wisdom. Through the karma conducive to the corruption of wisdom that they have performed, accumulated, fully accumulated, and amassed, then when this Perfection of Wisdom is being explained, taught, and demonstrated, they will reject it, they will slander it, and they will speak ill of it; and having slandered it, they will drift away.

"Subhūti, moreover, by rejecting, slandering, and speaking ill of this Perfection of Wisdom, they reject, slander, and speak ill of the omniscience of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present. Having ruined and scorched their own mental continuum, these are persons of small intellect, small wisdom, small merit, and small roots of virtue. Others, those who possess merely a little faith, a little joy, a little clarity, a little aspiration, beginners who are by nature without the fortune for it, these people too they turn back, separate, and cause to reverse even that little faith, joy, and aspiration. They say, 'One should not train in this,' and they declare in words, 'This is not the word of the Buddha.'

"Thus, having ruined and torn away their own mental continuum, and having ruined and torn away the mental continuum of others, they come to slander the Perfection of Wisdom. If one slanders the Perfection of Wisdom, one slanders omniscience. If one slanders omniscience, one slanders the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present. In this way they drift away from the presence of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones; they are abandoned by the Dharma; and they become wholly cast out from the Saṅgha. Thus, in every way and in every respect, they become entirely outside the Three Jewels.

"Because they cut off the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, they gather a karma conducive to ripening in the great hells. Because of having performed, established, and set in motion such karma, and by that very nature which is conducive to deprivation of the Dharma and to the corruption of wisdom, they will fall into the great hells for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, many millions of years, many tens of millions of years, many hundreds of millions of years, many thousands of millions of years, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of years.

"They go from one great hell to another great hell. While they pass for such a long time from great hell to great hell, the eon of destruction by fire arrives. When the eon of destruction by fire has arrived, they are cast away into whichever great hells exist in other world systems, and they fall into those great hells. Having been cast there, having fallen into those great hells, there too they pass from great hell to great hell. And while they pass there too from great hell to great hell, in exactly the same way the eon of destruction by fire arrives there as well."

"When the eon of destruction by fire arrives for them, then, immediately upon dying and passing away, they are cast away into whichever great hells of sentient beings exist in other world systems, and they come to be born in those great hells. There too, in exactly the same way, they pass from great hell to great hell. And while they pass there too, for a long time, from great hell to great hell, the eon of destruction by fire arrives there as well. When the eon of destruction by fire has arrived, they die and pass away from there as well. Because their karma is not exhausted and a remainder is still left, by that very karma they are cast back once more into this world system, and when they have been cast away they are again born in the great hells. Once more, in the great hells, they undergo those great sufferings of the hells, and they undergo them for as long as the destruction by fire has yet to come. In this way they experience a karma that accords with undergoing great suffering. Why is that? Because they spoke such harmful words."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the deeds of the five heinous crimes, done and accumulated, are not even a reflection, an approximation, or a likeness of this misconduct of mind and misconduct of speech."

The Blessed One declared: "So it is, Śāriputra, so it is. Śāriputra, the deeds of the five heinous crimes, done and accumulated, are not even a reflection, an approximation, or a likeness of this deed of misconduct of mind and misconduct of speech, done and amassed, fully accumulated and gathered.

"Those who, toward the teaching, demonstration, and explanation of this profound Perfection of Wisdom, think to turn away from it, who slander it and speak of it in unpleasant terms, who say, 'One should not train in this,' who declare, 'This was not spoken by the Tathāgata,' and who cause other beings too to be separated from it, such persons destroy their own mental continuum and also ruin the continuum of others. Having poisoned their own continuum, they poison the continuum of others as well. Having ruined themselves, they bring others to ruin too. They themselves neither know nor realize the profound Perfection of Wisdom, and they lead others to hold that one should not train in it.

"Śāriputra, I would not even permit myself to look upon a person of such a nature, still less to keep company with them, still less to give them gain and honor, still less to dwell with them. Why is that? Śāriputra, persons of such a nature should be recognized as rejecters of the Dharma. Śāriputra, persons of such a nature should be recognized as having become like rotten leaves. Śāriputra, such persons should be recognized as being of dark nature and as nurturing what is dark. Śāriputra, whatever anyone thinks to hear or to believe from such persons, all of that is wrongful and leads to ruin. Śāriputra, those who reject the Perfection of Wisdom should be recognized as persons who reject the Dharma."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, you have shown the measure of the body of the person who is born there and dwells in the great hells."

The Blessed One said: "Śāriputra, leave aside the measure of the body of the person, the being, who is born in that great hell. Why? Hearing the measure of the body of a person of such a nature would cause one to vomit hot blood from the mouth and to die, or to come near to dying, or to fall into unbearable suffering. Illness would strike and burn one; the thorn of sorrow would pierce one; one would fall into a great abyss, or wither, or be crushed. That cannot be allowed. So let no one hear of the measure of a body that has such faults, a measure so terrifying." Thus the Blessed One did not open the way for the venerable Śāriputra by declaring, "The measure of that body will be this much."

A second time and a third time the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: "The measure of that person's body would be made manifest to later beings, so that they would know: by the deeds of speech and mind that have been done, gathered, accumulated, and amassed, one takes on such a vast body as a being in the great hells. Blessed One, please explain this to me."

The Blessed One said: "Śāriputra, whoever commits wrongdoing through speech and mind, and brings about, brings together, gathers, accumulates, and amasses non-virtuous action, will experience suffering for this long a time. Precisely this will be made manifest to later beings. Śāriputra, because that very suffering is immeasurable and is spoken of as manifold, sons and daughters of good family who have the fortune of the white side will grow weary of it. From then on they will turn away from the actions that lead to being deprived of the Dharma, and will do nothing but bring about merit. They will think: 'So that I too will not meet with suffering like that, I will not abandon the sacred Dharma even for the sake of my life.'"

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, sons and daughters of good family should restrain with great care their actions of body, speech, and mind. Why? Blessed One, because one who speaks wrongly with speech, being of such a nature, gives rise to this great mass of demerit. Blessed One, by what action does this great mass of demerit arise?"

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, by speaking wrongly with speech, being of such a nature, this great mass of demerit, this vast, arises. Subhūti, there are foolish people who think to refute this profound Perfection of Wisdom, who think to denigrate it, who think to cast it back. They go forth in this very Dharma and Vinaya that is well taught. If this Perfection of Wisdom is cast back, then the awakening of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is also cast back. If the awakening of the buddhas is cast back, then the omniscience of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present is cast back. If omniscience is cast back, then the sacred Dharma is cast back. If the sacred Dharma is cast back, then the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's hearers is cast back."

If the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata's hearers is cast back, then in every way, entirely and completely, they have placed themselves outside the Three Jewels, and so they take up and accumulate immeasurable, countless great unwholesome karma."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which a son or daughter of good family comes to think of rejecting this Perfection of Wisdom?"

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, that son or daughter of good family has been influenced by Māra, or, through verbal actions that accord with the corruption of wisdom, they have no faith in these profound teachings and do not come to have clear faith in them. Subhūti, because they possess these two evil factors, that son or daughter of good family comes to cast back this Perfection of Wisdom.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, when this profound Perfection of Wisdom is being explained, taught, and expounded, whoever comes to think of rejecting it will possess these four features. That son or daughter of good family will have fallen into the hands of an evil friend; or will not strive earnestly; or will become attached to the aggregates; or will praise themselves and disparage others, seeking out faults."

This is the seventh chapter, called "Hell," from the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. Ninth bundle.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to have faith in, because of lack of earnest effort, because of being bereft of roots of virtue, and because of having fallen into the hands of an evil friend."

The Blessed One said: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to have faith in for those who do not strive earnestly, whose roots of virtue are slight, whose intelligence is weak, who do not seek the meaning, who have heard little, whose wisdom is feeble, who are supported by evil friends, who do not listen well, who are by nature not inclined to ask questions, and who do not strive in virtuous things."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, how profound is this Perfection of Wisdom, that it should be so difficult to have faith in!"

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Subhūti, because form has no intrinsic nature, form is neither bound nor liberated. In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Subhūti, because consciousness has no intrinsic nature, consciousness is neither bound nor liberated.

"Subhūti, the former extreme of form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, form has no intrinsic nature of a former extreme. Subhūti, the later extreme of form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because form has no intrinsic nature of a later extreme. Subhūti, the present arising of form is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because form has no intrinsic nature of a present arising.

"In the same way, Subhūti, the former extreme of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, consciousness has no intrinsic nature of a former extreme."

Subhūti, the later extreme of consciousness is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because consciousness has no intrinsic nature of a later extreme. Subhūti, the present arising of consciousness is neither bound nor liberated. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, consciousness has no intrinsic nature of a present arising.

Subhūti then said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to have faith in, and supremely difficult to have faith in, for those who lack diligence, who have not accumulated roots of virtue, who have fallen into the hands of bad friends, who have come under the power of Māra, who are lazy, weak in effort, lacking in mindfulness, and confused in wisdom."

The Blessed One declared: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. The Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to have faith in for those who lack diligence, who have not accumulated roots of virtue, who have fallen into the hands of bad friends, who have come under the power of Māra, who are lazy, weak in effort, lacking in mindfulness, and confused in wisdom. Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom is supremely difficult to have faith in.

"Why is that? Subhūti, whatever is the purity of form is the purity of the result, and whatever is the purity of the result is the purity of form. Thus, Subhūti, the purity of form and the purity of the result are not two, and cannot be made into two; they are not different, and not divided. Thus, Subhūti, because the result is pure, form is pure; and because form is pure, the result is pure.

"In the same way, Subhūti, whatever is the purity of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is the purity of the result, and whatever is the purity of the result is the purity of consciousness. Thus, Subhūti, the purity of consciousness and the purity of the result are not two, and cannot be made into two; they are not different, and not divided. Thus, Subhūti, because the result is pure, consciousness is pure; and because consciousness is pure, the result is pure.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, whatever is the purity of form is the purity of omniscience, and whatever is the purity of omniscience is the purity of form. Thus, Subhūti, the purity of form and the purity of omniscience are not two, and cannot be made into two; they are not different, and not divided. Thus, Subhūti, because omniscience is pure, form is pure; and because form is pure, omniscience is pure.

"In the same way, Subhūti, whatever is the purity of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness is the purity of omniscience, and whatever is the purity of omniscience is the purity of consciousness. Thus, Subhūti, the purity of consciousness and the purity of omniscience are not two, and cannot be made into two; they are not different, and not divided. Thus, Subhūti, because omniscience is pure, consciousness is pure; and because consciousness is pure, omniscience is pure."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound."

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, it is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom brings clarity."

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, it is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said:

"Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom illuminates."

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, it is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom has no junction."

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, it is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom has no affliction whatsoever."

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, it is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom has no attainment and no realization."

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, it is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom has no accomplishment."

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, it is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom has no birth at all in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm."

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, it is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is without grasping, without grasping in the full sense."

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, it is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, then what is it that the Perfection of Wisdom does not grasp, and does not fully grasp?"

The Blessed One declared: "Śāriputra, the Perfection of Wisdom does not know form, and does not fully know it. Why is that? Śāriputra, it is because of its purity. In the same way, Śāriputra, the Perfection of Wisdom does not know feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, and does not fully know them. Why is that? It is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom neither harms omniscience nor benefits it."

The Blessed One declared: "It is because of its purity."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom neither fully holds onto any phenomenon nor fully lets go of any."

The Blessed One declared: "It is because of its purity."

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, because I am pure, form is pure."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is because of utter purity."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, because I am pure, feeling, perception, and formations are pure. Blessed One, because I am pure, consciousness is pure."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is because of utter purity."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, because I am pure, the result is pure."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is because of utter purity."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, because I am pure, omniscience is pure."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is because of utter purity."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, because I am pure, there is no attainment, and there is no realization either."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is because of utter purity."

Subhūti said:

"Blessed One, because I am without end, form is without end."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is because of utter purity."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, because I am without end, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are without end."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is because of utter purity."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, whatever realization that great bodhisattva has in this way, that is this bodhisattva's Perfection of Wisdom."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is because of utter purity."

The venerable Subhūti said: "Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom does not abide on this shore, nor does it abide on the far shore, nor does it abide in the long stretch between the two."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is because of utter purity."

The venerable Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if a great bodhisattva perceives it in this way, he will abandon this Perfection of Wisdom, and he will make this Perfection of Wisdom distant."

The Blessed One declared: "Excellent, Subhūti, excellent! It is so, Subhūti, it is so. Why is that? Subhūti, one may become attached through a name, and one may also become attached through a sign."

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti spoke to the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, in this way, by speaking of the very things to which one becomes attached, the Blessed One has taught this Perfection of Wisdom well and shown it well; it is wonderful, utterly complete."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, what are those attachments?"

Subhūti replied: "Venerable Śāriputra, the thought 'form is empty' is attachment. Likewise, venerable Śāriputra, the thought 'feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are empty' is attachment. To know correctly of past phenomena that they are past phenomena is attachment. To know correctly of future phenomena that they are future phenomena is attachment. To know correctly of present phenomena that they are present phenomena is attachment. To know correctly that a person who has entered the bodhisattva vehicle, by giving rise to the first thought of awakening, produces this much of a mass of merit, is attachment."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), said to the venerable Subhūti: "Noble Subhūti, in what manner does attachment come about?"

Subhūti replied: "Kauśika, suppose someone knows, 'This is the first thought of awakening,' and dedicates that awakening mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, saying, 'I dedicate it.' Then that son or daughter of good family who has properly entered the Great Vehicle is unable to dedicate the intrinsic nature of mind. Therefore, Kauśika, those who teach others rightly, establish them rightly, praise them rightly, and gladden them rightly should, through realizing in accord with the true nature of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, rightly instruct, rightly establish, rightly praise, and rightly gladden others,

In this way that son or daughter of good family does no harm even to themselves, and by rightly establishing others in the way the buddhas have permitted, they cause others to be rightly established; and all these extremes of attachment are completely abandoned.

Then the Blessed One said "Excellent!" to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, it is excellent, truly excellent, that you thus bring bodhisattvas, the great beings, to understand these extremes of attachment. Therefore, Subhūti, I shall also speak of other, extremely subtle attachments. Listen well, attend carefully, and keep it in mind, and I will explain it to you."

Subhūti said, "Excellent, Blessed One," and the venerable Subhūti listened as the Blessed One instructed. Then the Blessed One spoke as follows:

"Subhūti, suppose that sons or daughters of good family with faith take the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete buddha as a sign and attend to him in that way. Subhūti, for as long as there is a sign, there is attachment. Why is that? Subhūti, it is from a sign that attachment arises. Now suppose one thinks: 'I rejoice in whatever undefiled qualities belong to the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, the future, and the present.' And having so rejoiced, one dedicates the roots of virtue that accompany that rejoicing toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, saying, 'I dedicate them.' Subhūti, the nature of phenomena, whatever it is, is neither past, nor future, nor present. What is neither past, nor future, nor present is utterly liberated from the three times. What is utterly liberated from the three times cannot be dedicated, cannot be made into a sign, and cannot be taken as an object. It is also not something seen, heard, realized, or cognized."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, the intrinsic nature of phenomena is profound."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, it is because it is secluded."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound in its intrinsic nature."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, because its intrinsic nature is utterly pure, and because, Subhūti, its intrinsic nature is secluded, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound in its intrinsic nature."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, because the Perfection of Wisdom is secluded in its intrinsic nature, I pay homage to the Perfection of Wisdom."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, all phenomena are likewise secluded in their intrinsic nature. Subhūti, that very seclusion of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is the Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because all phenomena were fully and perfectly awakened to without being made by the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete buddha."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, in that case the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete buddha has not fully and perfectly awakened to any phenomena at all."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, that is so, because in their intrinsic nature those phenomena do not exist at all. What is intrinsic nature is without intrinsic nature; and what is without intrinsic nature is intrinsic nature. That is to say, because all phenomena have no defining characteristic, they have a single characteristic. Therefore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete buddha has not fully and perfectly awakened to any phenomena. Why is that? Subhūti, the nature of phenomena is not twofold. Subhūti, the nature of all phenomena comes down to one alone."

Subhūti, whatever is the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is without intrinsic nature; and whatever is without intrinsic nature is intrinsic nature. In this way, Subhūti, all those extremes of attachment are completely abandoned.

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, is the Perfection of Wisdom profound?"

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound because space is profound."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, is the Perfection of Wisdom difficult to realize?"

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, it is so, in that no one fully and perfectly awakens to it."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, is the Perfection of Wisdom inconceivable?"

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, it is so, in that the Perfection of Wisdom is not to be known by the mind and not to be realized by the mind."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, is the Perfection of Wisdom something that has not been made?"

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, because no maker is observed, the Perfection of Wisdom is unmade."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, that being so, how should a bodhisattva, a great being, practice in the Perfection of Wisdom?"

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in the Perfection of Wisdom does not engage with form, he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom. In the same way, if he does not engage with feeling, nor with perception, nor with formations, and if he does not engage with consciousness, he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom.

"If he does not engage with form by thinking, 'Form is impermanent,' he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom. In the same way, if he does not engage with feeling, perception, and formations, and if he does not engage with consciousness by thinking, 'Consciousness is impermanent,' he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom.

"If he does not engage with form by thinking, 'Form is empty,' he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom. In the same way, if he does not engage with feeling, nor with perception, nor with formations, and if he does not engage with consciousness by thinking, 'Consciousness is empty,' he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom.

"If he does not engage with form by thinking, 'Form is incomplete,' or 'Form is complete,' he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom. The incompleteness or the completeness of form is not form; and if he does not engage in that way either, he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom. In the same way, if he does not engage with feeling, nor with perception, nor with formations, and if he does not engage with consciousness by thinking, 'Consciousness is incomplete,' or 'Consciousness is complete,' he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom. The incompleteness or the completeness of consciousness is not consciousness; and if he does not engage in that way either, he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, it is wonderful that, as long as it is so, the bodhisattvas, the great beings, are said to be both with attachment and without attachment."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, does not engage with form by thinking, 'It is with attachment,' or 'It is without attachment,' he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom. In the same way, if he does not engage with feeling, perception, and formations, and if he does not engage with consciousness by thinking, 'It is with attachment,' or 'It is without attachment,' he practices in the Perfection of Wisdom."

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, does not engage in the thought, "The eye is accompanied by attachment," or "It is free of attachment," then that bodhisattva practices the Perfection of Wisdom. In the same way, if one does not engage in the thought, "The feeling arising from the contact that is the coming together of mind is accompanied by attachment," or "It is free of attachment," then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom. If one does not engage in the thought, "The earth element is accompanied by attachment," or "It is free of attachment," then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom. And likewise, up to the element of consciousness, if one does not engage in the thought, "It is accompanied by attachment," or "It is free of attachment," then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

If one does not engage in the thought, "The perfection of generosity is accompanied by attachment," or "It is free of attachment," then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom. In the same way, if one does not engage in such thoughts about the perfection of moral discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom, then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

In the same way, if one does not engage in the thought, "The thirty-seven factors of awakening, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the individual exact knowledges, and the eighteen unshared qualities of a buddha are accompanied by attachment," or "They are free of attachment," then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

If one does not engage in the thought, "The fruit of stream-entry is accompanied by attachment," or "It is free of attachment," then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom. In the same way, if one does not engage in such thoughts about the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the state of an arhat, then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom. If one does not engage in the thought, "The state of a pratyekabuddha is accompanied by attachment," or "It is free of attachment," then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom. If one does not engage in the thought, "Buddhahood is accompanied by attachment," or "It is free of attachment," then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, if one does not engage in the thought, "Omniscience itself is accompanied by attachment," or "It is free of attachment," then one practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way does not generate attachment to form. In the same way, one does not generate attachment to feeling, nor to perception, nor to formations, nor to consciousness. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way does not generate attachment to the eye, and so on up to the feeling arising from the contact that is the coming together of mind. One does not generate attachment to the earth element, and so on up to the element of consciousness. One does not generate attachment to the perfection of generosity. One does not generate attachment to the perfection of moral discipline, nor to the perfection of patience, nor to the perfection of diligence, nor to the perfection of meditative concentration, nor to the perfection of wisdom. One does not generate attachment to the factors of awakening, nor to the powers, nor to the fearlessnesses, nor to the individual exact knowledges, nor to the eighteen unshared qualities of a buddha.

One does not generate attachment to the fruit of stream-entry, nor to the fruit of once-returning, nor to the fruit of non-returning, nor to the state of an arhat. One does not generate attachment to the state of a pratyekabuddha. One does not generate attachment to buddhahood. One does not generate attachment even to omniscience.

Why is that?

Subhūti, omniscience is unattached, unbound, unliberated, and has not fully passed beyond. Subhūti, it is thus, in order to turn away completely from all attachment, that a bodhisattva, a great being, should practice the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, this teaching called the Perfection of Wisdom is profound. It is wondrous that it does not diminish when it is taught and does not diminish when it is not taught, and that it does not increase when it is taught and does not increase when it is not taught.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows: Excellent, Subhūti, excellent! It is so, Subhūti, it is so. Subhūti, it is just as when the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, remains for as long as he lives and speaks in praise of space: space does not thereby increase, and if he does not praise it, space does not thereby decrease. Subhūti, it is also like a conjured man: if he is praised, he does not become attached, nor is he afflicted; if he is not praised, he does not become angry, nor is he afflicted. In the same way, Subhūti, the nature of phenomena, whatever it may be, is only so much whether it is taught or not taught.

The elder Subhūti said: Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices this profound Perfection of Wisdom and meditates on the Perfection of Wisdom, who is not discouraged and does not become faint-hearted, who applies himself to it and does not turn back, performs a difficult deed. Blessed One, meditating on the Perfection of Wisdom is meditating on space. Blessed One, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have put on this armor are worthy of homage. Why is that? Blessed One, to wish to put on armor for the sake of beings is to wish to put on armor together with space. To wish to put on armor for the sake of beings who are equal to space and equal to the dharmadhātu is, Blessed One, for a bodhisattva, a great being, to have put on the great armor; Blessed One, such a bodhisattva, a great being, is a hero. To wish to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening is, Blessed One, to wish to set space entirely free. It is, Blessed One, to wish to carry space away. Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to put on armor for the sake of beings who are equal to space and equal to the dharmadhātu has obtained the great armor of the perfection of diligence.

Then another monk, in the direction where the Blessed One was, bowed with palms joined, and said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, I pay homage to the Perfection of Wisdom. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom does not produce any phenomenon and does not bring any phenomenon to cessation.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the venerable Subhūti: Noble Subhūti, when one practices this Perfection of Wisdom in this way, in what does one practice? Subhūti replied: Kauśika, one who practices this Perfection of Wisdom practices in space.

Kauśika, one who studies this Perfection of Wisdom and sets his mind on practicing it is practicing in a way that is unsurpassed.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, when a son or daughter of good family comes to hold this Perfection of Wisdom, what protecting, guarding, and sheltering should be done for them? Please instruct me.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, do you rightly perceive any phenomenon that could be protected, guarded, or sheltered?

Śakra said: Noble Subhūti, I do not.

Subhūti said: Kauśika, if a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in this Perfection of Wisdom just as it has been explained, then that very abiding will protect, guard, and shelter him. But if he should become separated from the Perfection of Wisdom, then humans and nonhumans who watch for an opening and seek an opening will find one.

Furthermore, Kauśika, anyone who thinks of protecting, guarding, and sheltering a bodhisattva, a great being, who is practicing the Perfection of Wisdom is thinking of protecting, guarding, and sheltering space. Kauśika, what do you think? Would you be able to protect, guard, and shelter an echo?

Śakra said: Noble Subhūti, I would not.

Subhūti said: Kauśika, in just the same way, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices and abides in this Perfection of Wisdom fully understands all phenomena to be like an echo. Therefore he has no pride in this. He does not rightly perceive it, does not know it, and does not truly know it. He abides in the understanding that those phenomena do not exist, do not truly appear, are truly nonexistent, and cannot be apprehended. If he abides in this way, he is practicing the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then, through the power of the Buddha, in the great trichiliocosm world-system, the Four Great Kings, all the Śakras, lords of the gods, all the great Brahmās, and the great Brahmā who is lord of the Sahā world, as many as there were, all came to where the Blessed One was. Having come, they bowed with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circled him three times, and sat to one side.

When they were seated to one side, those Great Kings, all the Śakras, lords of the gods, all the great Brahmās, and the great Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, came to know, through the power of the Buddha and the blessing of the Buddha, that a thousand buddhas had taught this very Perfection of Wisdom and this very chapter on the Perfection of Wisdom, with these very names, these very words, and these very letters, through this very monk called Subhūti. They also knew that in this very place the Śakras, lords of the gods, themselves had questioned and made requests, and that this very Perfection of Wisdom had been explained here. And they knew that the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, too, after he becomes fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, will teach this very Perfection of Wisdom in this very place.

This is the eighth chapter, called Purification, from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this thing called the perfection of wisdom is a mere name. And even that name is not apprehended as 'this'; it is only the basis of speech that is called a name. The perfection of wisdom, too, does not exist and is not apprehended. As the name is, so is the perfection of wisdom; and as the perfection of wisdom is, so is the name. Since these two phenomena do not exist and are not apprehended, Blessed One, why is it that the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, after fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, will teach this very perfection of wisdom in this very place, using just these names, just these words, and just these letters?"

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, it is in this way. The bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, will awaken fully to the understanding that form is neither permanent nor impermanent, that form is neither bound nor liberated, and that therefore it is beyond extremes and perfectly pure. In the same way, he will awaken fully to the understanding that feeling, perception, and the formations are likewise so, and that consciousness is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither bound nor liberated, and that therefore it is beyond extremes and perfectly pure. Subhūti, it is for this reason that the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, after fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, will teach this very perfection of wisdom in this very place, using just these names, just these words, and just these letters."

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how wonderful! This perfection of wisdom is utterly pure."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom is utterly pure. In the same way, Subhūti, because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are pure, the perfection of wisdom is utterly pure. Subhūti, because form is without arising, without cessation, without affliction, and without purification, it is pure, and so the perfection of wisdom is utterly pure. In the same way, Subhūti, because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are without arising, without cessation, without affliction, and without purification, they are pure, and so the perfection of wisdom is utterly pure. Subhūti, because space is pure, the perfection of wisdom is utterly pure. Subhūti, because form is unstained and without grasping, the perfection of wisdom is utterly pure. In the same way, Subhūti, because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are unstained and without grasping, the perfection of wisdom is utterly pure. Subhūti, because space and the echo are non-existent, inexpressible, and not apprehended, the perfection of wisdom is utterly pure. Subhūti, because all phenomena, whether stained or unstained, are unstained, the perfection of wisdom is utterly pure."

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One:

Blessed One, even those sons or daughters of good family into whose ears this Perfection of Wisdom resounds have gained a gain, a truly good gain. How much more, then, those who hold it, bear it in mind, read it, fully comprehend it, recite it, teach it, explain it, give instruction in it, and learn it by heart. No disease of the eye will arise in them, nor disease of the ear, nose, or tongue, nor disease of the body. They will not become deluded. Free from dread, they will not meet a time of death. Many hundreds of thousands of sons of the gods will follow close behind them. On the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth days of the lunar month, wherever that son or daughter of good family who teaches the Dharma expounds the Perfection of Wisdom, in that very place they will generate very great merit.

When Subhūti had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Close behind that son or daughter of good family, hundreds of thousands of gods will follow. Hundreds of thousands of gods will come to that place. All those who wish to hear the Dharma from the teacher who expounds this Perfection of Wisdom will protect, shelter, and conceal that teacher. Why is that? Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom is the unsurpassed jewel of the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Therefore, Subhūti, that son or daughter of good family will generate much merit on that basis.

Subhūti, however, many obstacles will arise for anyone who writes down this profound Perfection of Wisdom, or holds it, bears it in mind, reads it, fully comprehends it, recites it, teaches it, explains it, gives instruction in it, or learns it by heart. Why is that? Subhūti, a great jewel has many enemies, and the more precious it is, the heavier the enemies become. Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom, this great jewel, is the unsurpassed jewel in the world. It has entered the world for the sake of the world's benefit and happiness, so that all phenomena may be unarisen and unceasing, and so that there may be no afflictions whatsoever. It abides in a manner that does not perish.

Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom does not abide in any phenomenon, is not joined with any phenomenon, and does not fully grasp any phenomenon. Why is that? Subhūti, because all those phenomena are nonexistent and cannot be apprehended. Subhūti, because nothing has arisen, the Perfection of Wisdom is unstained.
