Subhūti, what is called unstained is this very Perfection of Wisdom. Subhūti, because form is unstained, the Perfection of Wisdom is unstained. In the same way, because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are unstained, Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom is unstained.

Subhūti, even so, a bodhisattva, a great being, who does not truly understand this, still practices the Perfection of Wisdom. Furthermore, Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom does not cause entry into any phenomenon, nor cause definite entry; it does not demonstrate any phenomenon, nor definitely demonstrate it; it does not cause any phenomenon to be obtained, nor definitely obtained.

Then many thousands of sons of the gods appeared in the sky, shouting and laughing, tossing up their garments, and they said, "Oh, it appears that the wheel of the Dharma has now been turned twice in Jambudvīpa!"

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable elder Subhūti, "Subhūti, this is not a twice-turning of the wheel of the Dharma. For there is no turning forth and no turning back of any phenomenon whatsoever. Subhūti, such is the Perfection of Wisdom of the bodhisattva, the great being."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, this is the great perfection of that bodhisattva, that great being, who is free from attachment to all phenomena; who, although he wishes to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, does not awaken to any phenomenon at all; and who, although he turns the wheel of the Dharma, does not truly teach any phenomenon at all. Why is that? Because there is no phenomenon to be observed, and no phenomenon to be taught, and there is no one who turns anything for anyone."

"Why is that? Blessed One, because all phenomena are utterly unestablished; no phenomenon will be turned back, and none will be turned forth. Why is that? Blessed One, because all phenomena are unestablished from the very beginning. All phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, there is no entering into emptiness, and no turning back from it. Subhūti, there is no entering into the signless, and no turning back from it. Subhūti, there is no entering into the wishless, and no turning back from it. Subhūti, this teaching is the teaching of all phenomena. No one has taught it, no one has heard it, no one has received it, no one realizes it directly, no one is realizing it directly, and no one will realize it directly. Through this teaching of the Dharma no one has passed completely beyond sorrow, no one will pass completely beyond sorrow, and no one is passing completely beyond sorrow. And through this teaching of the Dharma, no one has been made a worthy recipient of offerings."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, because space does not exist, this is the perfection that does not exist. Blessed One, because all phenomena are equal in being unobservable, this is the perfection of the unequal and of equality itself. Blessed One, because of utter emptiness, this is the perfection of seclusion. Blessed One, because all phenomena are not observed, this is the perfection of what is not to be forgotten. Blessed One, because there is no name and no body, this is the perfection of having no abode. Blessed One, because there is no going and no coming, this is the perfection of having no essential nature. Blessed One, because all phenomena are free of conceptual thought, this is the perfection of the inexpressible. Blessed One, because the five aggregates are not observed, this is the perfection of having no name. Blessed One, because all phenomena do not go anywhere, this is the perfection of not going. Blessed One, because all phenomena have nothing to be grasped, this is the perfection of what cannot be seized."

Blessed One, because it is endowed with qualities that do not diminish, this is the perfection of non-diminishing. Blessed One, because no phenomenon is truly established, this is the perfection of the non-arising of all phenomena. Blessed One, because no agent is apprehended, this is the perfection without an agent. Blessed One, because all phenomena are without self, this is the perfection without a knower. Blessed One, because death, transmigration, and birth do not truly arise, this is the perfection of non-transmigration. Blessed One, because neither the past extreme, nor the future extreme, nor the present time is apprehended, this is the perfection that has nothing to be tamed.

Blessed One, because it makes known that nothing is born, this is the perfection that is like a dream, an echo, a mirage, a shimmering haze, and an illusion. Blessed One, because attachment, aversion, and delusion are without intrinsic nature, this is the perfection without total affliction. Blessed One, because no support is apprehended, this is the perfection without purification. Blessed One, because space is unstained, this is the perfection without stain. Blessed One, because it goes beyond all conceit, this is the perfection without conceptual elaboration. Blessed One, because there is no movement, this is the perfection without conceit.

Blessed One, because the dharmadhātu abides as it is, this is the perfection that does not move. Blessed One, because all phenomena are suchness, unmistaken, this is the perfection free from attachment. Blessed One, because all phenomena are nonconceptual, this is the perfection without arising. Blessed One, because the signs of all phenomena are not apprehended, this is the perfection of peace. Blessed One, because it is the perfection of good qualities, this is the perfection without fault. Blessed One, because there is no thorough imputation, this is the perfection without affliction.

Blessed One, because of the limit of reality, this is the perfection without sentient beings. Blessed One, because no phenomenon arises, this is the perfection without measure. Blessed One, because there is no clinging to any phenomenon, this is the perfection that does not realize the two extremes. Blessed One, because all phenomena are without division, this is the perfection without difference. Blessed One, because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas have no desire for anything, this is the perfection that grasps nothing as supreme. Blessed One, because conceptual thought is pacified, this is the perfection of nonconceptuality. Blessed One, because the nature of reality is immeasurable, this is the perfection that cannot be measured. Blessed One, because there is no attachment to any phenomenon, this is the perfection without attachment.

Blessed One, because all phenomena are uncompounded, this is the perfection of impermanence. Blessed One, because all phenomena are equal to space, this is the perfection of suffering. Blessed One, because no phenomenon is apprehended, this is the perfection of emptiness.

Blessed One, because all phenomena are not clung to, this is the perfection of selflessness. Blessed One, because all phenomena are not truly accomplished, this is the perfection of the absence of characteristics. Blessed One, because it has no limit and no extremity, this is the perfection of all emptinesses.

Blessed One, because those factors of awakening are not apprehended, this is the perfection of the factors of awakening, beginning with the establishments of mindfulness. Blessed One, because the three doors of liberation are not apprehended, this is the perfection of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Blessed One, because these are not apprehended, this is the perfection of the eight liberations. Blessed One, because the first meditative concentration and the rest are not apprehended, this is the perfection of the nine successive absorptions. Blessed One, because suffering and the rest are not apprehended, this is the perfection of the Four Truths. Blessed One, because generosity and the rest are not apprehended, this is the perfection of the ten grounds.

Blessed One, because it is not forgotten, this is the perfection of the powers. Blessed One, because it is utterly undaunted, this is the perfection of fearlessness. Blessed One, because all wisdoms are free from attachment and free from obstruction, this is the perfection of the fully discriminating knowledges. Blessed One, because it passes entirely beyond enumeration, this is the perfection of all the distinctive qualities of a buddha. Blessed One, because all phenomena are unmistaken suchness, this is the perfection of the suchness of the Tathāgata. Blessed One, because all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, this is the perfection of the self-arisen. Blessed One, because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fully known in all its aspects, this Perfection of Wisdom is the perfection of the wisdom of omniscience.

This is the ninth chapter, the chapter of praise, from the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. Tenth volume.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, thought: "Those sons or daughters of good family in whose ears this Perfection of Wisdom comes to be heard have surely performed special service to the Victors of the past, have planted roots of virtue under many buddhas, and are held by spiritual friends. How much more so are those who take up this profound Perfection of Wisdom, hold it, read it, fully understand it, recite it, teach it, explain it, give instruction in it, and learn it by heart; and who, having taken it up, held it, read it, fully understood it, taught it, explained it, given instruction in it, and learned it by heart, study it just as it is, practice it just as it is, and apply themselves to it in yoga just as it is. These will not have merely meager roots of virtue. Those sons and daughters of good family will have honored and served many buddhas."

Those who even now will listen to this Perfection of Wisdom, and having listened will hold it, bear it in mind, read it, fully understand it, recite it, teach it, explain it, give transmission of it, memorize it, train in it just as it is, practice it just as it is, and apply themselves to it in yoga just as it is: such sons or daughters of good family have already, in the presence of the former Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly awakened Buddhas, heard this Perfection of Wisdom, and have questioned and inquired about it thoroughly from those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. And those who, when this profound Perfection of Wisdom is being spoken, taught and explained, are not stunned, do not shrink back, are not alarmed, do not tremble, whose minds do not turn away, who do not become disheartened and turn back, who are not frightened, who are not utterly terrified, and who are not seized by dread: it should be known that those sons and daughters of good family have planted roots of virtue under many buddhas.

Then the venerable Śāriputra, knowing by his own mind the thought that had arisen in the mind of Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, if a son or daughter of good family, when this very profound Perfection of Wisdom is being taught, shown and explained, has faith in it, thinks on it and is inclined toward it, with a clear and believing mind arouses the thought of awakening, and holds, bears in mind, reads, fully understands, recites, teaches, explains, gives transmission of, memorizes, trains in just as it is, practices just as it is, and applies themselves in yoga just as it is to this Perfection of Wisdom, then such a person should be regarded as a bodhisattva, a great being, who is irreversible, exactly as such.

Why is that? Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Blessed One, those whose roots of virtue are slight, who have not heard it directly in the presence of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and have not questioned them, who by nature are of that kind, and who have not practiced in the past and so lack the foundation, are unable to have confidence in this Perfection of Wisdom that is so profound.

Blessed One, moreover, those who have no confidence in it, and who, through not understanding it, think of rejecting it: those sons and daughters of good family rejected this very profound Perfection of Wisdom in earlier times too, when it was being taught. Why is that? Blessed One, because their roots of virtue are slight and they did not practice in the past, they cannot in any way have confidence in this profound Perfection of Wisdom.

Those who come to reject this profound Perfection of Wisdom when it is being taught should be understood in the same way: they too rejected this very profound Perfection of Wisdom when it was taught in earlier times. For they have no faith in the teaching of this profound Perfection of Wisdom, no forbearance, no longing, no aspiration, no diligence, no clarity of mind, and no inclination toward it. They did not question or inquire of the former buddhas, the Blessed Ones, or of the buddhas' hearers.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Śāriputra: Noble Śāriputra, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound.

Bodhisattvas, great beings, who have not practiced before, may not take delight when this profound Perfection of Wisdom is taught; what is surprising in that?

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, I pay homage to the Perfection of Wisdom. Blessed One, to pay homage to the Perfection of Wisdom is to pay homage to omniscient wisdom."

The Blessed One declared, "So it is, Kauśika, so it is. To pay homage to the Perfection of Wisdom is to pay homage to omniscient wisdom. Why is that? Kauśika, the omniscience of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is born from this. And Kauśika, the Perfection of Wisdom has also been fully revealed through the wisdom that is born of omniscience. In this way one should practice in this Perfection of Wisdom; in this way one should abide in this Perfection of Wisdom; in this way one should engage in yogic practice in this Perfection of Wisdom."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, abide in the Perfection of Wisdom when practicing the Perfection of Wisdom? How, when practicing the Perfection of Wisdom, does one engage in yogic practice in the Perfection of Wisdom?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to Śakra, lord of the gods, "Excellent, excellent, Kauśika! It is excellent, Kauśika, that you think to inquire and to question the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete buddha, about this matter. Kauśika, this confidence of yours has also been born through the power of the buddha.

"Kauśika, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices this Perfection of Wisdom, he does not abide in form, and he does not abide thinking, 'It is form.' Kauśika, in that a bodhisattva, a great being, does not abide in form and does not abide thinking, 'It is form,' in that way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva, a great being, engages in yogic practice in form. In the same way, he does not abide in feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and does not abide thinking, 'It is consciousness.' Kauśika, in that a bodhisattva, a great being, does not abide in consciousness and does not abide thinking, 'It is consciousness,' in that way, Kauśika, a bodhisattva, a great being, engages in yogic practice in consciousness.

"Kauśika, he does not apply himself to the notion 'It is form.' Kauśika, in that he does not apply himself to the notion 'It is form,' in that way he does not abide in the thought 'It is form.' In the same way, Kauśika, he does not apply himself to the notion 'It is feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness.' Kauśika, in that he does not apply himself to the notion 'It is consciousness,' in that way he does not abide in the thought 'It is consciousness.' Thus he abides in the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, and thus he engages in yogic practice in it."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is hard to fathom. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is hard to grasp. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is immeasurable."

The Blessed One declared, "So it is, Śāriputra, so it is. Śāriputra, one does not abide thinking, 'Form is profound.'

Śāriputra, when one does not abide in the thought, "Form is profound," in that very way one is practicing yoga with respect to form. So too with feeling, perception, and the formations. Śāriputra, one does not abide in the thought, "Consciousness is profound"; Śāriputra, when one does not abide in the thought, "Consciousness is profound," in that very way one is practicing yoga with respect to consciousness.

Śāriputra, one does not practice in the thought, "Form is profound." Śāriputra, when one does not practice in the thought, "Form is profound," in that way one is not abiding in the thought, "Form is profound." So too with feeling, perception, and the formations. Śāriputra, one does not practice in the thought, "Consciousness is profound"; Śāriputra, when one does not practice in the thought, "Consciousness is profound," in that way one is not abiding in the thought, "Consciousness is profound."

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Should it be taught in the presence of bodhisattvas, great beings, who have received the prediction of irreversibility? Why is that? Blessed One, such beings feel no dismay; they will have no doubt, no confusion, and no dispute."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Noble Śāriputra, what fault would there be if this Perfection of Wisdom were taught in the presence of a bodhisattva, a great being, who has not received a prediction?"

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Śāriputra said to Śakra, lord of the gods: "Kauśika, consider a bodhisattva, a great being, who has not received a prediction, yet who gains the opportunity to see, to pay homage to, to honor and serve, and to hear this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and who, on hearing it, does not tremble, is not terrified, and is not seized by terror. Kauśika, you should know that such a bodhisattva, a great being, has come from far away. You should know that he entered the Great Vehicle long ago and that his roots of virtue have fully ripened. Before long he will receive the prediction to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening; you should know that he is close to receiving the prediction.

"That bodhisattva, a great being, will not pass beyond one, two, or three Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas before he receives the prediction to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. Moreover, he will please those Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas, and having pleased them, he will never cause them to be disheartened. His seeing the Tathāgatas will also bear fruit through the prediction. From that very seeing of the Tathāgatas he will receive the prediction to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

"For as long as he has not received the prediction to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, for that long, by seeing the Tathāgatas, paying homage to them, honoring them, serving and attending them, and up until he becomes manifestly and perfectly awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, his seeing them will bear fruit."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, as for the bodhisattva, the great being, who gains the opportunity to see, to pay homage to, to honor and serve, and to hear this profound Perfection of Wisdom, that bodhisattva, great being…"

Blessed One, they have come from far away. I would say that they entered the Great Vehicle properly long ago, and that their roots of virtue have fully ripened. How much more is this so for those who, having heard this Perfection of Wisdom, take it up, hold it, read it, thoroughly understand it, recite it, teach it, explain it in detail, give instruction in it, and know it by heart.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, Śāriputra, so it is. Any bodhisattva, any great being, who has gained the opportunity to see this profound Perfection of Wisdom, to pay homage to it, to honor and serve it, and to hear it, should be known as one who has come from far away, who entered the Great Vehicle properly long ago, and whose roots of virtue have fully ripened. How much more is this so for one who, having heard it, takes it up, holds it, reads it, thoroughly understands it, recites it, teaches it, explains it in detail, gives instruction in it, and knows it by heart."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I am inspired to offer an illustration. Sugata, I am inspired. Blessed One, suppose a son or daughter of good family who follows the bodhisattva vehicle dreams, even in a dream, of sitting at the heart of awakening. Blessed One, that bodhisattva, that great being, is close to the unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, for the sake of fully awakening to it. In just the same way, Blessed One, if any son or daughter of good family gains the opportunity to see this profound Perfection of Wisdom, to pay homage to it, to honor and serve it, and to hear it, then, Blessed One, that person who follows the bodhisattva vehicle has come from far away; and if they entered the Great Vehicle properly long ago and their roots of virtue have fully ripened, how much more is this so for one who, having heard it, takes it up, holds it, reads it, thoroughly understands it, recites it, teaches it, explains it in detail, gives instruction in it, and knows it by heart.

"That person who follows the bodhisattva vehicle is close to receiving the prophecy. It should be known that the buddha, the Blessed One, will give that bodhisattva, that great being, the prophecy of fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. A bodhisattva, a great being, who obtains even the mere hearing of this profound Perfection of Wisdom should be known as one who entered the Great Vehicle properly long ago and whose roots of virtue have fully ripened. How much more is this so for a son or daughter of good family who takes up this profound Perfection of Wisdom, holds it, reads it, thoroughly understands it, recites it, teaches it, explains it in detail, gives instruction in it, and knows it by heart.

"Why is that? Blessed One, most beings have not been free from accumulated karma that accords with being impoverished of the Dharma. For the most part, the minds of such beings do not accord with this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and their minds turn away from it. Beings who have not accumulated roots of virtue for the most part do not enter into this true limit, and do not come to have faith in it.

Those sons and daughters of good family who enter into this ultimate limit and come to have faith in it, O Blessed One, are those who have accumulated roots of virtue. They should be known as ones who have accumulated roots of virtue in abundance.

Blessed One, it is like this. Suppose a man has come out of a wilderness a hundred leagues wide, or two hundred, or three hundred, or four hundred, or five hundred, or a thousand leagues wide. As he comes out, he sees the signs that show a village, a town, or a city to be near: the signs seen earlier, such as herdsmen of cattle or of other livestock, a boundary, a lovely park, a lovely grove, or other signs besides these. When he sees those earlier signs, he thinks, "Because these earlier signs appear, I have drawn near to a village, a town, or a city." Then he has found relief and breathes freely, and from then on he gives no thought to bandits.

In the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, abides close to this profound Perfection of Wisdom, that bodhisattva, a great being, should be known as one who has drawn near to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. It should be known that before long this bodhisattva, this great being, will receive the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. Such a one will also feel neither fear nor terror at the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas. Why is that? Because, just as that man saw the earlier signs, so this bodhisattva has attained the seeing of this profound Perfection of Wisdom, the paying of homage to it, the honoring of it, and the hearing of it.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Śāriputra as follows. "Śāriputra, so it is, so it is. Just as you speak, and will speak, through the power of the Buddha, so too you should have confidence about this matter."

When he had said this, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One as follows. "Blessed One, it is like this. Suppose a certain man wishes to see the great ocean. As he goes toward the great ocean, the more he goes to see it, the more he may notice a tree, or the sign of a tree, or a mountain, or the sign of a mountain. If he does, he should think, 'From here the great ocean is still far away.' If later he no longer sees a tree, or the sign of a tree, or a mountain, or the sign of a mountain, he should think, 'From here the great ocean is near.' Why is that? The great ocean slopes down gradually, and so within the great ocean there is no tree or sign of a tree, no mountain or sign of a mountain. Even though he has not yet seen that great ocean directly with his eyes, he thinks, 'I have drawn near to the great ocean; from here the great ocean is not far.'

In the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, hears this profound Perfection of Wisdom, he should know this. Even though those Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly and completely awakened buddhas, have not yet given me a prophecy face to face, I should nonetheless know that I am drawing near to receiving the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. Why is that?"

They are so for this reason: it is in order to obtain the sight of this profound Perfection of Wisdom, to pay homage to it, to honor and revere it, and to hear it.

Blessed One, it is like this. When the spring season draws near, the old leaves fall from the branches of the various trees, and new leaves of many kinds appear. When the leaves appear, the people of Jambudvīpa see those earlier signs in the forests and become glad, thinking, "Before long, flowers and fruits will come." Why is this so? Because such signs were previously present in the trunks of the trees.

In the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, draws near in order to obtain the sight of this profound Perfection of Wisdom, to pay homage to it, to honor and revere it, and to hear it, it should be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, has brought his roots of virtue to full maturity with regard to this profound Perfection of Wisdom. This profound Perfection of Wisdom has been brought near to him by that very root of virtue from before.

Then the gods who had seen the buddhas in the past think, "In the case of those earlier bodhisattvas, great beings, the signs of being prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening also appeared beforehand. So this bodhisattva, this great being, will before long receive the prophecy to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening." Thinking so, they become delighted, rejoice, and feel a gladdened mind.

Blessed One, it is like this. When a pregnant woman is heavy with child and moves her body, she becomes very weary. She has little desire to walk about, she wants little food, she becomes drowsy and sleeps little, she speaks little, her strength is small, and her suffering is great. She often stays alone, brooding, and has little enthusiasm for company. She thinks, "Because I have attended to things improperly, and have indulged in, relied upon, cultivated and often done such things, my body is experiencing such sensations." At that time, Blessed One, just as one sees these earlier signs, so one should understand that this woman will give birth to a child before long.

In the same way, Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, whose roots of virtue have matured, draws near in order to obtain the sight of this profound Perfection of Wisdom, to pay homage to it, to honor and revere it, and to hear it, and when, on hearing it, he rejoices in it and gives rise to a mind that seeks the Perfection of Wisdom, at that time, Blessed One, it should be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, will before long receive the prophecy to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Śāriputra: "Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra! This too, Śāriputra, you have been inspired to say through the power of the Buddha."

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is wonderful that the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly and completely awakened buddha, has so well embraced, so well trained, and so well entrusted these bodhisattvas, these great beings."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, it is so. These bodhisattvas, these great beings, have set out for the benefit of many beings, for the happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, benefit and happiness of the great multitude of people."

out of compassion for gods and humans, wishing to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and, having become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, wishing to teach the unsurpassed Dharma.

Subhūti asked: Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices this perfection of wisdom, how does the cultivation of the perfection of wisdom become fully complete?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive any increase of form, then he is practicing the perfection of wisdom. In the same way, if he does not perceive any increase of feeling, of perception, of formations, or of consciousness, then he is practicing the perfection of wisdom. If he does not perceive any decrease of form, then he is practicing the perfection of wisdom. In the same way, if he does not perceive any decrease of feeling, of perception, of formations, or of consciousness, then he is practicing the perfection of wisdom. If he does not perceive any phenomenon, then he is practicing the perfection of wisdom. If he does not perceive any non-phenomenon, then he is practicing the perfection of wisdom. In this way, his cultivation of the perfection of wisdom becomes fully complete.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, this teaching is inconceivable.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, form is inconceivable. In the same way, feeling, perception, and formations are inconceivable, and, Subhūti, consciousness is inconceivable. Subhūti, if he does not even know that form is inconceivable, then he is practicing the perfection of wisdom. In the same way, if he does not even know that feeling, perception, and formations are inconceivable, and, Subhūti, that consciousness is inconceivable, then he is practicing the perfection of wisdom.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, who will have faith in this perfection of wisdom, which is so profound?

The Blessed One said: Śāriputra, whichever bodhisattva, great being, has become one who has practiced the perfection of wisdom, he will have faith in this perfection of wisdom.

The venerable Śāriputra asked: Blessed One, in what way is a bodhisattva, a great being, one who has practiced? Blessed One, in what way does he obtain the name "one who has practiced"?

The Blessed One said: Śāriputra, here a bodhisattva, a great being, has no conceptual thought about the powers, no conceptual thought about the fearlessnesses, no conceptual thought about the qualities of a buddha, and no conceptual thought even about omniscience. Why is that? Śāriputra, the powers are inconceivable, the fearlessnesses are also inconceivable, the qualities of a buddha are also inconceivable, omniscience is also inconceivable, and all phenomena are also inconceivable. Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has practiced in this way, and who does not dwell in anything at all, is practicing the perfection of wisdom. In that way he is called "one who has practiced," and he obtains the name "one who has practiced."

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One:

Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is a heap of jewels. Blessed One, because space is pure, the Perfection of Wisdom is a mass of purity. Blessed One, it is wonderful that when sons and daughters of good family take up this Perfection of Wisdom, hold it, read it, master it, recite it, teach it, explain it, give instruction in it, memorize it, and copy it down in writing, many obstacles arise for them.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, when sons or daughters of good family take up this Perfection of Wisdom, hold it, read it, master it, recite it, teach it, explain it, give instruction in it, memorize it, and copy it down in writing, many obstacles do arise. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because Māra the Evil One strives to create obstacles for those sons and daughters of good family who take up this Perfection of Wisdom, hold it, read it, master it, recite it, teach it, explain it, give instruction in it, memorize it, and write it down. Therefore they should write it quickly. Even if it will be requested to be written in one month, two months, or three months, they should still write it. And if it will be requested to be written after a year or more, even then, Subhūti, those sons or daughters of good family should write this Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that? Subhūti, it is just so: for anything that is a great and precious jewel, many obstacles arise.

When he had said this, the venerable Subhūti spoke to the Blessed One: Blessed One, when this Perfection of Wisdom is taken up, held, read, mastered, recited, taught, explained, given in instruction, memorized, and copied in writing, Māra the Evil One will give rise to many kinds of eagerness to act as an obstructer, and will make an effort to do so.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, although it is so that Māra the Evil One will strive to carry out the work of obstruction against those who take up, hold, read, master, recite, teach, explain, give instruction in, memorize, and copy down this Perfection of Wisdom, even so he cannot create obstacles for bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have not lost their commitment.

Then the venerable Śāriputra spoke to the Blessed One: Blessed One, at a time when Māra the Evil One becomes eager to create obstacles for sons and daughters of good family who take up, hold, read, master, recite, teach, explain, give instruction in, memorize, and copy down this Perfection of Wisdom, then, Blessed One, how will sons and daughters of good family in these times come to take up, hold, read, master, recite, teach, explain, give instruction in, memorize, and copy down this Perfection of Wisdom?

Blessed One, through whose power do those sons and daughters of good family come to hold this Perfection of Wisdom, to bear it in mind, to recite it, to master it fully, to read it aloud, to teach it, to explain it, to give its transmission, to recite it from memory, and to inquire into its written text?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Śāriputra as follows.

Śāriputra, it is through the power of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Tathāgatas, arhats, fully awakened buddhas, that those sons and daughters of good family come to hold this Perfection of Wisdom, to bear it in mind, to recite it, to master it fully, to read it aloud, to teach it, to explain it, to give its transmission, to recite it from memory, and to inquire into its written text; and they will also study it just as it is, practice it just as it is, and apply themselves to it in yoga just as it is.

Why is this so? Śāriputra, this is the nature of phenomena: in the immeasurable, innumerable world systems, whatever buddhas, Blessed Ones, are dwelling, living, and sustained, those buddhas keep in mind and take under their care those who hold this Perfection of Wisdom, who bear it in mind, recite it, master it fully, read it aloud, teach it, explain it, give its transmission, recite it from memory, and inquire into its written text.

Sons and daughters of good family who hold this Perfection of Wisdom, who expound it, recite it, master it fully, read it aloud, teach it, explain it, give its transmission, recite it from memory, and inquire into its written text, and who study it just as it is, practice it just as it is, and apply themselves to it in yoga just as it is: those too are kept in mind and taken under their care by those buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Śāriputra, no one is able to create obstacles for those sons and daughters of good family who are kept in mind by the buddhas and taken under the buddhas' care.

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, all those bodhisattvas, the great beings, who listen to this Perfection of Wisdom, hold it, bear it in mind, recite it, master it fully, read it aloud, teach it, explain it, give its transmission, recite it from memory, and inquire into its written text, and who study it just as it is, practice it just as it is, and apply themselves to it in yoga just as it is, will so practice through the power of the buddhas, through the blessing of the buddhas, and through being taken under the buddhas' care.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Śāriputra as follows: Śāriputra, so it is, so it is.

Śāriputra, all those bodhisattvas, those great beings, through the power of the buddhas, through the blessing of the buddhas, and through being embraced by the buddhas, will listen to this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and will hold it, bear it in mind, read it, master it fully, recite it, teach it, explain it, give transmission of it, memorize it, and have it written down in books. They will also train in accordance with suchness, practice in accordance with suchness, and apply themselves in yoga in accordance with suchness.

Śāriputra, those bodhisattvas, those great beings, who listen to this Perfection of Wisdom, hold it, bear it in mind, read it, master it fully, recite it, teach it, explain it, give transmission of it, memorize it, and have it written down in books, and who train in accordance with suchness, practice in accordance with suchness, and apply themselves in yoga in accordance with suchness, are known by the Tathāgata. Śāriputra, they are blessed by the Tathāgata. Śāriputra, they are seen by the Tathāgata. Śāriputra, they are looked upon by the Tathāgata with the buddha eye.

Having heard it, they hold it, bear it in mind, read it, master it fully, recite it, teach it, explain it, give transmission of it, memorize it, and write it down in books. Training in accordance with suchness, practicing in accordance with suchness, and applying themselves in yoga in accordance with suchness, they come near to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, and they will abide in unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening and in suchness.

Śāriputra, there will be those who write down this Perfection of Wisdom and hold it, read it, master it fully, recite it, teach it, explain it, give transmission of it, memorize it, and have it copied into books, but who do not train in accordance with suchness, do not practice in accordance with suchness, and do not apply themselves in yoga in accordance with suchness. Because they do not train, practice, and apply themselves in yoga in accordance with suchness, they will not come to abide in suchness and in unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. Even so, Śāriputra, those too are known by the Tathāgata; those too are blessed by the Tathāgata; those too are seen by the Tathāgata. Śāriputra, those too are looked upon by the Tathāgata with the buddha eye. Śāriputra, their effort and their exertion will also bring great benefit, great advantage, great results, and a great karmic maturation.

Why is this so? Because the Perfection of Wisdom is endowed with the ultimate meaning of all phenomena, and it abides close to all sentient beings so that they may realize things exactly as they are.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, these sūtras endowed with the six perfections will appear in the south when the Tathāgata has passed away and the time has come for the true Dharma to decline, when the Dharma and Vinaya have reached their essence and their last remnant. From the south they will go on to appear in Vartani. From Vartani they will appear again in the north.

Śāriputra, at that time, those sons and daughters of good family who take up, hold, read, comprehend, recite, teach, explain, expound, and memorize this Perfection of Wisdom, and who even set it down in a book and keep it, are regarded by the Tathāgata. They are known by the Tathāgata. Śāriputra, they are blessed by the Tathāgata. Śāriputra, they are seen by the Tathāgata. Śāriputra, they are beheld by the Tathāgata with the buddha eye.

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, will a Perfection of Wisdom as profound as this also flourish, in the later time, in the later age, in the northern country and the northern region?"

The Blessed One said: "Śāriputra, in that northern country and northern region, those who hear this profound Perfection of Wisdom and then practice it will cause it to flourish. Śāriputra, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who hear, ask about, hold, keep, read, comprehend, recite, teach, explain, expound, and memorize this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and who train in it just as it is, accomplish it just as it is, and practice it just as it is, should be understood to have set out well upon the vehicle long ago."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, in the northern country and northern region, how many will there be of those bodhisattvas, great beings, who hear, ask about, hold, keep, read, comprehend, recite, teach, explain, expound, and memorize this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and who train in it just as it is, accomplish it just as it is, and practice it just as it is? Will they be few, or will they be many? How many will there be?"

The Blessed One said: "Śāriputra, in the northern country and northern region there will be many bodhisattvas, great beings, very many indeed. Śāriputra, though they are many, among those many there will be very few bodhisattvas, great beings, who hear, ask about, hold, keep, read, comprehend, recite, teach, explain, expound, and memorize this Perfection of Wisdom, who train in it just as it is, accomplish it just as it is, and practice it just as it is, and who, when this Perfection of Wisdom is being taught, do not become stunned, do not become utterly discouraged, do not become timid, do not shrink back, do not turn their minds away, do not tremble, do not become utterly terrified, and are not gripped by utter terror. Those bodhisattvas, great beings, should be understood to have set out well upon the vehicle long ago."

They have followed the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas of the past, and have questioned them, inquired of them, and asked them repeatedly; those sons and daughters of good family who belong to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas have made offerings to the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas of the past. They will bring their moral discipline to complete fulfillment. Beginning from this very unsurpassed, perfect awakening, they will work for the benefit of many beings.

Why is this so? Because I myself have spoken with those sons and daughters of good family about matters connected with omniscience. Even when their lives change, they will practice rightly in this very way that is connected with omniscience and with the perfection of wisdom. Beginning from unsurpassed, perfect awakening, they will speak of it, and they will take delight in speaking of it. They will abide well in these, and they will rest in meditative equipoise in this perfection of wisdom, and Māra will not be able to divert them. How much less could other beings divert them by means of desire or by means of spells! Why is this so? Because their strength is firm in unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

When those sons and daughters of good family hear this, they will gain great joy, faith, and deep faith in this perfection of wisdom. Through them, the roots of virtue of many beings will be brought forth toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Why is this so? Because in my very presence those sons and daughters of good family spoke these words: "While I practice the conduct of a bodhisattva, I will establish many hundreds of living beings, many thousands of living beings, many hundreds of thousands of living beings, many millions of living beings, many thousands of millions, many hundreds of thousands of millions, and many hundreds of thousands of billions of living beings in unsurpassed, perfect awakening. I will instruct them, encourage them, praise them, bring joy to them, and clearly distinguish the path for them. I will make them abide in complete awakening. I will make them irreversible."

Why is this so? Looking into the minds of those sons and daughters of good family who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle, who spoke these words, I rejoiced in them. Thus those sons and daughters of good family are possessed of great aspiration, in the place where the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas, present before them, will teach the Dharma, and

In the buddha fields where this Perfection of Wisdom is heard extensively from the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, they will think of going to one buddha field after another. And in those buddha fields they will establish, instruct, set in place, praise, fill with joy, distinguish, and cause to awaken, and make irreversible in unsurpassed, perfect awakening many hundreds of living beings, many thousands of living beings, many hundreds of thousands of living beings, many hundreds of millions of living beings, many thousands of millions of living beings, many hundreds of thousands of millions of living beings, and many hundreds of thousands of billions of living beings.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, there is nothing in the dharmas of the past, the future, and the present that the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha has not seen, not heard, not directly known, or not fully known. There is no dharma that he does not fully know, and no conduct of sentient beings that he does not fully know. And, Blessed One, that you know the conduct of those future bodhisattvas, the great beings who seek awakening, who have perfect lofty intention and who have undertaken diligent effort, those who, at that time, hold, bear, recite, understand, thoroughly master, teach, explain, give instruction in, memorize, and write down this profound Perfection of Wisdom, is wonderful.

At that time, for the sake of these six perfections and for the sake of all sentient beings, they will generate diligence, and there are sons and daughters of good family who seek, search out, and go on seeking. Among these, some bodhisattvas who seek, search out, and go on seeking will find this profound Perfection of Wisdom when they seek it. Some, even though they seek it, will not find this profound Perfection of Wisdom. And some, even though they do not seek it, will find it. Blessed One, what is the cause of this?

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Śāriputra: So it is, Śāriputra, so it is. There is nothing among the dharmas of the past, the future, and the present that the Tathāgata has not seen, not heard, not known, or not fully known. Śāriputra, at that very time, some bodhisattvas will seek this Perfection of Wisdom, will seek it again and again, and will search it out thoroughly, yet will not find it. But some bodhisattvas, even though they do not seek it, do not seek it again and again, and do not search it out, will find it. Why is this? In the very distant past, those bodhisattvas sought and thoroughly searched out this Perfection of Wisdom without letting their diligence lapse. Therefore, through the very aspiration of the roots of virtue they formed in the past, they will find this Perfection of Wisdom even though they do not seek it, do not seek it again and again, and do not search it out.

Other sūtras as well, those that proclaim this very Perfection of Wisdom, will also come to them of their own accord, and will incline and turn toward them. Why is that? Śāriputra, it is like this: a bodhisattva, a great being, who seeks and thoroughly seeks this Perfection of Wisdom with unflagging diligence will, even after passing from this life into later lives, find this Perfection of Wisdom again. And the other sūtras that are accompanied by the Perfection of Wisdom will likewise come to that bodhisattva's side of their own accord, and will incline and turn toward him.

When this was said, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One: Blessed One, will only these sūtras, which are endowed with the six perfections, come to those sons and daughters of good family, and incline and turn toward them? Will others not do so?

The Blessed One said: Śāriputra, whatever other profound and deep sūtras there are, these also will come to those sons and daughters of good family of their own accord, and will incline and turn toward them. Why is that? Śāriputra, it is like this: those bodhisattvas, great beings, who establish beings in unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, who rightly teach them, rightly set them in it, rightly praise it to them, rightly bring them delight in it, rightly open it up for them, who bring them to abide in perfect awakening and make them irreversible, and who themselves train in it as well, Śāriputra, even after passing from this life, profound and deep sūtras that are endowed with non-apprehension, endowed with emptiness, and endowed with the six perfections will come to them of their own accord, will incline toward them of their own accord, and will turn toward them of their own accord.

This is the tenth chapter, called "Praise of the Qualities of Upholding," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, the eleventh volume.

Then the venerable Subhūti addressed the Blessed One: Blessed One, if the Blessed One speaks of these qualities of those sons and daughters of good family, then what manner of obstacles will arise for them?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, many deeds of Māra that create obstacles will arise.

Subhūti asked: Blessed One, what sorts of many deeds of Māra, obstructing and hindering them, will arise?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, for those bodhisattvas, great beings, who teach the Perfection of Wisdom, eloquence will arise only after a very long time. Subhūti, this should be recognized as the first deed of Māra. Subhūti, even when that eloquence does arise, it will become a cause of distraction, and this too should be recognized as a deed of Māra. Subhūti, if they become frivolous, boisterous and laughing, and are inquisitive about the letters, this too should be recognized as a deed of Māra. Subhūti, if they come to understand with a mind that is scattered and distracted, this too should be recognized as a deed of Māra.

Subhūti, if those who are writing it down question one another with their minds distracted by mutual consciousness, this too should be understood as the work of Māra. Subhūti, if they cannot hold the teaching in mind, this too should be understood as the work of Māra. Subhūti, if they laugh and joke with one another while writing it down, this too should be understood as the work of Māra. Subhūti, if they quarrel with one another while writing it down, this too should be understood as the work of Māra. Subhūti, if their eyes wander while they write, this too should be understood as the work of Māra. Subhūti, if those who are writing it down fall out with one another and cannot agree as a gathering, this too should be understood as the work of Māra.

Subhūti, if someone says, "I cannot fathom the depth of this, I cannot taste its flavor," and gets up from the seat and leaves, this too should be understood as the work of Māra. Subhūti, if someone gets up from the seat and goes away, without faith, thinking, "In this Perfection of Wisdom I have not been given any prophecy," this too should be understood as the work of Māra.

Subhūti, suppose someone thinks: "The name of the village, town, or city where I was born is not mentioned here. My own name and lineage are not mentioned here. The names and lineages of my father and mother are not mentioned here. The family into which I was born is not mentioned here." And so, deciding not to listen to the Perfection of Wisdom, he resolves to leave. As many as give rise to such thoughts, in whatever way they go off, in just that way, wherever they must again practice yoga, for that many eons they will be held fast in saṃsāra.

Why is that? Subhūti, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who do not listen to this Perfection of Wisdom will not become emancipated from worldly and transcendent phenomena. Subhūti, this too should be understood as their work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, there will be persons who belong to the bodhisattva vehicle who abandon and cast aside this Perfection of Wisdom, which accomplishes omniscient wisdom, and who think to seek out instead those sūtras that do not accomplish omniscient wisdom. Subhūti, this too should be understood as their work of Māra.

Subhūti, just as they do not wish to train in worldly and transcendent phenomena, and do not wish to become emancipated from worldly and transcendent phenomena, so too they do not train in this Perfection of Wisdom. Because they have not trained in this Perfection of Wisdom, they will not become emancipated from worldly and transcendent phenomena. Thus those of small intellect abandon and cast aside the Perfection of Wisdom, the root of fully knowing worldly and transcendent phenomena exactly as they are, and think to seek the branches.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a dog, giving up begging for scraps from its own master, were to think of seeking morsels from a servant. In the same way, Subhūti, in the future, in the final time, there will be certain persons of the bodhisattva vehicle who cast aside this root of omniscient wisdom, the Perfection of Wisdom, and think to seek the essence, buddhahood, from the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, which are like branches, leaves, and foliage. Subhūti, this too should be understood as the work of Māra for those bodhisattvas.

Why is that? Because those of small intellect do not know how this Perfection of Wisdom accomplishes omniscient wisdom.

Having abandoned and cast aside the Perfection of Wisdom, they will think of seeking, as something superior, whatever other sūtras show the stage of the śrāvakas and show the stage of the pratyekabuddhas. Bodhisattvas of this kind should be understood to have entered upon branches, leaves, and foliage.

Why is that? Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should not train in the way that persons of the śrāvaka vehicle and persons of the pratyekabuddha vehicle train.

Subhūti, how do persons of the śrāvaka vehicle and of the pratyekabuddha vehicle train? Subhūti, they think: "I alone shall be tamed. I alone shall be pacified. I alone shall pass completely beyond sorrow." For the sake of their own taming, their own pacification, and their own complete nirvāṇa alone, they undertake the practice of bringing about all roots of virtue. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should not train in that way.

Rather, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should train as follows: "For the benefit of the entire world, I shall myself abide in suchness, and I shall also establish all sentient beings in suchness. I shall lead the immeasurable realm of sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa." A bodhisattva, a great being, should undertake the practice of bringing about all roots of virtue in this way, and should not become conceited because of it.

Subhūti, suppose, for example, that there were a man who had never seen an elephant and went looking for the color and shape of an elephant. In the dark he came upon an elephant and judged it to be like whatever he felt of it. Having judged it so, he thought of searching for the elephant's trail, and thought of taking the color and shape of the elephant from the elephant's trail. Subhūti, what do you think? Would that man be of a skilled nature?

Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, in just the same way, there are persons of the bodhisattva vehicle who do not know this Perfection of Wisdom and do not ask about it, but abandon it. Though they wish to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, they think of seeking out those sūtras that show the stage of the śrāvakas and show the stage of the pratyekabuddhas. Such persons should be understood in this way. Subhūti, this too should be understood as their work of Māra.

Subhūti, suppose, for example, that there were a man in need of jewels who saw the great ocean. Without investigating, thinking about, or entering into the jewels there, he thought to search for the cause of jewels in a cow's hoofprint, and thought to make the cow's hoofprint equal to the great ocean. Subhūti, what do you think? Should that man be considered to be of a skilled nature?

Subhūti said: "No, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, in just the same way, there are persons of the bodhisattva vehicle who, even when they have found this Perfection of Wisdom, do not understand it, and, not knowing it, cast it aside. Wishing to remain with little effort, they think of seeking those sūtras that show the stage of the śrāvakas and show the stage of the pratyekabuddhas. Such persons should be understood in this way, wherever the bodhisattva vehicle has not been taught.

"I alone will be tamed, I alone will be pacified, I alone will pass completely into nirvāṇa." Thinking in this way, and settling the mind inward, they resolve: "I shall attain the fruit of the stream-enterer; I shall attain the fruit of the once-returner, the fruit of the non-returner, and the fruit of arhatship; I shall attain solitary awakening. In this very life, without clinging, I shall free my mind from the defilements and pass completely into nirvāṇa." Such an aspiration is said to belong to the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, great beings, should not give rise to the mind in this way. Why is that? Subhūti, bodhisattvas, great beings, have properly entered the Great Vehicle and put on the great armor. They never set their minds on a feeble enthusiasm. Why is that? Because these superior beings lead the world completely and work for the benefit of the world. Therefore they should always train well, without interruption, in the six perfections.

Furthermore, Subhūti, there are persons of the bodhisattva vehicle whose roots of virtue have not fully ripened, who are of small intelligence and weak in their higher intention. They do not know or comprehend the sūtras that are endowed with the six perfections. Abandoning and casting aside this Perfection of Wisdom, they think to seek out those sūtras that expound the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti, in the case of such persons of the bodhisattva vehicle who act in this way, this too should be recognized as the work of Māra.

Subhūti, it is as if a carpenter or a carpenter's apprentice wished to build and complete a house of the size of the Vaijayanta palace. He would go looking for the measure and the layout of the palace of the sun and moon. Having sought it, he would see the palace of the sun and moon and think to take its measurements as his own. Subhūti, what do you think? If he wished to build and complete a house of the size of the Vaijayanta palace, would he have to take the measure of the palace of the sun and moon?

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, he would not."

The Blessed One said: "In just the same way, Subhūti, in a future time there will be some persons of the bodhisattva vehicle who hear this Perfection of Wisdom and find this Perfection of Wisdom, yet abandon this Perfection of Wisdom and cast it aside. They think to seek omniscience from sūtras endowed with the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, from those sūtras that proclaim: 'I alone will be tamed; I alone will be pacified; I alone will pass completely into nirvāṇa.' They seek out sūtras in such a way, by which they alone attain taming, pacification, and nirvāṇa, and they think to train in that manner. Subhūti, what do you think? Should those bodhisattvas be recognized as skilled by nature?"

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, they should not."

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, this too should be recognized as the work of Māra on their part.

Subhūti, it is as if a certain man wished to see a wheel-turning king. He saw a wheel-turning king, and having seen him, he fixed in his mind the sign of his color, his form, his splendor, and his miraculous power, thinking, 'He is like this.' Then, if he were to see a ruler of a fortress, he would take the color, form, splendor, miraculous power, and signs of that ruler of a fortress,

Since they cannot tell the particulars apart, they say, "That wheel-turning king looks just like this: such is his color, form, splendor, miraculous power, and appearance." Subhūti, what do you think? Should a person who thinks to equate the wheel-turning king with the king of a city be regarded as wise by nature?

Subhūti said, "Certainly not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said, "In just the same way, Subhūti, in a future time there will be persons following the bodhisattva vehicle who hear this Perfection of Wisdom and obtain it, and yet abandon the Perfection of Wisdom, cast it aside, hold it at a distance, and think to seek omniscience in sūtras that belong to the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti, this too should be understood as the work of māra for them.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, I do not say that bodhisattvas, great beings, should seek omniscience in these sūtras connected with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Rather, Subhūti, unless bodhisattvas, great beings, train in the skillful means of bodhisattvas, great beings, that the Tathāgata has taught in the Perfection of Wisdom, they will not come forth definitively toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Why is that? Because in other sūtras it is difficult for a bodhisattva to be truly accomplished.

"Therefore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, seeing the benefits of the Perfection of Wisdom correctly, in many ways truly teaches this Perfection of Wisdom to bodhisattvas, great beings, truly establishes them in it, truly praises it, truly delights them in it, truly engages them in it, and truly sets them firmly in it. In this way bodhisattvas, great beings, become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

"Subhūti, what do you think? Suppose some, having obtained and accomplished the irreversible vehicle, the Great Vehicle, abandon it and think to seek the lesser vehicle. Would those bodhisattvas too be wise by nature?"

Subhūti said, "Certainly not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a hungry man found a food with a hundred flavors, nourishing, delicious, one that would end hunger and thirst for the rest of his life. He casts it aside and thinks to seek rice of sixty days' keeping, and having found that rice, he casts aside the food of a hundred flavors and thinks to eat the sixty-day rice. Subhūti, what do you think? Would that man be wise by nature?"

Subhūti said, "Certainly not, Blessed One."

The Blessed One said, "In just the same way, Subhūti, in a future time there will be some bodhisattvas who hear this Perfection of Wisdom and obtain it, and yet abandon the Perfection of Wisdom, cast it aside, hold it at a distance, and think to seek sūtras connected with the vehicle of the śrāvakas and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas,

If they should think to seek omniscience and skillful means in those sūtras that set forth the grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, Subhūti, what do you think? Should those bodhisattvas also be regarded as skilled by nature?

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, they should not."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, this too should be recognized as their work of Māra. Subhūti, it is as if a certain man had found a priceless jewel and thought to put it on a par with a jewel of small value and little worth. Subhūti, what do you think? Should that man be regarded as skilled by nature?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, he should not."

The Blessed One said, "In the same way, Subhūti, in the future there will be certain individuals of the Bodhisattva Vehicle who, having heard and found this profound, luminous, precious Perfection of Wisdom, will think to put it on a par with the vehicle of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. They will think to seek omniscience and skillful means from the grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti, what do you think? Should those bodhisattvas also be regarded as skilled by nature?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, they should not."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, this too should be recognized as the work of Māra for those bodhisattvas.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, as they explain, teach, and demonstrate this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and as they hold it, retain it, read it, give transmission of it, recite it from memory, and, while they are still young, inquire into it in writing, many obstacles will arise that distract the mind. Subhūti, this too should be recognized as the work of Māra for those bodhisattvas."

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, can the Perfection of Wisdom be written down in letters?"

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, it cannot. Subhūti, there may be those who, having written the Perfection of Wisdom in letters, think that they have written the Perfection of Wisdom, or say that it does not exist, or cling to the Perfection of Wisdom as being in the letters, or think that without letters there is none. Subhūti, this too should be recognized as their work of Māra.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, as they inquire into the Perfection of Wisdom in writing, thoughts about places will arise. Thoughts will arise about villages, towns, market towns, regions, provinces, and royal palaces and courts. Thoughts will arise about parks and pleasure groves. Thoughts will arise about teachers. Thoughts will arise about those who instruct in everything. Thoughts will arise about bandits. Thoughts will arise about predators. Thoughts will arise about Viśikhā. Thoughts will arise about Śivika. Thoughts will arise about prostitutes. Thoughts will arise about happiness, thoughts about suffering, and thoughts about fear. Thoughts will arise about women, thoughts about men, and thoughts about those who are neither. Thoughts will arise about those who are friendly and those who are unfriendly. Thoughts will arise about parents."

Thoughts about brothers and sisters will arise. Thoughts about relatives and friends will arise, and thoughts about companions, kinsfolk, and blood relations. Thoughts about wife, sons, and daughters will arise. Thoughts about house, food, and drink will arise, and thoughts about clothing, about bedding and seats, about the requisites of livelihood, and about immediate tasks. Thoughts of attachment will arise, thoughts of aversion, and thoughts of delusion. Thoughts about the seasons will arise, about auspicious times and inauspicious times. Thoughts about songs, about cymbals, and about dance will arise, and thoughts about poetry, lyrics, and stories. Thoughts about treatises will arise, about worldly conventions, about laughter and jesting, and about flirtation. Thoughts of sorrow will arise, thoughts of the afflictions, and thoughts of the self.

Subhūti, these thoughts and others like them are brought about by the evil Māra, and they will become obstacles and distractions for the bodhisattva, the great being, when he explains this Perfection of Wisdom, teaches it, instructs others in it, upholds it, retains it, reads it, gives the oral transmission of it, recites it, and even when he questions about it in writing. The bodhisattva, the great being, should recognize these deeds of Māra, and having recognized them, should abandon them.

Furthermore, Subhūti, thoughts about kings will arise, thoughts about princes, about elephants, about horses, about chariots, and about the sight of the amusements of the handed, the sporting entertainers. Subhūti, these too should be recognized as the deeds of Māra for those bodhisattvas, those great beings.

Furthermore, Subhūti, thoughts about fire will arise, thoughts about objects of desire, and thoughts about the abundance of wealth and grain. Subhūti, these too should be recognized by the bodhisattva, the great being, as the deeds of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, while the bodhisattva, the great being, explains this Perfection of Wisdom, teaches it, instructs others in it, gives the oral transmission of it, recites it, and even questions about it in writing, gains, honors, robes, alms food, bedding and seats, medicines for the sick, and other requisites may come to him, but they become an obstacle to him. Then, as he tastes the flavor of gains, honors, and praises in verse, torment may arise in his mind. Subhūti, these too should be recognized by bodhisattvas, great beings, as the deeds of Māra. They should recognize all these deeds of Māra, and having recognized them, they should abandon them.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when bodhisattvas, great beings, explain this Perfection of Wisdom, teach it, instruct others in it, give the oral transmission of it, recite it, and even question about it in writing, the evil Māra may come in the guise of a monk and offer them whatever profound sūtras there are that belong to the level of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. He says: "Train in this. Write this down. Receive the transmission of this. Memorize this. From this, omniscience will be attained." Subhūti, the bodhisattva, the great being, skilled in means, should not take delight in them. Why is that? Subhūti, although it is true that those sūtras do teach emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness,

Moreover, in those sūtras the skillful means of the bodhisattva, the great being, is not taught. Those bodhisattvas who do not clearly know the distinctions within the wisdom of skillful means will think to abandon this profound Perfection of Wisdom. Having abandoned this profound Perfection of Wisdom, they will think to seek skillful means in sūtras connected with the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti, this should be recognized by the bodhisattva, the great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the listeners of the Dharma are keen and wish to take up the Perfection of Wisdom, but the Dharma speaker is lazy and does not wish to teach the Dharma. Subhūti, this lack of harmony should be recognized by the bodhisattva, the great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the Dharma speaker is not lazy and wishes to give the Perfection of Wisdom, but the listener to the Dharma is lazy and has many tasks to attend to. Subhūti, this lack of harmony should be recognized by the bodhisattva, the great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the listeners of the Dharma are keen and wish to take up, to hold, to read, to master, and to recite the Perfection of Wisdom, and even wish to write it down, and they are endowed with comprehension, intelligence, and mindfulness. But the Dharma speaker is about to go to another region, or is unable to grasp the text from its very beginning, or elaborates it in a confused way and so does not understand it, or does not clearly know it. Subhūti, for the one who would explain, teach, point out, and give prophecies concerning this Perfection of Wisdom, who would recite it, study it, and even write it down, there will be a lack of harmony. Subhūti, this should be recognized by the bodhisattva, the great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the Dharma speaker is not lazy and clearly knows the meaning, and wishes to give this Perfection of Wisdom and to have it read. But the listener to the Dharma is about to go to another region, or cannot grasp the text from its very beginning, or elaborates it in a confused way and so does not understand it, or does not clearly know it. Subhūti, this lack of harmony should be recognized by the bodhisattva, the great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the Dharma speaker is intent on wealth, intent on gain and honor, intent on robes, while the listener to the Dharma has few desires and is content, delights in solitude, and does not wish to give away wealth. Subhūti, for the one who would train in and write out this Perfection of Wisdom, there will be a lack of harmony. Subhūti, this should be recognized by the bodhisattva, the great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the listener to the Dharma has faith and wishes to hear this Perfection of Wisdom, to fully grasp its meaning, and to give up all wealth, but the Dharma speaker has no faith, or does not wish to accept wealth, or has few desires, or does not wish to speak. Subhūti, this too, because of the lack of harmony, should be recognized as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the listener to the Dharma has faith, wishes to listen, and wishes to fully grasp the meaning, but the Dharma speaker has become an obstacle to the Dharma, so that those sūtras are lacking or he does not engage with them. Subhūti, because of this too, the listener to the Dharma, not finding a Dharma speaker, will fall into discord.

Subhūti, if someone has heard this Perfection of Wisdom and is holding it, retaining it, reading it, or writing it down, and he is not provided with a gathering, then this too should be recognized by a bodhisattva, a great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the Dharma speaker wishes to explain, but the Dharma listeners do not wish to listen. Then, Subhūti, the one who has heard this Perfection of Wisdom and holds it, retains it, reads it, or writes it down is not provided with a gathering. This too should be recognized by a bodhisattva, a great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the Dharma listeners become very sleepy and their bodies heavy, and, being possessed of that sleepiness and that bodily torpor, they do not wish to listen, while the Dharma speaker does wish to explain. Then, Subhūti, there is no gathering. This should be recognized by a bodhisattva, a great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose the Dharma speaker becomes very sleepy and his body heavy, and, being possessed of that sleepiness and that bodily torpor, he does not wish to explain, while the Dharma listeners do wish to listen. Then, Subhūti, the writing, reading, and full understanding of this text are not provided with a gathering. This too should be recognized by a bodhisattva, a great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose that while the Perfection of Wisdom is being written down, explained, and studied, someone comes there and speaks of the faults of the beings in the hells, speaks of the faults of the animal realm, speaks of the faults of the realm of hungry ghosts, and speaks of the faults of the body of an asura. He says: "The beings in the hells suffer in this way. The animal realm is a place of suffering in this way. The realm of hungry ghosts is a place of suffering in this way. The realm of the asuras is a place of suffering in this way. Conditioned things are suffering in this way. So bring suffering to its end right here." Then, Subhūti, this should be recognized by a bodhisattva, a great being, as the work of Māra, since it is not provided with a gathering.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose that while the Perfection of Wisdom is being written down, explained, and studied, someone comes there and speaks in praise of the gods. He says: "The gods are happy in this way. The higher realms are happy in this way. In the desire realm one enjoys desires in this way. In the form realm one rests in meditative concentrations in this way. In the formless absorptions one rests in equipoise in this way." And he says: "If everything is examined with wisdom, all birth is suffering. Even the Blessed One said: 'Monks, I do not praise any rebirth, not even one as brief as a fingersnap, as something that can be achieved.' All conditioned things are impermanent. All that has gone into existence is suffering. All that belongs to the three realms is empty. All phenomena are without self. Having recognized all these as unstable, impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, the wise should attain right here the fruit of stream-entry. They should attain the fruit of the once-returner and the fruit of the non-returner, and right here they should fully attain arhatship. Otherwise we may again meet with the ruin of wealth and the decline into those many sufferings." If in this way he makes some bodhisattvas weary and disheartened, then, Subhūti, this too should be recognized by a bodhisattva, a great being, as the work of Māra, since it is not provided with a gathering.

Subhūti, furthermore, there may be a Dharma teacher, a monk, who delights in being alone, while those who listen to the Dharma are devoted to a retinue. And that Dharma teacher may say, "To those who attend on me, I will give this Perfection of Wisdom; to those who do not attend on me, I will not give it." Then those sons and daughters of good family, longing for the Dharma, wishing for it and respecting it, may attend on the Dharma teacher, yet he does not give them the opportunity. The Dharma teacher desires only a small amount of material goods, and even that he is unwilling to give up. Moreover, he will go to wherever there is famine, or lack of success and happiness, or danger to life. When those who listen to the Dharma hear from others that famine has struck that region, that there is no success or happiness there, and that it is also dangerous to life, they should understand it so. Then the Dharma teacher may say to those sons of good family, "Sons of good family, in such and such a region there is the terror of famine. Son of good family, if you go there, you will regret it afterward because of the terror of famine." In this way the Dharma teacher turns them away by subtle means. They too become disheartened and understand thus: "These are signs of rejection; they are not signs of willingness to give. He does not wish to give this." Knowing this, they do not attend on him. In this way, for one who asks about this Perfection of Wisdom, studies it, teaches it, expounds it, gives its transmission, and recites it, there is a lack of harmony. Subhūti, this too should be recognized as the work of Māra by the bodhisattva, the great being.
