Subhūti, furthermore, that Dharma teacher may enter a place where there is the danger of living creatures, or the danger of beasts of prey, or the danger of non-humans; he goes there or stays there. He may go to a wilderness of beasts of prey, a wilderness of poisonous snakes, a wilderness of robbers, a wilderness of water, or a wilderness of famine. And he says to those who listen to the Dharma, "Sons of good family, understand this: I am going to a land where there is danger from living creatures, danger from beasts of prey, danger from flesh-eaters, a wilderness of poisonous snakes, a wilderness of robbers, a wilderness of water, a wilderness of famine. Sons of good family, understand this. Are you able to endure these sufferings?" Saying this, he turns them away by subtle means. Then they too become disheartened. Disheartened, they do not attend on him and turn back. Subhūti, these obstacles will arise for the giving of the transmission of the Perfection of Wisdom, for its recitation, and even for its writing down. Subhūti, this too, because of the lack of harmony, should be recognized as the work of Māra by the bodhisattva, the great being.

Subhūti, furthermore, a Dharma teacher, a monk, may become fixated on the houses of his friends and the houses of those who give alms. Being fixated on the houses of friends and almsgivers, he constantly thinks of going near to look at those houses. Because of his constant looking, he has much to do, and so he abandons those who listen to the Dharma, saying, "For now there is something I must look in on."

If he says, "I have something I must attend to, I have to go," then, Subhūti, he becomes one who lacks the gathering needed for writing out and understanding this Perfection of Wisdom. Subhūti, this too should be recognized by a bodhisattva, a great being, as the work of Māra: a lack of the necessary gathering.

Subhūti, in this way the evil Māra strives by every such means so that no one at all will take up this Perfection of Wisdom, or hold it, or read it, or fully comprehend it, or recite it thoroughly, or teach it, or explain it, or give transmission of it, or learn it by heart, or write it down, or have it written. Therefore, Subhūti, whatever obstacles there are, whatever causes a lack of the necessary gathering, a bodhisattva, a great being, should recognize all of them as the work of Māra, and having recognized them, should abandon them.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, for what reason does the evil Māra strive so hard, and apply every means, so that no one at all will take up this Perfection of Wisdom, or hold it, or read it, or fully comprehend it, or recite it thoroughly, or teach it, or explain it, or give transmission of it, or learn it by heart, or write it down, or have it written?

When he had said this, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, the omniscience of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is born from the Perfection of Wisdom. The teaching of the Tathāgatas arises from omniscience. And from the teaching of the Tathāgatas comes the abandoning of afflictions by immeasurable, countless, inconceivable beings. For one who has abandoned the afflictions, the evil Māra finds no opening. Finding none, his mind is tormented by suffering, he is unhappy, and the dart of sorrow pierces him to the heart.

For this reason he takes great displeasure in anyone writing out, fully comprehending, or studying the Perfection of Wisdom, and he exerts himself with great effort and vigor, applying every means, so that no one at all will write out, fully comprehend, or study this Perfection of Wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the evil Māra will come in the guise of a renunciant and cause division. Subhūti, he will separate in this way those sons of good family who are newly set out in the Great Vehicle as bodhisattvas, who are of small intelligence, weak intelligence, inferior intelligence, who are dull, and who have not been given a prediction of unsurpassed, perfect awakening. He says: "Venerable one, what you hear is not the Perfection of Wisdom. Rather, only what is included within my sūtras, only what belongs among my sūtras, is the Perfection of Wisdom." Subhūti, in this way the evil Māra makes them doubt, and causes them to abandon it.

Subhūti, in just this way the evil Māra, coming in the guise of a renunciant and creating division, makes doubt arise in bodhisattvas who are newly set out in the Great Vehicle, who are of small, weak, and inferior intelligence, who are dull, and who have not been given a prediction of unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Being thrown into doubt, they will not take up this Perfection of Wisdom, will not hold it, will not read it, will not fully understand it, will not recite it, will not teach it or explain it to others, will not give instruction in it, will not memorize it, will not copy it, and will not have it copied. Subhūti, this too should be recognized by a bodhisattva, a great being, as the work of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the evil Māra may take the form of a monk and come in the guise of a buddha. Concerning a bodhisattva who practices the profound teachings, he will say: "This one is realizing the true limit, and so he will become a śrāvaka and will not become a bodhisattva." And he will give an example, saying: "A bodhisattva is just like this." In this way he brings about the work of Māra. Subhūti, this too should be recognized by a bodhisattva, a great being, as the work of Māra.

Subhūti, in this way, as people copy, fully understand, and study this Perfection of Wisdom, the evil Māra will bring about many further works of Māra, one after another. A bodhisattva, a great being, should recognize these, and having recognized them, should abandon them completely and should not rely on them. Rather, he should undertake diligence and should be endowed with mindfulness and vigilance.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to him: "So it is, Blessed One. So it is, Sugata. Blessed One, those who possess great and precious jewels have many enemies. Why is that? Blessed One, it is because such jewels are hard to find and very precious. They are treasures, and therefore those who hold them come to have many enemies. In just the same way, Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom too will for the most part meet with many obstacles.

"Blessed One, under the power of these obstacles some will become lazy. And those bodhisattvas who think of not taking up this Perfection of Wisdom, of not holding it, not reading it, not fully understanding it, not reciting it, not teaching it, not explaining it, not giving instruction in it, not memorizing it, not copying it, and who think of not even having it copied in small part, should be known as those whom Māra has empowered. Blessed One, they are newly set out in the Vehicle. They are of small intellect, of inferior intellect, of weak intellect. Blessed One, their intellects are inverted, and their minds do not enter the vast and extensive teachings. This too should be recognized."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Those bodhisattvas who think of not taking up this Perfection of Wisdom, of not holding it, not reading it, not fully understanding it, not reciting it, not teaching it, not explaining it, not giving instruction in it, not memorizing it, not copying it, and who think of not even having it copied in small part, should be recognized, Subhūti, as those whom Māra has empowered. Subhūti, those bodhisattvas are newly set out in the Vehicle. They are of small intellect. They are of inferior intellect. They are of weak intellect."

Subhūti, these bodhisattvas are those whose minds are inverted, and in that way they will not turn their minds to the vast and great phenomena of the Dharma.

Subhūti, in this way too the works of Māra will arise, and many faults of Māra and many obstructions will appear. Yet even so, Subhūti, when any of them think of upholding this Perfection of Wisdom, of bearing it in mind, reading it, mastering it, reciting it, teaching it, expounding it, giving its transmission, memorizing it, writing it down, or, even if they are of lesser capacity, think of having it written down, then, Subhūti, it should be understood that this is through the power of the buddhas, through the blessing of the buddhas, and through being held by the buddhas, that they uphold it, bear it in mind, read it, master it, recite it, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, memorize it, write it down, or cause it to be written down. Why is that? Because the evil Māra makes great effort to create obstacles here, and the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, in holding it, also make great effort.

This is the eleventh chapter, called "The Works of Māra," from the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, the twelfth volume.

Then the Blessed One again spoke to the venerable Subhūti. Subhūti, suppose, for example, that a certain woman has many sons, five, or ten, or twenty, or thirty, or forty, or fifty, or a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand. If their mother should fall ill, they would all strive and exert themselves, thinking: "May our mother by no means come to any danger to her life. May our mother live a long life. May our mother's body by no means become unwell. May our mother remain for a long time. May our mother by no means become weakened. May no painful feeling arise in our mother. May nothing here be unknown to her, and may nothing disagreeable arise in her body." Why is that? Because they think: "She bore us. She did the hard work of giving us life. She showed us the world." So, so that no painful feeling or painful contact at all should arise in her, those sons carefully take hold of the mother by every means of bringing her comfort, carefully guard her, and carefully tend her. They think: "May no wind, bile, phlegm, or combination of the humors, no bee, no gadfly, no snake, no human or non-human being, no falling thing, no calamity, no sudden misfortune, nothing undesired, arise in her body." In this way those sons, reflecting on their mother, tend her and protect her, and make her their own, by every means of bringing her comfort, saying: "She is our mother who bore us, who rejoiced in doing so. She is the one who gave us life and showed us the world."

Subhūti, in the same way the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, also have this Perfection of Wisdom in mind. All those who write it down, uphold it, bear it in mind, read it, master it, recite it, teach it, expound it, give its transmission, and memorize it, all of them, too, come about through the power, the blessing, and the intention of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas.

In other world systems, whatever Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas there may be who are presently living and sustained for the benefit of many beings, for the happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, and out of compassion for gods, humans, and all sentient beings, all of them, too, hold this very Perfection of Wisdom in mind. Through their power they see to it that this Perfection of Wisdom will endure for a long time, that the name of this Perfection of Wisdom will not perish, and that no evil Māra, nor any gods of Māra's host, will become an obstacle to those who expound it, write it down, or study it.

Subhūti, in this way the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas also care for this Perfection of Wisdom, make it their own, and guard it. Why is that? Because this is the mother of the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas; it gives them birth, it shows omniscience, it shows it throughout the world.

Subhūti, the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas are born from this. Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom gives rise to the wisdom of omniscience in the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas, and shows it. In this way it shows it throughout this world. Subhūti, the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas is born from this.

Subhūti, in past times, all the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas who fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening did so by relying on this very Perfection of Wisdom. In future times, all the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas who will arise and attain complete buddhahood in unsurpassed, perfect awakening will do so by relying on this very Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, at the present time, in the immeasurable and innumerable world systems of the ten directions, there are Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas who live and are sustained for the benefit of many beings, for the happiness of many beings, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, and out of compassion for gods, humans, and all sentient beings. All of them, too, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening by relying on this very Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, I too, the Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly awakened buddha, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening by relying on this very Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, in this way the Perfection of Wisdom gives rise to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, and thus it is what shows the world.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, you have said that the Perfection of Wisdom shows the world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas. Blessed One, how does the Perfection of Wisdom show the world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas? Blessed One, what is it that the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, has spoken of as the world?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows: "Subhūti, the Tathāgata has spoken of the five aggregates as the world. Which five? They are form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. Subhūti, these five aggregates are what the Tathāgata has called the world."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, how does the Perfection of Wisdom teach the five aggregates to the Tathāgata? Blessed One, what does the Perfection of Wisdom teach?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows: "Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom teaches the Tathāgatas that the five aggregates are the world because they are indestructible and utterly indestructible."

"Why is it taught that they are indestructible and utterly indestructible? Subhūti, because the five aggregates have no intrinsic nature, their intrinsic nature is emptiness. Subhūti, emptiness is neither destroyed nor utterly destroyed. Thus, Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom shows this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas.

"Subhūti, the signless, the wishless, the unconditioned, the unarisen, the nonexistent, and the dharmadhātu are indestructible and utterly indestructible. Thus, Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom shows this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata fully knows, correctly and just as it is, that sentient beings are immeasurable and sentient beings are innumerable.

"Subhūti, how is it that, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata fully knows, correctly and just as it is, that sentient beings are immeasurable and sentient beings are innumerable? Subhūti, because sentient beings have no intrinsic nature, the Tathāgata fully knows, correctly and just as it is, that sentient beings are immeasurable and innumerable. Thus, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata fully knows, correctly and just as it is, the immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, because sentient beings are without any real entity, the Tathāgata also fully knows the workings of the minds of those immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings. Thus, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata fully knows, correctly and just as it is, the immeasurable and innumerable workings of the minds of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings."

Subhūti, in this way the Perfection of Wisdom reveals this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly and completely awakened buddhas.

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, "These are the minds of immeasurable, innumerable sentient beings, and these minds are contracted." How, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know exactly as it is that the contracted minds of immeasurable, innumerable sentient beings are contracted? He knows exactly as it is that the contracted mind, together with its contraction, is exhausted, and that even its exhaustion is inexhaustible. In this way, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is that the contracted minds of immeasurable beings are contracted.

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, "These are the minds of immeasurable beings, and these minds are distracted." How, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know exactly as it is that the distracted minds of immeasurable beings are distracted? Subhūti, in the nature of reality those minds that are distracted have no defining characteristic. Those minds are inexhaustible and utterly inexhaustible; they are not distracted. The Tathāgata knows those minds exactly as they are. In this way, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is that the distracted minds of immeasurable beings are distracted.

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, "These are the minds of immeasurable, innumerable sentient beings, and in these immeasurable and inexhaustible minds, the mind is immeasurable and inexhaustible." How, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know exactly as it is that, in the immeasurable and inexhaustible minds of immeasurable, innumerable sentient beings, the mind is immeasurable and inexhaustible? Subhūti, because the mind is immeasurable and inexhaustible like space, one who knows exactly as it is that the mind is immeasurable and inexhaustible has a mind that is blessed by the Tathāgata. It is without cessation, without arising, without abiding, without support, immeasurable, and inexhaustible. In this way, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is that, in the immeasurable and inexhaustible minds of immeasurable, innumerable sentient beings, the mind is immeasurable and inexhaustible.

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, "These are the minds of immeasurable beings, and these minds are afflicted." How, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know exactly as it is that the afflicted minds of immeasurable beings are afflicted?

Subhūti, those minds are not afflicted by affliction, and there is no designation for them. In just this way, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows as it truly is, "The afflicted minds of immeasurable beings are afflicted minds."

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows as it truly is, "The unafflicted minds of immeasurable beings are unafflicted minds."

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know as it truly is that the unafflicted minds of immeasurable beings are unafflicted minds? Subhūti, those minds are luminous by their intrinsic nature. In just this way, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows as it truly is, "The unafflicted minds of immeasurable beings are unafflicted minds."

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows as it truly is, "The abiding minds of immeasurable beings are abiding minds."

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know as it truly is that the abiding minds of immeasurable beings are abiding minds? Subhūti, those minds abide in what has no ground. In just this way, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows as it truly is, "The abiding minds of immeasurable beings are abiding minds."

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows as it truly is, "The grasping minds of immeasurable beings are grasping minds."

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know as it truly is that the grasping minds of immeasurable beings are grasping minds? Subhūti, those minds are not grasped, and they are not something that is to be grasped. In just this way, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows as it truly is, "The grasping minds of immeasurable beings are grasping minds."

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows as it truly is, "The minds with defilement of immeasurable beings are minds with defilement."

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know as it truly is that the minds with defilement of immeasurable beings are minds with defilement? Subhūti, those minds have no essential nature and are like what does not exist.

Subhūti, in this way, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are with outflows are minds with outflows.

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are without outflows are minds without outflows.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are without outflows are minds without outflows? Subhūti, those minds are inclined toward the absence of real entities, and this is spontaneously accomplished. Subhūti, in this way, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are without outflows are minds without outflows.

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are with attachment are minds with attachment.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are with attachment are minds with attachment? Subhūti, the attachment that a mind has is not the true suchness of the mind. And the true suchness of the mind is not a mind with attachment. Subhūti, in this way, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are with attachment are minds with attachment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are free of attachment are minds free of attachment.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are free of attachment are minds free of attachment? Subhūti, the freedom of the mind is not itself a mind with attachment. And the true suchness of the mind that is free of attachment is not a mind with attachment. Subhūti, in this way, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are free of attachment are minds free of attachment.

Furthermore, Subhūti, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, the Tathāgata knows, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are with aversion are minds with aversion.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know, exactly as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are with aversion are minds with aversion?

Subhūti, the mind that has aversion is not the very suchness of mind. And the very suchness of mind is not a mind that has aversion. Subhūti, it is thus that the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who have aversion are minds that have aversion.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are free of aversion are minds that are free of aversion.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are free of aversion are minds that are free of aversion? Subhūti, the freedom of the mind is not a state of having aversion. And the very suchness of the mind that is free of aversion is not a mind that has aversion. Subhūti, it is thus that the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are free of aversion are minds that are free of aversion.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who have delusion are minds that have delusion.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who have delusion are minds that have delusion? Subhūti, the mind that has delusion is not the very suchness of mind. And the very suchness of mind is not a mind that has delusion. Subhūti, it is thus that the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who have delusion are minds that have delusion.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are free of delusion are minds that are free of delusion.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are free of delusion are minds that are free of delusion? Subhūti, the freedom of the mind is not a state of having delusion. And the very suchness of the mind that is free of delusion is not a mind that has delusion. Subhūti, it is thus that the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings who are free of delusion are minds that are free of delusion.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, that the minds of immeasurable beings whose minds are not expansive are minds that are not expansive.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are not vast are not vast? Subhūti, those minds are without the arising of motivation; they are included within the absence of motivation. Subhūti, in just this way the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are not vast are not vast.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are vast are vast. Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are vast are vast? Subhūti, those minds do not diminish and do not increase, and because minds are never separated from their nature, those minds are not separated at all. Subhūti, in just this way the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are vast are vast.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that have not become exalted are not exalted. Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that have not become exalted are not exalted? Subhūti, those minds are nothing other than being without coming and without going. Subhūti, in just this way the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that have not become exalted are not exalted.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that have become exalted are exalted. Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that have become exalted are exalted? Subhūti, those minds are equal through equality; they are equal by their very nature. Subhūti, in just this way the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that have become exalted are exalted.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, knows in accordance with reality, as it truly is, that the minds of immeasurable sentient beings that are measureless are measureless.

Subhūti, how is it that the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the immeasurable minds of immeasurable beings are immeasurable minds? Subhūti, those minds are immeasurable minds because they have no support. In just this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the immeasurable minds of immeasurable beings are immeasurable minds.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that can be shown are minds that can be shown. Subhūti, how is it that the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that can be shown are minds that can be shown? Subhūti, those minds are shown to be equal to the essential nature of mind. In just this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that can be shown are minds that can be shown.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that cannot be shown are minds that cannot be shown. Subhūti, how is it that the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that cannot be shown are minds that cannot be shown? Subhūti, because it has no defining characteristic and is empty of any real object, that mind does not appear; it does not become manifest to the three eyes, nor to any of them. In just this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that cannot be shown are minds that cannot be shown.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that have obstruction are minds that have obstruction. Subhūti, how is it that the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that have obstruction are minds that have obstruction? Subhūti, those minds are imputed onto what does not exist; they are empty, and come within the range of what is apprehended. In just this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that have obstruction are minds that have obstruction.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that are without obstruction are minds that are without obstruction. Subhūti, how is it that the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows correctly, exactly as it is, that the minds of immeasurable beings that are without obstruction are minds that are without obstruction? Subhūti, in just this way the Tathāgata knows it correctly, exactly as it is.

Subhūti, those minds have become non-dual; they have not arisen, and yet they have fully arisen. Subhūti, in this way the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows perfectly and exactly as it is that the unobstructed minds of immeasurable sentient beings are unobstructed minds.

Subhūti, furthermore, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows perfectly and exactly as it is that the surpassable minds of immeasurable sentient beings are surpassable minds. Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know perfectly and exactly as it is that the surpassable minds of immeasurable sentient beings are surpassable minds? Subhūti, whatever the surpassable mind is, exactly as it is, regarding that there is no conceit.

Subhūti, furthermore, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows perfectly and exactly as it is that the surpassable minds of immeasurable sentient beings are surpassable minds.

Subhūti, furthermore, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows perfectly and exactly as it is that the unsurpassable minds of immeasurable sentient beings are unsurpassable minds. Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know perfectly and exactly as it is that the unsurpassable minds of immeasurable sentient beings are unsurpassable minds? Subhūti, those minds are free of conceptual elaboration, because not even a subtle particle of mind is apprehended. Subhūti, in this way the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows perfectly and exactly as it is that the unsurpassable minds of immeasurable sentient beings are unsurpassable minds.

Subhūti, furthermore, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows perfectly and exactly as it is that the unconcentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings are unconcentrated minds. Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know perfectly and exactly as it is that the unconcentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings are unconcentrated minds? Subhūti, those minds engage in the unequal through the equal and the equal through the unequal, and in that way the mind is unconcentrated. Subhūti, in this way the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows perfectly and exactly as it is that the unconcentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings are unconcentrated minds.

Subhūti, furthermore, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows perfectly and exactly as it is that the concentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings are concentrated minds. Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know perfectly and exactly as it is that the concentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings are concentrated minds? Subhūti, those minds engage the equal through the equal, and those minds that are concentrated in this way are like space. Subhūti, in this way the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows perfectly and exactly as it is that the concentrated minds of immeasurable sentient beings are concentrated minds.

Subhūti, furthermore, relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, in the right way, the unliberated minds of immeasurable beings: "These are unliberated minds."

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know exactly as it is, in the right way, the unliberated minds of immeasurable beings: "These are unliberated minds"? Subhūti, those minds are by their intrinsic nature already liberated; their nature is to have no inherent identity. Thus, Subhūti, relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, in the right way, the unliberated minds of immeasurable beings: "These are unliberated minds."

Subhūti, furthermore, relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, in the right way, the liberated minds of immeasurable beings: "These are liberated minds."

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know exactly as it is, in the right way, the liberated minds of immeasurable beings: "These are liberated minds"? Subhūti, it is because mind does not exist. The Tathāgata does not apprehend mind as past, and does not apprehend it as future or as arisen in the present. Thus, Subhūti, relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, in the right way, the liberated minds of immeasurable beings: "These are liberated minds."

Subhūti, furthermore, relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, in the right way, the unseeable minds of immeasurable beings: "These are unseeable minds."

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know exactly as it is, in the right way, the unseeable minds of immeasurable beings: "These are unseeable minds"? Subhūti, because it does not exist, mind is thus nonexistent; because it has not arisen, it is not something to be cognized; and because it is not truly established, it cannot be grasped even by the eye of wisdom or the divine eye. Since it does not appear at all, how much less could it be seen by the eye of flesh! Thus, Subhūti, relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, in the right way, the unseeable minds of immeasurable beings: "These are unseeable minds."

Subhūti, in this way the perfection of wisdom reveals this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas.

Subhūti, furthermore, relying on this perfection of wisdom, the Tathāgata knows exactly as it is, in the right way, the open and the closed in other sentient beings and other persons, immeasurable and innumerable: "These are open, and these are closed."

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, know exactly as it is, in the right way, the open and the closed in other sentient beings and other persons, immeasurable and innumerable: "These are open, and these are closed"? Subhūti, he knows exactly as it is, in the right way, that all those beings arise by abiding in form.

Subhūti, in the same way, the Tathāgata knows, exactly as it is, that all those beings arise by resting upon feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata come to know that those who are of open mind and those who are of closed mind rest upon form? And likewise, how does he come to know that those who are of open mind and those who are of closed mind rest upon feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness?

The view "One who has gone thus will exist after death" depends upon form. The view "One who has gone thus will not exist after death" depends upon form. The view "One who has gone thus will both exist and not exist after death" depends upon form. The view "One who has gone thus will neither exist nor not exist after death" depends upon form.

In the same way, for feeling, perception, and formations, and likewise for consciousness: the view "One who has gone thus will exist after death" depends upon consciousness. The view "One who has gone thus will not exist after death" depends upon consciousness. The view "One who has gone thus will both exist and not exist after death" depends upon consciousness. The view "One who has gone thus will neither exist nor not exist after death" depends upon consciousness.

The claim "The self and the world are permanent; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon form. The claim "The self and the world are impermanent; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon form. The claim "The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon form. The claim "The self and the world are neither permanent nor impermanent; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon form.

In the same way, for feeling, perception, and formations: the claim "The self and the world are permanent; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon consciousness. The claim "The self and the world are impermanent; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon consciousness. The claim "The self and the world are both permanent and impermanent; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon consciousness. The claim "The self and the world are neither permanent nor impermanent; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon consciousness.

Here ends the twelfth fascicle of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. Now begins the thirteenth fascicle.

The claim "The self and the world have an end; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon form. The claim "The self and the world are endless; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon form. The claim "The self and the world both have an end and are endless; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon form. The claim "The self and the world neither have an end nor are endless; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon form.

In the same way, for feeling, perception, and formations: the claim "The self and the world have an end; this alone is true, anything else is delusion" depends upon consciousness.

"The self and the world have no end": this very view holds that this alone is true and anything else is delusion, and it rests on consciousness. "The self and the world both have an end and have no end": this very view holds that this alone is true and anything else is delusion, and it rests on consciousness. "The self and the world neither have an end nor are without an end": this very view holds that this alone is true and anything else is delusion, and it rests on consciousness.

"The life force is the same as the body": this very view holds that this alone is true and anything else is delusion, and it rests on form. "The life force is one thing and the body another": this very view holds that this alone is true and anything else is delusion, and it rests on form. In the same way, for feeling, perception, and formations, and likewise for consciousness: "The life force is the same as the body": this very view holds that this alone is true and anything else is delusion, and it rests on consciousness. "The life force is one thing and the body another": this very view holds that this alone is true and anything else is delusion, and it rests on consciousness.

Subhūti, in this way the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly complete Buddha, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, has fully known that the open and the closed minds of immeasurable, innumerable other sentient beings and other persons rest on form. In the same way he has fully known that those open and closed minds rest on feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows precisely, just as they really are, the open and the closed minds of immeasurable, innumerable other sentient beings and other persons.

Subhūti, how does the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, know precisely, just as they really are, the open and the closed minds of immeasurable, innumerable other sentient beings and other persons? Subhūti, here the Tathāgata knows form. And how, Subhūti, does the Tathāgata know form? Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows form exactly according to its suchness. In this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows form. The same applies to feeling, perception, and formations. Here, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows consciousness. And how does the Tathāgata know consciousness? Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows consciousness exactly according to its suchness. In this way, Subhūti, the Tathāgata knows consciousness.

Subhūti, in this way the Tathāgata, relying on this Perfection of Wisdom, knows precisely, just as they really are, the open and the closed minds of immeasurable, innumerable other sentient beings and other persons.

Subhūti, thus the Tathāgata designates, within suchness, the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of the aggregates, and the suchness of the open and the closed minds. Subhūti, the suchness of the aggregates is also the suchness of the world. Why is that? Subhūti, the Tathāgata has given the name "world" to the five aggregates. Therefore, Subhūti, the suchness of the aggregates is the suchness of the world. The suchness of the world is the suchness of all phenomena. The suchness of all phenomena is the suchness of the fruit of stream-entry.

The suchness of the fruit of stream-entry is the suchness of the fruit of the once-returner. The suchness of the fruit of the once-returner is the suchness of the fruit of the non-returner. The suchness of the fruit of the non-returner is the suchness of the fruit of the arhat. The suchness of the fruit of the arhat is the suchness of the pratyekabuddha. The suchness of the pratyekabuddha is the suchness of the Tathāgata. Subhūti, in this way, the suchness of the Tathāgata, the suchness of the aggregates, the suchness of all phenomena, and the suchness of all the noble ones, the hearers and the solitary buddhas, are this one suchness, free from the many entities and non-entities. This is because it is not one, because it is not different, because it is inexhaustible, because it is unchanging, because it is non-dual, and because it cannot be made dual.

Subhūti, it is in this way that the Tathāgata, relying on this perfection of wisdom, fully and perfectly awakened to this suchness. Subhūti, in this way this perfection of wisdom reveals this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas. Subhūti, the Tathāgata reveals the world to this world as it truly is, and in this way the whole of this world has been revealed. Subhūti, in this way the perfection of wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, their begetter and the one who brings them forth. Subhūti, having fully and perfectly awakened to suchness, the Tathāgata knows the suchness of the world. He knows the unmistaken suchness. He knows the suchness that is not otherwise. Subhūti, because the Tathāgata has fully and perfectly awakened to suchness, he is called the Tathāgata.

The elder Subhūti said: Blessed One, suchness is profound. Blessed One, it is from this suchness that the awakening of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is distinguished and fully revealed. Blessed One, who else would have faith in this? Only irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, or arhats whose examination is complete, or persons endowed with perfect view. Blessed One, the Tathāgata fully and perfectly awakened to such supremely profound matters as these, and then taught them.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti thus: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. The Tathāgata fully and perfectly awakened to these supremely profound matters, and then explained them. Subhūti, the suchness to which the Tathāgata fully and perfectly awakened is inexhaustible. Having fully and perfectly awakened, he taught the inexhaustible as the inexhaustible.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), and the other sons of the gods who move in the desire realm, together with two hundred thousand sons of the gods of the Brahmā class, went to where the Blessed One was. Having come, they bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One and sat to one side. Seated to one side, those sons of the gods who move in the desire realm and in the form realm spoke to the Blessed One thus: Blessed One, when you teach profound phenomena, how, Blessed One, do you establish their defining characteristic?

The Blessed One declared: Sons of the gods, the defining characteristic is established as emptiness.

Sons of the gods, it is the signless. It is the wishless. In this way the defining characteristic is established. Sons of the gods, it is the unborn. It is the unceasing. It is without thorough affliction. It is without purification. It is without entities. It is nirvāṇa; it is the dharmadhātu; it is suchness. In this way the defining characteristic is established.

Why is this so? Sons of the gods, these characteristics are non-abiding; these characteristics are like space. Sons of the gods, these characteristics were not established by the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha. These characteristics are not counted as form. They are not counted as feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. These characteristics do not depend on form. They do not depend on feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. These characteristics were not established by gods, humans, or non-humans. These characteristics cannot be shaken by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Why is this so? Because the world with its gods, humans, and asuras is itself nothing but these very characteristics. These characteristics were not set down by anyone's hand.

Sons of the gods, if someone were to say, "Who established this space?", sons of the gods, would that person be speaking truthfully?

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, those sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm and the form realm said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, space was established by no one. Why is that? Blessed One, space is unconditioned, and so space was established by no one."

Then the Blessed One said to those sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm and the form realm: "Sons of the gods, so it is, so it is. Whether tathāgatas appear or tathāgatas do not appear, these characteristics abide just so. Why is that? Just as these abide, so the Tathāgata has fully awakened to them in perfect buddhahood and has taught them. Therefore, sons of the gods, the Tathāgata is called the Tathāgata."

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Tathāgata has fully awakened in perfect buddhahood to these profound characteristics. That is to say, the Perfection of Wisdom is the unattached wisdom of the tathāgatas. Because it is unattached wisdom, the Perfection of Wisdom is the domain of the Tathāgata."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, so it is, so it is. Subhūti, in just this way, this Perfection of Wisdom truly reveals this world to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha. Subhūti, just as the tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas rely upon and abide in this Dharma of the Perfection of Wisdom, so, because they do not abide in those phenomena, they abide constantly. And just as they are, so the Tathāgata has fully awakened in perfect buddhahood. Therefore they rely upon and abide in the Dharma alone. They honor the Dharma. They hold it as their teacher. They esteem it. They make offerings to it. They paint it in images. They serve and revere it. Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom is the very nature of all phenomena.

For this reason the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, show reverence to the Perfection of Wisdom, hold it as their teacher, honor it, make offerings to it, paint its image, and attend upon it. Why is that? Subhūti, it is from this Perfection of Wisdom that the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, is brought forth and made distinct. The Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, are those who know what has been done for them and who feel gratitude for what has been done.

Subhūti, if anyone says, "The Tathāgata knows what has been done for him and feels gratitude for what has been done," that person speaks truly. If one says, "He knows what has been done for him and feels gratitude for what has been done," one speaks in accord with what is true.

Subhūti, in what way is the Tathāgata one who knows what has been done for him and feels gratitude for it? Subhūti, whatever vehicles the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, has gone by, and whatever practices he has relied on, by which he fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, those very vehicles and those very practices are what he knows and feels gratitude for, and for that very reason the Tathāgata upholds and protects them. Subhūti, this is to be understood as the Tathāgata's knowing what has been done for him and feeling gratitude for it.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the Tathāgata has fully awakened to the fact that all phenomena are unmade, that is, unmade. He has fully awakened to the fact that they are unchanging, that is, unchanging. He has fully awakened to the fact that they are not constructed by any conditioning activity, that is, not constructed by any conditioning activity. Subhūti, this too is to be understood as the Tathāgata's knowing what has been done for him and feeling gratitude for it.

Subhūti, relying on the Perfection of Wisdom, the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, enters into all phenomena. Subhūti, by this way of explaining as well, the Perfection of Wisdom is that which truly reveals this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to him: Blessed One, when all phenomena are without a knower and without a seer, then, Blessed One, in what way does the Perfection of Wisdom truly reveal this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas?

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, it is excellent, truly excellent, that you should put such a question to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, and that you should reflect on it in this way. Subhūti, when you say that all phenomena are without a knower and without a seer, then, Subhūti, it is just so, it is just so. All phenomena are without a knower and without a seer.

Subhūti, in what way are all phenomena without a knower and without a seer? Subhūti, all phenomena are empty. Subhūti, all phenomena are without abiding. In this way, Subhūti, all phenomena are without a knower and without a seer. In this way, Subhūti, it is by relying on the Perfection of Wisdom that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to all these phenomena.

Subhūti, in this way too, the Perfection of Wisdom truly shows this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas. It shows it truly because they do not see form, and do not see feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. Thus, Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom truly shows this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas.

Subhūti asked, "Blessed One, how is it that form is not seen? How is it that feeling, perception, and formations are not seen? Blessed One, how is it that consciousness is not seen?"

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, if no consciousness arises that takes form as its object, then in that way form is not seen. In the same way, if no consciousness arises that takes feeling, perception, and formations as its object, then they are not seen. Subhūti, if one does not give rise to a mind that takes consciousness as its object, then in that way consciousness is not seen. Subhūti, the non-seeing of form, the non-seeing of feeling, perception, and formations, and the non-seeing of consciousness: in this way the Tathāgata sees the world. Thus, Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom truly shows this world to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas.

"Subhūti, and how does the Perfection of Wisdom truly show the world? In this way: the world is empty. In this way the world is expressed. In this way the Tathāgata makes the world known. In this way he causes the world to be seen. In this way the world is inconceivable, in this way the world is peaceful, in this way the world is secluded, in this way the world is utterly pure. So the world is spoken of, so it is made known, and so he causes the world to be seen."

This is the twelfth chapter, called "Truly Showing the World," from the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines of the Noble One.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Blessed One, how marvelous! This Perfection of Wisdom abides as a great deed. Blessed One, how marvelous! This Perfection of Wisdom abides as an inconceivable deed, an unequaled deed, an immeasurable deed, an innumerable deed, and a deed equal to the unequaled."

The Blessed One said, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom abides as a great deed. Subhūti, this Perfection of Wisdom abides as an inconceivable deed, an unequaled deed, an immeasurable deed, an innumerable deed, and a deed equal to the unequaled.

"Subhūti, how does this Perfection of Wisdom abide as an inconceivable deed? Subhūti, the state of being a Tathāgata, the state of being a buddha, the state of being self-arisen, the state of being omniscient, are inconceivable. Subhūti, in this way this Perfection of Wisdom abides as an inconceivable deed, and it cannot be conceived by the mind. Why is that? Because mind, mental activity, and mental factors do not enter into it.

"Subhūti, how does this Perfection of Wisdom abide as an unequaled deed?"

Subhūti, the Tathāgata's state of being a tathāgata, his buddhahood, his self-arisen nature, and his omniscience cannot be thought of or matched. In this way, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom abides through an activity that has no equal.

Subhūti, how does this perfection of wisdom abide through an activity that is immeasurable? Subhūti, the state of being a tathāgata, buddhahood, the self-arisen nature, and omniscience are immeasurable. In this way, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom abides through an activity that is immeasurable.

Subhūti, how does this perfection of wisdom abide through an activity that is innumerable? Subhūti, the state of being a tathāgata, buddhahood, the self-arisen nature, and omniscience are innumerable. In this way, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom abides through an activity that is innumerable.

Subhūti, how does this perfection of wisdom abide through an activity that is both unequal and equal? Subhūti, if there is not even an equal to the state of being a tathāgata, to buddhahood, to the self-arisen nature, and to omniscience, how much less is there anything greater! In this way, Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom abides through an activity that is unequal and equal.

The elder Subhūti then said: Blessed One, is the state of being a tathāgata inconceivable, without equal, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal? Likewise, are buddhahood, the self-arisen nature, and omniscience inconceivable, without equal, immeasurable, unequal and equal? Or, Blessed One, is form also inconceivable, without equal, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal? Likewise, are feeling, perception, and the formations, or consciousness also inconceivable, without equal, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal? Or are all phenomena also inconceivable, without equal, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, form too is inconceivable, without equal, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal. Likewise, Subhūti, feeling, perception, the formations, and consciousness are inconceivable, without equal, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal. Likewise, Subhūti, all phenomena are inconceivable, without equal, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal.

Why is this so? Subhūti, in the nature of form there is no mind, no thought, and no mental factors, and so there is no thinking of "it is so." Likewise, Subhūti, in the nature of feeling, perception, the formations, and consciousness there is no mind, no thought, and no mental factors, and so there is no thinking of "it is so." Subhūti, in the nature of all phenomena there is no mind, no thought, and no mental factors, and so there is no thinking of "it is so."

In this way, Subhūti, form is inconceivable and without equal. Likewise, Subhūti, feeling, perception, the formations, and consciousness are inconceivable and without equal. Likewise, Subhūti, all phenomena are inconceivable and without equal. Subhūti, form is also immeasurable.

Subhūti, in the same way feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also immeasurable. Subhūti, all phenomena are also immeasurable. Why is this? Subhūti, one does not know the measure of form. In the same way, Subhūti, one does not know the measure of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; and one does not know the measure of any phenomenon at all.

Subhūti, why does one not know the measure of form? In the same way, why does one not know the measure of feeling, perception, and formations? Subhūti, why does one not know the measure of consciousness? Subhūti, why does one not know the measure of any phenomenon at all? Subhūti, it is because form has no measure. In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness have no measure; Subhūti, all phenomena have no measure.

Subhūti, why does form have no measure? Why do feeling, perception, and formations have no measure? Why does consciousness have no measure? Why do all phenomena have no measure? Subhūti, it is because all phenomena are without measure.

Subhūti, form is also innumerable. In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also innumerable. Subhūti, all phenomena are also innumerable, because they are beyond all counting.

Subhūti, form is also unequal and equal. In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are also unequal and equal. Likewise, Subhūti, all phenomena are unequal and equal, because, Subhūti, all phenomena are equal to space.

Subhūti, what do you think? In space, is there any equality, number, measure, comparison, mind, thought, or mental factor whatsoever? Subhūti replied: Blessed One, there is not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it is just so. By this line of explanation, all these phenomena are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal. Subhūti, these are the qualities of the Tathāgata. Subhūti, by this line of explanation too, all phenomena are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal. Subhūti, these qualities of the Tathāgata are inconceivable because they are free of mind. They are incomparable because they have utterly passed beyond comparison.

Subhūti, what is called the inconceivable and the incomparable is a designation for the Dharma that has become consciousness. The same holds for what is called the immeasurable, the innumerable, the unequal and equal. Subhūti, what is called immeasurable, innumerable, and unequal and equal is so because it is free of equality, number, and measure. The qualities of the Tathāgata are immeasurable, innumerable, and unequal and equal.

These phenomena, being equal to space, being innumerable and immeasurable, are unequal and equal, innumerable and immeasurable. Ah, these phenomena, being equal to space, do not enter into either inequality or equality. Therefore, Subhūti, these phenomena are said to be incomparable.

Because space is inconceivable, these phenomena are inconceivable. Because space is incomparable, these phenomena are incomparable. Because space is immeasurable, these phenomena are immeasurable. Because space is innumerable, these phenomena are innumerable. Because space is unequal and equal, these phenomena are unequal and equal.

Even as the Blessed One spoke of these things that are inconceivable, incomparable, immeasurable, innumerable, unequal and equal, five hundred monks had their minds fully liberated from the defilements without grasping. Two thousand nuns likewise had their minds fully liberated from the defilements without grasping. Six thousand laymen attained the Dharma eye, free of dust and stain, utterly pure, with regard to all phenomena. Three thousand laywomen likewise attained the Dharma eye, free of dust and stain, utterly pure, with regard to all phenomena. Twenty thousand bodhisattvas attained the acceptance of the nonarising of phenomena. And the Blessed One prophesied that, in this very Fortunate Eon, they would reach unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. As for those laymen and laywomen who attained the Dharma eye, free of dust and stain, utterly pure, the Blessed One also gave them a prophecy: they too would have their minds fully liberated from the defilements without grasping.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound. Blessed One, how wonderful that this perfection of wisdom is established for the sake of a great purpose."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. The perfection of wisdom is profound. Subhūti, this perfection of wisdom is established for the sake of a great purpose. Why is that? Subhūti, it is fully endowed with omniscience. It is fully endowed with the stage of the solitary buddhas. It is fully endowed with the stage of the hearers.

"Subhūti, it is like this. Consider a king of the warrior caste, consecrated on the crown of his head, who has gained power and diligence over the people of his country. Whatever the tasks of the king, whatever the tasks of the cities, and whatever the tasks of the provinces, all of these are bound up with his ministers. For that reason the king exerts little effort and is relieved of the burden. In the same way, Subhūti, whatever the qualities of the buddhas, or the qualities of the solitary buddhas, or the qualities of the hearers may be, all of them are fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom, and so it is the perfection of wisdom itself that does the work for them. Subhūti, for this reason this perfection of wisdom is established for the sake of a great purpose.

"The perfection of wisdom is established so that one will not grasp at form or cling to it, and likewise so that one will not grasp at feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, or cling to them. It is established so that one will not grasp at the fruit of stream-entry or cling to it, and likewise so that one will not grasp at the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and arhatship, or cling to them. It is established so that one will not grasp at self-arisen awakening or cling to it, and so that one will not grasp at omniscience or cling to it."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, in what way is the perfection of wisdom established so that one will not grasp at omniscience or cling to it?"

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Do you perceive any arhatship at all that one could grasp at or cling to?"

Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, no. I do not see, Blessed One, any such factor as arhatship by which one would be grasping or clinging."

The Blessed One declared, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. I too do not see the Tathāgata; and because I do not see that Tathāgata, I do not grasp at him or cling to him. Therefore, Subhūti, even in omniscience there is no grasping and no clinging."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, when bodhisattvas, great beings, who have newly entered the vehicle and whose roots of virtue are slight hear this teaching, that even omniscience is not grasped and not clung to, they will tremble and become utterly terrified. Blessed One, however, those bodhisattvas, great beings, whose causes are complete, who in the past served the Victors and for a long time have planted roots of virtue, will have faith when they hear this profound perfection of wisdom."

The Blessed One declared, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is."

Then the sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm and those who dwell in the form realm said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, the perfection of wisdom is profound, difficult to behold, difficult to realize. Blessed One, those bodhisattvas who have faith on hearing this profound perfection of wisdom have served the Victors in the past and have planted roots of virtue for a long time. Blessed One, suppose all the sentient beings in the great thousand worlds of the three-thousandfold universe were to practice for an eon, or for more than an eon, on the stage of those who follow through faith. And suppose someone were to endure this profound perfection of wisdom, even for a single day, and to desire, seek, reflect upon, weigh, examine, and ponder it. Blessed One, that one would be superior to all of them."

When they had spoken, the Blessed One said to the sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm and the form realm, "Sons of the gods, if any sons or daughters of good family listen to this profound perfection of wisdom, then, sons of the gods, they should expect to reach nirvāṇa very swiftly, which is not so for those who practice for an eon or more than an eon on the stage of those who follow through faith."

Then the sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm and the form realm said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, this perfection of wisdom is indeed the great perfection." Having said this, they bowed their heads to the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and departed from the presence of the Blessed One. When they had gone a short distance, they vanished from sight. The sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm returned to the desire realm, and the sons of the gods who dwell in the form realm returned to the world of Brahmā.

This is the thirteenth chapter, "The Inconceivable," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, on the very moment of hearing this profound Perfection of Wisdom being taught, is drawn to it with faith. He is not stunned by it, not discouraged, does not hesitate, is not bewildered, and feels neither doubt nor perplexity, but takes delight in the Perfection of Wisdom. Blessed One, after dying and passing away from where does he come to be reborn there?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who on the very moment of hearing this profound Perfection of Wisdom being taught is drawn to it with faith, who is not stunned, not discouraged, does not hesitate, is not bewildered, and feels neither doubt nor perplexity, takes delight just in looking at it. He will hold and cultivate this profound Perfection of Wisdom. He does not abandon attention that is endowed with the Perfection of Wisdom, and he does not turn his mind away from it. He generates the wish to grasp it, retain it, read it, fully comprehend it, and recite it. He follows after it and walks behind it, and he does not abandon the Dharma teacher.

Subhūti, it is like a young calf, which does not leave its mother cow. In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has heard this profound Perfection of Wisdom, does not abandon the Dharma teacher for as long as this Perfection of Wisdom has not been taken up in his body, that is, committed to memory, or set down in a book. Such a bodhisattva, a great being, Subhūti, has died and passed away from among humans and been reborn as a human.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, is there a bodhisattva, a great being, endowed with these qualities who, having died and passed away from another buddha-field, has been reborn here?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, there are also bodhisattvas, great beings, who have honored and served other buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and have questioned them thoroughly and inquired of them in detail, and who, having died and passed away from those other buddha-fields, have been reborn here. These too should be understood as endowed with these very qualities.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has died and passed away from among the gods of Tuṣita and been reborn here should also be understood as endowed with these very qualities. One who has honored the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, and has questioned him thoroughly and inquired of him in detail concerning this Perfection of Wisdom should likewise be understood as endowed with these qualities.

Again, Subhūti, a bodhisattva who has heard this profound Perfection of Wisdom but who, even in the past, never questioned thoroughly, never inquired, and never asked for details, is reborn among humans, yet he becomes stupefied, bewildered, and discouraged when this profound Perfection of Wisdom is taught. Subhūti, such a bodhisattva should be understood as being by nature one who did not question even in the past. Why is that? Because he became stupefied, bewildered, and discouraged when this profound Perfection of Wisdom was taught.

Furthermore, Subhūti, there is a bodhisattva who, even in the past, heard this profound Perfection of Wisdom for only one, two, three, four, or five days.

If, having shown respect and attended, a bodhisattva has questioned and inquired thoroughly, that faith lasts only for a while; it will be lost again, and it will be carried off by the very questioning. Why is that? Subhūti, it is like this. A bodhisattva who has not previously inquired about this profound Perfection of Wisdom, has not questioned it properly, has not examined it through questioning, and has not followed it, will sometimes follow it with eagerness in order to listen to this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and sometimes will have no eagerness. Because of that, he becomes distracted and discouraged, his mind turns restless, and he becomes like a tuft of cotton blown about. You should understand that this bodhisattva entered the Vehicle not long ago, and has come to it newly.

That bodhisattva will abandon that faith, that clarity of mind, and that eagerness. That is, he will not take up this profound Perfection of Wisdom, will not engage in it, and will not rely on it. So he should look forward to one or the other of the two levels, the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a ship that has set out on the great ocean breaks apart. If those aboard do not hold on to a plank or a piece of wood, or do not cling to a corpse, then, Subhūti, you should understand that they will meet their death in the water without reaching the far shore. Subhūti, but if those aboard a ship that has broken apart on the great ocean do hold on to a plank or a piece of wood or a corpse, then you should understand that they will not die in the water, but will reach the far shore in safety, and will stand on dry land unharmed and uninjured.

In the same way, Subhūti, even if a bodhisattva has faith, joy, clarity of mind, and eagerness, if he does not rely on the Perfection of Wisdom, you should understand that he will be ruined midway along the path, and without attaining omniscience will remain at the level of a śrāvaka or a pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, Subhūti, take those great bodhisattvas who have faith, patience, longing, eagerness, diligence, earnestness, devotion, a lofty intention, generosity, respect, delight, contentment, clarity of mind, great joy, and unfailing perseverance for the sake of fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. If they rely on the Perfection of Wisdom, then that faith of theirs, that patience, that longing, that eagerness, that diligence, that earnestness, that devotion, that lofty intention, that generosity, that respect, that delight, that contentment, that clarity of mind, that great joy, and that unfailing perseverance, having obtained the Perfection of Wisdom, will come to rest in omniscience.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a woman or a man were to fill a new, unbaked pot with water. Subhūti, you should understand that such a pot will not last long; it will quickly break and fall apart. Why is that? Because the pot has not been fired, it will in the end turn back into earth.

Subhūti, in the same way, there may be some bodhisattva, a great being, who has faith in fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, who has patience, who has aspiration, who has zeal, who has diligence, who has conscientiousness, who has conviction, who has superior intention, who has the capacity to give up, who has reverence, who has joy, who has great delight, who has serenity, who has gladness of mind, and who does not abandon perseverance. And yet, if that bodhisattva is not held by the perfection of wisdom and by skillful means, Subhūti, it should be understood that this bodhisattva will be destroyed midway along the path.

Subhūti, what is the destruction of a bodhisattva midway along the path? It is the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a woman or a man has a well-baked pot and draws water with it from a spring, a pool, a pond, a lake, a well, or some other source of water. If that person carries the water away, Subhūti, it should be understood that the pot will reach home safely. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, the pot was well baked.

In the same way, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, has faith in fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and has patience, aspiration, zeal, diligence, conscientiousness, conviction, superior intention, the capacity to give up, reverence, joy, great delight, serenity, gladness of mind, and also does not abandon perseverance, and that bodhisattva is held by the perfection of wisdom and by skillful means, then, Subhūti, it should be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, will not be destroyed midway along the path. Unharmed and unobstructed, that bodhisattva will come to abide in omniscience.

This is the end of the fourteenth volume of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a man of confused discernment has a seagoing ship whose planks are not caulked and not repaired, and which was lashed together long ago. He drags it into the water, loads it with goods until it is full, and goes aboard weighed down by the burden. Subhūti, such a ship is bound to break apart in this way.
