It will not cross to the far shore of the water; the goods will be lost, and the ship itself will go to ruin. In just this way, that unskilled captain of confused discernment will suffer the loss of great wealth and will fall away from the great source of jewels.

In the same way, Subhūti, there may be some bodhisattva who has faith in fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, who has patience, aspiration, zeal, diligence, conscientiousness, conviction, superior intention, the capacity to give up, reverence, joy, contentment, serenity, great delight, and who does not abandon perseverance. Yet if that bodhisattva is not held by the perfection of wisdom and is without skillful means, Subhūti, then before reaching the source of the jewel of omniscience, that bodhisattva will be ruined midway and will fall into despair. He will fall away from his own great aim, and he will fall away from the heap of jewels that is the great aim of others. That is, he will fall away from the great source of jewels that is the great aim of omniscience. This should be understood.

Subhūti, and what is the ruin of a bodhisattva midway?

That is to say, the level of the hearers or the level of the solitary buddhas.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a skilled captain builds a ship for sailing the ocean. He binds it well, fits its lattice of planks well, and repairs whatever needs repair. He then draws the ship into the water, loads the cargo until it is full, arranges everything properly, and, joined with a favorable wind, sails gradually toward whatever destination he wishes. Subhūti, that ship will not be destroyed by the water. It will reach the destination toward which it was meant to go, and that captain will obtain great gains, namely, he will come to possess the jewels of the world. This is how it should be understood.

In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, may have faith in fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and have patience, longing, aspiration, diligence, carefulness, devotion, superior intention, generosity, respect, joy, delight, serene confidence, and great gladness, and may also not abandon his perseverance. If he is embraced by the Perfection of Wisdom and is not separated from skillful means, then, Subhūti, that bodhisattva, that great being, will not be wasted in the middle and will not become discouraged. It should be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, will abide in unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Why is that? Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose there are bodhisattvas, great beings, who have faith in fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and have patience, longing, aspiration, diligence, carefulness, devotion, superior intention, generosity, respect, joy, delight, serene confidence, and great gladness, and also do not abandon their perseverance. If these qualities of theirs are embraced by the Perfection of Wisdom and are not separated from skillful means, then they will actualize the qualities by which one becomes omniscient, and they will set out correctly toward fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. They will not instead accomplish the level of the hearers or the level of the solitary buddhas.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a man has been born and has reached the age of one hundred and twenty. He is old, aged, and bent over. If some illness arising from wind, or from bile, or from phlegm, or from a combination of these, strikes his body, what do you think, Subhūti? Could that man get up from his bed without support?

Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, he could not."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, even if that man were able to get up from his bed, being overcome by that old age and that illness, he would have no strength to walk even one league or even two leagues. Even if he could get up from his bed, he would have no strength to walk.

In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, may have faith in fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and have patience, longing, aspiration, diligence, carefulness, devotion, superior intention, generosity, respect, joy, delight, serene confidence, and great gladness, and may also not abandon his perseverance, and yet…

If such a bodhisattva is not embraced by the Perfection of Wisdom and is separated from skillful means, then even though he has properly set out to attain full and perfect awakening, Subhūti, he will be ruined and destroyed along the way. Know that he will come to rest in the stage of the śrāvakas or the stage of the pratyekabuddhas. Why is that? Because he is not embraced by the Perfection of Wisdom and is separated from skillful means.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a man has been born and has reached the age of a hundred and twenty. He is old, worn out with age, and bent. His body is struck by some illness, whether arising from wind, from bile, from phlegm, or from a combination of these. Two strong men, one on his right and one on his left, support him well, hold him up, grasp him firmly, and say to him: "Good man, until you reach the place where you wish to go, we two will support you, so you need not fear falling or collapsing along the way. Go wherever you wish to go." Then he would be able to rise from his bed.

In the same way, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, has faith, patience, longing, aspiration, diligence, carefulness, devotion, and a lofty intention for the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Suppose he also has generosity, reverence, joy, contentment, serene confidence, delight, and unflagging perseverance. If he is embraced by the Perfection of Wisdom and is not separated from skillful means, then, Subhūti, that bodhisattva, that great being, will not be ruined or destroyed along the way. Know that from that very position he will be able to reach the state of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

This is the fourteenth chapter, the chapter on similes, from the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva, a great being who is a beginner, abide in the Perfection of Wisdom, and how should he train?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being who is a beginner and wishes to train in the Perfection of Wisdom, should draw near to good spiritual friends, rely on them, and honor them. Those who counsel and instruct him in this Perfection of Wisdom, and those who explain the meaning of this Perfection of Wisdom, should be recognized, Subhūti, as that bodhisattva's good spiritual friends.

They will say to him: 'Come, child of good family, apply yourself to the perfection of generosity. In the same way, apply yourself to the perfection of moral discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom. Child of good family, whatever gifts you give, dedicate all of them fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.'"

Child of good family, do not take pride in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening as form. In the same way, do not take pride in it as feeling, as perception, or as formations. Child of good family, do not take pride in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening as consciousness. Why is that? Child of good family, because omniscience is without pride.

In the same way, whatever moral discipline you keep, and, joining all the others in the same manner, whatever patience you practice, whatever diligence you undertake, whatever meditative concentration you enter into in equipoise, and whatever wisdom you cultivate, dedicate all of it fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Child of good family, do not take pride in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening as form. In the same way, do not take pride in it as feeling, as perception, or as formations. Child of good family, do not take pride in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening as consciousness. Why is that? Child of good family, because omniscience is without pride. Child of good family, do not aspire to the ground of the śrāvakas or the ground of the pratyekabuddhas.

Thus they should give instruction on the meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom. In this way, Subhūti, the good spiritual friends should gradually introduce the novice bodhisattva, the great being, to the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, there are bodhisattvas, great beings, who have properly entered upon the path to fully and perfectly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Relying on generosity of such a nature, on moral discipline of such a nature, on patience of such a nature, on diligence of such a nature, on meditative concentration of such a nature, and on wisdom of such a nature, they have gained mastery over passing completely beyond sorrow, and yet they do not wish to pass completely beyond sorrow. Rather, seeing the realm of sentient beings so greatly afflicted by suffering, they wish to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and they are not frightened of saṃsāra. This, Blessed One, is a difficult thing they do."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas, great beings, who have set out for the benefit of the world, for the happiness of the world, and out of compassion for the world, thinking: 'Having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, I shall become a protector of the world. I shall become a refuge of the world. I shall become a resting place of the world. I shall become an ally of the world. I shall become an island for the world. I shall become a light for the world. I shall become a guide of the world. I shall become a support of the world.' To undertake diligence toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening of such a nature is a difficult thing to do."

"Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, become a protector of the world?"

Subhūti, whatever sufferings there are in the world of those who move in saṃsāra, from these he protects them; he strives to abandon those sufferings and arouses diligence. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, becomes the protector of the world.

Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, become the refuge of the world? Subhūti, there are beings who are subject to birth, subject to aging, subject to sickness, subject to death, subject to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and turmoil. Such beings he frees completely from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental distress, and turmoil. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, becomes the refuge of the world.

Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, become the resting place of the world? Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, teaches the Dharma to beings so that they may come to be without engagement. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, becomes the resting place of the world.

Subhūti asked: Blessed One, how is it that there is no engagement?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what is without connection to form is without engagement with form. What is without engagement with form is without connection to form. What is without connection to form is without the arising and without the cessation of form. What is without the arising and without the cessation of form is without engagement with form. That which is the absence of engagement with form is the absence of connection to form, and this absence of connection to form is the absence of engagement with form.

It is the same with feeling, perception, and the formations. Subhūti, what is without connection to consciousness is without engagement with consciousness. What is without engagement with consciousness is without connection to consciousness. What is without connection to consciousness is without the arising and without the cessation of consciousness. What is without the arising and without the cessation of consciousness is without engagement with consciousness. What is without engagement with consciousness is without connection to consciousness, and this absence of connection to consciousness is the absence of engagement with consciousness.

Subhūti, when consciousness sees in this way that all phenomena are without engagement and without connection, one comes to be without engagement. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, becomes the resting place of the world.

Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, become the ally of the world?

Subhūti, the far shore of form is not form. Subhūti, as the far shore is, so too is form. In the same way, the far shore of feeling, of perception, and of the conditioning factors is not feeling, perception, or the conditioning factors. And Subhūti, the far shore of consciousness is not consciousness. As the far shore is, so too is consciousness. Subhūti, as the far shore of form, feeling, perception, the conditioning factors, and consciousness is, so too are all phenomena.

Subhūti then spoke. Blessed One, if as the far shore of form, feeling, perception, the conditioning factors, and consciousness is, so too are all phenomena, then, Blessed One, is it not the case that bodhisattvas, the great beings, are already fully awakened to all phenomena? Why do I say so? Blessed One, because there is no conceptual thought whatsoever in this.

The Blessed One declared: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. In that which is the far shore there is no conceptual thought whatsoever. Subhūti, because there is no conceptual thought, bodhisattvas, the great beings, are indeed fully awakened to all phenomena. Subhūti, this too is a supremely difficult deed of bodhisattvas, the great beings: that when they have thus come to a firm conviction about all phenomena, they neither become arrogant nor become discouraged, and think, "We shall fully awaken to these phenomena. Having thus fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, we shall teach these phenomena and explain them thoroughly."

Subhūti, in this way a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, becomes a protector for the world.

Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, become an island for the world? Subhūti, for example, in the midst of rivers or oceans, a place that is surrounded on every side by water is called an island. In the same way, Subhūti, form is utterly cut off from its former limit and its later limit. In the same way, feeling, perception, and the conditioning factors, and likewise, Subhūti, consciousness, are utterly cut off from their former limit and their later limit. Subhūti, by this complete cutting off, all phenomena are completely cut off from their former limit and their later limit.

Subhūti, this complete cutting off of all phenomena is peace. It is stillness. It is complete nirvāṇa. It is things as they truly are. It is the unmistaken. Subhūti, in this way a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, becomes an island for the world.

Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, become a light for the world? Subhūti, here a bodhisattva, a great being, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, brings light through wisdom to beings who for a long time have been wholly enclosed in the shell and membrane of the egg of ignorance and overwhelmed by darkness, and dispels all the pitch darkness of unknowing.

Subhūti, in this way bodhisattvas, great beings, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, become the light of the world. Subhūti, how is it that bodhisattvas, great beings, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, become the guides of the world? Subhūti, here bodhisattvas, great beings, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, teach that form, by its intrinsic nature, is without arising and without cessation. In the same way, they teach that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, by their intrinsic nature, are without arising and without cessation. They teach that the qualities of ordinary beings, by their intrinsic nature, are without arising and without cessation. They teach that the qualities of the śrāvakas, by their intrinsic nature, are without arising and without cessation. They teach that the qualities of the pratyekabuddhas, by their intrinsic nature, are without arising and without cessation. They teach that the qualities of the bodhisattvas, by their intrinsic nature, are without arising and without cessation. They teach that the qualities of the buddhas, by their intrinsic nature, are without arising and without cessation. They teach that all phenomena, by their intrinsic nature, are without arising and without cessation. Subhūti, in this way bodhisattvas, great beings, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, become the guides of the world.

Subhūti, how is it that bodhisattvas, great beings, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, become the support of the world? Subhūti, here bodhisattvas, great beings, having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, teach the world that form rests on space. In the same way they teach that feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness rest on space. Subhūti, likewise all phenomena rest on space; they have no going and no coming, and are equal to space. Just as space has no coming and no going, is unmade, unchanging, unfabricated, nonabiding, without any true abiding, without any particular abiding, unarisen, and unceased, so too, Subhūti, all phenomena have no coming and no going, are unmade, unchanging, unfabricated, nonabiding, without any true abiding, without any particular abiding, unarisen, and unceased. Because they are equal to space, they are free of conceptualization.

Why is this so? Subhūti, the emptiness of form has neither coming nor going. In the same way, the emptiness of feeling, perception, formations, and, Subhūti, of consciousness has neither coming nor going. Subhūti, likewise the emptiness of all phenomena has neither coming nor going.

Why is this so? Subhūti, all phenomena rest on emptiness, and they do not go beyond that basis. Subhūti, all phenomena rest on signlessness, and they do not go beyond that basis. Subhūti, all phenomena rest on wishlessness, and they do not go beyond that basis. Subhūti, all phenomena rest on non-fabrication, and they do not go beyond that basis. Subhūti, all phenomena rest on non-occurrence, and they do not go beyond that basis. Subhūti, all phenomena rest on non-arising, and they do not go beyond that basis.

Subhūti, all phenomena have the absence of entities as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have the dream as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have the self as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have the boundless as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have peace as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have nirvāṇa as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have the unextractable as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have the absence of coming as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have the absence of going as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have the immovable as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have form as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Likewise, Subhūti, all phenomena have feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support. Subhūti, all phenomena have the arhat, the pratyekabuddha state, and unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening as their support, and they do not pass beyond that support.

Therefore, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, the bodhisattva, the great being, teaches the Dharma, saying that all phenomena have space as their support. Subhūti, in this way, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, the bodhisattva, the great being, becomes a support for the world.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, who will understand this profound Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, you should know that this profound Perfection of Wisdom will be understood by those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have practiced in the presence of the buddhas of the past, the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas, and whose roots of virtue have fully matured.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, what is the essential nature of those bodhisattvas, great beings, who will understand this profound Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who will understand this profound Perfection of Wisdom are those whose nature is solitude, arisen from the Vinaya.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, do those bodhisattvas, great beings, become dependent on precisely such supports? And having fully awakened, do they teach these very supports to sentient beings, and in that way become a support for sentient beings?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, those bodhisattvas, great beings, become those who have such supports. Having fully awakened to these supports, they teach these supports to sentient beings, and in that way they become a support for sentient beings.

Subhūti, in this way a bodhisattva, a great being, after fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, complete awakening, becomes a support for immeasurable, countless sentient beings.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has put on this armor with the thought, "I shall bring immeasurable, countless sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa," is doing something difficult.

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. A bodhisattva, a great being, who has put on this armor with the thought, "I shall bring immeasurable, countless sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa," is doing something difficult.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the armor of a bodhisattva, a great being, who has put on the great armor is not connected with form, nor is it connected for the sake of form. In the same way, it is not connected with feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness, nor is it connected for the sake of consciousness. It is not connected with the stage of the śrāvakas, nor connected for the sake of the stage of the śrāvakas. It is not connected with the stage of the pratyekabuddhas, nor connected for the sake of the stage of the pratyekabuddhas. It is not connected with the stage of the buddhas, nor connected for the sake of the stage of the buddhas. Why is that? Subhūti, this armor of a bodhisattva, a great being, who has put on the great armor, is not connected with any phenomena at all.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has put on the great armor and practices in this way in the profound Perfection of Wisdom, should not hope for three things. What are the three? They are the stage of the śrāvakas, the stage of the pratyekabuddhas, and the stage of the buddhas.

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, what purpose do you see, that you say: "A bodhisattva, a great being, who has put on the great armor and practices in this way in the profound Perfection of Wisdom, should not hope for three things: the stage of the śrāvakas, the stage of the pratyekabuddhas, and the stage of the buddhas"?

Subhūti, for a bodhisattva, a great being, who has put on the great armor and practices in this way in the profound Perfection of Wisdom, to hope for the stage of the śrāvakas or the stage of the pratyekabuddhas is impossible, and there is no occasion for it. Yet whoever has put on this great armor for the sake of all sentient beings should hope for buddhahood itself.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound. It is not cultivated by anyone. It has not been cultivated by anyone, no one cultivates it, and no one will cultivate it. There is nothing at all to be cultivated, and there is nowhere in which to cultivate it. Why is that? Blessed One, because in the Perfection of Wisdom no phenomenon whatsoever is truly established.

Blessed One, this cultivation of the Perfection of Wisdom is a cultivation of space. Blessed One, this cultivation of the Perfection of Wisdom is a non-cultivation of all phenomena.

Blessed One, this cultivation of the Perfection of Wisdom is the cultivation of non-attachment. Blessed One, this cultivation of the Perfection of Wisdom is the cultivation of the limitless. Blessed One, this cultivation of the Perfection of Wisdom is the cultivation of the non-existence of things. Blessed One, this cultivation of the Perfection of Wisdom is the cultivation of the absence of any grasping.

When Subhūti had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows. Subhūti, it is just so, it is just so. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in the way of abiding of the profound Perfection of Wisdom should be recognized as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Subhūti, such a bodhisattva, a great being, does not become fixated on this profound Perfection of Wisdom. Nor does he become fixated on what others say or what others discuss. Nor does he follow others out of faith placed in them. Subhūti, when this profound Perfection of Wisdom is being taught, this bodhisattva, this great being, is not stunned, is not discouraged, does not tremble, is not terrified, and does not become possessed by terror. He does not hesitate, does not fall into doubt, and is not bewildered. He understands and has confidence, and he delights to see and to hear the Perfection of Wisdom. Therefore, Subhūti, it should be understood that in the past, too, he has thoroughly questioned the Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that? Subhūti, it is because when this profound Perfection of Wisdom is being taught, he does not tremble, is not terrified, and is not possessed by terror.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, if a bodhisattva, a great being, does not tremble, is not terrified, and is not possessed by terror when this profound Perfection of Wisdom is being taught, then Blessed One, in what way has he examined the Perfection of Wisdom in detail?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it is by a mental continuum inclined toward omniscience that a bodhisattva, a great being, has examined the Perfection of Wisdom in detail.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, how has he examined in detail the continuum inclined toward omniscience?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it is by a continuum inclined toward space, Subhūti, one that flows down toward space, Subhūti, one that is directed toward space, that the continuum inclined toward omniscience has been examined in detail. Subhūti, moreover, whatever is examined in detail through a continuum inclined toward omniscience is thus examined in detail. Why is that? Subhūti, omniscience is immeasurable. Subhūti, omniscience is without measure. Subhūti, whatever is immeasurable and without measure is not form, not feeling, not perception, not formations, not consciousness. It is not an attainment, not a realization, not a comprehension. It is not a path, not the fruit of the path, not wisdom, not consciousness. It is not arising, not ceasing, not increase, not decrease, not cessation. It is not cultivation, not cultivation in particular. It is made by no one, comes from nowhere, goes nowhere, abides in no object, and abides in no direction.

Otherwise, it would fall into the category of what is called the immeasurable and the unfathomable. Because space is unmeasurable, omniscience is unmeasurable. What is unmeasurable cannot be fully and perfectly awakened to by anyone. It is not awakened to by means of form, nor by feeling, nor by perception, nor by formations, nor by consciousness. It is not awakened to by the perfection of generosity, nor by the perfection of moral discipline, nor by the perfection of patience, nor by the perfection of diligence, nor by the perfection of meditative concentration. Nor can anyone fully and perfectly awaken by means of the Perfection of Wisdom.

Why is that? Subhūti, form itself is omniscience. In the same way, feeling itself, perception itself, and formations themselves are omniscience, and, Subhūti, consciousness itself is omniscience. Subhūti, the perfection of generosity itself is omniscience. In the same way, the perfection of moral discipline itself, the perfection of patience itself, the perfection of diligence itself, and the perfection of meditative concentration itself are omniscience, and, Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom itself is omniscience.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, together with the sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm, and Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, together with the sons of the gods who dwell in the form realm, approached the Blessed One. Having arrived, they bowed with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and sat to one side. When they were seated, Śakra, lord of the gods, together with the sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm, and Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, together with the sons of the gods who dwell in the form realm, spoke to the Blessed One as follows.

Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to fathom. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to behold. Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to realize. It was in view of this very point that the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, having fully and perfectly awakened to unsurpassable, perfect awakening, and while abiding at the heart of awakening, inclined his mind toward little exertion and did not incline it toward teaching the Dharma.

When they had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to Śakra, lord of the gods, and the sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm, and to Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, and the sons of the gods who dwell in the form realm: Sons of the gods, it is so. It is just so. Sons of the gods, alas, this Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Sons of the gods, this Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to fathom. Sons of the gods, this Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to behold. Sons of the gods, this Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to realize. It was in view of this very point that the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, immediately after fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassable, perfect awakening, while abiding at the heart of awakening, thought, "Alas, I have fully awakened to this profound Dharma," and inclined his mind toward little exertion, and did not incline it toward teaching the Dharma. This is the profundity of the Dharma: that in it, no one has ever become fully awakened, no one becomes fully awakened, and no one will become fully awakened.

Because space is profound, this Dharma is profound. Because the self is profound, this Dharma is profound. Because no phenomenon comes, this Dharma is profound. Because no phenomenon goes, this Dharma that I have fully awakened to is profound.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Śakra, lord of the gods, together with the sons of the gods who move in the desire realm, and Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, together with the sons of the gods who move in the form realm, said to the Blessed One: "How wondrous, Blessed One! How marvelous, Sugata! Blessed One, this Dharma has been taught as running counter to the entire world. Blessed One, this Dharma has been taught so that no phenomenon is grasped, whereas the people of the world dwell in grasping."

This is the fifteenth chapter, called "The Gods," of the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, fifteenth volume.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Alas, Blessed One, in this Dharma that has been taught, no phenomenon is apprehended. Blessed One, this Dharma is obstructed by nothing. Blessed One, because it is like space, and nothing in any place is apprehended, this Dharma has the characteristic of being unobstructed. Blessed One, because there is no duality, this Dharma has the characteristic of having no equal. Blessed One, because there is no one to dispute it, this Dharma has the characteristic of having no counterpart. Blessed One, because nothing is truly accomplished, this Dharma has no abiding. Blessed One, because no arising of any kind has arisen, this Dharma has no coming into being. Blessed One, because no path of any kind is apprehended, this Dharma has no path."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, and Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, and those sons of the gods who move in the desire realm and the form realm, said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this noble elder Subhūti, a śrāvaka of the Blessed One, has been born in accord with the Blessed One. Why is that? Blessed One, it is because whatever Dharma this elder Subhūti teaches, he teaches that very Dharma on the basis of emptiness."

Then the venerable Subhūti said to those sons of the gods, Śakra, lord of the gods, Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world, and those who move in the desire realm and the form realm: "Sons of the gods, you say that this elder Subhūti has been born in accord with the Tathāgata. It is because he has not been born that the elder Subhūti has been born in accord with the Tathāgata. The elder Subhūti follows the suchness of the Tathāgata. Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes, so the suchness of the elder Subhūti neither comes nor goes. In this way the elder Subhūti follows the suchness of the Tathāgata. From the very beginning the elder Subhūti has followed the suchness of the Tathāgata. Why is that? The suchness of the Tathāgata is the suchness of all phenomena. The suchness of all phenomena is the suchness of the Tathāgata.

The suchness of the Tathāgata, and the suchness of all phenomena, is the suchness of the elder Subhūti. The elder Subhūti has followed that very suchness, and so he has been born in the wake of the Tathāgata. Yet that suchness of the Tathāgata is not itself a suchness apart; it is that to which he conforms. In this way the elder Subhūti is born in the wake of the Tathāgata. By the very abiding in which the suchness of the Tathāgata abides, by that abiding the elder Subhūti is born in the wake of the Tathāgata.

Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is without change, without alteration, without conceptual thought, and without discursive conceptualization, so too the suchness of the elder Subhūti is without change, without alteration, without conceptual thought, and without discursive conceptualization. In this way the elder Subhūti too, by that suchness which is unchanging, unaltering, and free of thought and conceptualization, is born in the wake of the Tathāgata.

Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is unchanging, unaltering, free of thought and conceptualization, and unobstructed in regard to anything, so too the suchness of all phenomena is unchanging, unaltering, free of thought and conceptualization, and unobstructed in regard to anything. Why is this so? Because this suchness of the Tathāgata and this suchness of all phenomena are one; there is no duality, and it cannot be made dual. The nondual suchness is not the suchness located in anything, nor arising from anything, nor belonging to anything. Since it belongs to nothing at all, that suchness is nondual, and the nondual suchness cannot be made dual.

In this way the elder Subhūti is born in the wake of the Tathāgata through the uncreated suchness. That uncreated suchness never becomes other than suchness. Because it never becomes other than suchness, that suchness is nondual, and the nondual suchness cannot be made dual. In this way the elder Subhūti is born in the wake of the Tathāgata.

Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata, in every respect, does not conceptualize or discursively conceptualize any phenomenon, so too the suchness of the elder Subhūti, in every respect, does not conceptualize or discursively conceptualize any phenomenon. Likewise the Tathāgata and Subhūti are manifested by suchness; these two are neither distinct in kind nor different, since nothing that would make them different is perceived. In this way the elder Subhūti is born in the wake of the Tathāgata.

Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is not other than the suchness of all phenomena, so too the suchness of Subhūti is not other than the suchness of all phenomena. And what is not other than the suchness of all phenomena can never become not the suchness of anything, for that very suchness is the suchness of all phenomena.

Venerable Subhūti has accepted that he follows along with that suchness, a suchness that is not other, and yet here there is no one who follows along with anything anywhere. In this way, Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata. Just as the suchness of the Tathāgata is not past, not future, and not present, so too the suchness of all phenomena is not past, not future, and not present. Thus, because Subhūti follows along with that suchness, he is said to be born after the Tathāgata.

Moreover, the suchness of the Tathāgata follows along with suchness. The suchness of the Tathāgata follows along with the suchness of the past, and the suchness of the past follows along with the suchness of the Tathāgata. The suchness of the Tathāgata follows along with the suchness of the future, and the suchness of the future follows along with the suchness of the Tathāgata. The suchness of the Tathāgata follows along with the suchness of the present, and the suchness of the present follows along with the suchness of the Tathāgata. The suchness of the Tathāgata follows along with the suchness of the past, the future, and the present, and the suchness of the past, the future, and the present follows along with the suchness of the Tathāgata. Thus, the suchness of Subhūti, the suchness of the past, the future, and the present, and the suchness of the Tathāgata are not two; they cannot be made into two. In the same way, the suchness of all phenomena and the suchness of Subhūti are not two; they cannot be made into two.

Blessed One, the suchness of one who has become a bodhisattva is none other than the suchness of the Blessed One who has fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. It is by this very suchness that a bodhisattva, a great being, having become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, obtains the name Tathāgata. This is that suchness. At the very time when this suchness of the Tathāgata was taught, just as when a Tathāgata fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, this great earth trembled in the six ways and the eighteen great signs: it shook, shook strongly, and shook all over; it quivered, quivered strongly, and quivered all over; it heaved, heaved strongly, and heaved all over; it was stirred, stirred strongly, and stirred all over; it resounded with a rumbling, resounded strongly, and resounded all over; it roared, roared strongly, and roared all over.

Then venerable Subhūti spoke further to those sons of the gods: Sons of the gods, in this way Subhūti is born after the Tathāgata. Moreover, Subhūti is not born after form; he is not born after feeling, nor perception, nor the formations, nor consciousness. He is not born after the fruit of stream-entry; nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor the fruit of an arhat. He is not born after the state of a pratyekabuddha, and he is not born after the state of a buddha. Why is that so?

For in this way, those by whom there is a following in birth, and the phenomena that are followed in birth, do not truly exist and are not apprehended. In this way, the elder Subhūti was born in the wake of the Tathāgata.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, this very suchness is a profound practice.

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Śāriputra: So it is, Śāriputra, so it is. Śāriputra, this very suchness is a profound practice. Even as this teaching of suchness was being expounded, three hundred monks, without grasping, had their minds fully liberated from the defilements. Five hundred nuns obtained the pure, stainless Dharma eye with regard to phenomena. Five thousand sons of the gods, who had previously trained, attained the acceptance that phenomena are unborn. And sixty bodhisattvas, without grasping, had their minds fully liberated from the defilements.

Then the venerable Śāriputra, knowing that those bodhisattvas had their minds fully liberated from the defilements without grasping, said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, what is the cause and what is the condition by which these bodhisattvas have their minds fully liberated from the defilements without grasping?

The Blessed One said: Śāriputra, these bodhisattvas have attended and honored five hundred buddhas. Throughout, they gave gifts, kept moral discipline, cultivated patience, undertook diligence, and developed meditative concentration. Yet all of this was not embraced by the Perfection of Wisdom, and they were separated from skillful means. Śāriputra, although the path of these bodhisattvas was one of practice in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, even so, because they were not endowed with skillful means, they made the true limit manifest and definitively emerged into the level of the śrāvakas, not into the level of the buddhas.

Śāriputra, it is like this. Suppose there were a bird whose body measured a hundred leagues, or two hundred, or three hundred, or four hundred, or five hundred leagues. It lives among the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, and it thinks, I shall go to this Jambudvīpa. But, Śāriputra, that bird has no wings grown, or its wings have been plucked out, or its wings have been cut off. Thinking, I shall stay in Jambudvīpa, it hurls itself from the realm of the gods of the Thirty-Three, and the bird falls from there. While it remains in the space of the sky, it thinks, Alas, I shall go back and dwell among the gods of the Thirty-Three. What do you think, Śāriputra? Would that bird be able to go back and stay among the gods of the Thirty-Three?

The venerable Śāriputra said: Blessed One, it would not.

The Blessed One said: Śāriputra, suppose it thinks, Alas, I shall stay in Jambudvīpa unharmed and uninjured. What do you think, Śāriputra? Would that bird come to stay in Jambudvīpa unharmed and uninjured?

Śāriputra said: Blessed One, it would not. Having fallen to Jambudvīpa, it would be harmed and injured, and it would suffer pain amounting to death or close to death. Why is that? Blessed One, it is like this: because its body is huge, it has no wings, and it has fallen from a great height.

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, Śāriputra, so it is. Śāriputra, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, has given rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā has remained giving gifts, guarding moral discipline, cultivating patience, undertaking diligence, and resting in meditative concentration. Suppose he has entered into all this on a vast scale, and has greatly strengthened his resolve to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Even so, if he is not held by the Perfection of Wisdom and is separated from skillful means, he will fall to the ground of the śrāvakas or the ground of the pratyekabuddhas.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, suppose a bodhisattva thinks about and clings, through the mode of signs, to the moral discipline, the concentration, the wisdom, the liberation, and the vision of the wisdom of liberation of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present. Such a person does not know or see the moral discipline of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas. It is not concentration, it is not wisdom, it is not liberation; and he does not know or see the vision of the wisdom of liberation of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas.

"Because he does not know and does not see, he listens to the sound 'emptiness,' and he makes a sign of that sound. Having made that sound into a sign, he wishes to dedicate it toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening. For this reason, it should be understood that he will come to abide on the ground of the śrāvakas or the ground of the pratyekabuddhas. Why is that? Śāriputra, whoever is not held by the Perfection of Wisdom and is separated from skillful means will come to be in this way."

Śāriputra said: "Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has explained, if a bodhisattva possesses a very great accumulation of merit, yet is not held by the Perfection of Wisdom, is separated from skillful means, and does not have a spiritual friend, then it becomes doubtful whether he will attain unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Therefore, Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening should cultivate the Perfection of Wisdom and should also strive in skillful means."

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "So it is, Śāriputra, so it is. Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva, a great being, is not held by the Perfection of Wisdom and is separated from skillful means, then even though he possesses a great accumulation of merit, if he is also separated from spiritual friends, it becomes doubtful whether he will attain unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Therefore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening should cultivate the Perfection of Wisdom and should also be endowed with skillful means."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, together with the sons of the gods who move in the desire realm, and Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world (Sahāṃpati), together with the sons of the gods who move in the form realm, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom is profound."

Blessed One, unsurpassed, perfect awakening is hard to come by. Blessed One, to fully and perfectly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening is exceedingly hard to come by.

Then the Blessed One spoke to the sons of the gods of the desire realm, with Śakra, lord of the gods, at their head, and to the sons of the gods of the form realm, with Brahmā, lord of the world of endurance, at their head. He said: "Sons of the gods, so it is, so it is. Sons of the gods, this Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Unsurpassed, perfect awakening is also hard to come by. For those whose wisdom is confused, whose diligence is weak, whose faith and interest are weak, who are unskilled in means, and who rely on bad friends, fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening is exceedingly hard to come by."

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, the Blessed One has said that unsurpassed, perfect awakening is hard to come by, and that fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening is exceedingly hard to come by. But if there is nothing at all that one could fully awaken to, then, Blessed One, how is it that unsurpassed, perfect awakening is hard to come by, and that fully and perfectly awakening to it is exceedingly hard to come by? Why do I ask? Blessed One, because all phenomena are empty, there is no phenomenon at all that could be fully awakened to. Blessed One, all phenomena are empty in just this way. Blessed One, there is also no phenomenon taught for the sake of being abandoned. In the same way, whatever full and perfect awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening there is, whatever is to be awakened to, whatever is realized, and whatever is to be realized, all of those phenomena are empty. Blessed One, by this way of explaining too, it occurs to me that fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening is easy to come by, and that it is not hard to come by."

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, because there is no arising, unsurpassed, perfect awakening is hard to come by. Subhūti, because it is not truly real, unsurpassed, perfect awakening is hard to come by. Subhūti, because it is free of conceptual thought, unsurpassed, perfect awakening is hard to come by. Subhūti, because it is not brought about by any construction, unsurpassed, perfect awakening is hard to come by. Fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening is supremely hard to come by."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, by this way of explaining too, which is called emptiness, unsurpassed, perfect awakening is hard to come by, and fully and perfectly awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening is supremely hard to come by. Why is that? Venerable Subhūti, space does not think, 'I shall fully and perfectly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.' Venerable Subhūti, in just the same way, these phenomena too are not something to be fully awakened to."

Why is this so? Venerable Subhūti, it is because all phenomena are equal to space. Venerable Subhūti, if unsurpassed, perfect awakening were truly something that could come about, then the bodhisattvas, as many as the sands of the Ganges, would have become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Yet, Venerable Subhūti, bodhisattvas as many as the sands of the Ganges do turn back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Therefore, Venerable Subhūti, you should understand that unsurpassed, perfect awakening is difficult to come about, and that fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening is supremely difficult to come about.

When this was said, the Venerable Subhūti spoke to the Venerable Śāriputra as follows. Venerable Śāriputra, does form turn back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it does not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is there, apart from form, some phenomenon that turns back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, there is not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, do feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness turn back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, they do not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is there, apart from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, some phenomenon that turns back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, there is not.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, does the suchness of form turn back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it does not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, does the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of formations, and the suchness of consciousness turn back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it does not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is there, apart from the suchness of form, some phenomenon that turns back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, there is not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is there, apart from the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of formations, and the suchness of consciousness, some phenomenon that turns back from unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, there is not.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, does form fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it does not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, do feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, they do not.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, does the phenomenon that is fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening exist apart from form? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it does not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, does the phenomenon that is fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening exist apart from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it does not.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is whatever is the suchness of form fully awakened to as unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it is not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is whatever is the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of formations, and the suchness of consciousness fully awakened to as unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it is not.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, does whatever phenomenon is fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening exist apart from the suchness of form? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it does not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, does whatever phenomenon is fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening exist apart from the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, and the suchness of formations, or apart from the suchness of consciousness? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it does not.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is whatever is form to be known as unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it is not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is whatever is feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness to be known as unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it is not.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is whatever phenomenon is other than form to be known as unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it is not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is whatever phenomenon is other than feeling, perception, and formations, and other than consciousness, to be known as unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it is not.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is whatever is the suchness of form to be known as unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it is not. Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is whatever is the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, the suchness of formations, and the suchness of consciousness to be known as unsurpassed, perfect awakening? Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, it is not.

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, is whatever phenomenon is other than the suchness of form to be known as unsurpassed, perfect awakening?

Śāriputra said, "Venerable Subhūti, it is not so."

Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, is there any phenomenon, other than the suchness of feeling, other than the suchness of perception, other than the suchness of the formations, other than the suchness of consciousness, that is to be known as unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?"

Śāriputra said, "Venerable Subhūti, there is not."

Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, what do you think: does suchness turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?"

Śāriputra said, "Venerable Subhūti, it does not."

Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, what do you think: does that phenomenon which turns back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening exist in suchness?"

Śāriputra said, "Venerable Subhūti, it does not."

Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, then what is that phenomenon which turns back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, abiding in the manner of not abiding in that very nature of reality? And what is that phenomenon which has become suchness? Venerable Śāriputra, can suchness itself ever turn back?"

Śāriputra said, "Venerable Subhūti, it cannot."

Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, since all phenomena, in this way, in truth and in their abiding, cannot be apprehended, what is that phenomenon which could turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?"

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Subhūti, "By the manner of the Dharma as the venerable elder Subhūti has explained it, there is no phenomenon at all that turns back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Venerable Subhūti, the three kinds of persons belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas were taught by the Tathāgata. But according to what the venerable Subhūti has shown, there would be no establishing of three; there would be only one vehicle, namely the Buddha vehicle, the bodhisattva vehicle."

Then the venerable Pūrṇa, son of Maitrāyaṇī, said to the venerable Śāriputra, "Venerable Śāriputra, does the venerable elder Subhūti not acknowledge even a single follower of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, or of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or a bodhisattva of the Great Vehicle? Let us first put this question to the elder, the venerable Subhūti."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable elder Subhūti, "Venerable Subhūti, do you not acknowledge even a single follower of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, or of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or a bodhisattva of the Great Vehicle?"

Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, in the suchness of suchness, do you perceive even a single follower of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, or of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or a bodhisattva of the Great Vehicle?"

Śāriputra said, "Venerable Subhūti, I do not. Since suchness itself cannot be apprehended in any of the three ways, how much less a bodhisattva."

Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, then is suchness apprehended in even a single way?"

Śāriputra said, "Venerable Subhūti, it is not so."

Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, do you then see, correctly and in accordance with reality, even a single dharma of a bodhisattva in suchness?"

Śāriputra said, "Venerable Subhūti, it is not so."

Subhūti said, "Venerable Śāriputra, since in this way even that dharma of a bodhisattva is not apprehended in true reality and in the abiding nature, why do you think, 'This one belongs to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, this one belongs to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and this one belongs to the Great Vehicle'?

"Śāriputra, when bodhisattvas, great beings, hear that all the distinctions made within suchness are without difference, without distinction, and incapable of being made separate, and if that bodhisattva, that great being, is not discouraged, is not utterly disheartened, and does not turn back, then it should be known that this bodhisattva, this great being, is certain to go forth to awakening."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti, "Subhūti, so it is. So it is. Subhūti, it is by the power of the Tathāgata and the blessing of the buddhas that you have the confidence to speak in this way. Excellent, Subhūti! Excellent! Indeed, when bodhisattvas, great beings, hear that all the distinctions made within suchness are without difference, without distinction, and incapable of being made separate, and are not discouraged, are not utterly disheartened, and do not turn back, then, Subhūti, it should be known that such a bodhisattva, such a great being, is certain to go forth to awakening."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, by what awakening will this bodhisattva, this great being, be certain to go forth?"

The Blessed One said, "Śāriputra, it is by unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening that this bodhisattva, this great being, will be certain to go forth."

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to go forth with certainty to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, how should he abide, and how should he train?"

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to go forth with certainty to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening should abide in evenness toward all sentient beings. He should generate a mind of evenness toward all sentient beings. That is, he should regard others with a mind free of partiality. He should regard others with a mind of loving-kindness. He should regard others with a mind of benefit. He should regard others with a mind of virtue. He should regard others with a mind that has broken down pride. He should regard others with a mind free of hostility. He should regard others with a mind free of harmfulness. He should regard others with a mind free of enmity. He should establish the perception that every sentient being is a mother, and the perception that every sentient being is a father, a son, or a daughter, and in this way regard others.

"Subhūti, in this way a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to attain manifest, complete awakening in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening should abide toward all sentient beings in this manner, and should train in this manner. He should resolve, 'I shall become the protector of all sentient beings.' And he himself should abide in turning away from all evil."

Practice generosity, guard moral discipline, cultivate patience, undertake diligence, settle in meditative concentration, and become fully developed in wisdom. Observe dependent origination, both in its accordant and in its non-accordant order. Urge others as well to do likewise, speak in praise of this, and rejoice in it in accord with them. In the same way, from the truths up to the bodhisattva's entry into the state beyond fault, and while abiding in the full maturing of sentient beings, one should urge others as well to this, speak its praise, and rejoice in it in accord with them. One who wishes in this way and trains in this way will come, through the manner of being without obscuration, to abide in the sacred Dharma, and will come as far as the nature that is without obscuration.

This is the sixteenth chapter, called "Suchness," of the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what are the aspects of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being? What are the signs, and what are the marks? Blessed One, how am I to recognize an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being?"

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, the ground of ordinary beings, the ground of the śrāvakas, the ground of the pratyekabuddhas, and the ground of the buddhas are all called the ground of suchness. For the suchness of all of these there is no duality and nothing that can be made into two; it is without thought and without conceptualization. One who enters into that suchness and that nature of reality, who abides in suchness, does not think about suchness and does not conceptualize it. One who thus enters and has thus entered, having heard suchness just as it is, and having gone even beyond that, does not feel regret, saying 'It is not like this.' He feels no doubt, no hesitation, and no bewilderment. Rather, he is convinced and he comprehends, saying 'This is suchness; it is just so.' He does not come to speak at random, but speaks words that are connected with meaning, never words disconnected from meaning. And he does not look to what others have done or left undone.

"Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, does not look to the faces of other ascetics and brahmins, thinking 'These people know what is to be known and have seen what is to be seen.' He does not pay homage to other gods. He does not think of offering flowers, incense, perfume, garlands, unguents, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, flags, or lamps to other gods, and he does not rely on other gods. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who also possesses these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

"Moreover, Subhūti, those irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, are not born in the lower realms, and they do not take on the condition of a woman.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, takes up and abides in the ten paths of virtuous action. He himself abstains from taking life, and he also establishes others in abstaining from taking life."

He himself abstains from taking what is not given, and he also establishes others in abstaining from taking what is not given. He himself abstains from sexual misconduct, and he also establishes others in abstaining from sexual misconduct. He himself abstains from the occasion of heedlessness that comes from grain liquor and prepared liquor, and he also establishes others in abstaining from it. He himself abstains from false speech, and he also establishes others in abstaining from false speech. He himself abstains from divisive speech, and he also establishes others in abstaining from divisive speech. He himself abstains from harsh speech, and he also establishes others in abstaining from harsh speech. He himself abstains from idle chatter, and he also establishes others in abstaining from idle chatter. He himself abstains from covetousness, and he also establishes others in abstaining from covetousness. He himself abstains from malice, and he also establishes others in abstaining from malice. He himself abstains from wrong view, and he also establishes others in abstaining from wrong view.

Subhūti, in this way an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, himself takes up and abides in the ten paths of virtuous action, and he also teaches others the ten paths of virtuous action, establishes them in them, encourages them, delights them, and makes them steadfast. Even in a dream, none of the ten paths of non-virtuous action, whether one or many, ever arises in him in any way whatsoever, and he does not engage in them even in thought.

Furthermore, Subhūti, even in the dreams of that irreversible bodhisattva, that great being, the ten paths of virtuous action become manifest. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, whatever Dharma an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, comes to understand and gives to others, he understands and gives it with this thought: "I shall give this Dharma for the sake, the benefit, and the happiness of all sentient beings. May all sentient beings, through this teaching of the Dharma, come to have their aspiration for the Dharma fulfilled." And he shares this gift of the Dharma in common with all sentient beings. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, is not discouraged when profound Dharma is being taught; he has no hesitation and no doubt, and he does not become bewildered. His speech becomes beneficial, his speech becomes fitting, and his speech becomes gentle. He becomes free of dullness and sleeps little. He is free of latent tendencies. Whether he is coming or going, he goes and comes with a mind that is not confused. He goes with mindfulness well established, and he comes with mindfulness well established. He does not set his feet down on the ground slowly or lift them slowly. He sets them down and lifts them comfortably, he does not raise his feet or place them on the ground carelessly or clumsily, and he steps forward on the ground with full awareness, seeing where he steps.

Subhūti, the robes that an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, wears on his body also do not wear out. His conduct becomes careful, he is little troubled by harm, and he has few faults. The eighty thousand kinds of worms that live in the bodies of other beings do not arise at all, in any way, anywhere in his body. Why is that? Subhūti, the roots of virtue of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, are exalted above the whole world. As those roots of virtue grow, in just that way the bodhisattva, the great being, also comes to hold a body that is utterly pure, a speech that is utterly pure, and a mind that is utterly pure.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, how should one recognize the utter purity of the mind of a bodhisattva, a great being?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, as the roots of virtue of the bodhisattva, the great being, grow, in just that way he comes to have a mind with little to do. He holds a mind that is not agitated, a mind without deceit, a mind without crookedness, and a mind without pretense. Subhūti, because his mind is utterly pure, he passes beyond the grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Subhūti, this is how one should recognize the utter purity of the mind of a bodhisattva, a great being. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, does not hanker after gain, honor, and praise. He is not eager for robes, alms food, bedding and seats, medicines for illness, and requisites. He is not given to jealousy or to much miserliness. When profound teachings are expounded he does not shrink back but becomes steady of mind and deep of understanding. He listens to the Dharma from others with full respect, and whatever Dharma he hears from others, he connects all of it with the Perfection of Wisdom. Whatever worldly crafts and occupations there are, he relies on the Perfection of Wisdom and connects every one of them with the nature of reality. He sees no phenomenon whatsoever that is not connected with the dharmadhātu; he sees everything correctly as joined with it. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose Māra the Evil One were to conjure up the eight great hells. In each of those great hells he would conjure up many hundreds of bodhisattvas, many thousands of bodhisattvas, and many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas. And he would say to the irreversible bodhisattva, the great being: "These bodhisattvas, great beings, whom the Tathāgata prophesied to be irreversible, have been born in these eight great hells.

Since you too have been prophesied to be irreversible, you too will be born among these eight great hells. So you should confess that mind of awakening and give it up. If you are born in those eight hells, what will buddhahood do for you? If you do this, you will go to the world of the gods.

Even when he says this, if the bodhisattva, the great being, remains unshaken and unmoved in mind, and understands, "For an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, to be born in the lower realms is impossible; there is no occasion for it," then, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, endowed with these aspects, signs, and marks should also be taken to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, in the guise of an ascetic, may come to an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, and say: "Confess what you heard before. Give up what you formerly took up. If you confess this and give it up, then I will come to you again and again. What you have heard in this way is not the word of the Buddha. It was fabricated by poets for their own display. But what I am teaching is what the Buddha has taught; this is the word of the Buddha." If, hearing this, the bodhisattva is shaken and moved, then, Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva has not been prophesied by the Tathāgatas, is not certain to attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and does not abide in the state of irreversibility.

But, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, hears these words from Māra the Evil One and is neither shaken nor moved, relying on the nature of reality, relying on non-arising, non-cessation, and the absence of conditioned activity, and does not go along with others out of faith in them, then he is like this. Subhūti, just as a monk who is an arhat, whose defilements are exhausted, does not follow another out of faith, because he has realized the nature of reality directly and cannot be carried off by Māra the Evil One, so too, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, cannot be turned aside by persons of the Śrāvaka Vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle. He is of a nature never to fall back to the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas. He is certain of omniscience and inclines toward complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when that bodhisattva, a great being, comes to abide in the state of irreversibility, then he will not be placed in the keeping of others. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, endowed with these aspects, signs, and marks should be taken to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, sixteenth volume.

Furthermore, Subhūti, someone may come to an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, and say: "This conduct of a bodhisattva is the conduct of saṃsāra. Bring your suffering to an end right here. Do not undergo the suffering and unhappiness of conduct in repeated saṃsāra."

"Alas, mother! For now, in this very life, these aggregates of yours will not come to be accomplished; how then could you even think of taking up other aggregates?" If, being spoken to in this way, that bodhisattva is not disturbed and does not waver, then Māra the Evil One will come in person and say to him: "There were bodhisattvas, great beings, who for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges served buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with robes, almsfood, bedding and seats, medicines for the sick, and requisites. They lived the holy life in the presence of as many buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. They honored and attended those buddhas, and for the sake of this very vehicle of the bodhisattvas they inquired, questioned, and asked again and again: 'How should bodhisattvas, great beings, abide?' And they abided just as those Tathāgatas taught them, practiced just so, and trained in yoga just so. Yet even they did not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. If even those who stayed within such instruction and guidance, and who trained in this way, did not attain omniscience, then how could you possibly attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?"

If even after such words he is not disturbed and does not waver, then Māra the Evil One will magically conjure monks in that very place, and they will say: "Those monks who are arhats, whose defilements are exhausted, had set out for awakening, and yet now they have attained only arhatship and abide in arhatship. So how could you possibly attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?" If such things are said and shown to the bodhisattva, the great being, and his mind is still not disturbed and does not waver, then that bodhisattva, great being, should be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

If, having heard such words meant to turn him away from others, that bodhisattva, great being, does not fall away from the nature of reality, his mind does not turn back, his mind does not change, and he knows all these deeds of Māra for what they are, then, Subhūti, it is impossible, there is no occasion, for a bodhisattva, great being, who practices the perfections in this way, to fail to attain omniscience.

A bodhisattva, great being, who practices and trains in this way, who is not separated from the conduct that the Tathāgata has taught, and who is not separated from those attentions that accord with the perfections, cannot possibly give Māra the Evil One an opening. That is impossible, there is no occasion for it.

If that bodhisattva, great being, understands the deeds of Māra, and having heard from others words meant to turn him away does not fall away, his mind does not turn back, and his mind does not change, because he knows those deeds of Māra in this way, then, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, great being, who has these aspects, these signs, and these marks should likewise be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Subhūti, furthermore, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, does not form the perception of form, and does not generate the perception of form. In the same way, he has no perception of feeling, no perception of perception, and no perception of formations; he does not form the perception of consciousness, and does not generate the perception of consciousness. Why is that? Because an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, being empty of intrinsic characteristics, enters without fault into the bodhisattva's path through phenomena. Yet he does not apprehend those phenomena, and does not form or generate any notion of them. Therefore he is said to have attained the forbearance of the wisdom of non-arising. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be taken to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Subhūti, furthermore, Māra the Evil One, having transformed himself into the guise of a monk, may come into the presence of a bodhisattva, a great being, and try to turn back the bodhisattva's resolve. He says: "Omniscience is like space. This thing called omniscience does not exist. This thing called omniscience is not something that is. Who could know it? Who could become fully and completely awakened to it? Nothing at all comes forth from it. That which fully awakens, that which is to be fully awakened to, that which knows, and that which is to be known, all these phenomena are like space. You are tormenting yourself for no purpose. The claim that one should become fully and completely awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is shown to be Māra's work. This was not taught by the Buddha." And the son or daughter of good family should understand, think, and recognize in this way: "Whatever draws one away from awakening, this is the work of Māra." Having thought in this way, he should make his mind steadfast regarding it, keeping his mind unshaken and not letting it be carried away.
