Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be taken to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Subhūti, furthermore, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, turns away from the grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and enters into omniscience. If he wishes, he enters into the first meditative concentration. In the same way he enters the second, the third, and the fourth meditative concentration. He abides in those four concentrations and becomes thoroughly familiar with meditative concentration. Although he enters into these concentrations, he is not reborn through the power of concentration. Instead, by his own wish, he abides in the states of the desire realm. Subhūti, this too should be understood as a defining mark of the irreversibility of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti, furthermore, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, does not make a great matter of his name. He does not make a great matter of fame, reputation, or verses of praise, and he has no attachment to a name. His mind is undisturbed, and his mind becomes one of benefit toward all sentient beings. When he goes and when he comes, he does not go with a confused mind and does not come with a confused mind; he comes mindfully and goes mindfully.

Even if such a bodhisattva dwells in the household life, he does not become attached to the objects of desire, nor does an excessive inclination toward them arise in him. He engages with desires while perceiving them as a source of weariness, and while perceiving them as fearsome. Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a man goes into a wilderness haunted by bandits and takes a meal there. He eats in a state of fear, and he eats thinking only of moving on, reflecting, "How long before I get out of this bandit-ridden wilderness?" Perceiving things in this way, he eats in haste. In just the same way, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, even when dwelling in the household life, engages with whatever objects of desire he enjoys without seeking them, without craving them, and without clinging to them. He becomes one who does not seek after the five strands of sensual pleasure, whose nature is delight and whose nature is bliss.

While dwelling in the household life, they do not make their living by means fair or unfair. They live by the Dharma alone and do not live by what is contrary to the Dharma. Even at the cost of their lives, they would not readily harm another. Why is this? It is because those who are noble persons, great persons, supreme persons, most excellent persons, beautiful persons, the best of the herd among persons, vast persons, chief persons, foremost persons, cherished persons, lotus persons, white lotus persons, wise persons, elephant persons, lion persons, those who turn the reins of those to be trained, bring all beings to hold to the supreme of bliss. Subhūti, such bodhisattvas, great beings, dwell in the household life because they have gained the power produced by the Perfection of Wisdom. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, endowed with these aspects, these signs, and these marks should also be held to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the great yakṣa Vajrapāṇi constantly follows close behind an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being. Such a bodhisattva is hard to overcome, and neither humans nor non-humans are able to get past him. He becomes hard for all beings to approach. His mind is not distracted. He does not have deficient faculties; his faculties are fully complete, and he is never without fully complete faculties. He is endowed with the faculties of the best of the herd among persons, and he is never other than a noble person. He never applies, in any way whatever, to women the classes of mantras, ointments, spells, medicines, and other means of bringing them under his control. His livelihood becomes entirely pure, and he does not live by wrong livelihood. He does not become one who is by temperament quarrelsome or given to contentious speech. He does not disparage those whose views are upright, and he does not slander others. He is endowed with these good qualities and with others as well. He does not make predictions to men or women, saying, "You will have a son," or "You will have a daughter." Such faults of a prognosticator do not arise in him; no such nature is found in him.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who is endowed with these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be held to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, I shall now set forth the aspects, the signs, and the marks by which one should know a bodhisattva, a great being, to be irreversible from unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. What are they?

Such bodhisattvas do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice, and the continued practice, of the aggregates, the sense sources, the elements, and dependent origination. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice, and the continued practice, of talk that delights in company and idle gatherings. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about kings, nor of talk about thieves, nor of talk about armies, nor of talk about quarrels. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about villages, towns, market towns, regions, countries, and royal palaces and their retinues. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about themselves. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about ministers and chief ministers. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about men, women, and eunuchs. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about conveyances, pleasure groves, monasteries, palaces, ponds, lakes, pools, tanks, forests, parks, and mountains. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about yakṣas, rākṣasas, hungry ghosts, flesh-eating piśācas, crawling ghouls, and kumbhāṇḍas. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about food and drink, clothing, ornaments, incense, garlands, and ointments. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about the marketplace, crossroads, rest houses, gatherings of merchants, and the bearing of children. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about song, dance, the reciting of praises, clapping and dancing, and musicians. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk about oceans, rivers, and continents. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk that runs contrary to the Dharma. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice of talk that delights ordinary people.

Rather, they dwell in strenuous application to the practice, and the continued practice, of talk about the Perfection of Wisdom, and they are never separated from the attentive engagement of the mind that is joined with omniscience. They do not dwell in strenuous application to the practice, and the continued practice, of talk about quarrels, disputes, contention, and debate. They desire only the Dharma, and do not desire what is contrary to the Dharma.

They do not delight in quarrels that cause division; they speak words that bring harmony and do not speak words that create discord. They wish for friendship and do not wish for enmity. They speak the Dharma and do not speak what is contrary to the Dharma. They long with yearning only to see the Tathāgata. In other world systems there are Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas who dwell, live and abide there; they give rise to the thought of being born in the presence of those buddhas, and if they wish it, they are born there. Thus they are never separated from seeing the Tathāgata and from serving and honoring the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, pass away from among the gods who move in the desire realm, from among the gods who move in the form realm, or from among the gods who move in the formless realm, they are born in this very central region of Jambudvīpa. They are born among human beings who are skilled in the arts, skilled in poetry, skilled in mantras, skilled in the sciences, skilled in treatises, skilled in signs, and skilled in the meaning of the Dharma. Few are born among the people of the border regions; for the most part they are born in the central region. Even those who are born among the people of the border regions are born in great cities, and they too possess these qualities. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses these aspects, these signs and these marks should be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, does not think, "Am I irreversible, or am I not irreversible?" For regarding his own stage he feels no doubt and no hesitation, and he does not become wholly discouraged. Subhūti, it is just as a stream-enterer feels no vacillation and no doubt about his own fruit of stream-entry. In the same way, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, feels no vacillation, doubt or hesitation about his own bodhisattva stage, and he does not become wholly discouraged regarding his own stage. He also quickly recognizes the actions of Māra as they arise and occur, and he does not come under the sway of those actions of Māra that arise and occur.

Subhūti, it is just as when a person has committed a deed of immediate retribution: until the time of death he is never separated from the mind of that deed. He can neither dispel nor suppress that mind, and it follows him until the time of death. In the same way, Subhūti, the irreversible mind of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, abides firmly, and he does not stir from his own irreversible stage. Neither the world with its gods, humans and asuras can move or shake him. He also recognizes the actions of Māra as they arise and occur, and he does not come under their sway. Because he feels no vacillation or doubt about his own stage, even when he passes away, the mind of a śrāvaka and the mind of a pratyekabuddha do not arise in him. Even when he passes away, he thinks, "I will certainly not fail to attain full awakening."

Thinking, "I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening," he remains on his own ground, and he will not be left at the mercy of others; he will not be shaken from his own ground. Why is that? Because he abides endowed with an unplundered mind and unplundered wisdom.

Suppose Māra the Evil One approaches in the guise of a buddha, and having approached, says: "Realize arhatship right here. You have not been prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. The modes, the signs, and the marks by which a bodhisattva, a great being, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect awakening are not found in you; those signs are absent, those marks are absent. Since they do not exist in you, why do you practice this?" If the mind of that bodhisattva, that great being, were to change, then, Subhūti, it should be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, has not been prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening by the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past.

But suppose he thinks, "Alas, this is Māra the Evil One, who has magically appeared in the guise of a buddha; or he is under Māra's empowerment, or is an emanation of Māra. This is not the Tathāgata. What the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, has declared is exactly so, and not otherwise." Or suppose he reflects carefully and thinks, "Alas, Māra the Evil One has taken on the appearance of a buddha, wishing to separate me from unsurpassed, perfect awakening." Subhūti, if Māra the Evil One then turns back, it should be understood that this bodhisattva, this great being, has been prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening by the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past, and that he abides on the ground of an irreversible bodhisattva.

Subhūti, if these modes, these signs, and these marks are present in a bodhisattva, a great being, then, in accord with his possessing these qualities, one should understand: "Surely this bodhisattva, this great being, has been prophesied by the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past, and abides on the ground of an irreversible bodhisattva." Why is that? Because those modes, those signs, and those marks of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, are present in him. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, endowed with those modes, signs, and marks should likewise be taken as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, in order to uphold the sacred Dharma, gives up even his own self and gives up even his life. Therefore, Subhūti, the irreversible bodhisattva, the great being, strives with intense diligence in order to uphold the sacred Dharma.

Out of delight in and reverence for the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present, and out of delight in and reverence for the Dharma, thinking, "The buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are the body of the Dharma," he takes up the sacred Dharma. He thinks: "This is not only the taking up of the sacred Dharma by the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past. The taking up of the sacred Dharma by the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the present is this very same thing, and so too is that of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have yet to come. I too am counted among those future buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Therefore I too will be prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. This is my own taking up of the sacred Dharma as well." Seeing this significance, he gives up even his own body for the sake of taking up the sacred Dharma. He even gives up his life, and in this he does not become discouraged and is not lazy.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has these aspects, these signs, and these marks should be understood to be irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, has no regret and no doubt when the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly complete buddha, teaches the Dharma.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, is it only with regard to the Tathāgata's teaching of the Dharma that he has no regret and no doubt, and not with regard to that of a śrāvaka?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, he feels no regret and has no doubt even when a śrāvaka teaches the Dharma. Why is that? Because that bodhisattva, that great being, has attained acceptance of the unborn nature of phenomena. For that reason he listens in a way that does not contradict the nature of all phenomena, and having heard, he feels no regret and has no doubt. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has these qualities is irreversible. Subhūti, these too should be recognized as the aspects, signs, and marks of a bodhisattva, a great being, who is irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

This is the seventeenth chapter, "The Aspects, Signs, and Marks of Irreversibility," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, it is marvelous that a bodhisattva, a great being, possesses such a vast collection of qualities, that a bodhisattva, a great being, possesses immeasurable qualities, and that a bodhisattva, a great being, possesses incalculable qualities.

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, so it is, so it is. Why is that? Subhūti, an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, attains boundless, limitless wisdom, which cannot be taken away by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, even if the Blessed One were to set forth the aspects, signs, and marks of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, he would still go on practicing.

Therefore, Blessed One, please teach the profound, profound points that are connected with the Perfection of Wisdom to the bodhisattva, the great being.

When he had spoken in this way, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, it is excellent, truly excellent, that you wish to know about the profound, profound points. Subhūti, 'profound' is a synonym for emptiness. Subhūti, 'profound' is a synonym for the signless, the wishless, the unconditioned, the unarisen, the unborn, the non-existent, freedom from attachment, cessation, and nirvāṇa, and for what has become free."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, is this a synonym only for those phenomena, or is it also a synonym for all phenomena?"

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, this is a synonym for all phenomena as well. Why is that? Subhūti, form is profound. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are profound."

"Subhūti, how is form profound? And how, Subhūti, are feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness profound? Subhūti, form is profound in just the way that suchness is. In the same way, feeling, perception, and formations are profound, and, Subhūti, consciousness is profound in just the way that suchness is. Subhūti, in this regard, form is profound in just the way that the suchness of form is. In the same way, feeling, perception, and formations are profound in just the way that the suchness of feeling, the suchness of perception, and the suchness of formations are; and, Subhūti, consciousness is profound in just the way that the suchness of consciousness is.

"Subhūti, that in which there is no form is the profundity of form. In the same way, Subhūti, that in which there is no feeling, no perception, no formations, and no consciousness is the profundity of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, it is wonderful that, through subtle skillful means, one is turned away even from form and nirvāṇa is shown; and in the same way, that through subtle skillful means one is turned away even from feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and nirvāṇa is shown."

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, whoever reflects on, weighs, and thoroughly considers these profound, profound points connected with the Perfection of Wisdom, thinking, 'I shall abide just as it is taught in the Perfection of Wisdom; I shall train just as it is explained in the Perfection of Wisdom; I shall accomplish just as it is closely taught in the Perfection of Wisdom'; and who practices in that way, reflects closely in that way, examines thoroughly in that way, applies himself in that way, makes effort in that way, and strives in that way, and who practices yoga in this for even a single day, how much activity does that bodhisattva, that great being, accomplish in that one day?

"Subhūti, suppose, for example, there were a man of passionate temperament, given to conceptual thought. And suppose that this man of passionate temperament, given to conceptual thought, had made an assignation with a beautiful woman, lovely to behold and delightful to see, and that this woman was one who was held by another."

If he has no power to leave the household and come and go as he wishes, Subhūti, what do you think? What kinds of conceptual thoughts would arise in that man?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, the thoughts that arise in that man would be only those connected with the woman. He would think, "I will go to her, and with her I will indulge in such pleasures; in this way I will take delight, in this way I will play, in this way I will wander about in enjoyment."

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Until the day has passed, how many conceptual thoughts would arise in that man?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, until the day has passed, a great many conceptual thoughts would arise in that man.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, however many conceptual thoughts arise in that man until the day has passed, for that many eons a bodhisattva, a great being, turns his back on saṃsāra, casts it aside, and brings it to an end. As for one who abides in this Perfection of Wisdom, who studies it, realizes it, reflects on it closely, and practices it in yoga, just as it is set forth, taught, closely explained, shown, and thoroughly demonstrated, such a one also removes those faults through which a bodhisattva, a great being, would turn back from unsurpassable, perfect awakening.

Subhūti, in this way the bodhisattva, the great being, who exerts himself in the practice of the Perfection of Wisdom and who abides in this manner, accomplishes this much in a single day through the attention that accompanies the Perfection of Wisdom.

Suppose a bodhisattva, devoid of the Perfection of Wisdom, were to remain for eons as many as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, giving gifts. And suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, were to practice the Perfection of Wisdom in yoga for even a single day. This latter is more excellent than the former.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva were to remain for eons as many as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, giving gifts to stream-enterers and establishing them in the Dharma. Likewise he gives gifts to once-returners, to non-returners, and to arhats, and establishes them. He gives gifts to pratyekabuddhas and establishes them. He gives gifts to the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, and establishes them. Yet he is devoid of the Perfection of Wisdom. And suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, were to practice in yoga, for even a single day, just as it is closely explained, taught, and thoroughly demonstrated in the Perfection of Wisdom. This bodhisattva, this great being, generates far greater merit.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva were to remain for eons as many as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, giving gifts to beings from stream-enterers up to the perfectly awakened buddhas and establishing them, and were also to bring moral discipline to complete perfection, yet were devoid of the Perfection of Wisdom. And suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in the Perfection of Wisdom, were to attend to it, and rising from that attention were to teach the Dharma.

Subhūti, this bodhisattva, this great being, generates far more merit than the former bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva remains for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, and from the stream-enterers up to the perfectly complete buddhas, offers gifts to them and establishes them in virtue. Suppose he also brings moral discipline to full perfection and is endowed with patience, yet is separated from the Perfection of Wisdom. And suppose another, a bodhisattva, a great being who abides in the Perfection of Wisdom, rises from that very attention and gives the gift of the Dharma. Then, Subhūti, this bodhisattva, this great being, generates far more merit than the former bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva remains for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, and from the stream-enterers up to the perfectly complete buddhas, offers gifts and establishes them in virtue. Suppose he brings moral discipline to full perfection, is endowed with patience, and undertakes diligence, and devotes himself to the meditative concentrations and to the factors that are on the side of awakening, yet is separated from the Perfection of Wisdom. And suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, having given the gift of the Dharma in this way, dedicates it to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. Then, Subhūti, this bodhisattva, this great being, generates far more merit than the former bodhisattva.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, gives the gift of the Dharma in this way and dedicates it to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening through the dedication taught in the Perfection of Wisdom. Then he generates far more merit than the one before.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, gives the gift of the Dharma in this way and dedicates it to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening through the dedication taught in the Perfection of Wisdom, but, having dedicated it, does not practice by correctly establishing it within. And suppose another bodhisattva, a great being, gives the gift of the Dharma in this way, dedicates it to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening through the dedication taught in the Perfection of Wisdom, and, having dedicated it, does practice by correctly establishing it within. When he practices by correctly establishing it within, that correct establishing within is embraced by the Perfection of Wisdom and is not separated from the Perfection of Wisdom. This bodhisattva, this great being, generates far more merit.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, when the Blessed One has said that this manifest composing is conceptual construction, in what way, then, is it said that much merit is generated?

The Blessed One replied: Subhūti, the merit that a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom manifestly composes, even that, as things now appear, appears just like something shown; it appears as something accumulated; it appears as something nourished; it appears as something without essence.

Furthermore, Subhūti, to whatever extent a bodhisattva, a great being, discerns all phenomena individually in this way, to that same extent, Subhūti, the bodhisattva, the great being, is not separated from the Perfection of Wisdom. And furthermore, Subhūti, to whatever extent a bodhisattva, a great being, is not separated from the Perfection of Wisdom, to that same extent he generates merit that is immeasurable and incalculable.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, what difference is there, what distinction, between the immeasurable and the incalculable?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, "immeasurable" means that to which no measure applies. Subhūti, "incalculable" means that which cannot be exhausted by counting.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, is there a way of speaking by which even form comes to be immeasurable? And likewise, Blessed One, is there a way of speaking by which feeling, perception, and formations, and also consciousness, come to be immeasurable?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, you have asked in these words: "Blessed One, is there a way of speaking by which even form comes to be immeasurable? And likewise feeling, perception, and formations; and, Blessed One, is there a way of speaking by which even consciousness comes to be immeasurable?" Subhūti, there is a way of speaking by which form itself comes to be immeasurable. Likewise, there is a way of speaking by which feeling itself, perception itself, formations themselves, and consciousness itself come to be immeasurable.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, of what is this "immeasurable" a synonym?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, this "immeasurable" is a synonym for emptiness. This "immeasurable" is a synonym for the signless. Subhūti, this "immeasurable" is a synonym for the wishless.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, is this "immeasurable" a synonym for emptiness alone? Blessed One, is this "immeasurable" a synonym for the signless and the wishless alone, and not for other phenomena?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Has it not been taught that all phenomena are empty?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, the Tathāgata has taught that all phenomena are emptiness.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, whatever is emptiness is inexhaustible, and whatever is emptiness is also immeasurable. Therefore, Subhūti, these phenomena are not found to be distinct or different in meaning. Subhūti, they are merely verbal designations, as the Tathāgata has shown and declared.

Whether it is called the immeasurable, the incalculable, the inexhaustible, emptiness, the signless, the wishless, the non-constructed, the non-arising, the unborn, the non-entity, freedom from attachment, cessation, or nirvāṇa, Subhūti, all of this has been spoken of by the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, as the establishing of the teaching.

Subhūti said:

How wondrous that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, has taught even this, the very nature of all phenomena, and that this nature of all phenomena is itself inexpressible! Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said, all phenomena are indeed inexpressible.

The Blessed One declared: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, all phenomena are inexpressible. Why is that? Subhūti, because the emptiness of all phenomena cannot be expressed.

Subhūti asked: Blessed One, is there then any increase or decrease in the meaning of the inexpressible?

The Blessed One declared: Subhūti, there is not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, if there is no increase and no decrease in the meaning of the inexpressible, then there would be neither increase nor decrease in the perfection of generosity either. In the same way, Blessed One, there would be neither increase nor decrease in the perfection of moral discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom. Blessed One, if there is neither increase nor decrease in these six perfections, then how, Blessed One, could a bodhisattva, a great being, by the power of six perfections that do not increase, come to be fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening? Or how could he draw near to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening? Blessed One, without bringing the perfections to completion, a bodhisattva, a great being, cannot draw near to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

The Blessed One declared: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, although there is indeed no increase or decrease in the meaning of the perfections, nevertheless, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and meditates on the Perfection of Wisdom, and who is skilled in means, does not think, "This perfection of generosity is increasing; this perfection of generosity is decreasing." Rather, he thinks, "This so-called perfection of generosity is merely a name." Having thought so, he practices giving, and he dedicates those attentions, those aspirations of mind, and those roots of virtue to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, dedicating them just as unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening truly is.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and meditates on the Perfection of Wisdom, and who is skilled in means, thinks, "This perfection of moral discipline is increasing."

He does not think, "This perfection of moral discipline is increasing," nor "This perfection of moral discipline is declining." Rather, he thinks, "What is called the perfection of moral discipline is merely a name." Having thought this, he takes up moral discipline properly and abides in it, and he dedicates those acts of attention, those generations of the mind of awakening, and those roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. He dedicates them just as unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening truly is.

Subhūti, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and meditates on the Perfection of Wisdom, being skilled in means, does not think, "This perfection of patience is increasing," nor "This perfection of patience is declining." Rather, he thinks, "What is called the perfection of patience is merely a name." Having thought this, he cultivates patience, and he dedicates those acts of attention, those generations of the mind of awakening, and those roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. He dedicates them just as unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening truly is.

Subhūti, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and meditates on the Perfection of Wisdom, being skilled in means, does not think, "This perfection of diligence is increasing," nor "This perfection of diligence is declining." Rather, he thinks, "What is called the perfection of diligence is merely a name." Having thought this, he undertakes diligence, and he dedicates those acts of attention, those generations of the mind of awakening, and those roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. He dedicates them just as unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening truly is.

Subhūti, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and meditates on the Perfection of Wisdom, being skilled in means, does not think, "This perfection of meditative concentration is increasing," nor "This perfection of meditative concentration is declining." Rather, he thinks, "What is called the perfection of meditative concentration is merely a name." Having thought this, he settles in meditative equipoise in the concentrations, and he dedicates those acts of attention, those generations of the mind of awakening, and those roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. He dedicates them just as unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening truly is.

Subhūti, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and meditates on the Perfection of Wisdom, being skilled in means, does not think, "This perfection of wisdom is increasing," nor "This perfection of wisdom is declining." Rather, he thinks, "This perfection of wisdom is merely a name." Having thought this, he practices the Perfection of Wisdom and meditates on the Perfection of Wisdom, and he dedicates those acts of attention, those generations of the mind of awakening, and those roots of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. He dedicates them just as unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening truly is.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what then is this that is called unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?"

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, what is called unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is suchness. Subhūti, suchness neither increases nor diminishes. If a bodhisattva, a great being, remains for long without interruption, endowed with those modes of attention, then he is close to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Subhūti, in the same way, in what is inexpressible there is neither increase nor decrease. By those modes of attention nothing diminishes. Subhūti, in the same way, in the perfections there is neither increase nor decrease. Subhūti, in the same way, in all phenomena there is neither increase nor decrease. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, abides with such modes of attention, then he is close to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening."

This is the eighteenth chapter, called the chapter on emptiness, from the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. The seventeenth volume.

Then the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, does a bodhisattva, a great being, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening through the first arising of the mind? Or does a bodhisattva, a great being, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening through a later arising of the mind? Blessed One, the earlier arising of the mind does not meet with the later arising of the mind, and the later arising of the mind does not meet with the earlier arising of the mind. Then, Blessed One, how do the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva, a great being, come to completion?"

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, what do you think? When the flame of an oil lamp is burning, is the wick burned by the first flame that touches it, or is the wick burned by a later flame that touches it?"

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, not so. The wick is not burned by the first flame that touches it, yet without depending on the first flame having arisen, the wick would not be burned. Blessed One, nor is the wick burned by the later flame that touches it, yet without depending on the later flame touching it, the wick would not be burned."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, what do you think? Is that wick burned?"

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, it is burned. Sugata, it is burned."

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, in the same way, a bodhisattva, a great being, does not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening through the first arising of the mind, yet without depending on the first arising of the mind he would not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Nor does he awaken through the later arising of the mind, yet without depending on the later arising of the mind he would not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Nor is it that he awakens through those arisings of the mind alone, and neither does he fully awaken through anything other than those arisings of the mind."

A bodhisattva, a great being, also fully awakens to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

When this was said, the venerable Subhūti spoke to the Blessed One as follows. Blessed One, this dependent origination is profound. Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, does not fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening through the first generation of the awakening mind; yet without relying on that first generation of the awakening mind, he also does not fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. A bodhisattva, a great being, does not fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening through the final generation of the awakening mind; yet without relying on the final generation of the awakening mind, he also does not fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. He does not fully awaken through those generations of the awakening mind, nor through any generation of mind other than those; and yet a bodhisattva, a great being, does fully awaken to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows. Subhūti, what do you think? Does a mind that has ceased arise again afterward?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it does not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Is a mind that arises of a nature to cease?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it is of a nature to cease.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Does a mind that is of a nature to cease go on to cease?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it does not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Is a mind that has not arisen of a nature to cease?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it is not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Does a mind that is not of a nature to cease go on to cease?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it does not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Does a mind that neither arises nor ceases, being of a nature that does not cease, go on to cease?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it does not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Does a phenomenon whose essential nature is, by its intrinsic nature, already ceased go on to cease?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it does not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Does the nature of reality of phenomena, whatever it is, go on to cease?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it does not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Does suchness abide just as it is?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, suchness abides just as it is.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? If suchness abides just as it is, then would it not at that time be something that is not permanently fixed?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it would not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Is suchness not profound?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it is profound.

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does mind exist in suchness?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, it does not."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Is the mind itself suchness?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, it is not."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does mind exist apart from suchness?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, it does not."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, do you correctly perceive suchness?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, I do not."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does one who practices in this way practice in the profound?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, one who practices in this way does not practice in anything at all. Why is that? Because in this there are no engagements to enter into, and no engaging at all."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom, in what does he practice?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, he practices in the ultimate."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in the ultimate, practice in signs?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, he does not."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Has he not destroyed that sign?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, that is not so."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom, thereby destroy signs?"

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, when that bodhisattva, that great being, practices the conduct of a bodhisattva, he does not apply himself with the thought, 'May I attain, right here, the abandoning of signs.' For if he were to attain it, then, because the qualities of a buddha would not have been completed, he would become a śrāvaka. Blessed One, he knows what the defining characteristic is and what the sign is, and he also understands that sign, and yet he becomes thoroughly familiar even with the absence of that sign. This is the skillful means of a bodhisattva, a great being."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, cultivates in a dream the three doors of liberation, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, will his Perfection of Wisdom increase?"

Subhūti replied, "Venerable Śāriputra, if it increases through cultivation by day, then it increases in dreams as well. Why is that? Venerable Śāriputra, the Blessed One has said that dream and daytime are without conceptual distinction. Venerable Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva, a great being, who has found the Perfection of Wisdom practices the Perfection of Wisdom throughout a whole day, then for that bodhisattva, that great being, who is accustomed to the Perfection of Wisdom, the Perfection of Wisdom will also grow in dreams."

Śāriputra said, "Venerable Subhūti, if any man or woman performs in a dream some virtuous or non-virtuous action, does that action accumulate, or become fully accumulated?"

Subhūti replied,

As the Blessed One taught that all phenomena are like a dream, in that way that action is not accumulated, nor is it fully accumulated. Venerable Śāriputra, but suppose that man, having awakened, conceptualizes and generates the perception of having killed; then that action is accumulated and fully accumulated. Venerable Śāriputra, moreover, suppose that someone has taken life in a dream, and then, having awakened, he too thinks in this way: "Ah! I killed it! I killed it well! I killed it thoroughly! It was I who killed it!" If he thinks like that and generates the perception of rejoicing in it, then, venerable Śāriputra, that action is accumulated and fully accumulated.

Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, if that man, having awakened, thinks in this way, conceptualizes, and generates the perception of killing, thinking, "Ah! I killed it! I killed it well! I killed it thoroughly! It was I who killed it!", and if in that case the action is accumulated and fully accumulated, then, since the Buddha, the Blessed One, also brings about the conceptualization that perceives exhaustion, would his action too be accumulated and fully accumulated?

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, that is not so. Why? Because the Tathāgata is free from all thought and conceptualization; he is, as it were, just like space. Venerable Śāriputra, in the same way, without an object of focus no action arises, and without an object of focus no mind arises. Venerable Śāriputra, therefore action arises only together with an object of focus, and not without an object of focus. Mind arises only together with an object of focus, and not without an object of focus. Venerable Śāriputra, the mind engages with phenomena that are seen, heard, understood, and cognized. With some of these the mind takes hold of what is thoroughly afflicted, and with others it takes hold of what is purified. Venerable Śāriputra, therefore volition arises only together with an object of focus, and not without one. Mind arises only together with an object of focus, and not without one.

Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, when the Blessed One has taught that all objects of focus are empty and secluded, then, venerable Subhūti, why does volition arise only together with an object of focus, and not arise without one?

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, volition arises together with an object of focus because one has fixed on a sign and has taken as one's object what is in fact nonexistent; it does not arise without an object of focus. Venerable Śāriputra, volition is secluded, and the sign is also secluded. In the same way, the formations conditioned by ignorance are also secluded. Consciousness conditioned by the formations is also secluded, and so on, up to aging and death conditioned by birth, which are also secluded. Venerable Śāriputra, in the same way all those objects of focus are secluded. Volition too is secluded from signs, yet depending on worldly convention, a mind together with an object of focus arises.

Śāriputra said: Venerable Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, in a dream practices generosity, and also fully dedicates that generosity to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Is that generosity then said to have been fully dedicated?

Subhūti said: Venerable Śāriputra, this bodhisattva, this great being Maitreya, is present here.

"He has been prophesied by the Tathāgata to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, without any interruption. This matter he realizes directly in his own person. Ask him, and he will answer this question."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya: "Venerable Maitreya, the elder Subhūti says that the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, will give the answer to this question. Venerable Invincible One, please give the answer to this question."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, said to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, you say that the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, will give the answer to this question. Venerable Subhūti, is the name 'Maitreya' what gives the answer to this question? Or is it form that gives the answer? Or is it feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that give the answer? Or is it color that gives the answer? Or is it shape that gives the answer? Or is it the emptiness of form, whatever that is, that gives the answer? Or is it the emptiness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, whatever that is, that gives the answer?

"Venerable Subhūti, that which is the emptiness of form cannot give the answer. In the same way, venerable Subhūti, that which is the emptiness of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness cannot give the answer. Venerable Subhūti, I do not see, as a genuine fact, any phenomenon that gives an answer. I do not see, as a genuine fact, any phenomenon to which an answer is to be given. I do not see, as a genuine fact, any phenomenon by which an answer is to be given. And I do not see, as a genuine fact, any phenomenon that is prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening."

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya: "Venerable Maitreya, just as these phenomena have been taught in words, have you realized them directly in that way?"

Maitreya said: "Venerable Śāriputra, I have not realized these phenomena directly in the way they are taught in words. Venerable Śāriputra, even those phenomena that are expressed in words or conceived by the mind, I do not know in that way, I do not apprehend them, and I do not see them as a genuine fact. Venerable Śāriputra, just as that which cannot be touched by the body, cannot be expressed in words, and cannot be conceived by the mind is so, in the same way all phenomena too are without intrinsic nature, because they have no inherent existence."

Then the venerable Śāriputra thought: "Ah, this bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, is profound in wisdom. He teaches as one who has practiced the Perfection of Wisdom for a very long time."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, why do you think, 'Ah, this bodhisattva, the great being Maitreya, is profound in wisdom'? Śāriputra, by possessing which phenomenon are you distinguished as an arhat? Do you see that phenomenon as a genuine fact?"

Śāriputra replied: "Blessed One, I do not."

The Blessed One said:

Śāriputra, in the same way, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom, he does not think: "This Dharma has been prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. This Dharma will be prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. This Dharma is being prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Through this Dharma I will become fully awakened in unsurpassed, perfect awakening." A bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way is practicing the Perfection of Wisdom. While practicing, he is not alarmed, he is not frightened, and he does not come to be possessed by terror. Nor does he reflect: "Because I have obtained the power that has been developed, I will not fail to become fully awakened." If he practices like this, he is practicing the Perfection of Wisdom.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva, a great being, enters a wilderness haunted by predatory beasts, he should not be alarmed, should not be frightened, and should not be possessed by terror. Why is that? Because he has given up everything for the sake of all sentient beings. He should generate the thought in this way: "If I am eaten by predatory beasts, then I will have given them that gift, and my perfection of generosity will also be fully completed. I will draw close to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. And may it be so that in the buddha field where I become fully awakened in unsurpassed, perfect awakening, those sentient beings who have gone to the animal realm will never, in any way, anywhere, appear at all, nor even be known of, but instead will possess the enjoyments of the gods and the full use of them." This is how he thinks.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva, a great being, enters a wilderness haunted by bandits, he should not be alarmed, should not be frightened, and should not be possessed by terror. Why is that? Because a bodhisattva, a great being, delights in the root of virtue that consists in giving up all possessions. A bodhisattva, a great being, must completely abandon even his own body, and likewise all his belongings and necessities. He should generate the thought in this way: "If they plunder all my belongings and necessities, may I have given those gifts to those beings. If someone takes my life, I will not generate malice, anger, or hatred toward him, and I will not harm even those people with body, speech, or mind. In this way, my perfection of generosity, my perfection of moral discipline, and my perfection of patience will be fully completed, and I will draw close to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. And in the buddha field where I become fully awakened in unsurpassed, perfect awakening, may all wildernesses haunted by bandits never, in any way, anywhere, appear at all, nor even be known of." In this way he acts, and in this way he accomplishes it. He thinks: "In the buddha field where I become fully awakened in unsurpassed, perfect awakening, may those faults and others like them never, in any way, anywhere, appear at all, nor even be known of. For the sake of completely purifying the buddha field, I will strive."

Śāriputra, furthermore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, goes into a wilderness that has become a waterless waste, he should not tremble, should not be terrified, should not be possessed by terror. Why is that? A bodhisattva, a great being, is by nature one who does not tremble and is not terrified. He should arouse the thought in this way: "I train in order to cut off the craving for existence in all sentient beings. If I were to die of thirst, I would be born in the world of hungry ghosts." Even so, the bodhisattva, the great being, should not tremble, should not be terrified, should not be possessed by terror. Rather he should think, "Alas, these beings have little merit, for such waterless wastes are seen in this world," and thus arouse a mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings. "In the buddha field of the buddha I shall become, when I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, waterless wastes shall be wholly, entirely, in every way and by every means nonexistent and unknown. I shall bring it about that all sentient beings find water endowed with the eight qualities. Just so I shall hold fast to merit. Just as my perfection of diligence will then be fully perfected, so for the sake of all sentient beings I shall undertake diligence with firm resolve."

Śāriputra, furthermore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, goes into a wilderness of famine, he should not tremble, should not be terrified, should not be possessed by terror. He should put on the armor in this way: "In the buddha field of the buddha I shall become, when I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, wildernesses of famine such as these shall be wholly, entirely, in every way and by every means nonexistent and unknown, and all those beings shall be endowed with well-being and happiness and shall meet with every happiness. For this I undertake diligence with firm resolve. In this way I shall purify the buddha field. I shall bring it about that whatever those beings wish, whatever they think of in their minds, is accomplished, just as for the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three everything arises merely by being thought of in the mind. Likewise for those beings everything shall be accomplished merely by being thought of in the mind, and everything thought of shall arise. Just as my perfection of meditative concentration will then be fully perfected, so for the sake of all sentient beings I shall strive to purify my own mind." Thinking thus, he undertakes diligence with firm resolve, so that the Dharma aspirations of those beings may be fully perfected, and so that all the necessities of life of all sentient beings may never, at any time, in any way, be lacking.

Śāriputra, furthermore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, goes into a wilderness of sickness, he should not tremble, should not be terrified, should not be possessed by terror. He should examine, reflect, and weigh it in this way: "In this, there is no phenomenon that makes one sick, and no phenomenon that is called sickness." Thus he should examine it as empty, and not tremble, not be terrified, not be possessed by terror. Śāriputra, a bodhisattva, a great being, is one who

He should not give rise to the thought, "After a very long time I shall become fully and perfectly awakened in unsurpassable, perfect awakening." He should not generate such a thought, and he should not tremble, should not be terrified, should not be seized by terror. Why is that? Because this single moment of mind is the very end of the beginningless, which is to say that it is endless.

Śāriputra, the bodhisattva, the great being, should not give rise to the perception of difficulty, thinking, "This end of the beginningless is vast and long. This end of the beginningless is joined to a single moment of mind, which is to say it is endless." Thus, Śāriputra, the bodhisattva, the great being, should not tremble, should not be terrified, should not be seized by terror at the thought, "Only after a very long time shall I become fully and perfectly awakened in unsurpassable, perfect awakening."

Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva, a great being, does not tremble, is not terrified, and is not seized by terror when he sees, hears, understands, and cognizes these and other unbearable terrors, then, Śāriputra, you should know that this son of good family or daughter of good family has the destiny to become fully and perfectly awakened in unsurpassable, perfect awakening.

Śāriputra, the bodhisattva, the great being, having donned the great armor, should act and should undertake steadfast diligence in such a way that, in the buddha field where he becomes fully awakened in unsurpassable, perfect awakening, the illnesses of all sentient beings will in every respect, completely and entirely, not arise and will be unknown. He should act in such a way that he speaks what the Tathāgata has spoken and does just as it has been spoken. And so that the Perfection of Wisdom may be brought to full completion in him at that time, he should become thoroughly familiar with the Perfection of Wisdom for the sake of all sentient beings.

Then, in that assembly, a woman called the goddess Gaṅgā was gathered and seated. She rose from her seat, arranged her upper robe over one shoulder, set her right knee on the ground, and, turning toward the Blessed One, joined her palms, paid homage, and said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I shall not tremble at this matter, I shall not be terrified, I shall not be seized by terror. Without trembling and without terror, I shall teach the Dharma to all sentient beings."

Then, at that time, the Blessed One smiled, a smile like the color of gold. That light pervaded boundless, limitless world systems and reached as far as the world of Brahmā. Returning, it circled the Blessed One three times and disappeared into the crown of the Blessed One's head.

As soon as the Blessed One had smiled, the woman took golden flowers and scattered them over the Blessed One, strewing them, showering them forth. Then those golden flowers remained unattached in the open space of the sky.

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, set his right knee on the ground, and, turning toward the Blessed One, joined his palms, paid homage, and said to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, does not smile without a cause and without a condition. What, then, is the cause and what is the condition for the Blessed One's smiling?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, this sister, the goddess of the Gaṅgā River, will in a future time become a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly awakened buddha called Golden Flower, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of those to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One, who will appear in the world. In the eon called Star-like, he will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

"Ānanda, this sister, the goddess of the Gaṅgā, will change from a female body and obtain a male body. After she passes away from here, she will be born in the buddha field of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Akṣobhya, in the world realm called Abhirati, Manifest Joy. Born there, she will practice the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Akṣobhya. Passing away from there, she will never be parted from the sight of the Tathāgatas, and will go from buddha field to buddha field. Then again, from the buddha field where she is never separated from the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, she will go from buddha field to buddha field, going to this one and that one.

"Ānanda, it is just as a wheel-turning king goes from palace to palace. For as long as he lives, he goes without the soles of his feet touching the ground, and even at the time of death he dies without the soles of his feet having touched the ground. In just the same way, Ānanda, this sister, the goddess of the Gaṅgā, will go from buddha field to buddha field, and until she fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, she will never be parted from the buddhas, the Blessed Ones."

Then the venerable Ānanda thought: "The bodhisattvas, the great beings, who sit in the presence of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Akṣobhya, should be known as those who have gathered into the Tathāgata himself."

Then the Blessed One, knowing with his mind the thought in the mind of the venerable Ānanda, spoke to him: "So it is, Ānanda, so it is. Those bodhisattvas, the great beings, have crossed over the mire, and they practice the holy life in the buddha field of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Akṣobhya. Ānanda, those bodhisattvas, the great beings, should be known as those who are close to the full accomplishment of awakening.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, the community of śrāvakas of that Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Golden Flower, will not be a finite number. Why is that? Ānanda, in that field the śrāvakas will be so many that they will be immeasurable, and what is called the countless and the incalculable will be the number into which they fall.

"Furthermore, Ānanda, at that time, in that period, in that buddha field there will be no wilderness of wild beasts, no wilderness of bandits, no wilderness of water, no wilderness of famine, no wilderness of disease.

Ānanda, those wildernesses of misfortune, and other misfortunes besides, will in that buddha-field be entirely absent, in every respect and in every way, and will not even be known. Ānanda, when the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Suvarṇapuṣpa became fully and perfectly awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, such fearsome and unbearable wildernesses were then wholly absent, in every respect and in every way, and were not even known.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda said to him: "Blessed One, in the presence of which Tathāgata did this sister, the goddess Gaṅgādevī, first generate the root of virtue of giving rise to the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect awakening?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, this sister, the goddess Gaṅgādevī, first generated the root of virtue of giving rise to the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect awakening in the presence of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Dīpaṃkara. At that time, with a mind that sought unsurpassed, perfect awakening, she scattered golden flowers before the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and dedicated them, thinking: 'When I scatter these five stalks of lotus to the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Dīpaṃkara, may I also attain acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.' Then the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Dīpaṃkara prophesied to me, to unsurpassed, perfect awakening: 'Young brahmin, in a future time you will become the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha named Śākyamuni, perfect in knowledge and conduct, the Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of those to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a buddha, a Blessed One.' When this sister heard that prophecy given to me, the thought arose in her: 'Oh, mother! Just as this young brahmin has been prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, what would be wrong if I too were prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening?' In this way, Ānanda, this sister first generated the root of virtue of giving rise to the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect awakening in the presence of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Dīpaṃkara."

When he had said this, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how wonderful! This sister, the goddess Gaṅgādevī, has indeed trained thoroughly and brought her training to completion, and she has been prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening."

When he had said this, the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "So it is, Ānanda, so it is, just as you have said. Indeed, this sister, the goddess Gaṅgādevī, has trained thoroughly and brought her training to completion, and she has been prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening."

This is the nineteenth chapter, called "The Goddess Gaṅgādevī," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One:

Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom become thoroughly familiar with emptiness? How should he enter into the meditative absorption of emptiness?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, here a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom should closely examine, thinking, "Form is empty." In the same way he should closely examine, "Feeling, perception, the formations, and consciousness are empty." And as he examines in this way, he does not correctly see, in that very nature of things, any intrinsic nature that exists by virtue of that nature. With an undistracted stream of mind he examines in this way; yet because he does not correctly see even that nature of things, he does not make the true limit directly manifest.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Subhūti said to him: Blessed One, you have said that a bodhisattva, a great being, should not make emptiness directly manifest. Blessed One, if a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in that meditative absorption, how is it that he does not make emptiness directly manifest?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, in this regard a bodhisattva, a great being, contemplates emptiness endowed with the supreme of all aspects. Yet he does not think, "I shall make it directly manifest," nor does he think, "I am making it directly manifest." He thinks only, "I shall become thoroughly familiar with it." He thinks, "This is the time for becoming thoroughly familiar, not the time for making it directly manifest." And thinking, "I shall be held by the Perfection of Wisdom, and I shall not make it directly manifest," he fixes his mind on an object while not yet resting in full equipoise. In that interval, the bodhisattva, a great being, does not fall away from the factors that belong to awakening, and he does not bring about the exhaustion of defilements; and yet he does become thoroughly familiar with this.

When a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in the meditative absorption of emptiness, the door of liberation, then he should also abide in the meditative absorption of the signless, but he should not make the signless directly manifest. Why is this? Because a bodhisattva, a great being, who has firm roots of virtue and possesses the qualities that bring them to full maturity, should closely consider, "This is the time for becoming thoroughly familiar with this, not the time for making it directly manifest." He is held by the Perfection of Wisdom, and he does not make the true limit directly manifest.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose there were a man who is exceedingly courageous, endowed with great diligence, steady and firmly grounded. He is of fine appearance, handsome, and pleasing to behold. He has many good qualities and the finest qualities, such as moral discipline, supreme power, learning, and generosity. He is trustworthy, able to speak and able to answer, accomplished in eloquence, endowed with skill in carrying out tasks. He knows the right time, the right region, and the right place. He has reached the summit of skill in archery, and he can turn aside many weapons and even the hardest weapons. He is highly skilled in all the arts, thoroughly accomplished, and has reached the utmost perfection in every field of craft.

He is mindful, intelligent, and discerning; he has faith, he knows the proper way of doing things, and he is fearless in every field of learning. He has friends, wealth, and an army. He lacks no limb and has all his faculties complete; he is perfectly provided with every resource and with a fine retinue. He is dear and pleasing even to many people, and whatever undertaking he begins, he is able to bring it through to completion. He is also one who conducts himself according to sound reasoning. In all of this he has great gain, and because he possesses such great gain, he is kind to many people: he honors those who should be honored, treats as teachers those who should be treated as teachers, esteems those who should be esteemed, and makes offerings to those who deserve offerings.

Subhūti, what do you think? Would that man, on this account, feel great delight, satisfaction, exhilaration, and happiness?

Subhūti replied: Blessed One, he would indeed. Sugata, he would indeed.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, suppose further that this man, endowed with such great good fortune, takes his parents, his children, and his wife, and, together with a certain party of travelers, enters a vast and terrifying wilderness, dreadful and harsh for the simple-minded, called "Hair-Raising." Having arrived there, he reassures his parents, children, and wife, saying: "I will quickly and safely bring you out of this terrible, frightful wilderness, and you will soon be free of it. Do not be afraid; do not be afraid!" And so he grants them fearlessness.

Subhūti, now suppose that in that wilderness many enemies and hostile men appear against this man. What do you think, Subhūti? Would that man, a hero who never turns back, who has insight, diligence, and strength, who is wise, gentle, clever, and steadfast, and who is accompanied by a great company, abandon his parents, children, and wife, and think to go forth alone out of that terrifying, dreadful wilderness?

Subhūti replied: Blessed One, he would not. Why is that? Blessed One, because the man would not abandon his parents, children, and wife. He is also equipped with an army both within and without, and in that wilderness there are others who oppose those enemies and hostile men, who are far more numerous, braver, more heavily armed, and mightier, and who protect him. Therefore those hostile enemies who seek faults and watch for an opening do not find an opportunity. Blessed One, for that reason that powerful man, without being harmed or injured, is able to bring his parents, children, and wife, and himself as well, out of that terrible, dreadful wilderness, and he will soon and safely reach a village, a town, or a market settlement.

When Subhūti had spoken thus, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Subhūti with these words.

Subhūti, in the same way, a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in loving-kindness, which is the wish to benefit all sentient beings and a tender affection for them. He abides in compassion, abides in joy, and abides in equanimity. He is embraced by skillful means and by the Perfection of Wisdom, and he dedicates his roots of virtue through the dedication that the perfectly awakened buddhas have approved. In this way he enters the gateways to liberation, the absorptions of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Even so, he does not make any true limit directly manifest on the ground of the śrāvakas or on the ground of the pratyekabuddhas.

Why is that? Because what embraces him is supremely powerful and supremely stable, namely the Perfection of Wisdom and skillful means. Therefore he does not abandon any sentient being, and for that reason he is able to awaken fully and manifestly, in virtue and in happiness, to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, brings to mind the thought of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and having brought it to mind, unites himself with them through the supreme of loving-kindness, then that bodhisattva, that great being, has passed far beyond the side of the afflictions and the side of Māra. He has passed far beyond the ground of the śrāvakas and the ground of the pratyekabuddhas, and he abides in that absorption.

Subhūti, even when he sees the exhaustion of defilements, he makes himself thoroughly familiar with emptiness, the supreme of the perfections.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in the absorption of emptiness, the gateway to liberation, then during that time he does not abide in the absorption of signlessness, and he has not made the absorption of signlessness directly manifest.

Subhūti, it is like this. A bird moves through the sky. It does not fall to the ground, and it rests on nothing, remaining without support. Though it stays in the very midst of the sky, it neither relies on it nor dwells in it.

In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, abides by abiding in emptiness, and also makes himself thoroughly familiar with emptiness. He abides by abiding in signlessness, and also makes himself thoroughly familiar with signlessness. He abides by abiding in wishlessness, and also makes himself thoroughly familiar with wishlessness. Yet before the qualities of a buddha are fully perfected, he does not fall into emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness.

Subhūti, it is like this. A powerful master archer, well trained in the weapon of the arrow and fully accomplished in it, shoots an arrow upward. Having shot it, he sends other arrows to turn it back, and so keeps that arrow from falling to the ground. Against the first arrow he shoots later arrows in an unbroken series, and does not let it fall. For as long as he has not thought, "Alas, let that arrow fall to the ground," the arrow does not fall.

In the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and is embraced by skillful means, does not make that true limit directly manifest, for as long as the roots of virtue directed toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening have not ripened, and have not become fully ripened.

But when those roots of virtue directed toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening have fully ripened and become thoroughly ripe, then he realizes the ultimate true limit directly. Therefore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva, the great being, should practice the Perfection of Wisdom and should meditate on the Perfection of Wisdom. In this way he should examine and closely contemplate the nature of these profound phenomena, but he should not realize it directly.

Here ends the eighteenth volume of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

When this had been said, the venerable Subhūti spoke to the Blessed One as follows. Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices emptiness, abides in emptiness, rests in the meditative absorption of emptiness, and yet does not realize the true limit directly, performs a difficult deed. Blessed One, that bodhisattva, that great being, performs a very difficult deed. Blessed One, this is wonderful. Sugata, this is truly wonderful.

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. A bodhisattva, a great being, who practices emptiness, abides in emptiness, rests in the meditative absorption of emptiness, and yet does not realize the true limit directly, performs a difficult deed. That bodhisattva, that great being, performs a very difficult deed.

Why is that? Subhūti, it is because that bodhisattva, that great being, does not abandon any sentient being. For him there arise special aspirations of this kind: "I shall liberate all these sentient beings." When a bodhisattva, a great being, sets his mind thus, "I will not abandon any sentient beings; I will bring all of them to liberation," and at the same time brings about the door of liberation that is the meditative absorption of emptiness, brings about the door of liberation that is the meditative absorption of signlessness, and brings about the door of liberation that is the meditative absorption of wishlessness, at that time the bodhisattva, the great being, should be known as one endowed with skillful means. Until the qualities of a buddha are fully complete, he will not, in the interim, realize the true limit directly.

Why is that? Because he is protected by skillful means. His not abandoning any sentient beings is itself his generation of the awakening mind. One who has generated the mind in this way and is endowed with such skillful means will not, in the interim, realize the true limit directly.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, has come to dwell in the profound, that is, in the doors of liberation, namely the meditative absorption of emptiness, the meditative absorption of signlessness, and the meditative absorption of wishlessness, and when he examines these, or wishes to examine them, he should set his mind in this way:

"These beings have long engaged with objects through the perception of a sentient being. Having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, I will teach the Dharma to these beings in order to abandon the view of those who hold to objects." Thinking thus, the bodhisattva rests in equipoise in the concentration of the door of liberation of emptiness, yet does not make the true limit manifest. He rests in equipoise in the concentration of the door of liberation of signlessness, yet does not make the true limit manifest. He rests in equipoise in the concentration of the door of liberation of wishlessness, yet does not make the true limit manifest.

Thus, when a bodhisattva, a great being, possesses this generation of the mind and this skillful means, then even in the interim he does not make the true limit manifest, and he does not fall away from the concentration of loving-kindness. Nor does he fall away from compassion, nor from joy, nor does he completely fall away from the concentration of equanimity. Why is that? Because he is held by skillful means, the bodhisattva, the great being, greatly increases through white, virtuous qualities. His faculties of faith and the rest also become very keen, and he attains the powers, the limbs of awakening, and the paths.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva, the great being, thinks thus: "These beings have long engaged with objects through the perception of phenomena. Having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, I will teach the Dharma in order to abandon the view of those who hold to objects." Thinking thus, for the sake of all beings he rests in equipoise in the concentration of the door of liberation of emptiness. Possessing that generation of the mind and that earlier skillful means, he rests in equipoise in the concentration of the door of liberation of emptiness, yet does not make the true limit manifest. He does not fall away from the concentrations of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity. Why is that? Because the bodhisattva, the great being, held by skillful means, greatly increases through white, virtuous qualities. His faculties of faith and the rest also become very keen, and he attains the powers, the limbs of awakening, and the paths.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva, the great being, thinks thus: "These beings have long engaged with signs through the perception of signs.
