Having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, I will teach the Dharma to them in order to abandon the perception of signs." Thinking thus, for the sake of all beings he rests in equipoise in the concentration of the door of liberation of signlessness. Possessing that generation of the mind and that earlier skillful means, he rests in equipoise in the concentration of the door of liberation of signlessness, yet does not make the true limit manifest, and he does not completely fall away from the concentrations of loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, nor from any concentration. Why is that? Because he is held by skillful means, the bodhisattva, the great being, greatly increases through white, virtuous qualities. His faculties of faith and the rest also become very keen, and he attains the powers, the limbs of awakening, and the paths.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva, the great being, thinks thus: "These beings have long been mistaken, through the perception of permanence, the perception of happiness, the perception of self, and the perception of the pleasant,

"May I, having awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, teach the Dharma so as to remove the inversions of beings who have been deluded by the perception of permanence, the perception of happiness, the perception of self, and the perception of the beautiful. I will teach that all this is impermanent, and that this is not permanent; that all this is suffering, and that this is not happiness; that all this is without self, and that this is not possessed of a self; that all this is unlovely, and that this is not lovely." One should proceed in just this way.

Endowed with that aspiration to awakening, and skilled in means, and held firmly by the earlier skillful means and by the Perfection of Wisdom, the bodhisattva does not, before the qualities of a buddha are fully perfected, realize the true limit in the interim. In the same way, while abiding in meditative equipoise in the samādhi of the aspirationless door of liberation, the bodhisattva does not realize the true limit. Nor does the bodhisattva fall away from loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.

Why is this so? A bodhisattva, a great being, who is held firmly by skillful means grows greatly in the white qualities, and the faculties of faith and the rest become exceedingly keen. Such a bodhisattva also gains the powers, the factors of awakening, and the paths.

Subhūti, when any bodhisattva, any great being, generates this aspiration, thinking: "For a long time these beings have engaged with a focus of attention, and even now they engage with a focus of attention. They have engaged in the perception of signs, and even now they engage in the perception of signs. They have engaged in inversion, and even now they engage in inversion. They have engaged in the perception of wholes, and even now they engage in the perception of wholes. They have engaged in mistaken perception, and even now they engage in mistaken perception. They have engaged in wrong views, and even now they engage in wrong views. How might none of these faults arise in them at all, in any way, in every respect? I will see to it that, through not knowing, they do not fall into these." In this way the bodhisattva thinks of all beings.

That bodhisattva, a great being, being endowed with such knowing mindfulness and such an aspiration to awakening, and also being endowed with skillful means and held firmly by the Perfection of Wisdom, examines in this way the nature of these profound phenomena, seeing it as emptiness, or as signlessness, or as aspirationlessness, or as non-conditioning, or as non-arising, or as non-production, or as the absence of any real entity.

Subhūti, for a bodhisattva, a great being, who is endowed with such knowing qualities, to fall into the state of non-conditioning, or to remain together with the three realms, is not possible; there is no opportunity for it.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening should put this question to other bodhisattvas, great beings: "Do you not bring emptiness into direct experience? Do you not bring the signless into direct experience? Do you not bring the wishless into direct experience? Do you not bring non-conditioning into direct experience? Do you not bring non-arising into direct experience? Do you not bring non-production into direct experience? Do you not bring the absence of entities into direct experience? And while you also cultivate the Perfection of Wisdom, what is it that you should become thoroughly familiar with in these teachings? And when you bring about such states of mind, in what kind of intrinsic nature should you bring them about?"

Subhūti, suppose that a bodhisattva, a great being, is questioned in this way by another bodhisattva, a great being. If he replies, "A bodhisattva, a great being, should attend to emptiness. A bodhisattva, a great being, should attend to the signless, the wishless, non-conditioning, non-arising, non-production, and the absence of entities," and so gives his prediction in this way, but does not set forth that mind which never abandons any sentient being, and does not show skillful means, then, Subhūti, you should know that this bodhisattva, a great being, was not predicted by the Tathāgatas of the past, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Why is that? Because he does not teach, does not distinguish, does not explain, and does not understand those unshared qualities that belong to the irreversible bodhisattva, the great being. Even when questioned he gives no prediction and no reply, and he does not stand upon the ground that belongs to the irreversible bodhisattva, the great being.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, is there a way by which a bodhisattva, a great being, becomes irreversible?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, there is a way by which a bodhisattva, a great being, becomes irreversible. If a bodhisattva, a great being, whether he has heard this Perfection of Wisdom or not, understands it in this way and answers in this way, he should be recognized as an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then although many practice for awakening, few answer in this way.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, so it is. Those bodhisattvas, great beings, who are predicted to the stage of irreversible wisdom are few; but those who have been so predicted do answer in this way. You should know that these bodhisattvas, great beings, have made their roots of virtue blaze. These bodhisattvas, great beings, cannot be swept away by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, even in a dream, rightly sees all phenomena as like a dream and does not bring them into direct experience, then, Subhūti, you should recognize this too as a defining mark of the irreversibility of the irreversible bodhisattva, the great being.

Subhūti, furthermore, if a bodhisattva, a great being, even in a dream has no longing for the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas or for the three realms, and does not generate a mind that seeks their benefits, then, Subhūti, this too should be understood as a mark of irreversibility in an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti, furthermore, if a bodhisattva, a great being, even in a dream sees himself seated in the middle of an assembly of many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands, many hundreds of millions, many thousands of millions, many hundreds of thousands of millions, and many hundreds of thousands of billions of beings, in the center of the circle of that assembly, surrounded by the community of monks and with the community of bodhisattvas gathered before him, and sees himself, having become a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly complete buddha, teaching the Dharma, then, Subhūti, this too should be understood as a mark of irreversibility in an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti, furthermore, if a bodhisattva, a great being, even in a dream rises into the sky and teaches the Dharma to beings; or if he knows that his light fills a fathom's breadth; or if he goes to other directions and, in another world-realm, performs the deeds of a buddha, and there too emanates monks and teaches the Dharma; if, Subhūti, in this way even in a dream he is recognized as an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, then, Subhūti, this too should be understood as a mark of irreversibility in an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti, furthermore, if a bodhisattva, a great being, even in a dream does not tremble, is not frightened, and is not seized by terror, even when harm comes upon a village, or upon a town, or upon a market town, or upon a region, or upon a district, or a wildfire breaks out; or when he sees beasts of prey, or wild animals, or other kinds of lesser creatures; or when he is about to be beheaded, or any other great, unbearable danger, painful and distressing, arises; and even when he sees the suffering, distress, and great unbearable fear of other beings, no unbearable fear arises in him; he does not tremble, is not frightened, and is not seized by terror; and then, awakening from sleep, as soon as he rises he thinks: "All these three realms are like a dream. Having fully and completely awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, I shall teach the Dharma exactly as the Teacher truly teaches it" — then, Subhūti, this too should be understood as a mark of irreversibility in an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti, furthermore, if an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, even in a dream sees beings in the hells and thinks: "How might I act so that, in the buddha-field of the one who has fully and completely awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, all the bad destinies will altogether, entirely, in every respect, and everywhere cease to occur?" then, Subhūti, this too should be understood as a mark of the purification of the bad destinies in this irreversible bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti, how is one to know that, in the buddha field of that irreversible bodhisattva, that great being, who has awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, the evil destinies will never arise at all, in any way, in any aspect whatsoever?

Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, sees in a dream beings who belong to the hells, or to the animals, or to the realm of hungry ghosts, and thereupon recalls this. Having recalled it, he thinks: "How may it come about that in the buddha field of me, who have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, the evil destinies will never arise at all, in any way, in any aspect whatsoever?" Subhūti, this should be known as the mark of the purification of the evil destinies of a bodhisattva, a great being, and this too should be known as a mark of the irreversibility of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, dreams of a city on fire, or of a village that has been burned. Having woken from that dream, he thinks: "By whatever aspects, signs, and marks I saw in the dream, a bodhisattva, a great being, is to be taken as irreversible. If those aspects, signs, and marks are present in me, then by this truth and by these words of truth, may this burning city and this burned village be extinguished, may they be cooled, may they cease to be." If he speaks thus, Subhūti, and the burning village or city is extinguished, cooled, and ceases to be, then that bodhisattva, that great being, should be known to have been prophesied by the Tathāgatas of the past, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect awakening. If it is not extinguished, not cooled, and does not cease to be, then that bodhisattva, that great being, should be known not to have been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Again, Subhūti, suppose the fire spreads from house to house, from street to street, passing on to some other street or some other house, and burns on without being extinguished, cooled, or ceasing to be. Then, Subhūti, it should be known that this bodhisattva, this great being, has accumulated karma that accords with rejecting the Dharma and with confusing wisdom. Therefore the ripening of that karma, which accords with rising up in this very life, is a ripening with a remainder, arising from that very rejection of the Dharma.

Subhūti, such is the cause and such is the condition of the mark of irreversibility of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being. And by this, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, is to be taken as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, I shall explain to you the aspects, signs, and marks by which an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, is to be taken as irreversible. Listen well, and keep it in mind. I shall teach it to you.

Then the venerable Subhūti said, "Excellent!" to the Blessed One, and listened as the Blessed One had instructed. The Blessed One spoke as follows.

Subhūti, suppose a man or a woman, a boy or a girl, has been seized and possessed by a non-human being. Then a bodhisattva, a great being, should come and reflect with a blessing in this way: "If I have been prophesied by the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past, to unsurpassed, perfect awakening; and if my intention toward fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect awakening is utterly pure; and if I wish to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, with my attention to unsurpassed, perfect awakening utterly pure, and free of any mind of a śrāvaka or of a pratyekabuddha; then I shall become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. It is not that I will fail to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. I will certainly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Moreover, in those immeasurable, innumerable world systems there dwell, live and are sustained the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas; and for them nothing is unknown, unseen, uncomprehended, unrealized before their eyes, or not fully awakened to. If those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, know my intention, and so I will awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, then by this truth and by these words of truth, let the non-human possession that has seized and overpowered this man, woman, boy or girl depart!"

Subhūti, if the bodhisattva, the great being, speaks in this way and the non-human being does not depart, then you should understand that this bodhisattva, this great being, has not been prophesied by the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. And, Subhūti, if the bodhisattva, the great being, speaks in this way and the non-human being departs, then you should understand that this bodhisattva, this great being, has been prophesied by the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

This is the twentieth chapter, called "Practice in Skillful Means," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Subhūti, furthermore, in that case a bodhisattva, a great being, may speak these words: "By whatever truth and words of truth I have been prophesied by the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, by that truth and those words of truth, let this non-human being depart!" Then, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One strives to make that non-human being go away. Why is that?

Then, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One, who is exceedingly powerful and exceedingly splendid, strives to make the non-human spirit depart, thinking, "How might this non-human depart?" And so the non-human departs through the blessing of Māra. Even so, that bodhisattva, that great being, thinks, "The departing of this non-human is due to my power," and does not understand that the non-human departs through the power of Māra. He does only that much striving, and because of that striving he comes to look down on other bodhisattvas, great beings. He disparages them, belittles them, makes light of them, scorns them, and reviles them. He thinks, "I have been prophesied by the former Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, to unsurpassable, perfect awakening." On that ground alone, again and again he gives rise to pride. He fully produces pride, increases pride, greatly increases pride, relies on pride, depends upon pride, makes pride grow, makes pride flourish, and brings pride forth.

Through that pride, through great pride, through pride upon pride, through conceit and through false pride, he puts omniscience far away. He puts far away the unsurpassed wisdom of a buddha, the self-arisen wisdom, the wisdom of omniscience. He puts far away unsurpassable, perfect awakening.

In that way, when he sees bodhisattvas, great beings, who are spiritual friends, who have virtuous qualities, who have vast inclination, who are endowed with superior intention, who are skilled in means, and who possess the qualities of irreversibility, he gives rise to conceit and looks down on them. He does not associate with such spiritual friends, does not rely on them, does not honor or revere them, and does not question them. He only makes more firm the bond by which Māra binds him. He should be understood as belonging to one of two grounds, namely, the ground of the śrāvakas or the ground of the pratyekabuddhas.

Subhūti, in this way, through the blessing of that truth, Māra the Evil One obstructs unsurpassable, perfect awakening for a bodhisattva, a great being, who has newly entered the vehicle, who has little faith and little learning, who is separated from spiritual friends, who is not held by the Perfection of Wisdom, and who lacks skill in means. Subhūti, this too should be understood as a deed of Māra for a bodhisattva, a great being.

Furthermore, Subhūti, pointing out a bodhisattva's name also becomes a deed of Māra. Subhūti, how does pointing out a bodhisattva's name become a deed of Māra? Here, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One draws near to a bodhisattva, a great being, by pointing out his name and by blessing the name. Coming in some guise or other, whatever suits, he says this: "You were prophesied by the former Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, to unsurpassable, perfect awakening. Why is that so? Your name is such and such. Your mother's name is such and such. Your father's name is such and such. Your brother's name is such and such. Your sister's name is such and such.

Mara will say, "Your friends, your ministers, your relatives and your kin by blood and marriage have such and such names," and he will recite the names going back seven generations on both the paternal and maternal sides. He will say, "You were born in such and such a region, in such and such a village, town, or hamlet." If the person is by nature dull, Mara will say, "You were dull in the past as well." If the person is by nature sharp in faculties, Mara will say, "You had sharp faculties in the past as well."

Suppose the person is a forest dweller, or an alms-gatherer, or one who wears rag robes, or one who does not take food after the meal, or one who sits in a single session, or one who keeps to the seat as laid out, or one who has only the three robes, or a charnel-ground dweller, or one who lives at the foot of a tree, or one who sits in the open air, or one who has no shelter, or one who wears felt, or one with few desires, contentment, and deep seclusion, or one who goes barefoot, or one who speaks gently and sparingly. To such a person Māra the Evil One, drawing on these qualities of this present life, will say, "In the past too you possessed these very qualities. You were definitely prophesied by the Tathāgatas of the past, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, to irreversibility from unsurpassable, perfect awakening, to the stage of an irreversible bodhisattva. Why is that? Because you have these ascetic qualities, you surely possessed them in the past as well." In this way he exhorts the person.

Then, relying on the names recounted from the past and on the ascetic qualities and the few possessions he now has, the person will give rise to conceit. He will think, "I was prophesied by the Tathāgatas of the past, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, to unsurpassable, perfect awakening, for I have these qualities." And Māra the Evil One will say to him, "You were prophesied by the Tathāgatas of the past, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, to irreversibility from unsurpassable, perfect awakening. Why is that? Because you have such ascetic qualities."

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One will sometimes think to appear in the guise of a monk, sometimes in the guise of a nun, sometimes in the guise of a layman, sometimes in the guise of a laywoman, sometimes in the guise of a brahmin, sometimes in the guise of a householder, sometimes in the guise of a mother, sometimes of a father, sometimes of a brother, sometimes of a sister, and sometimes in the guise of a friend, a minister, a relative, or a kinsman by blood or marriage. Having come, he will say, "You were prophesied by the Tathāgatas of the past, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, to the irreversible stage of unsurpassable, perfect awakening. Why is that? Because you have the ascetic qualities of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being." Furthermore, Subhūti, if those qualities, those aspects, signs, and marks of irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, which I have taught are absent in him,

Subhūti, in such a case another bodhisattva, a great being, should recognize, "Alas, this bodhisattva, this great being, is under the sway of Māra." Why is that? Because the aspects, signs, and marks of the bodhisattvas, the great beings who never turn back, are absent in him.

Furthermore, Subhūti, through the sway of such a power, that bodhisattva, that great being, becomes inflated with conceit. Having generated conceit, he is overpowered by it and puffed up with pride, overcome by the sway of Māra. As a result he comes to belittle other bodhisattvas, great beings; he treats them with contempt, ridicules them, derides them, and disparages them. Subhūti, this too should be recognized by the bodhisattva, the great being, as the work of Māra, brought about through the sway of Māra.

Furthermore, Subhūti, the bodhisattva, the great being, should recognize as the work of Māra any teaching of a name and any prophecy of a name. Subhūti, how should a bodhisattva, a great being, recognize a teaching of a name or a prophecy of a name as the work of Māra? Subhūti, in this case Māra the Evil One comes in the guise of a monk and gives a prophecy to a bodhisattva, a great being, in these words. Whatever name the bodhisattva has been thinking, "Oh, may I become known by this name when I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening," following after that name, reflecting on it and examining it in his mind, exactly that name does the monk prophesy: "You will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening and be called by this very name."

Then that bodhisattva, whose wisdom is flawed by nature and who is unskilled in means, thinks, "Just as I followed after the name, reflecting on it and examining it, thinking, 'Oh, may I become known by this name when I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect awakening,' so has this monk declared it." Having thought this, he reasons, "The name that I reflected upon, and the name spoken by Māra the Evil One himself, or by a monk emanated by those of Māra's following, or by a monk under Māra's sway, are the same in both cases. As the thought arose in my mind, so this monk has declared my name; the two names coincide." And he comes to think, "I have been prophesied to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, by name, by the buddhas of the past, the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened ones."

Subhūti, the aspects, signs, and marks that I have taught for bodhisattvas, great beings who never turn back, are absent in him, and he is bereft of them. Yet through that teaching and prophecy of his name, he generates conceit about it.

Having conceived this arrogance, he thinks, "I have received the prediction to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, but these others have not received the prediction to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening," and so he holds other bodhisattvas, great beings, in contempt. Through that contemptuous mind, through pride, great pride, pride beyond pride, wrong pride, and the pride of presumption, he holds other bodhisattvas, great beings, in contempt, and so he makes omniscience distant and makes the wisdom of the buddhas distant. Not being embraced by the Perfection of Wisdom, lacking skillful means, lacking spiritual friends, and being held by evil companions, he should expect only one of two grounds: the ground of the śrāvakas or the ground of the pratyekabuddhas.

Now suppose that, after training and taming himself for a long time, indeed a very long time, he comes to rely on this Perfection of Wisdom and wishes to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Suppose too that he were to follow spiritual friends and always go to the presence of spiritual friends. Even so, in this very life, with his body fully formed, he would be one who disparages those who have generated the awakening mind, who disgraces them, harms them, abandons them, and denounces them one by one. Even then, it would be hard for him to reach the ground of a buddha.

Why is that? Subhūti, the ground of downfall that arises from the arrogance of a bodhisattva, a great being, is this heavy.

Subhūti, take for example a monk of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, on the ground of the śrāvakas. The four root downfalls are heavy for him. If he commits any one of these downfalls, or any other, he is not a monk, not an ascetic, not a son of the Śākya. Yet generating arrogance and a contemptuous mind is heavier than those four downfalls. That is to say, when the mind of great nonvirtue, the mind of contempt, arises on the occasion of the naming of a bodhisattva, a great being, you should know that generating this mind is heavier than those downfalls.

Subhūti, leave aside the four root downfalls. Even compared with those five acts of immediate retribution, when a bodhisattva, a great being, names another and the mind arises that is accompanied by arrogance, you should know that generating this mind is heavier, and heavier than the downfall of those five acts of immediate retribution.

Subhūti, even a declaration of a name like that can give rise to the subtle, very subtle works of Māra. The bodhisattva, the great being, should recognize them. Having recognized them, he should abandon them completely, and he should help others to understand and cause them to give them up.

Furthermore, Subhūti, Māra the Evil One comes into the presence of a bodhisattva, a great being, and urges and reminds him with the qualities of solitude. Subhūti, how does Māra the Evil One come into the presence of a bodhisattva, a great being, and urge and remind him with the qualities of solitude? Subhūti, in this case Māra the Evil One approaches the bodhisattva, the great being, and having approached him says, "The Tathāgata speaks in praise of solitude. You should dwell in the wilderness, in forest thickets, in mountain caves, in charnel grounds, in heaps of straw, and the like."

Subhūti, I do not say that the various dwelling places, such as forests, remote borderlands, uninhabited regions, woodland thickets, mountain caves, charnel grounds, and heaps of straw, constitute the seclusion of a bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti then asked: Blessed One, if the seclusion of a bodhisattva, a great being, does not come from dwelling in the various places such as forests, remote borderlands, uninhabited regions, woodland thickets, mountain caves, charnel grounds, and heaps of straw, then what other seclusion is there? Blessed One, what is that other seclusion of a bodhisattva, a great being, like?

When he had spoken in this way, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, becomes secluded from thoughts associated with the śrāvakas, and secluded from thoughts associated with the pratyekabuddhas, then that bodhisattva, a great being, is dwelling in seclusion. Even if such a one lives in the midst of a village, that one abides with the perfection of wisdom, with skillful means, and with loving-kindness and great compassion toward all sentient beings. One who abides in this way is truly abiding in seclusion.

Subhūti, I also grant this seclusion from thoughts associated with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to a bodhisattva, a great being: if a bodhisattva, a great being, spends day and night abiding in this seclusion, then that one is dwelling in seclusion. And if a bodhisattva, a great being, dwells in forests, woodland thickets, mountain caves, charnel grounds, and remote dwelling places while abiding in this very way, then that bodhisattva, a great being, is dwelling in seclusion.

Subhūti, there is also the seclusion of dwelling in forests, woodland thickets, mountain caves, charnel grounds, and remote dwelling places that Māra the Evil One presents as though it were seclusion. By that seclusion, one becomes mixed up with thoughts associated with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. One does not strive earnestly for the perfection of wisdom, and one does not bring omniscient wisdom to completion. One abides in this mixed-up way, and because one abides with thoughts that are not thoroughly purified, the activities of one's body, speech, and mind are not thoroughly purified.

Because the activities of body, speech, and mind are not thoroughly purified, such a bodhisattva, a great being, despises those other bodhisattvas who live in the midst of villages yet are not mixed up with thoughts associated with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and who abide in the way of wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion. Though living in the wilderness, that one's bodily, verbal, and mental activities remain impure, and one keeps abiding in a mixed-up way. Such a one is not dwelling in seclusion.

But the others abide in wisdom, skillful means, and great compassion. They live in villages, their bodily, verbal, and mental activities are thoroughly purified, they are secluded from thoughts associated with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and they are not mixed up with those thoughts. When one despises them, one will not attain the meditative concentrations, the absorptions, the attainments, the liberations, and the higher knowledges, and these will not be brought to completion in one. Why is that? Because such a one is unskilled in means.

Subhūti, suppose there is a bodhisattva, a great being, who dwells for a year, or a hundred years, or a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years, or a million, or a hundred million, or a billion, or a trillion years, or even longer, in a wilderness a hundred leagues wide, with no beasts of prey, no wild animals, no flocks of birds, no lesser wild animals or predators, where no yakṣas or rākṣasas roam, where there are no bandits, in a terrifying, intolerable wilderness that is nevertheless free of harm. Suppose that bodhisattva has entered upon that seclusion with a superior intention and abides possessed of a perfect superior intention. If he does not understand the seclusion that I have taught, then that bodhisattva, unskilled in means, because of this lack of understanding, makes the wilderness his sole concern and dwells there. He relies on that seclusion, clings to it, is attached to it, and is strongly attached to it. Subhūti, by that much that bodhisattva, that great being, has not pleased my mind. Why is that? Subhūti, dwelling in this kind of seclusion does not accord with the seclusion that I have taught for bodhisattvas, great beings.

Then Māra the Evil One will come, and sitting in the space of the sky above, he will say to that bodhisattva: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! This is the seclusion that the Tathāgata taught for bodhisattvas, great beings. Son of good family, abide in just this seclusion. If you do so, son of good family, you will quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening."

And that bodhisattva, through that seclusion in the wilderness, will despise other bodhisattvas, great beings, who have entered villages, who are monks living the holy life, who possess virtuous qualities, whose attention is not mixed up with that of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and whose bodily, verbal, and mental activities and livelihood are thoroughly pure. He will say: "Alas, these venerable ones dwell in a mixed-up way; they do not dwell in seclusion. These venerable ones dwell in constant mixing; they do not dwell in seclusion." And he will quarrel with those who abide in the seclusion of bodhisattvas, great beings, because they dwell mixed with others; he will quarrel with them for living in constant mixture. Of those who dwell mixed with others, he will say that they practice dwelling in seclusion, and he will generate reverence for them. But toward those for whom reverence is truly appropriate, he will generate pride.

Why is that, Subhūti? Because he thinks: "The places where I dwell are indeed dwelling places; I am urged on by nonhuman beings, and I am remembered by nonhuman beings. But for whom among those dwelling in villages do nonhuman beings give encouragement? For whom among those dwelling in villages do those nonhuman beings keep remembrance?" In this way that person despises those who follow the vehicle of the bodhisattvas.

Subhūti, such a one should be known as an outcaste among bodhisattvas. Such a one should be known as a refuter of bodhisattvas. Such a one should be known as a mere reflection of a bodhisattva. Such a one should be known as a counterfeit bodhisattva. Such a one should be known as a bodhisattva sprout gone to waste. He is a bandit who has disguised himself in the garb of a renunciant. He is a bandit among those who follow the bodhisattva vehicle. He is a bandit of the world with its gods.

Subhūti, furthermore, a person of such a nature should not be relied upon, should not be revered, and should not be served or honored. Why? Such a person should be understood to have fallen into manifest arrogance. Such a person also criticizes and rebukes others who are of little strength and who have entered the vehicle only a short while ago. Such a person should be known as one whose qualities are impure; such a person should be known as one who lacks a true teacher; and such a person should be known as one who lacks the qualities of the noble ones.

Subhūti, furthermore, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has not abandoned any sentient being, who has not abandoned omniscience, and who has not abandoned unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, who with a superior intention wishes to become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening and wishes to accomplish the benefit of all sentient beings, should not rely upon, revere, serve, or honor a person of that kind.

Subhūti, however, in order to understand these works of Māra and others as well, one who strives for the sake of all sentient beings should always keep the mind free of discouragement. For the sake of showing the path to all sentient beings who have not found it, one should not let the mind be frightened, and should not mix it with the three realms. And in that very effort, one should first generate great compassion, with a mind of loving-kindness and a mind of compassion, holding tender care for others. One should feel joy toward those beings who have rightly entered the path, and, through the nature of phenomena as non-apprehension, maintain equanimity toward phenomena. In this way, one should generate the thought: "May every fault of the works of Māra, in every way, never arise and never occur at all; and should any such fault occur, may I swiftly abandon it. Thus I shall train." Know too that this is how bodhisattvas, great beings, overcome others through their own direct knowledge. And Subhūti, this too should be understood by a bodhisattva, a great being, as a work of Māra, namely a quality of seclusion that has gone astray.

This is the twenty-first chapter, called "The Works of Māra," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, nineteenth volume.

Then the Blessed One spoke again to the venerable Subhūti. Subhūti, here a bodhisattva, a great being, who has rightly entered upon a superior intention and wishes to become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, should from the very first rely upon, revere, serve, and honor spiritual friends.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has rightly entered upon a superior intention and wishes to become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, should from the very first rely upon, revere, serve, and honor which spiritual friends? Who are those spiritual friends of a bodhisattva, a great being? Please explain.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows. Subhūti, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones themselves, and those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have become irreversible and are skilled in the conduct of bodhisattvas, who rightly instruct and guide others in these perfections, and those who teach and expound this Perfection of Wisdom: Subhūti, these should be known as the spiritual friends of a bodhisattva, a great being.

Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom itself should be recognized as the spiritual friend of a bodhisattva, a great being. Subhūti, all six perfections should be recognized as the spiritual friend of a bodhisattva, a great being. The six perfections themselves are the teacher. The six perfections are the path. The six perfections are the illumination. The six perfections are the lamp. The six perfections are the light. The six perfections are the protector. The six perfections are the refuge. The six perfections are the resting place. The six perfections are the ally. The six perfections are the island. The six perfections are the mother. The six perfections are the father. The six perfections are what brings about understanding, realization, and the state of being established for the sake of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Why is this so? Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom depends on these, that is to say, on the six perfections.

Subhūti, the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who became fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening and then passed completely into nirvāṇa, was likewise born from these six perfections. Subhūti, the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the future, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who will become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, will likewise be born from these six perfections. Subhūti, the omniscience of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas who now, in immeasurable, innumerable, boundless, inconceivable world systems, having become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, remain, live, sustain themselves, and teach the Dharma, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is likewise born from these six perfections. Subhūti, my own omniscience also, I who am now a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly awakened buddha, and who have become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, is born from these six perfections.

Why is this so? Subhūti, within these six perfections are gathered the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening, the four immeasurables, the four means of gathering disciples, and all the qualities of a buddha that exist: the wisdom of a buddha, self-arisen wisdom, inconceivable wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, innumerable wisdom, incomparable wisdom, the wisdom that is unequal and equal, and the wisdom of omniscience. All of these are gathered within the six perfections.

Therefore, Subhūti, these six perfections themselves are the spiritual friend of a bodhisattva, a great being. These six perfections themselves are the teacher. The six perfections are the path. The six perfections are the illumination. The six perfections are the lamp. The six perfections are the light. The six perfections are the protector. The six perfections are the refuge. The six perfections are the resting place. The six perfections are the ally.

The six perfections are the island. The six perfections are the mother. The six perfections are the father. The six perfections will stand for the sake of knowing, realizing, attaining omniscience, and attaining unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. When a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in the six perfections, he becomes a benefactor even to all those who cannot repay him.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to train in these six perfections should listen to this very Perfection of Wisdom, grasp it, hold it, read it, fully understand it, recite it, teach it, explain it, study it aloud, memorize it, examine it thoroughly through its meaning, its Dharma, and its method, reflect on it, question it, and inquire into it fully.

Why is that? This Perfection of Wisdom is the forerunner of these six perfections. It is their leader, their guide, the one who shows them correctly and teaches them fully. It gives them birth; it is their mother. Why is that? Without the Perfection of Wisdom, the other five perfections are not apparent, and they would not even obtain the name "perfection."

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to go without relying on others, and who wishes to abide in the state of a bodhisattva, a great being, who does not rely on others, should train in this very Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, what is the defining mark of the Perfection of Wisdom?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom has the defining mark of non-attachment.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, is there a way of speaking by which, through that very defining mark of non-attachment by which the Perfection of Wisdom exists, all phenomena exist?

The Blessed One said: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Subhūti, there is a way of speaking by which, through that very defining mark of non-attachment by which the Perfection of Wisdom exists, all phenomena exist. Why is that? Subhūti, all phenomena are secluded. Subhūti, all phenomena are empty. Therefore, Subhūti, through that very defining mark of non-attachment by which the Perfection of Wisdom is secluded and empty, all phenomena are secluded and empty.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, if all phenomena are secluded and all phenomena are empty, then, Blessed One, how will sentient beings be known to be afflicted? Blessed One, how will sentient beings be known to be purified? Blessed One, what is secluded does not become afflicted. Blessed One, what is secluded does not become purified. Blessed One, what is empty does not become afflicted. Blessed One, what is empty does not become purified.

Blessed One, solitude, or emptiness, does not fully awaken into unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And, Blessed One, apart from solitude and emptiness itself, no phenomenon is found that becomes a buddha, or fully awakens, or will come to fully awaken into unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Blessed One, how then should I understand the meaning of this teaching? Blessed One, please explain it. Sugata, please explain it.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows. Subhūti, what do you think? Have beings, since a long time ago, been engaged in grasping at "I" and grasping at "mine"?

Subhūti answered: So it is, Blessed One. So it is, Sugata. Beings have, since a long time ago, been engaged in grasping at "I" and grasping at "mine."

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Are grasping at "I" and grasping at "mine" empty?

Subhūti answered: They are empty, Blessed One. They are empty, Sugata.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Is it through grasping at "I" and grasping at "mine" that beings wander in saṃsāra?

Subhūti answered: So it is, Blessed One. So it is, Sugata. It is through grasping at "I" and grasping at "mine" that beings wander in saṃsāra.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, in this way one should understand how beings become defiled. It is just as beings grasp and cling that they become defiled; yet in this there is no one at all who becomes defiled. Subhūti, it is just as there is no grasping and no clinging that one does not know grasping at "I" and grasping at "mine" at all. In this way, Subhūti, one should understand how beings become purified. It is just as beings have no grasping and no clinging that they become purified; yet in this there is no one at all who becomes purified. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices in this way, he is practicing in the Perfection of Wisdom. Subhūti, in this way, with all phenomena in solitude and all phenomena empty, one should understand the defilement and the purification of beings.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it is wondrous that, with all phenomena in solitude and all phenomena empty, the defilement and purification of beings are nevertheless understood. Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices in this way, he is practicing in the Perfection of Wisdom.

Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices in this way, he does not practice in form. He does not practice in feeling, nor in perception, nor in formations, nor in consciousness.

Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices in this way, he cannot be overcome by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

Blessed One, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices in this way, he overpowers the conduct of all persons of the śrāvaka vehicle and the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and he also attains the state of being unable to be overpowered. Why is that? Blessed One, because buddhahood, the state of the Tathāgata, the state of the self-arisen one, and omniscience cannot be overpowered.

Blessed One, if a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses the Perfection of Wisdom abides in that state of attention and lets day and night pass in it, that bodhisattva comes close to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, so it is, so it is. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way practices the Perfection of Wisdom. A bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way does not practice in form; likewise, he does not practice in feeling, nor in perception, nor in the formations, nor in consciousness.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way cannot be overcome by the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way surpasses the conduct of all individuals who belong to the vehicle of the śrāvakas and the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and also attains the state that cannot be overcome. Why is that? Subhūti, because buddhahood, the state of the Tathāgata, the self-arisen state, and omniscience cannot be overcome.

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses the Perfection of Wisdom abides in this state of attention and lets day and night pass in it, he has come close to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect awakening.

Furthermore, Subhūti, suppose that all the sentient beings there are in Jambudvīpa, without exception, were to obtain a human body, and having obtained a human body, were to generate the mind of unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Having generated that mind, they would remain for as long as they live, and while they live they would honor all the Tathāgatas, revere them, hold them as their teachers, make offerings to them, worship them, depict them in images, and attend upon them. And likewise they would give gifts to all sentient beings, and dedicate that giving too to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Subhūti, what do you think? Would those bodhisattvas, great beings, generate much merit on that basis?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, much! Sugata, much!

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, even more merit than that is generated by the son or daughter of good family who, at the very least, abides for a single day in attention that possesses the Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that? Subhūti, to the extent that a bodhisattva, a great being, abides day and night in attention that possesses the Perfection of Wisdom, to that extent he becomes a worthy recipient of the gifts of all sentient beings. Why is that? Subhūti, because a mind endowed with loving-kindness such as that bodhisattva's, a great being's, is found in no other sentient beings, except the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Why is that? Subhūti, because the Tathāgata is an individual without an equal. Subhūti, the Tathāgata has no comparison. Subhūti, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, is endowed with inconceivable qualities.

Subhūti, how is it that a son or daughter of good family brings about such a quantity of merit? Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, has come to possess what kind of wisdom does he see all sentient beings as if they were about to be slain? At that very time he is wholly seized by great compassion. Looking with the divine eye, he sees immeasurable, innumerable, incalculable, boundless beings bound up with the deeds of immediate retribution. He also sees others who are in the unfavorable states, who have fallen away, who are covered by the net of wrong views, who have not found the path, and who are in unfavorable circumstances, and he sees those who have wasted the freedoms and endowments of a human life. Seeing them, he is overcome with great dismay. Then he pervades all those beings with that great loving-kindness and that great compassion, and he comes to think: "I shall become the protector of all these beings, and I shall free all these beings from suffering." In this way he comes to possess a wisdom in which he does not dwell together with signs or with anything else.

Subhūti, this is for the bodhisattva, the great being, the great light of wisdom for fully awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in this way is held to be a worthy recipient of the offerings of the whole world, and he does not turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Those donors and lords of giving who use robes, alms food, bedding, medicines for the sick, and requisites, having firmly set their minds on this Perfection of Wisdom, purify their gifts and offerings, and all of them draw near to omniscience.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to enjoy the alms of the country with fruitful result, who wishes to show the path to all sentient beings, who wishes to bring forth a vast illumination, who wishes to free the beings who dwell in saṃsāra from saṃsāra, and who wishes to purify the eyes of all sentient beings, should abide in this mental engagement that is accompanied by the Perfection of Wisdom. If he wishes to abide in this mental engagement, he should come to know the mental engagement that is accompanied by the Perfection of Wisdom.

Why is that? Whatever it is that he thinks of knowing, that very thing becomes his mental engagement. No opening should be given to any mental engagement apart from this, one that is separated from the Perfection of Wisdom. He should act in such a way that day and night are exhausted through this mental engagement accompanied by the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose a certain man who is skilled in knowing precious jewels, knowing the kinds of jewels, comes upon a great precious jewel such as he had never found before. Having found that great precious jewel, he becomes joyful and greatly delighted, filled with a wide and spacious happiness. But then he loses that great precious jewel, and because of this he becomes possessed of great suffering and unhappiness.

Thinking in this way, "Alas, I am parted from that great and precious jewel," he would constantly and without interruption be gripped by the thought of being parted from it. And so, until he found either that same great precious jewel or another that was like it in qualities and of the same kind, that man would not forget the great precious jewel.

Subhūti, in the same way, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has fallen away from the great precious jewel of the Perfection of Wisdom, just like one who has lost the great precious jewel and perceives it as precious, is endowed with attention to the Perfection of Wisdom and is never apart from attention to the Perfection of Wisdom. With a mind set on omniscience, for as long as he has not found it, he should go on seeking. And for that long he should remain endowed with the attention of one who has found the great precious jewel of the Perfection of Wisdom, and never be parted from the attention of one who has found the great precious jewel of omniscience itself.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, the Blessed One has taught that all phenomena and all acts of attention are devoid of intrinsic nature and are empty. Then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva, a great being, come to be endowed with attention to the Perfection of Wisdom and with attention to omniscience, and never be parted from them?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows: Subhūti, suppose a bodhisattva, a great being, thinks, "All phenomena are secluded by their intrinsic nature; all phenomena are empty by their intrinsic nature." Attention of this kind is endowed with attention to the Perfection of Wisdom and with attention to omniscience, and is never parted from them. Why is that? Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom is empty, and it neither increases nor decreases.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, if the Perfection of Wisdom is empty and neither increases nor decreases, then how does a bodhisattva, a great being, come to accomplish awakening through a Perfection of Wisdom that has no increase? How does he fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows: Subhūti, the practice of a bodhisattva, a great being, in the Perfection of Wisdom has neither increase nor decrease. Subhūti, just as the Perfection of Wisdom is empty and so has neither increase nor decrease, in the same way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, is also empty and so has neither increase nor decrease. Subhūti, precisely because the Perfection of Wisdom is empty and so has neither increase nor decrease, and likewise a bodhisattva, a great being, is empty and so has neither increase nor decrease, for that very reason a bodhisattva, a great being, strives for the sake of awakening, and in this way fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Subhūti, if, when this is being taught, a bodhisattva, a great being, is not frightened, not terrified, not overcome by dread, and does not lose heart, then it should be understood that this bodhisattva, a great being, is practicing this Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, does the Perfection of Wisdom practice the Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it does not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then does the emptiness that is the Perfection of Wisdom practice the Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it does not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then, apart from the emptiness that is the Perfection of Wisdom, is any phenomenon found that practices the Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it is not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then does emptiness practice the Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it does not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then is any phenomenon that practices the Perfection of Wisdom found within this emptiness?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it is not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then does emptiness practice emptiness?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it does not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then does form practice the Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it does not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then do feeling, perception, and the formations, and does consciousness, practice the Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, they do not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then, apart from form, is any phenomenon found that practices the Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it is not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then, apart from feeling, perception, and the formations, and apart from consciousness, is any phenomenon found that practices the Perfection of Wisdom?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it is not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then how does a bodhisattva, a great being, come to practice the Perfection of Wisdom?

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, do you perceive, rightly and correctly, any phenomenon that practices the Perfection of Wisdom?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, I do not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, do you perceive, rightly and correctly, that Perfection of Wisdom in which a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, I do not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Do you rightly perceive any phenomenon that is not apprehended? And is that very phenomenon one that has arisen, or is arising, or will arise, or has ceased, or is ceasing, or will cease?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it is not so.

The Blessed One said:

Subhūti, such is the very nature of the forbearance toward the unborn nature of phenomena possessed by a bodhisattva, a great being. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has this kind of forbearance will receive the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who has accomplished this fearless path of the Tathāgata, and who practices in this way, strives in this way, and exerts effort in this way, could not fail to attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a buddha, the great wisdom, the wisdom of omniscience, the wisdom of the great caravan leader. That is impossible.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, is it the unborn nature of all phenomena that receives the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, it is not.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, then in regard to what phenomenon is the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening given?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, do you then correctly perceive any phenomenon as that to which the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is given?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, I do not. Blessed One, I do not correctly perceive any phenomenon that is prophesied, or that will be prophesied, or that prophesies, as regards unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Blessed One, I also do not correctly perceive any phenomenon that is fully awakened to, or that is to be fully awakened to, or by which one will be fully awakened. Why is that? Blessed One, because all phenomena are without any basis to be apprehended, and so I do not think, "I fully awaken to this phenomenon," or "I will fully awaken to this phenomenon," or "I became fully awakened by this phenomenon."

This is the twenty-second chapter, called "The Spiritual Friend," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then at that time Śakra, lord of the gods, together with his retinue, came and gathered there and sat down. Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Alas, Blessed One, this Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to see and difficult to realize.

When he had said this, the Blessed One said this to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, so it is. So it is. Kauśika, this Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Kauśika, this Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to see and difficult to realize. Because space is profound, this Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Because it is secluded, this Perfection of Wisdom is difficult to see. Because it is empty, it is difficult to realize.

When he had said this, Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, those beings who come to hear this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and who, having heard it, also hold it, retain it, read it, master it, recite it, teach it, explain it, give instruction in it, recite it from memory, and write it down, are surely not possessed of an inferior root of virtue.

When he had said this, the Blessed One said this to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, so it is, so it is.

Kauśika, those beings who come to listen to this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and who, having heard it, also grasp it, hold it, read it, master it, recite it aloud, teach it, explain it, expound it, memorize it, and write it down in letters, are not endowed with a poor or inferior root of virtue.

Kauśika, suppose that all the beings who live in Jambudvīpa were established in the ten paths of virtuous action. What do you think, Kauśika? Would those beings produce abundant merit on that basis?

Śakra said: Blessed One, they would produce much. Sugata, they would produce much.

The Blessed One declared: Kauśika, a son or daughter of good family who does the following produces more merit than that. That is, one who listens to this Perfection of Wisdom, and, having heard it, grasps it, holds it, reads it, masters it, recites it aloud, teaches it, explains it, expounds it, memorizes it, and writes it down in letters. Kauschika, as for any son or daughter of good family who listens to this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and, having heard it, grasps it, holds it, reads it, masters it, recites it aloud, teaches it, explains it, expounds it, memorizes it, and writes it down in letters, and who becomes endowed with whatever root of virtue results from this, the former mass of merit arising from the moral discipline of all the beings of Jambudvīpa does not come near even to a hundredth part of this mass of merit. It does not come near to a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred ten-millionth part, nor a thousand ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part of a ten-million ten-millionth. It does not come within any count. It cannot be reckoned, nor expressed by an analogy, nor demonstrated through a comparison, and it cannot bear comparison on the basis of any ground or cause.

Then another monk said to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, a son or daughter of good family who listens to this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and, having heard it, grasps it, holds it, reads it, masters it, recites it aloud, teaches it, explains it, expounds it, memorizes it, and writes it down in letters, will overwhelm you.

When he had said this, Śakra, lord of the gods, said to that monk: Noble one, if such a son or daughter of good family would overwhelm me with just a single generation of the awakening mind, how much more would this be so for one who listens to this profound Perfection of Wisdom, grasps it, holds it, reads it, masters it, recites it aloud, teaches it, explains it, expounds it, memorizes it, and writes it down in letters. And how much more still for one who, having heard it, grasps it, holds it, reads it, masters it, recites it aloud, teaches it, explains it, expounds it, memorizes it, and writes it down in letters, and who then trains in it just as it is, practices it just as it is, and engages in yogic cultivation of it just as it is. Such bodhisattvas, great beings, will go on overwhelming the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Such bodhisattvas, great beings, will not only go on overwhelming the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, but

They will surpass all the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas as well. Yet these bodhisattvas, great beings, do not merely surpass the stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas. They will also surpass all those bodhisattvas, great beings, who are great lords of giving but who lack the Perfection of Wisdom and skill in means. And these bodhisattvas, great beings, do not merely surpass the bodhisattvas, great beings, who are great lords of giving. They will also surpass all those bodhisattvas, great beings, whose moral discipline is perfectly pure, whose mass of moral discipline is unimpaired, flawless, unspotted, complete, entirely pure, and free of stain, but who lack the Perfection of Wisdom and skill in means.

And these bodhisattvas, great beings, do not merely surpass those bodhisattvas, great beings, who possess a mass of moral discipline that is unimpaired, flawless, unspotted, complete, entirely pure, and free of stain. They will also surpass all those bodhisattvas, great beings, who are endowed with perfect patience and perfect tranquillity, who would not give rise to a harmful thought even toward a small piece of wood that is burning them, but who lack the Perfection of Wisdom and skill in means.

And these bodhisattvas, great beings, do not merely surpass those bodhisattvas, great beings, who are endowed with perfect patience and perfect tranquillity and have no resentment in their minds. They will also surpass all those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have undertaken diligence, who are without idleness or laziness, and who have a body, speech, and mind that carry out their works without flagging, but who lack the Perfection of Wisdom and skill in means.

And these bodhisattvas, great beings, do not merely surpass those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have undertaken diligence and who carry out the works of body, speech, and mind without idleness, laziness, or flagging. They will also surpass all those bodhisattvas, great beings, who delight in meditative concentration, are devoted to it, have the power of concentration, are endowed with it, abide in it, and have mastery over it, but who lack the Perfection of Wisdom and skill in means.

Bodhisattvas, great beings, who practice the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught will surpass the entire world with its gods, humans, and asuras. They will surpass all those of the Śrāvaka Vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, and also those bodhisattvas, great beings, who are not skilled in means, while they themselves will not be surpassed.

Why is that? Because when a bodhisattva, great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught and follows after the Perfection of Wisdom, this bodhisattva, great being, has set out so that the lineage of omniscience may not be cut off.

This bodhisattva, this great being, will not be kept far from the Tathāgatas. If this bodhisattva, this great being, applies himself in this way, he will go to the heart of awakening before long. If this bodhisattva, this great being, trains in the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, he will draw out the beings who are sunk in the mire of the afflictions. If this bodhisattva, this great being, trains in this way, he is training in the training of a bodhisattva; he is not training in the training of the śrāvakas, and he is not training in the training of the pratyekabuddhas.

When a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, the Four Great Kings, the guardians of the world, will come into his presence and say: "Noble son, train swiftly in the training of a bodhisattva! Do not be slow in training! When you are seated at the heart of awakening and have become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, these are the four alms bowls you will receive."

Blessed One, it is not only the Four Great Kings, the guardians of the world, who will think of coming into the presence of a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in the Perfection of Wisdom as it has been taught. Even I think of going into the presence of that bodhisattva, a great being, so what need is there to speak of the other sons of the gods! That bodhisattva, that great being, will also be constantly held in mind by the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas. When a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, none of the sufferings of the world and none of the harms inflicted by others, whatever they may be, nor any others at all, will ever arise in any way whatsoever. Blessed One, this too is a quality of a bodhisattva, a great being, in this very life, when he practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then the venerable Ānanda thought: "Does Śakra, lord of the gods, speak through his own eloquence, or does he speak through the power of the Buddha?"

Then, through the power of the Buddha, Śakra, lord of the gods, knew the thought in the venerable Ānanda's mind, and said to him: "Noble Ānanda, you should understand this as the power of the Buddha. Noble Ānanda, you should understand this as the blessing of the Buddha. Noble Ānanda, I am not able to speak at all, taking the bodhisattva, the great being, as my starting point, by my own power."

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, it is just as Śakra, lord of the gods, has said. It is so, it is so. This is the power of the Tathāgata. It is through the blessing of the Tathāgata that Śakra, lord of the gods, has spoken."

This is the twenty-third chapter, called "The Chapter of Śakra," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. The twentieth volume.

Then the Blessed One spoke again to the venerable Ānanda, saying:

Ānanda, furthermore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in the Perfection of Wisdom, applies himself to the Perfection of Wisdom, and meditates on the Perfection of Wisdom, then, Ānanda, all the evil Māras of the great trichiliocosm world-system fall into doubt, thinking: "Will this bodhisattva, this great being, turn back midway and directly realize the true limit at the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas? Or will he awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?"

Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in the Perfection of Wisdom, then those evil Māras are pierced by the sting of sorrow.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom and applies himself to the Perfection of Wisdom, then those evil Māras try to harm that bodhisattva, that great being. They think: "May this bodhisattva, this great being, become discouraged and be struck with terror, so that even a single generation of his mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is exhausted." So they also conjure up terrors, and they let loose and display shooting stars falling in every direction, and things like blazing fires.

Ānanda, however, the evil Māra does not come intending harm into the presence of all bodhisattvas, great beings. He comes into the presence of some, and he does not come into the presence of others.

Ānanda said: "Blessed One, into the presence of what kind of bodhisattva, great being, does the evil Māra come intending harm?"

The Blessed One declared: "Ānanda, if a bodhisattva, a great being, has not, even in the past, generated a mind of devotion toward the teaching of the Perfection of Wisdom, then, Ānanda, the evil Māra comes to that bodhisattva, that great being, intending harm, and he finds an opening.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when the profound Perfection of Wisdom is being taught, a bodhisattva may fall into doubt and become double-minded, wondering, 'Is this the Perfection of Wisdom or is it not?' Ānanda, the evil Māra comes intending harm to such a bodhisattva, a great being, in whom doubt has arisen, and he finds an opening in him.

Furthermore, Ānanda, in this case a bodhisattva, a great being, may be parted from spiritual friends and held by evil companions. He does not listen when the Perfection of Wisdom, that most profound of subjects, is taught. Because he has not listened, he does not understand. Because he does not understand, he does not ask, 'How should one meditate on the Perfection of Wisdom?' Ānanda, the evil Māra comes intending harm to this bodhisattva, this great being, too, and he finds an opening in him.

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bodhisattva, a great being, may come to rely on and engage in the grasping of what is not the true Dharma. He thinks: 'This one is my friend, who will never abandon me in any matter. There are many other bodhisattvas, great beings, who are my friends, but they do not fulfill my wishes.'

Thinking, "I have found a friend who is in harmony with me, and he will fulfill my aspiration completely," Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will also come with harmful intent toward this bodhisattva, a great being, and will find an opening.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when such a bodhisattva, a great being, is expounding this profound Perfection of Wisdom, he says to other bodhisattvas, great beings: "Alas, this Perfection of Wisdom is profound. What use is it for you to listen to it? You will not succeed in it by striving in the way the Tathāgata taught in other sūtras. I myself cannot find its depth and cannot taste its flavor, so what use is it for you to listen to it or to write it down?" In this way he turns other bodhisattvas, great beings, away from it. Ānanda, Māra the Evil One will come with harmful intent toward this bodhisattva too, and will find an opening.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva looks down on other bodhisattvas and thinks, "I dwell in seclusion, while the others do not dwell in seclusion; they have no seclusion," then, Ānanda, Māra the Evil One becomes delighted, pleased, and glad. Great joy, exhilaration, and happiness arise in him; he is wholly satisfied, his mind is content, and great delight arises. Why is that? Because he thinks, "This one will keep unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening far away."

Furthermore, Ānanda, when a bodhisattva, a great being, is named, or his lineage is mentioned, or the qualities of his ascetic practice are fully described, then on that basis, a bodhisattva, a great being, who in fact lacks those qualities, looks down on others who possess virtuous qualities. And yet he himself does not have those qualities. He does not have the qualities, the aspects, the signs, and the marks of an irreversible bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom. Although he lacks them, he becomes afflicted with pride about the qualities of the irreversible ones. He says, "The qualities that appear to me do not appear to you," praising himself and disparaging others.

Then Māra the Evil One thinks: "The realm of Māra will not be emptied. The great hells of sentient beings will not be destroyed. The animal births, the realm of the hungry ghosts, and the host of the asuras will not be destroyed." Having thought this, Māra the Evil One empowers things so that those bodhisattvas, great beings, become people who are overcome by gain and honor, who become eloquent in speech, and who, through that eloquence, are followed by many people. He wills that many people listen to them and have faith in them. Then, seeing or hearing of them, people will imitate them. And in imitating what they have seen and heard, they will not train in suchness, will not practice in suchness, and will not apply themselves to yoga in suchness. Because they do not train in suchness, practice in suchness, or apply themselves to yoga in suchness, their afflictions will increase.

Because their mental continuum is inverted in this way, whatever actions of body, speech, and mind they perform will all turn out to be undesirable, unpleasant, joyless, and disagreeable. In this way those great hells of sentient beings will not be emptied. The birthplaces of animals, the realm of hungry ghosts, the hosts of the asuras, and the abodes of Māra will not be emptied either. Ānanda, seeing this very reason, Māra the Evil One becomes delighted, pleased, and rejoicing, and feels great joy, satisfaction, and happiness.

Ānanda, furthermore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, quarrels, disputes, and mocks with a person who follows the vehicle of the śrāvakas, and reviles and insults him, thinks of harming him, and generates aversion, then Māra the Evil One thinks: "Alas! This son of good family will keep far away from omniscience; he will dwell very far from omniscience."

And if a person who follows the vehicle of the bodhisattvas quarrels, disputes, and mocks with another person who follows the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, and reviles and insults him, thinks of harming him, and generates aversion, then Māra the Evil One becomes extremely delighted, pleased, and rejoicing, and feels great joy, satisfaction, and happiness. He thinks: "Both of these bodhisattvas will dwell far from omniscience."

Ānanda, furthermore, if a bodhisattva, a great being, who has not received a prediction quarrels, disputes, and mocks with a bodhisattva, a great being, who has received a prediction, and reviles and insults him, thinks of harming him, generates aversion, and injures his mind, then that bodhisattva, a great being, even if he does not abandon omniscience, must put on the armor for as many eons as the number of those thoughts of awakening.

When he had spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, for those who have generated those thoughts of awakening, is there any deliverance at all? Or must that bodhisattva, a great being, certainly put on the armor for that many eons?"

The Blessed One said: "Ānanda, to persons of the śrāvaka vehicle, to persons of the pratyekabuddha vehicle, and to persons of the bodhisattva vehicle, I have taught the Dharma that includes deliverance. Among these, Ānanda, if a person of the bodhisattva vehicle quarrels and disputes with another person of the bodhisattva vehicle, and reviles and insults him, thinks of harming him, and generates aversion, and then does not confess it individually, does not take up restraint afterward, but holds a grudge and remains clinging to resentment, Ānanda, I do not say that such a person has deliverance. Ānanda, that person will certainly have to put on the armor for that many eons.

"Ānanda, but if a person of the bodhisattva vehicle quarrels and disputes with another person of the bodhisattva vehicle, and reviles and insults him, thinks of harming him, and generates aversion, and then confesses it individually, and having confessed it takes up restraint afterward and generates this thought: 'I must settle the quarrels of all sentient beings, remove them, and completely pacify them. If I myself were to quarrel, or were to answer back when someone speaks to me, that would be a wretched gain, a bad acquisition and not a good one. I must become like a bridge for all sentient beings.'"

When speaking to others, I will not use harsh words such as "you," nor will I retort and reply with rough speech.
