When people quarrel, dispute, and mock, I will act like one who is stupid, deaf, and mute. When others speak ill, say hateful things, or utter abuse, I will hear their words without harboring ill will toward anyone. To make a point of knowing the faults and flaws of others does me no good; it is no part of my task. To think that I should listen for the faults and flaws of others is no part of my task.

Why is that? Because I must not disturb my own higher intention. I am to become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and then bring happiness to all sentient beings with every kind of comfort and lead them to complete nirvāṇa. How could I give rise to malice? Even when I and others are angry, I should not feel malice toward them. Would that not be my own disturbance? This is not for me to do. Rather, with firm and steady resolve, I will subdue others, and even when they threaten my life, I will not be disturbed or let anger and resentment arise in me.

Ānanda, I have declared that this is the way a bodhisattva, a great being, brings about his emergence from such pride.

Ānanda, a bodhisattva, a great being, should likewise abide in this way before persons who follow the Śrāvaka Vehicle. Just as he is not disturbed in the presence of any being, so should he abide in the presence of all beings.

Ānanda, how should a bodhisattva, a great being, abide in the presence of other persons who follow the Bodhisattva Vehicle? Ānanda, he should abide as he would before the Teacher, thinking: "These bodhisattvas, great beings, are my teachers. These bodhisattvas, great beings, have entered the same vehicle as I. These bodhisattvas, great beings, have entered the same path as I. These bodhisattvas, great beings, share my aspiration. These bodhisattvas, great beings, have rightly entered a vehicle in harmony with mine. Whatever they train in, I too will train in. However they train, so will I train. If some of them live in a mixed way, I will not live in a mixed way. And if they all live without mixing, with attention endowed with omniscience, then I too will train in the same way."

Ānanda, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way in omniscience, there will be no obstacle to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and he will swiftly awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

This is the twenty-fourth chapter, called "Pride," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, in what should a bodhisattva, a great being, train in order to be training in omniscience?"

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in exhaustion, he trains in omniscience."

Likewise, it is without arising, without cessation, without birth, without entity; it is secluded, free of attachment, space, and the dharmadhātu. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in nirvāṇa, he trains in omniscience.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, why is it that if a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in exhaustion, he trains in omniscience? Likewise, if he trains in what is without arising, without cessation, without birth, without entity, secluded, free of attachment, space, the dharmadhātu, and nirvāṇa, why does he train in omniscience?

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, you ask why it is that if a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in exhaustion, he trains in omniscience, and likewise why training in what is without arising, without cessation, without birth, without entity, secluded, free of attachment, space, the dharmadhātu, and nirvāṇa amounts to training in omniscience. Subhūti, what do you think? That suchness of the Tathāgata, and that by which the Tathāgata is designated "the Tathāgata," is it something that could be exhausted?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it is not. Why? Blessed One, what is exhausted is not exhausted; Blessed One, exhaustion is inexhaustible.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? That suchness of the Tathāgata, and that by which the Tathāgata is designated "the Tathāgata," does it arise, or cease, or become born, or become an entity, or become secluded, or become destroyed, or become free of attachment, or become space, or become the dharmadhātu?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it does not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? That suchness of the Tathāgata, and that by which the Tathāgata is designated "the Tathāgata," does it pass into nirvāṇa?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, it does not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, therefore a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains thus: suchness is inexhaustible. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains in omniscience. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains in the Perfection of Wisdom. He trains in the stage of a buddha. He trains in the powers. He trains in the fearlessnesses. He trains in all the qualities of the buddhas. He trains in the wisdom of omniscience.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way will attain the perfection of all trainings. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way cannot be overpowered by Māra, by Māra's retinue, or by the gods of Māra's host. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way will quickly attain the nature of irreversibility. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way will quickly come to be seated at the heart of awakening.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains in his own proper domain. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains in the qualities that make one a protector. He trains in great loving-kindness. He trains in great compassion. He trains in great joy. He trains in great equanimity. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains in setting the wheel of Dharma in motion, turned three times in twelve aspects. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains in the resolve, "I shall not let the realm of sentient beings diminish." Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains in keeping the lineage of the Tathāgatas from being cut off. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains in the resolve, "I shall open the door to the realm of the deathless."

Subhūti, this vast training cannot be trained in by one whose mind is weak, and one of little power cannot train in it. Why is that? Subhūti, those who train in this training are in harmony with all sentient beings and share in common with them. Subhūti, they are the protectors of all sentient beings. Those who train in this training wish to attain a state that rises supreme above all sentient beings.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way is not born among the beings of the hells, is not born in the animal realms, is not born in the realms of the hungry ghosts, and is not born in the body of an asura. He is not born among the people of the borderlands, is not born into the caste of outcastes, is not born into the caste of bamboo workers, and is not born into the families of hunters, fishermen, bandits, or butchers. He is not born into any other such low family of a wretched station and a wretched support.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way does not become blind, does not become deaf, does not become lame, does not become hunchbacked, does not become bent, does not become crippled, does not become leprous, does not become mute, does not become hoarse, does not become dull of hearing, and does not become impaired in his limbs. He does not become deficient in his limbs, does not become unsightly in his limbs, does not become ugly in complexion, does not become ugly in form, does not become impaired in his faculties, and does not become deficient in his faculties. Rather, he becomes complete in every aspect of the faculties, and his voice becomes perfectly excellent.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way does not take life, does not take what is not given, and does not engage in sexual misconduct. He does not lie, does not speak divisively, does not speak harshly, and does not engage in idle talk. He does not become covetous, does not become malicious, and does not hold wrong views. He does not make his living by wrong livelihood.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way is not born among the long-lived gods. He does not take up immoral conduct, and does not take up what is not the true Dharma. He is not born there through the power of meditative concentration and absorption. Why is that? Because the bodhisattva, the great being, who is endowed with skillful means has the skillful means by which he does not come to be born among the long-lived gods. Subhūti, what is that skillful means?

That is to say, a bodhisattva, a great being, who is endowed with skillful means in this very Perfection of Wisdom, enters even into meditative concentration, and yet through the power of that concentration is not reborn there. In just this way he practices this skillful means. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this manner has his powers fully purified, his fearlessnesses fully purified, and all the qualities of a buddha fully purified, and he will gain them in due course.

The venerable Subhūti said: Blessed One, since all phenomena are pure by their very nature, then, Blessed One, by what means do a bodhisattva, a great being, come to have their powers purified, their fearlessnesses purified, and the qualities of a buddha purified, and come to gain them?

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Why is that? Subhūti, all phenomena are pure by their very nature. Subhūti, when bodhisattvas, great beings, who train in the Perfection of Wisdom are neither discouraged nor dismayed with regard to all phenomena being thus pure by their very nature, then, Subhūti, that is the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, ordinary foolish beings do not know and do not see these phenomena as they are. Because they neither know nor see, they do not know or see the nature of phenomena. Subhūti, for the sake of those beings, a bodhisattva, a great being, makes effort and undertakes diligence, training in this training: I myself shall make known to beings what they do not know, and I myself shall make visible to beings what they do not see. A bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this training will gain the powers, will gain the fearlessnesses, and will gain all the qualities of a buddha.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way fully understands, exactly as they are, the conduct and the stirrings of the minds of other beings and other individuals, and by fully understanding them exactly as they are, goes to the far shore of knowing the conduct of others' minds.

Subhūti, consider this example. In the great earth, the regions where there are no stones and where gold, gems, and silver are found are few, while the regions of the great earth that are filled with salt-laden soil, gravel, grass, stumps, and thorns of many kinds are far more numerous. In just the same way, Subhūti, among beings, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who train in the training of the Perfection of Wisdom and of omniscience are few, while those beings who train in the training of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are far more numerous.

Furthermore, Subhūti, consider this example. Among beings, those who have undertaken and abide in the karma that leads to attaining the kingship of a wheel-turning king are few, while those beings who have undertaken and abide in the karma that leads to attaining the kingship of a king of a city are far more numerous.

Subhūti, in the same way, among beings those bodhisattvas, great beings, who enter the great path, that is, the path of the Perfection of Wisdom, with the thought "I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening," are few. Among beings those who enter the path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are very many.

Furthermore, Subhūti, take this example. Among beings, those who firmly undertake and abide in the actions that lead to becoming Śakra are few. Among beings, those who firmly undertake and abide in the actions that lead to birth in the world of the gods are very many.

In the same way, Subhūti, among beings those bodhisattvas, great beings, who train in the training of the Perfection of Wisdom are few. Among beings those who train in the training of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are very many.

Furthermore, Subhūti, take this example. Among beings, those who firmly undertake and abide in the actions that lead to becoming Brahmā are few. Among beings, those who firmly undertake and abide in the actions that lead to birth in Brahmā's retinue are very many.

In the same way, Subhūti, among beings those bodhisattvas, great beings, who do not turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening are few. Among beings those bodhisattvas, great beings, who do turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening are very many.

Therefore, Subhūti, among beings those who have rightly entered upon unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening are few. Fewer than those few are the beings who practice in accordance with suchness. Fewer still than those very few who practice in accordance with suchness are those who devote themselves to the Perfection of Wisdom. And fewer still than those few who devote themselves to the Perfection of Wisdom are the bodhisattvas, great beings, who do not turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, great being, who wishes to be counted among those irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, who are fewer even than the few, should train in this very Perfection of Wisdom and should devote himself to it.

Furthermore, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, great being, trains in the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, no mind accompanied by crookedness arises, no mind accompanied by doubt arises, no mind accompanied by envy arises, no mind accompanied by miserliness arises, no mind accompanied by immoral conduct arises, no mind accompanied by malice arises, no mind accompanied by laziness arises, no mind accompanied by distraction arises, and no mind accompanied by confused wisdom arises.

Subhūti, by training in the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, a bodhisattva, great being, will fully grasp all the perfections. He will wholly take hold of all the perfections. He will take up all the perfections as supreme. All the perfections will follow after him. All the perfections will be gathered within him.

Subhūti, it is like this. Take this example.

Within the view of the perishable aggregates, the sixty-two views are gathered. In just the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in the Perfection of Wisdom, all the perfections are gathered within it.

Subhūti, it is like this. Within a person's life faculty, all the faculties are gathered. In just the same way, Subhūti, when one trains in the Perfection of Wisdom, all the virtuous qualities of a bodhisattva, a great being, are gathered within it.

Subhūti, it is like this. When a person's life faculty ceases, all the faculties cease. In just the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in the Perfection of Wisdom, ignorance ceases and all unwholesome qualities cease, while all the perfections are gathered within and held fast.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to grasp all the perfections should train in the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in the Perfection of Wisdom, he trains as the supreme one among all sentient beings. Why is this? Because he is the supreme one in merit.

Subhūti, what do you think? Of all the sentient beings who exist in the great trichiliocosm world-system, however many are counted as sentient beings, are they all numerous?

Subhūti replied: Blessed One, even the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are numerous, so what need is there to speak of all the sentient beings of the great trichiliocosm world-system?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, suppose a single bodhisattva, a great being, were to remain for as long as he lives and attend to all those sentient beings with clothing, food, bedding, medicine for the sick, and all useful provisions. Subhūti, what do you think? Would that bodhisattva, a great being, produce a great deal of merit on that basis?

Subhūti replied: Blessed One, a great deal. Sugata, a great deal.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, meditates on this Perfection of Wisdom for even as short a time as it takes to snap the fingers, he produces far more merit than that. Why is this? Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom of a bodhisattva, a great being, is of such great significance, for the Perfection of Wisdom is what brings a bodhisattva, a great being, to the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening.

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should train in this Perfection of Wisdom if he wishes to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening; if he wishes to become unsurpassed among all sentient beings; if he wishes to become the protector of all sentient beings who have no protector; if he wishes to attain the realm of the buddhas; if he wishes to attain the state of being the supreme leader of the herd, the buddha; if he wishes to delight in the playful display of the buddhas; if he wishes to roar the lion's roar of the buddhas; if he wishes to attain the excellences of the buddhas; and if he wishes to speak the Dharma throughout the great trichiliocosm world-system.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in the Perfection of Wisdom, I do not see any excellence that he would fail to train in.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, does that bodhisattva, that great being, also train in the excellences of the śrāvakas?

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, that bodhisattva, that great being, does train in the excellences of the śrāvakas. Yet, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, does not train in the thought that he should abide in the excellences of the śrāvakas, nor in the thought that the excellences of the śrāvakas will belong to those who need no further training. He does not train in that way.

Subhūti, he also fully understands whatever qualities the śrāvakas have, but he does not abide in them. He examines them in this way without abiding, and he trains in the thought: "I shall explain these qualities of the śrāvakas, and I shall teach them."

Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, he becomes a worthy recipient of offerings for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, trains in this way, he overcomes all other recipients of offerings, those who possess the qualities of śrāvakas and those who possess the qualities of pratyekabuddhas, and he draws near to omniscience.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way does not abandon the Perfection of Wisdom. He practices the Perfection of Wisdom and is never separated from abiding in the Perfection of Wisdom. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices in this way, he should be known as one whose nature is never to fall away from omniscience. He keeps far from the level of the śrāvakas and the level of the pratyekabuddhas, and he draws near to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening.

Now suppose he were to think: "This is the Perfection of Wisdom, which brings about the attainment of this very omniscience." If he thinks and understands in that way, he is not practicing the Perfection of Wisdom. And suppose he does not truly know this Perfection of Wisdom either, in the thought: "This is the Perfection of Wisdom; this belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom; this Perfection of Wisdom is what attains omniscience." Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, neither truly knows nor truly sees it in this way, then, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way is practicing the Perfection of Wisdom.

This is the twenty-fifth chapter, called "Training," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. Volume twenty-one.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, thought: "Even by the conduct of a bodhisattva, a great being, all beings are overcome in this way. How much more so when he has become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening! Those beings whose minds turn toward omniscience have gained a good gain, and those beings live a good life. How much more so those who have given rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening!"

Those excellent beings who will fully awaken into unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening should be regarded as the ones to be wished for.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, magically conjured mandārava flowers, and holding them cupped in his hands he scattered them over the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, and he spoke these words: "May the awakening mind of those persons of the bodhisattva vehicle, who give rise to the thought of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, who aspire, who reflect, who take up that resolve, thinking, 'Having fully awakened to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, we shall establish on the ground of the buddhas, on the far shore, all sentient beings who are being swept along by the great ocean of saṃsāra,' be fulfilled. May those very qualities of a buddha be perfectly completed in them. May those very qualities that accompany omniscience be perfectly completed. May those very self-arisen qualities be perfectly completed. May those very qualities that cannot be taken away be perfectly completed.

"Blessed One, as for those bodhisattvas, great beings, endowed with great compassion, not one thought of turning back from unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening will arise in them. Blessed One, as for those persons of the bodhisattva vehicle who have properly entered upon fully awakening to unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening, not one thought of turning back from it will arise in them, for, seeing the sufferings that sentient beings experience in saṃsāra, they will give rise to vast aspirations for unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening.

"Why is that? Those who are endowed with such a resolve as this, 'Having crossed over myself, I shall bring sentient beings across; having been freed, I shall free them; having breathed freely, I shall give them breath; having completely passed beyond sorrow, I shall lead them to complete nirvāṇa,' those who abide in such a resolve are wishing for the sake of great compassion, are wishing to heal, and are showing tender concern with compassion for the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

"Blessed One, if one rejoices in the resolve of those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have newly entered the vehicle; and rejoices in the resolve of those who are practicing the conduct of bodhisattvas; and rejoices in the irreversible nature of the irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings; and rejoices in the nature of the bodhisattvas, great beings, who are bound to only one more birth, then, Blessed One, how much merit will that son or daughter of good family produce?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to Śakra, lord of the gods, in these words: "Kauśika, one could grasp the measure of Mount Sumeru, king of mountains, by weighing it on a scale, but, Kauśika, the measure of the merit of that resolve of a son or daughter of good family, endowed with rejoicing in bodhisattvas, great beings, cannot be grasped."

Kauśika, one might still be able to grasp the measure of the world-system of the fourth great continent, if it were weighed on a scale, but the measure of the merit of that mind generated together with rejoicing cannot be grasped. Kauśika, one might still be able to grasp the measure of a thousand-fold world-system, a small chiliocosm, if it were weighed on a scale, but the measure of the merit of that mind generated together with rejoicing cannot be grasped. Kauśika, one might still be able to grasp the measure of the second, middle thousand-fold world-system, if it were weighed on a scale, but the measure of the merit of that mind generated together with rejoicing cannot be grasped. Kauśika, one might still be able to grasp the measure of the great trichiliocosm world-system, if it were weighed on a scale, but, Kauśika, the measure of the merit of the mind generated together with rejoicing by a son or daughter of good family in the bodhisattva, the great being, cannot be grasped.

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One: Blessed One, those beings who do not listen to, do not accept, do not see, and do not rejoice in the merit of generating the mind of rejoicing in bodhisattvas, great beings, which is immeasurable in this way, from the first generation of the awakening mind up to the fully accomplished buddhahood of unsurpassed, perfect awakening, should be known as blessed, that is, possessed, by Māra. Blessed One, those beings who do not rejoice in this generation of the mind by bodhisattvas, great beings, have come over to the side of Māra. Blessed One, those beings who do not rejoice in this generation of the mind by bodhisattvas, great beings, have passed away and transmigrated from the realm of Māra, that is, they have left his domain.

Why is that? Blessed One, those who bring about these generations of mind, those who fully dedicate these generations of mind to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, or those who rejoice in these generations of mind, destroy the abode of Māra. Blessed One, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have generated the mind for unsurpassed, perfect awakening, those generations of mind should be rejoiced in. Blessed One, those sons or daughters of good family who have not abandoned the Tathāgata, have not abandoned the Dharma, and have not abandoned the Saṅgha should rejoice in this generation of the mind.

When he had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, it is so, it is just so. Kauśika, those sons or daughters of good family who have not abandoned the Tathāgata, have not abandoned the Dharma, and have not abandoned the Saṅgha should rejoice in these generations of mind. Kauśika, those sons or daughters of good family, whether followers of the bodhisattva vehicle, the pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the śrāvaka vehicle, who rejoice in this generation of the mind will quickly please the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas, and will not fail to please them.

When he had spoken thus, Śakra, lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:

Blessed One, it is just so. Sugata, it is just so. Those sons or daughters of good family, whether they follow the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the śrāvakas, who rejoice in these generations of the awakening mind, will very swiftly please the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, and will not displease them. And through the roots of virtue of generating the awakening mind accompanied by such rejoicing, wherever they are born, in each such place they will be honored, revered, offered gifts, worshipped, held in esteem, and attended with respect. They will not see unpleasing forms, they will not hear unpleasing sounds, they will not smell unpleasing odors, they will not taste unpleasing flavors, and they will not touch unpleasing tangibles. It should be understood that they will not be born in the lower realms; it should be understood that they will be born in the higher realms. Why is that? It is because those sons or daughters of good family rejoice in the roots of virtue, immeasurable and innumerable, that bring happiness to all sentient beings.

Blessed One, those persons who follow the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, and whose generations of the awakening mind I have rejoiced in with eager intention, will have those generations of awakening mind grow and increase, and they will attain unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, they will also lead immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings to complete nirvāṇa.

The Blessed One said: Kauśika, through the power of the Tathāgata, whatever you have said is just so; it is just so. Kauśika, if a son or daughter of good family rejoices in the generations of the awakening mind of persons who follow the vehicle of the bodhisattvas, then in this way, Kauśika, by rejoicing in those generations of the awakening mind of such persons, that son or daughter of good family comes to rejoice in the roots of virtue of immeasurable and countless sentient beings, and generates and accomplishes them.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, how can a mind that is like an illusion come to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, what do you think? Do you perceive the mind correctly as being like an illusion?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, I do not.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? Do you perceive the illusion correctly?

Subhūti said: Blessed One, I do not. Blessed One, I do not correctly perceive a mind like an illusion, nor do I correctly perceive an illusion.

The Blessed One said: Subhūti, what do you think? You who do not correctly perceive an illusory mind or a mind like an illusion, do you correctly perceive any phenomenon, other than the illusion or the mind like an illusion, that awakens fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening?

Subhūti said:

"Blessed One, it is not so. Apart from illusion, or apart from mind that is like an illusion, I do not perceive any phenomenon that would fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Since I do not perceive any such phenomenon apart from illusion or apart from mind that is like an illusion, what phenomenon could I speak of as existing or as not existing? Of that phenomenon which is utterly secluded, there is no realization that it exists or that it does not exist. For any phenomenon that is utterly secluded does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Why is that? Blessed One, a phenomenon that does not exist does not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

"Blessed One, therefore the Perfection of Wisdom is utterly secluded. And that phenomenon which is utterly secluded is not something to be cultivated; by it nothing is attained and nothing is abandoned. Then, Blessed One, how could a bodhisattva, a great being, relying on the Perfection of Wisdom that is utterly secluded, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening? Blessed One, unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is also utterly secluded. Blessed One, when the Perfection of Wisdom is utterly secluded, and unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is also utterly secluded, then, Blessed One, how could seclusion fully awaken to seclusion?"

When he had spoken in this way, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: "Excellent, Subhūti, excellent! It is just so, Subhūti, it is just so. The Perfection of Wisdom is utterly secluded, and unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is also utterly secluded. Subhūti, it is precisely because the Perfection of Wisdom is utterly secluded that one fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, which is utterly secluded.

"Subhūti, if a bodhisattva, a great being, were to know thoroughly that the Perfection of Wisdom is utterly secluded, that would not be the Perfection of Wisdom. Subhūti, in this way a bodhisattva, a great being, relying on the Perfection of Wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. And yet, Subhūti, there is no one who, relying on the Perfection of Wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Seclusion does not fully awaken to seclusion; nevertheless a bodhisattva, a great being, does fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and without relying on the Perfection of Wisdom, one does not fully awaken."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has taught, a bodhisattva, a great being, practices in a profound meaning."

The Blessed One said: "It is just so, Subhūti, it is just so. A bodhisattva, a great being, practices in a profound meaning. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in a profound meaning, and who yet does not make that meaning directly manifest at the stage of the śrāvakas or the stage of the pratyekabuddhas, performs a difficult deed."

Subhūti said: Blessed One, as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has taught, a bodhisattva, a great being, does not practice anything difficult. Why is that? Blessed One, it is because the phenomenon that is being realized directly is itself not apprehended; the phenomenon that is realized is not apprehended; and the phenomenon by which it is realized directly is not apprehended either.

Blessed One, if, when this is taught, a bodhisattva, a great being, is not discouraged, not dismayed, not utterly disheartened, does not turn away in mind, does not tremble, is not completely terrified, and does not become possessed of fright, then he practices the Perfection of Wisdom. If he does not view himself, in the right way, as thinking, "I am practicing," then he practices the Perfection of Wisdom. If he does not view himself, in the right way, as thinking, "I have come close to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening," then he practices the Perfection of Wisdom. If he does not think, "I have left the grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas far behind," then he practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

Blessed One, it is like space. Space does not think, "I am near to some things and far from others." Why is that? Blessed One, it is because space has no conceptual thought. In just the same way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom does not think, "I have come close to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, and the grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are far from me." Why is that? Blessed One, it is because the Perfection of Wisdom has no conceptual thought.

Blessed One, it is like a magical illusion of a man. The illusory man does not think, "The one who creates the illusion is near to me, but this other gathering of people assembled here is far from me." Why is that? Blessed One, it is because the illusory man has no conceptual thought. In just the same way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom does not think, "I have come close to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, and the grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are far from me." Why is that? Blessed One, it is because the Perfection of Wisdom has no conceptual thought.

Blessed One, it is like a reflection. A reflection does not think, "Whatever the support is from which the reflection arises, that is near to me, but those who have not come close to the mirror or the vessel filled with water are far from me." Why is that? Blessed One, it is because a reflection has no conceptual thought. In just the same way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom does not think, "I have come close to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, and the grounds of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are far from me." Why is that? Blessed One, it is because the Perfection of Wisdom has no conceptual thought.

Blessed One, it is like this. The Tathāgata holds neither fondness nor dislike toward anyone. Why is that? Because the Tathāgata has abandoned all conceptualization and discrimination. In just the same way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom holds neither fondness nor dislike toward anyone. Why is that? Blessed One, because there is no conceptualization in the Perfection of Wisdom. Blessed One, just as the Tathāgata has abandoned all conceptualization and discrimination, so too the Perfection of Wisdom has abandoned all conceptualization and discrimination.

Blessed One, it is like this. Suppose an emanation is magically produced by a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly awakened buddha. That emanation does not think, "I have come close to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and the level of the śrāvakas and the pratyekabuddhas is far from me." Why is that? Blessed One, because there is no conceptualization in an emanation. In just the same way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom does not think, "I have come close to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and the level of the śrāvakas and the level of the pratyekabuddhas are far from me." Why is that? Blessed One, because there is no conceptualization in the Perfection of Wisdom.

Blessed One, it is like this. An emanation performs whatever task it was emanated to perform, and yet that emanation has no conceptualization. Why is that? Because there is no conceptualization in that emanation. In just the same way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, accomplishes whatever task he undertakes to accomplish by cultivating this Perfection of Wisdom, and yet that Perfection of Wisdom has no conceptualization. Why is that? Blessed One, because there is no conceptualization in the Perfection of Wisdom.

Blessed One, it is like this. Suppose a skilled carpenter, or a carpenter's apprentice, assembles a mechanical figure of a man or a woman made of wood. Whatever task it was made to perform, it performs, and yet that assemblage of wood has no conceptualization. Why is that? Blessed One, because there is no conceptualization in that assemblage of wood. In just the same way, Blessed One, a bodhisattva, a great being, accomplishes whatever task he undertakes to accomplish by cultivating this Perfection of Wisdom, and yet that Perfection of Wisdom has no conceptualization. Why is that? Blessed One, because there is no conceptualization in the Perfection of Wisdom.

This is the twenty-sixth chapter, called "The Chapter on Being Like an Illusion," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the venerable Subhūti: "Venerable Subhūti, alas, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom practices in the essence."

When he had said this, the venerable Subhūti said to the venerable Śāriputra:

Venerable Śāriputra, alas! Whatever bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom practices in what is not the essence.

Then many thousands of sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm thought: Those beings who have generated the mind toward unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening and strive to accomplish it are worthy of homage. And those who practice this profound Perfection of Wisdom, and yet, though they practice in this way, do not directly realize the true limit at the level of the śrāvakas or the level of the pratyekabuddhas, and who, though they practice in the nature of phenomena, do not directly realize that nature of phenomena, by this account too one should know that these bodhisattvas, great beings, are doing what is difficult.

Then the Venerable Subhūti, knowing with his own mind the thoughts in the minds of those many thousands of sons of the gods who dwell in the desire realm, said to them: Sons of the gods, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who do not directly realize that true limit are not doing what is difficult. But, sons of the gods, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who put on the armor thinking, "I shall lead immeasurable, innumerable beings to complete nirvāṇa," are doing what is difficult; they are doing what is supremely difficult. For beings are empty, and those beings too are utterly nonexistent; being nonexistent, they are not apprehended. In the same way, those who are to be tamed are utterly nonexistent; being nonexistent, they are not apprehended. Thus bodhisattvas, great beings, who think, "I shall tame beings," have properly set out to become fully awakened in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Sons of the gods, to think "I shall tame beings" is to think "I shall tame space." Why is that? Sons of the gods, because space is empty, beings should be known as empty. Sons of the gods, if a bodhisattva, a great being, puts on the armor for the sake of beings who are nonexistent and not apprehended, then by this account he is doing what is difficult. Sons of the gods, to think "I shall put on the armor for the sake of beings" is to think "I shall contend with space." Yet this bodhisattva, a great being, has put on this armor for the sake of beings. And the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, have taught that those beings too are utterly unapprehended; and because beings are empty, it should be understood in this way. Thus, because those to be tamed are empty, the bodhisattva should be known as empty.

If, when this is explained, the bodhisattva, a great being, does not become discouraged, sons of the gods, you should know that this bodhisattva, a great being, is practicing the Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that? Because beings are empty, form should be known as empty. In the same way, because beings are empty, feelings, perceptions, and formations are empty; and because beings are empty, consciousness should be known as empty. In the same way, because beings are empty, all phenomena, up to the very last, should be known as empty. Sons of the gods, in this way one should view all phenomena as empty. Sons of the gods, when all phenomena are thus explained as empty, if the bodhisattva, a great being, does not become discouraged, then because of not becoming discouraged in this way, he practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then the Blessed One, knowing the answer, said to the venerable Subhūti, "Subhūti, why is it that when all phenomena are taught in this way as secluded, the bodhisattva, the great being, is not discouraged?"

Subhūti replied, "Blessed One, it is because of seclusion that he is not discouraged. Blessed One, for this reason the bodhisattva, the great being, is not discouraged when all phenomena are taught as secluded. Blessed One, there is no phenomenon at all by which he could become discouraged. Why is that? Blessed One, those phenomena by which one might become discouraged are not apprehended at all. Blessed One, a phenomenon by which some phenomenon might become discouraged is not apprehended either."

The Blessed One said, "So it is, Subhūti, so it is. Nevertheless, Subhūti, if, when this is spoken, taught, shown, and explained in this way, the bodhisattva, the great being, does not become discouraged, is not timid or anxious, is not dejected, is not utterly dejected, does not lose heart, does not turn back in mind, is not crushed and does not turn back, is not frightened, is not utterly terrified, and is free from terror, then he is practicing the Perfection of Wisdom."

Subhūti said, "Blessed One, so it is. Sugata, so it is. Blessed One, if the bodhisattva, the great being, practices in this way, he is practicing the Perfection of Wisdom. To a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way, the gods together with Indra, together with Brahmā, together with Prajāpati, together with Īśāna, together with the sages, and the assemblies of men and women, will bow from afar with palms joined."

The Blessed One said, "Subhūti, it is not only the gods together with Indra, together with Brahmā, together with Prajāpati, together with Īśāna, together with the sages, and the assemblies of men and women who will bow from afar with palms joined to the bodhisattva, the great being, who practices in this way. Subhūti, the gods of the Brahmā realms as well, the gods of Brahmā's Retinue, the Priests of Brahmā, the Great Brahmās, the gods of Limited Light, Immeasurable Light, and Radiant Light, the gods of Limited Virtue, Immeasurable Virtue, and Increasing Virtue, the gods of Cloudless, Merit-Born, and Great Fruit, the beings without discrimination, and the gods of Not Great, Not Afflicted, Beautiful in Appearance, Clear-Seeing, and Akaniṣṭha, all these, Subhūti, will bow to the bodhisattva, the great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom itself.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, in the immeasurable, innumerable world systems there are Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas who are now living, who remain and are sustained. Those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, regard with the buddha eye the bodhisattva, the great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom in this way. Subhūti, they assist him and keep him in mind, the one who practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

"Furthermore, Subhūti, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who practice the Perfection of Wisdom are assisted and kept in mind by the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas."

Subhūti, such bodhisattvas, great beings, should be understood as irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. No obstacle from Māra or from anyone else will arise for them. Why is this? Subhūti, suppose that all the beings in the great trichiliocosm world-system were to become Māra the Evil One, and that each of those evil Māras were to emanate that many armies of Māra. Even so, Subhūti, those evil Māras would be unable to create an obstacle to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening for a bodhisattva, a great being, who is cared for by the buddhas and who practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, let alone all the beings of one great trichiliocosm becoming evil Māras. Suppose that all the beings in as many great trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā were to become evil Māras, and that each of those evil Māras were to emanate that many armies of Māra. Even so, Subhūti, those evil Māras would be unable to create an obstacle to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening for a bodhisattva, a great being, who is cared for by the buddhas and who practices the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, possesses two qualities, it is difficult for the evil Māras or the gods of Māra's retinue to overcome that bodhisattva. What are the two? They are these: that bodhisattva has not abandoned any being, and that bodhisattva realizes all phenomena as empty. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses these two qualities is difficult for the evil Māras or the gods of Māra's retinue to overcome.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, possesses two other qualities, it is difficult for the evil Māras or the gods of Māra's retinue to overcome that bodhisattva. What are the two? They are these: that bodhisattva acts just as he speaks, and that bodhisattva is cared for by the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who possesses these two qualities is difficult for the evil Māras or the gods of Māra's retinue to overcome.

Subhūti, even the gods will think of approaching a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way. Having approached, they will think of questioning that bodhisattva, they will think of inquiring further, and they will think of honoring and revering that bodhisattva. They will also inspire joy in that bodhisattva, saying: "Son of good family, you will soon become fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Therefore, son of good family, you should abide in this very abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that? Son of good family, if you abide just as you now abide and practice in this way, you will become a protector for beings who have no protector. You will become a savior for beings who have no savior. You will become a refuge for beings who have no refuge. You will become a resting place for beings who have no resting place. You will become an ally for beings who have no ally. You will become an island for beings who have no island. You will become a light for beings who are blind. You will become a guide for beings who have no guide. You will become a support for beings who have no support."

Those who have strayed from the path, and those who have no deliverance, he will become the supreme path and the way of deliverance." In this way, those sons of the gods delight in that bodhisattva, that great being.

Why is this so? Subhūti, in immeasurable, countless world systems there are buddhas, Blessed Ones, who are surrounded by communities of śrāvakas and honored at the head of communities of bodhisattvas, and who dwell, live, and remain there. Those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, too, proclaim the names, lineages, powers, colors, and forms of the bodhisattvas, the great beings, who abide in this abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom, who practice the Perfection of Wisdom, and who possess such qualities of inherent nature, that is, the qualities that belong to abiding in the Perfection of Wisdom. They teach the Dharma and speak words of praise about that bodhisattva, that great being.

Subhūti, it is just as, at present, I myself teach the Dharma and speak words of praise by proclaiming the names, lineages, powers, colors, and forms of the bodhisattva, the great being, Ratnaketu, of the bodhisattva, the great being, Śikhin, and of whichever other bodhisattvas, great beings, are now practicing the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Akṣobhya. In just the same way, Subhūti, those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, also teach the Dharma and speak words of praise by proclaiming the names, lineages, powers, colors, and forms of those bodhisattvas, great beings, who are now practicing the holy life in my buddha field and who abide in this abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, do those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma and speak words of praise by proclaiming the names, lineages, powers, colors, and forms of all bodhisattvas, great beings?"

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, that is not so. Those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not teach the Dharma and speak words of praise by proclaiming the names, lineages, powers, colors, and forms of all bodhisattvas, great beings. Subhūti, rather, those buddhas teach the Dharma and speak words of praise by proclaiming the names, lineages, powers, colors, and forms of those bodhisattvas, great beings, who are irreversible and free from all attachment."

Subhūti said: "Blessed One, do the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, ever teach the Dharma and speak words of praise by proclaiming the names, lineages, powers, colors, and forms of other bodhisattvas, great beings, who are not irreversible?"

The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, apart from the irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, there are also individuals on the bodhisattva vehicle who possess the power of the antidote, and those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma and speak words of praise by proclaiming their names, lineages, powers, colors, and forms. And who are they?

Those who at present practice the conduct of bodhisattvas by training after the conduct of the bodhisattvas of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Akṣobhya, and who abide in the manner of training in it: Subhūti, apart from the irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, these are persons of the bodhisattva vehicle about whom those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma and make declarations, proclaiming their names, their lineages, their powers, their complexions, and their forms.

Again, Subhūti, those who practice the conduct of bodhisattvas by training after the conduct of the bodhisattva, the great being Ratnaketu, and who abide in the manner of training in it: Subhūti, apart from the irreversible bodhisattvas, great beings, these too are persons about whom those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma and make declarations, proclaiming their names, their lineages, their powers, their complexions, and their forms.

Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas, great beings, who practice the Perfection of Wisdom and who have the conviction that all phenomena are unborn, yet who have not yet attained the acceptance of the unborn nature of phenomena. And there are those who have the conviction that all phenomena are peaceful, yet who have not yet gained mastery over irreversibility in regard to all phenomena, nor become unshakable in it. About these bodhisattvas, great beings, who abide in this state, those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, likewise teach the Dharma and make declarations, proclaiming their names, their lineages, their powers, their complexions, and their forms.

Furthermore, Subhūti, those bodhisattvas, great beings, about whom those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma and make declarations, proclaiming their names, their lineages, their powers, their complexions, and their forms, are those who have left behind the level of the śrāvakas and the pratyekabuddhas. They aspire to the level of buddhahood itself, and they will also receive the prophecy of unsurpassable, perfect, complete awakening. Why is that? Subhūti, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who practice the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, and about whom those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma and make declarations, proclaiming their names, their lineages, their powers, their complexions, and their forms, will come to abide in irreversibility.

Furthermore, Subhūti, there are bodhisattvas, great beings, who, on hearing this profound Perfection of Wisdom being taught, have conviction in it. They do not become bewildered, they are not discouraged, and they have no doubt. Having conviction that it is just as the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha has taught, they listen to it in detail, and they give rise to the thought: "I shall listen in detail to this Perfection of Wisdom from the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Akṣobhya, and from those persons of the bodhisattva vehicle who lead the holy life in his buddha-field."

Through them as well, some will listen to this very Perfection of Wisdom and come to have faith in it. And when they have faith in this Perfection of Wisdom, they will have faith exactly as the Tathāgata has taught it, and by having faith in that way they will come to abide in irreversibility. Subhūti, if even hearing this way of the Perfection of Wisdom is shown to be of such great benefit, what need is there to speak of those who have faith in it, and, having faith, abide for the sake of suchness and practice for the sake of suchness; and who, having abided and practiced for the sake of suchness, come to abide in suchness itself and in omniscience, and then teach the Dharma?

Subhūti asked: Blessed One, when nothing other than suchness can be apprehended, then, Blessed One, what phenomenon will abide in suchness? What will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening? And what will teach this Dharma?

When he had spoken in this way, the Blessed One said to the venerable Subhūti: Subhūti, you ask, "When nothing other than suchness can be apprehended, then what phenomenon will abide in suchness, what will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and what will teach this Dharma?" Subhūti, apart from suchness, no other phenomenon that could abide in suchness is apprehended. Subhūti, since suchness itself is not apprehended, what need is there to speak of something that abides in suchness? Subhūti, suchness does not fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. For, Subhūti, no phenomenon that has become a perfect buddha in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, or that will become one, or that is fully awakening, is apprehended at all. Subhūti, suchness does not teach the Dharma. Subhūti, no phenomenon that is to be taught is apprehended either.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, the Perfection of Wisdom is profound. Blessed One, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who wish to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening are doing something difficult. Why is that? Blessed One, it is because no phenomenon abides in suchness, no phenomenon fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and no one teaches the Dharma, and yet in this they do not shrink back, do not become discouraged, and do not become bewildered.

Then the venerable Subhūti said to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, you say that bodhisattvas, great beings, who do not become discouraged or bewildered when such a profound Dharma is taught are doing something difficult. Kauśika, since all phenomena are empty, who here would become discouraged and bewildered?

Śakra said: Venerable Subhūti, whatever you have taught has been taught on the basis of emptiness, and so it meets with no obstruction anywhere. It is just as, when an arrow is shot into the sky, nothing obstructs it.

In the same way, the teaching of the Dharma given by the noble Subhūti is also unobstructed.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, when I say and teach such things with reference to the elder Subhūti, am I speaking as the Tathāgata has spoken? Am I speaking the Dharma? Am I explaining, with an explanation that accords with the Dharma, what is in keeping with the Dharma?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, what you have said is so. Kauśika, it is so. What you say and teach in this way is speaking as the Tathāgata has spoken. It is speaking the Dharma. It is explaining, with an explanation that accords with the Dharma, what is in keeping with the Dharma.

Why is that? Kauśika, whatever the elder Subhūti is inspired to say, Kauśika, he is inspired to say with reference to emptiness.

Why is that? Kauśika, the elder Subhūti does not even perceive or apprehend the perfection of wisdom, so how could there be any practicing of the perfection of wisdom? He does not apprehend even awakening, so how much less any becoming fully and perfectly awakened? He does not apprehend even omniscience, so how could there be any attaining of omniscience? He does not apprehend even suchness, so how could there be any becoming a Tathāgata? He does not apprehend even non-arising, so how could there be any making of non-arising manifest? He does not apprehend even bodhisattvas, so how could there be any becoming fully and perfectly awakened? He does not apprehend even the powers, so how could there be any possessing of the powers? He does not apprehend even fearlessness, so how could there be any becoming fearless? He does not even apprehend the Dharma, so how could there be any teaching of the Dharma?

Kauśika, the elder Subhūti abides in the abiding in which all phenomena are secluded and all phenomena are unapprehendable.

Kauschika, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices and abides in the perfection of wisdom does not come near to even a hundredth part of the abiding of the elder Subhūti, in which all phenomena are secluded and all phenomena are without any basis for apprehension. Nor does such a bodhisattva come near to a thousandth part, a hundred-thousandth part, a ten-millionth part, a hundred-ten-millionth part, a thousand-ten-millionth part, or a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part. Nor does he come near to even a hundred thousand billionth part. He does not come near in number. It cannot be counted, it cannot be compared with any example, it cannot be demonstrated by any simile, and it cannot bear a basis or a cause for comparison.

Kauśika, the abiding in which a bodhisattva, a great being, practices and abides in the perfection of wisdom overpowers all other abidings, except for the abiding of the Tathāgata, and whatever is not that. Kauśika, this abiding is called the supreme of all those abidings. It is called the sublime, the chief, the excellent, the most excellent, the highest, the foremost, the unsurpassed, the unexcelled, the incomparable, and the equal of the unequaled.

The abiding in which a bodhisattva, a great being, practices and abides in the perfection of wisdom overpowers all the abidings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Kauśika, therefore, any son or daughter of good family who wishes to be supreme among all beings, who wishes to be the best, the chief, the foremost, the most excellent, the highest, the unsurpassed, the unexcelled, who wishes to be unequaled, and who wishes to be equal to the unequaled, should abide in the abiding in which bodhisattvas, great beings, practice and dwell in the Perfection of Wisdom.

This is the twenty-seventh chapter, called "The Essence," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. The twenty-second section.

Then, at that time, another son of the gods, together with the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, took up mandārava flowers and great mandārava flowers and went to the place where the Blessed One was. At that time, six hundred thousand monks had gathered in the assembly and were seated there. They too rose from their seats, arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, set their right knees on the ground, and from where they were, bowed with palms joined toward the place where the Blessed One was. Through the power of the buddha, the alms bowls of those monks were filled with mandārava flowers and great mandārava flowers. With those mandārava flowers and great mandārava flowers they scattered, strewed, and showered the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, and they spoke these words:

Blessed One, we shall practice this Perfection of Wisdom. Blessed One, we shall abide in this unsurpassed abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then the Blessed One, at that moment, smiled. It is the nature of things that whenever buddhas, blessed ones, smile, rays of light of many colors issue from the mouth of the Blessed One, in many hues: blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, crystal, silver, and gold. These lights illuminated boundless, limitless, endless world systems, rose upward as far as the world of Brahmā, then returned, circled the Blessed One three times, and vanished into the crown of the Blessed One's head.

Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, set his right knee on the ground, bowed with palms joined toward the place where the Blessed One was, and said to the Blessed One: Blessed One, the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, do not smile without cause or condition. What is the cause, what is the condition, for the Blessed One's smile?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke these words to the venerable Ānanda: Ānanda, in a future time, in the Star-like eon, these six hundred thousand monks will awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Having become fully awakened buddhas, they will teach the Dharma to beings. All of them will bear the same name: they will appear in the world as Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas, Teachers, all called Spread of Flowers. And, Ānanda, the communities of śrāvakas of those Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas called Spread of Flowers will all be equal in number.

The life span of all those Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas called Scattered Flowers will likewise be equal, twenty thousand eons. The sacred scriptures of each of them will also flourish and spread widely and extensively among gods and humans. The sacred Dharma of each of them will likewise remain for twenty thousand eons, equal in length.

In whatever villages, towns, market towns, regions, countries, and royal palaces those buddhas appear, and having appeared, wherever they turn the wheel of Dharma, and having turned it, wherever they dwell, and from wherever to wherever they enter, and from wherever they come forth to wherever they go, in all those places, in entering and coming forth and dwelling, a rain of flowers of the five colors will fall.

Ānanda, therefore, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to dwell in the supreme abiding should dwell in the abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, one who wishes to dwell in the abiding of the Tathāgata should dwell in the abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom.

Ānanda, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who practice the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood to have died among humans and been born here, or to have passed away from the realm of the gods of Tuṣita and been born among humans. Why is that? Because it is among humans and among the gods of Tuṣita that this Perfection of Wisdom is extensively practiced.

Furthermore, Ānanda, those bodhisattvas, great beings, who practice this Perfection of Wisdom should be known to be seen by the Tathāgata.

Those who hold this Perfection of Wisdom, bear it in mind, read it, thoroughly understand it, recite it, teach it, explain it, expound it, memorize it, and ask about it, or at the least write it down in a book; who having held, borne in mind, read, thoroughly understood, recited, taught, explained, expounded, and memorized it, and having at the least written it in a book, instruct and guide bodhisattvas, great beings, correctly teach them, correctly establish them, correctly encourage them, and fill them with joy: Ānanda, those bodhisattvas, great beings, should be known to have planted roots of virtue under the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas.

Those who train in this Perfection of Wisdom have not planted roots of virtue merely under śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Rather, Ānanda, those bodhisattvas, great beings, have without fail planted roots of virtue under the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas.

Ānanda, those who train in this Perfection of Wisdom and are not afraid; those who hold this Perfection of Wisdom, bear it in mind, read it, thoroughly understand it, recite it, teach it, explain it, expound it, memorize it, and ask about it, at the least in writing; and who in this way come to realize it in accord with its meaning, its true nature, and its method: Ānanda, those bodhisattvas, great beings, should be understood to have certainly come face to face with the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas.

Ānanda, those who do not slander this Perfection of Wisdom, do not contradict it, do not disturb it, do not destroy it, do not reject it, do not obstruct it, and do not think of harming it, should be understood to be bodhisattvas, great beings, who have done their work under the Victors of the past.

Ānanda, it is also the case that when a bodhisattva, a great being, makes an aspiration toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening, that aspiration does not prove false. Therefore, when a bodhisattva, a great being, plants roots of virtue in the presence of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, he does not bring about the ripening of that virtue for the sake of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Rather, Ānanda, that bodhisattva, that great being, should for the most part practice in the Perfection of Wisdom.

Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this Perfection of Wisdom to you, and I entrust it to you again, so that it may by no means vanish. Hold it, master it, and keep it so that not even a single letter of it vanishes. Understand it fully, bring it to completion, and make it endure for a long time.

Ānanda, suppose you took hold of every teaching I have spoken to you directly, apart from the Perfection of Wisdom, and afterward wasted it, abandoned it, or forgot it. Even then, Ānanda, I would not count it as a fault in you. But Ānanda, if you were to waste, abandon, or forget even a single part of a phrase connected with the Perfection of Wisdom, then, Ānanda, you would have done me that much wrong, and you would not have pleased my mind.

Moreover, Ānanda, if after taking hold of the Perfection of Wisdom you later waste it, abandon it, and forget it, then you have not honored me, not revered me as your teacher, not served me, not made offerings to me, not made paintings of me, and not attended on me with respect. Ānanda, you will also have failed to honor, revere, serve, make offerings to, depict, and attend with respect all those blessed buddhas of the past, the future, and the present. Ānanda, if after taking hold of the Perfection of Wisdom you later waste it, abandon it, and forget it, you will have done me that much wrong, and you will not have pleased my mind.

Why is that? Ānanda, the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas have taught that this Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past, the future, and the present. She gives them birth, brings them forth, and causes them to attain omniscience.

Therefore, Ānanda, I entrust this Perfection of Wisdom to you, and I entrust it to you again, so that it may by no means vanish. Ānanda, take hold of this Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, keep this Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, read this Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, understand this Perfection of Wisdom fully. Ānanda, recite this Perfection of Wisdom aloud. Ānanda, teach this Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, explain this Perfection of Wisdom closely.

Ānanda, you should recite this Perfection of Wisdom aloud. Ānanda, you should commit this Perfection of Wisdom to memory. Ānanda, you should write down this Perfection of Wisdom, and Ānanda, you should meditate on this Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, you should attend to this Perfection of Wisdom well, grasp it well, understand it fully, and recite it well, taking up the letters, the words, and the clear articulation, and grasping rightly the syllables and the definitive expressions.

Why is this? Ānanda, take it as authoritative that this is the very nature of reality: it is the dharmakāya of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas of the past, the future, and the present.

Ānanda, just as you now think of me, the Tathāgata who is present, alive and sustained, with benevolent intent, with joy and reverence, wishing to do what is wholesome, to dwell in ease, or to relieve poverty, so, Ānanda, with that same benevolent intent, that same joy, that same reverence, and endowed with such qualities, you should hold this Perfection of Wisdom, bear it in mind, read it, understand it fully, recite it, teach it, and explain it. You should recite it aloud, commit it to memory, write it, meditate on it, honor it, regard it as your teacher, praise it, make offerings to it, depict it in paintings, and serve and revere it. In this way, Ānanda, you will be making offerings both to me and to those bodhisattvas, great beings, and you will also be generating joy, faith, and reverence in the presence of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present.

Ānanda, if you do not abandon your joy in me, the Tathāgata, and your delight in me, then in just the same way, so that not a single word is wasted or lost, do not abandon your joy and delight in this Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, with regard to entrusting this Perfection of Wisdom to you, if I were to speak at length, I could do so for an eon, or more than an eon, or a hundred eons, a thousand eons, a hundred thousand eons, a million eons, ten million eons, a hundred thousand million eons, or even longer. But in brief, Ānanda, just as I am your Teacher, so too the Perfection of Wisdom is your Teacher. Ānanda, just as the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present are the teachers of the worlds with their gods, humans, and asuras, so too the Perfection of Wisdom is the teacher of the worlds with their gods, humans, and asuras.

Therefore, Ānanda, the Perfection of Wisdom is immeasurable. For the benefit and happiness of the worlds with their gods, humans, and asuras, I entrust this Perfection of Wisdom to you with an immeasurable entrustment; I hand it over to you, and I entrust it to you for the future. Ānanda, whoever does not abandon the Tathāgata, does not abandon the Dharma, does not abandon the Saṅgha, and does not abandon the awakening of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present, should not abandon the Perfection of Wisdom. This is my final instruction.

Ānanda, if any person holds and bears this Perfection of Wisdom, reads it, understands it fully, recites it, teaches it, explains it, expounds it aloud, commits it to memory, and asks about it,

By cultivating it, one will come to be held in the awakening of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present. Ānanda, if anyone takes up this Perfection of Wisdom at the time when the Dharma is utterly decaying, that person will come to be held in the awakening of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the past, the future, and the present.

Why is that? Ānanda, the awakening of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is born from the Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, the unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening of those Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who appeared in the past, was likewise born from the Perfection of Wisdom, Ānanda. The unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening of those Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who will appear in the future, was likewise born from the Perfection of Wisdom, Ānanda. And the unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening of those Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who now dwell, live, and abide in all the immeasurable and innumerable world systems, Ānanda, is likewise born from this Perfection of Wisdom. My own unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, Ānanda, was also born from this Perfection of Wisdom.

Therefore, Ānanda, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to attain perfect buddhahood in unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and who wishes to train in the six perfections, should listen to this very Perfection of Wisdom, take it up, hold it, read it, thoroughly understand it, recite it, teach it, explain it, expound it, memorize it, and write it out; he should train in this very Perfection of Wisdom and practice it in yoga.

Why is that? Ānanda, because this Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the great beings; she gives them birth and brings them forth. Ānanda, all those bodhisattvas, great beings, who by training in the six perfections have definitively emerged, are emerging, and will emerge into unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, have trained in the six perfections in dependence on the Perfection of Wisdom, Ānanda. All of them were born from the six perfections in dependence on this very Perfection of Wisdom. Why is that? Ānanda, because all the perfections are born from the Perfection of Wisdom, and it is this that brings about the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Therefore, Ānanda, so that this Perfection of Wisdom may by no means vanish, I entrust it to you, and entrust it a second time, and hand it on to you.

Ānanda, this Perfection of Wisdom is the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas. Why is that? Ānanda, whatever Dharma the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have taught to sentient beings throughout the beginningless saṃsāra of the past, all of it has been taught from this very treasury of the Dharma, the Perfection of Wisdom.

Ānanda, whatever buddhas, blessed ones, in the future, through immeasurable cycles of time, will awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening and teach the Dharma to sentient beings, those buddhas, blessed ones, will likewise teach from this very treasury of the Dharma, the Perfection of Wisdom. And Ānanda, whatever buddhas, blessed ones, now dwell, live, and sustain themselves in countless, innumerable world-systems and teach the Dharma, those buddhas, blessed ones, too will expound it from this very treasury of the Dharma, the Perfection of Wisdom. Therefore, Ānanda, these treasuries of the Perfection of Wisdom are inexhaustible treasuries of the Dharma.

Ānanda, suppose you were to teach the Dharma of the śrāvaka stage to individuals of the śrāvaka vehicle, and as you taught it, all the sentient beings in the great trichiliocosm world-system were to realize arhatship directly. Even so, you, who turn the wheel of the Dharma after me and teach in my wake as my śrāvaka, would not thereby have done the work of a śrāvaka. But Ānanda, if you were to explain or reveal to a bodhisattva, a great being, even a single teaching that accords with the Perfection of Wisdom, then you, who turn the wheel of the Dharma after me and teach as my śrāvaka, would have pleased me. The earlier teaching would not please me in that way, even though through it all the sentient beings in the great trichiliocosm world-system had attained arhatship.

Ānanda, what do you think? Would the mass of merit arising from the basis of meritorious action through giving, the basis of meritorious action through moral discipline, and the basis of meritorious action through meditation, in all those arhats, be great?

Ānanda replied: It would be great, Blessed One. It would be great, Sugata.

The Blessed One said: Ānanda, one who teaches the Dharma that accords with the Perfection of Wisdom to a bodhisattva, a great being, generates far more merit than those individuals of the śrāvaka vehicle. Furthermore, Ānanda, a bodhisattva, a great being, who teaches the Dharma that accords with the Perfection of Wisdom to another bodhisattva, a great being, even for as little as a single day, generates far more merit than that. Ānanda, never mind a single day. Even for as little as a morning, or, Ānanda, never mind a morning, for as little as an hour, or never mind an hour, for a brief while, or, Ānanda, never mind a brief while, for a single moment of time, or, Ānanda, never mind a moment, for as little as an instant, whenever a bodhisattva, a great being, teaches another bodhisattva, a great being, the Dharma that accords with the Perfection of Wisdom, even for an instant, a moment, or a brief while, he generates far more merit than that.

Ānanda, this gift of the Dharma given by that bodhisattva, a great being, surpasses the roots of virtue of all individuals of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles.

Ānanda, as for bodhisattvas, great beings, who possess such roots of virtue, and bodhisattvas, great beings, who think upon such roots of virtue, that they should turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening is, Ānanda, impossible and out of the question. This is not a possibility.

Then the Blessed One, at that time, by the power of a miraculous display that he willed into being, caused the fourfold assembly of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen, together with gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, great mahoragas, humans and non-humans, all of them, through the buddha's power, to see the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Akṣobhya, surrounded by the community of monks and preceded by an assembly of bodhisattvas, teaching the Dharma. Akṣobhya was profound like the ocean, and his retinue consisted of bodhisattvas, great beings, endowed with inconceivable qualities.
