It included also arhats, all with their defilements exhausted and free of affliction, masters of themselves, with minds fully liberated and wisdom fully liberated, noble ones, great elephants, who had done what was to be done, laid down their burden, attained their own aim, utterly exhausted the fetters of becoming, who through right and complete knowledge were fully liberated in mind, and who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all minds. Such was the miraculous display that he willed into being.

Then the Blessed One withdrew that miraculous display. When the Blessed One had withdrawn the miraculous display that he had willed into being, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha Akṣobhya, became invisible. Those bodhisattvas, great beings, those great śrāvakas, all those buddha-fields, and also that fourfold assembly, the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, great mahoragas, humans and non-humans, all vanished from the sight of those beings. Why was this? Because the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha had withdrawn the miraculous display he had willed into being, all of this vanished from their sight.

Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda. Ānanda, in just this way all phenomena do not even appear before the eye. Phenomena do not appear to phenomena. Phenomena do not see phenomena, and phenomena do not know phenomena. Why is this? Ānanda, because no phenomenon is a knower or a seer, and none has the capacity to perform a function. Why is this? Ānanda, just as space has no activity, so all phenomena are without activity. Ānanda, all phenomena are inconceivable, like a person conjured by illusion. Ānanda, because phenomena have no real entity, none of them is a feeler.

Ānanda, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices in this way practices the Perfection of Wisdom and has no clinging to any phenomenon whatsoever. Ānanda, a bodhisattva, a great being, who trains in this way trains in the Perfection of Wisdom. A bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to attain the great awakening, the supreme perfection that surpasses all trainings, should train in the Perfection of Wisdom. Why is this?

Ānanda, these trainings are called the supreme of all trainings. They are called the excellent, the chief, the foremost, the most supreme, the most sublime, the highest, the unsurpassed, the one with nothing above it, the peerless, the one that is equal to the unequal. They bring benefit to all the world. They bring happiness to all the world. They become a protector for those who have no protector. They are permitted by the buddhas and praised by the buddhas.

Ānanda, having trained in this training and abiding in this training, the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas could lift up this great trichiliocosm world-system with a single toe and set it down again, and yet those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not think, "I am lifting up this great trichiliocosm world-system," or "I am setting it down." Why is that? Because the Perfection of Wisdom possesses immeasurable and countless qualities. Ānanda, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, having trained in this training of the Perfection of Wisdom, attained non-attachment toward all phenomena of the past, the future, and the present.

Ānanda, of all the trainings that exist in the past, future, and present times, this training of the Perfection of Wisdom is called the supreme. It is called the excellent, the chief, the foremost, the most supreme, the most sublime, the highest, the unsurpassed, the one with nothing above it, the peerless, the one that is equal to the unequal.

Ānanda, the Perfection of Wisdom is without measure. Ānanda, the Perfection of Wisdom is inexhaustible. Why is that? Because the Perfection of Wisdom is nonexistent. Ānanda, whoever thinks of grasping at a measure, an exhaustion, or an end of the Perfection of Wisdom is thinking of grasping at a measure, an exhaustion, or an end of space. Why is that? Ānanda, because the Perfection of Wisdom is without measure. Ānanda, the Perfection of Wisdom is inexhaustible. Ānanda, the Perfection of Wisdom is endless.

Ānanda, I have not spoken of a measure, an exhaustion, or an end of the Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, collections of names, collections of words, and collections of letters do have a connection with measure, but the Perfection of Wisdom has no connection with measure. Why is that? Ānanda, collections of names, collections of words, and collections of letters are not the Perfection of Wisdom. Ānanda, the Perfection of Wisdom is not endowed with measure. Ānanda, the Perfection of Wisdom is immeasurable.

Ānanda said, "Blessed One, why then did the Blessed One not state a measure of the Perfection of Wisdom?"

The Blessed One declared, "Ānanda, because the Perfection of Wisdom is inexhaustible, the Tathāgata did not teach a measure. Ānanda, because the Perfection of Wisdom is secluded, the Tathāgata did not speak of a measure. Ānanda, if in a secluded phenomenon not even seclusion can be found, how could there be a measure of it? Ānanda, in just this way, because the Perfection of Wisdom is unfathomable, it has no measure and is immeasurable."

Ānanda, in the past, whatever Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas have appeared, they too were all distinguished by this very Perfection of Wisdom; and yet, Ānanda, this Perfection of Wisdom is neither exhausted nor will it ever be exhausted. Ānanda, in the future, whatever Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas will appear, they too will be distinguished by this very Perfection of Wisdom; and yet, Ānanda, this Perfection of Wisdom is neither exhausted nor will it ever be exhausted. Ānanda, at present, in immeasurable and countless world systems, whatever Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas are dwelling, living, and sustained, they too are distinguished by this very Perfection of Wisdom; and yet, Ānanda, this Perfection of Wisdom is neither exhausted nor will it ever be exhausted. Ānanda, the present Tathāgata, arhat, perfectly awakened buddha is likewise distinguished by this very Perfection of Wisdom; and yet, Ānanda, this Perfection of Wisdom is neither exhausted nor will it ever be exhausted.

Why is that? Ānanda, whoever thinks of exhausting the Perfection of Wisdom thinks of exhausting space. Therefore, Ānanda, this Perfection of Wisdom is inexhaustible.

Then the venerable Subhūti thought: "This subject taught by the Tathāgata is profound. I shall ask the Tathāgata about this subject." Then the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, does the Perfection of Wisdom not come to an end?"

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, the Perfection of Wisdom is inexhaustible. It is just so: because space is inexhaustible, all phenomena are unborn."

Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how should a bodhisattva, a great being, bring about the Perfection of Wisdom?"

The Blessed One declared: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should bring about the Perfection of Wisdom through the inexhaustibility of form. Likewise, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should bring about the Perfection of Wisdom through the inexhaustibility of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. In this way, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should bring about the Perfection of Wisdom.

"Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should bring about the Perfection of Wisdom through the inexhaustibility of ignorance. Likewise, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should bring about the Perfection of Wisdom through the inexhaustibility of formations, the inexhaustibility of consciousness, the inexhaustibility of name and form, the inexhaustibility of the six sense sources, the inexhaustibility of contact, the inexhaustibility of feeling, the inexhaustibility of craving, the inexhaustibility of grasping, the inexhaustibility of becoming, the inexhaustibility of birth, the inexhaustibility of aging and death, and the inexhaustibility of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental unhappiness, and distress.

"Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva's, the great being's, way of viewing dependent origination, free of the two extremes."

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who views in this way sees dependent origination as without a limit and without a middle. Subhūti, this way of viewing dependent origination is the unmixed quality of a bodhisattva, a great being, who has entered the heart of awakening. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who views dependent origination in this way will attain omniscient wisdom.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom by this accomplishing of inexhaustibility, and who views dependent origination, will not come to rest on the ground of the śrāvakas or on the ground of the pratyekabuddhas, but will come to rest in omniscience itself.

Subhūti, all those bodhisattvas, great beings, who turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening do so because they do not know this attention and this skillful means, since they do not rely upon them.

If one asks how a bodhisattva, a great being, practicing the Perfection of Wisdom, should accomplish the Perfection of Wisdom by the accomplishing of inexhaustibility, and how, by accomplishing inexhaustibility, one should view dependent origination in the Perfection of Wisdom, then, Subhūti, all those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have turned back, are turning back, and will turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, have turned back, are turning back, and will turn back because they do not rely upon this skillful means. Subhūti, all those bodhisattvas, great beings, who have not turned back, do not turn back, and will not turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, have not turned back, do not turn back, and will not turn back because they rely upon this Perfection of Wisdom.

In this way a bodhisattva, a great being, practicing the Perfection of Wisdom, should accomplish the Perfection of Wisdom by the accomplishing of inexhaustibility. Having accomplished inexhaustibility in this way, one views dependent origination in the Perfection of Wisdom.

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who views dependent origination in this way does not perceive any phenomenon as arising without a cause. Nor does such a one perceive any phenomenon as permanent, stable, enduring, or of a nature that is without change. Nor does such a one perceive any phenomenon as an agent or as an experiencer.

Subhūti, this is how a bodhisattva, a great being, accomplishes the Perfection of Wisdom by the accomplishing of inexhaustibility, practices the Perfection of Wisdom, and views dependent origination.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, accomplishes the Perfection of Wisdom by the accomplishing of inexhaustibility, and views dependent origination, then, Subhūti, that bodhisattva, a great being, does not perceive form. In the same way, such a one does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness. Nor does such a one perceive ignorance.

In the same way, he does not observe the formations as such, nor consciousness, nor name and form, nor the six sense sources, nor contact, nor feeling, nor craving, nor grasping, nor becoming, nor birth, nor aging and death. He does not observe sorrow, lamentation, suffering, mental unhappiness, or agitation. He does not observe "this is a buddha-field," and he does not observe "this is another buddha-field." And he does not observe the very phenomenon by which one would fail to observe "this one" or "another" buddha-field. Subhūti, this is the Perfection of Wisdom of bodhisattvas, great beings.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom, then Māra the Evil One is pierced by the sharp sting of grief. Subhūti, it is like a man whose mother and father have just died: he is pierced by the sharp sting of grief. In just the same way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom, then Māra the Evil One is likewise pierced by the sharp sting of grief.

Subhūti said: Blessed One, is it a single Māra the Evil One who is pierced by the sharp sting of grief? Or are many Māras the Evil One so pierced? Or is it that all the Māras the Evil One there are in the great trichiliocosm world-system are pierced by the sharp sting of grief at that time?

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti as follows: Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, abides in the abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom, then all the Māras the Evil One that exist in the great trichiliocosm world-system are pierced by the sharp sting of grief, and they take no pleasure even in their own seats.

Why is that? Because the world, with its gods, humans, and asuras, finds no opening and no foothold against a bodhisattva, a great being, who abides in the Perfection of Wisdom. It finds no chance to think, "We shall seize this one and strike him down," or, "We shall turn him back from unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening."

Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to awaken fully to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening should practice the Perfection of Wisdom.

Why is that? Subhūti, by practicing the Perfection of Wisdom, a bodhisattva, a great being, brings to completion the cultivation of the perfection of generosity. In the same way, he brings to completion the cultivation of the perfection of moral discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, and the perfection of meditative concentration. Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom brings to completion the cultivation of all six perfections. He brings to completion the cultivation of all skillful means.

A bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom in this way will recognize whatever deeds of Māra may arise, at the very moment they arise, and having recognized them, will abandon them.

Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, who wishes to embrace all skillful means should practice the Perfection of Wisdom and should cultivate the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, whenever a bodhisattva, a great being, practices the Perfection of Wisdom and brings the Perfection of Wisdom to realization, at that time, Subhūti, the bodhisattva, the great being, should think: "In the immeasurable, innumerable world systems there are buddhas, Blessed Ones, who dwell, live, and sustain themselves; and their omniscience too has arisen from this very Perfection of Wisdom." Having thought thus, that bodhisattva, the great being, should also generate this thought: "Just as those buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have attained those qualities, so too shall I attain those same qualities."

Subhūti, in this way a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom should generate and bring about these thoughts for the span of a single day, or even for as short a time as it takes to snap the fingers.

Subhūti, compare a bodhisattva, a great being, who still apprehends objects and who gives gifts for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, with a bodhisattva, a great being, who for a single day brings about this Perfection of Wisdom, even if only for as short a time as a snap of the fingers. The latter generates far greater merit. This bodhisattva, this great being, comes to abide on the stage of non-regression.

A bodhisattva, a great being, who for a single day, even for as short a time as a snap of the fingers, practices this Perfection of Wisdom and generates this thought, should be known as one held in mind by the Tathāgata. How much more so, then, one who follows this thought from day to day.

Subhūti, as for a bodhisattva, a great being, who is held in the Tathāgata's mind, what destiny should such a one expect? Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, held in the Tathāgata's mind should fear no destiny other than unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Such a one will not be born in a fortunate-lacking condition or in the lower realms, but should expect birth in the higher realms. There too, such a one will never be separated from the tathāgatas, and will be born in a buddha field not separated from the Tathāgata, and will bring sentient beings to maturity.

Subhūti, since there are these qualities and these benefits for a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom even for as short a time as a snap of the fingers, who brings the Perfection of Wisdom to realization and generates this thought, how much more so for one who follows this thought from day to day.

Subhūti, it is just like the bodhisattva, the great being called Gandhahastin ("Fragrant Elephant"), who is at present leading the pure life in the presence of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha Akṣobhya.

This is the twenty-eighth chapter of the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, called "The Scattering of Flowers."

Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva, a great being, should come to know the Perfection of Wisdom in this way.

Because all phenomena are without attachment, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are indivisible, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are without arising, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are equal, being without change, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are realized through wisdom to be without self and without discriminating awareness, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are expressed through mere names and mere conventional designations, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. And yet the conventional designation is not for anything, nor by anything; no conventional designation exists at all. Because all phenomena are without convention, inexpressible, beyond speech, and without words, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are immeasurable, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known.

Because form is immeasurable, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. In the same way, because feeling is immeasurable, perception is immeasurable, the formations are immeasurable, and consciousness is immeasurable, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known.

Because all phenomena are without characteristics, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are definitively distinguished, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are utterly pure by their intrinsic nature, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are without words, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are without cessation, and what is to be abandoned is therefore equal, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena have attained nirvāṇa and are equal to suchness, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena do not come, do not go, are not known, are not born, and are utterly unborn, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because one does not view self and other, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are, like the noble arhat, utterly pure by their intrinsic nature, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena have laid down the burden and do not take up a burden, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known. Because all phenomena are without object and without direction, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known.

Why is this so? Subhūti, form, by the essence of its intrinsic nature, is without object and without direction. Subhūti, in the same way, feeling, perception, the formations, and consciousness, by the essence of their intrinsic nature, are without object and without direction.

Because all phenomena bring about the complete quieting of cessation, the Perfection of Wisdom should be known.

Because there is no joy and no separation from joy, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood. Because there is no one who is attached and no one who is free from attachment, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood.

Why is this so? Subhūti, form, in its own nature, which is in accord with suchness, neither becomes attached nor becomes free from attachment. Subhūti, in the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, in their own nature, which is in accord with suchness, neither become attached nor become free from attachment.

Because of being utterly pure by nature, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood. Because all phenomena are free from clinging, whether to attachment or to non-attachment, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood. Because of fully realizing the wisdom of the buddhas, one should understand the Perfection of Wisdom as the realization that all phenomena are awakening. Because all phenomena are emptiness, signless, and wishless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood.

With great loving-kindness going before, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as the realization that all phenomena are like medicine. Because all phenomena abide in loving-kindness, abide in compassion, abide in joy, and abide in equanimity, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood.

Because all phenomena have become Brahmā-like, they give rise to no aversion and take up no aversion at all; therefore the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood. Because all phenomena are without wishes and without hatred, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood.

Because the ocean is limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless. Because space is limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless. Because of the variegated nature of Mount Meru, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as variegated. Because form is limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless. In the same way, because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless.

Because the disk of the sun's rays shines without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless. Because all sounds are limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless. Because the full accomplishment of all the qualities of the buddhas is limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless. Because the accumulation of merit and wisdom of all realms of sentient beings is limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless.

Because the earth element is limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless. In the same way, because the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the element of consciousness are limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless.

Because the accumulation of virtuous and non-virtuous phenomena is immeasurable, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as immeasurable. Because the accumulation of all phenomena is immeasurable, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as immeasurable. Because of attaining the limitless meditative absorptions of all phenomena, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless. Because all the qualities of the buddhas are limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless. Because all phenomena are limitless, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as limitless.

Because emptiness is without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as without limit. Because mind and mental factors are without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as without limit. Because the activity of mind is without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as without limit. Because virtuous and non-virtuous phenomena are immeasurable, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as immeasurable. Because it sounds the lion's roar, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as such. Because all phenomena are free of disturbance, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as free of disturbance.

Why is this so? Subhūti, form is like the ocean. In the same way, Subhūti, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like the ocean.

Form is like space. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like space.

Form is like the many-colored Mount Meru. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like the many-colored Mount Meru.

Form is like the limitless. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like the limitless.

Form is like the rising of the rays of light from the disk of the sun. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like the rising of the rays of light from the disk of the sun.

Form is like the limitlessness of all sounds. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like the limitlessness of all sounds.

Form is like the limitless accomplishment of all the qualities of the buddhas. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like the limitless accomplishment of all the qualities of the buddhas.

Form is like the limitless accumulation of merit and wisdom of all the realms of sentient beings. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like the limitless accumulation of merit and wisdom of all the realms of sentient beings.

Form is like the earth. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like the earth.

Form is like water. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like water.

Form is like fire. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like fire.

Form is like wind. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like wind.

Form is like space. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like space.

Form is like consciousness. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are like consciousness.

Form is free of the accumulation of virtuous and non-virtuous phenomena. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are free of the accumulation of virtuous and non-virtuous phenomena.

Form is free of the accumulation of all phenomena.

In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are free of the accumulation of all phenomena. Form is equal to the boundless absorption of all phenomena. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are equal to the boundless absorption of all phenomena. Form is free, and the essential nature of form and the suchness of form are the qualities of a buddha. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are free, and the essential nature of consciousness and the suchness of consciousness are the qualities of a buddha. Form is the boundless nature of all phenomena. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are the boundless nature of all phenomena. Form is the boundless nature of emptiness. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are the boundless nature of emptiness. Form is without limit in mind and mental factors. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are without limit in mind and mental factors. Form arises from the activity of mind. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness arise from the activity of mind. Form extends to the virtuous, the non-virtuous, and the unapprehendable. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness extend to the virtuous, the non-virtuous, and the unapprehendable. Form is equal to the lion's roar. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are equal to the lion's roar. Form is without agitation. In the same way, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are without agitation.

Subhūti, in this way a bodhisattva, a great being, should come to know the Perfection of Wisdom.

Subhūti, when a bodhisattva, a great being, comes to know the Perfection of Wisdom in this way, and examines it, enters into it, realizes it, reflects on it, measures it, and contemplates it closely; and when he cultivates it with an attitude that has entirely abandoned deceit and dissimulation, an attitude that has entirely abandoned laziness, an attitude that has entirely abandoned conceit, an attitude that has abandoned self-praise, an attitude that has abandoned disparaging others, an attitude that has abandoned the perception of a self, an attitude that has abandoned the perception of a sentient being, an attitude that has abandoned gain, honor, and fame, an attitude that has abandoned the five obscurations, an attitude that has abandoned envy and miserliness, and an attitude that has abandoned all beings, then for him it will not be difficult to attain the perfection of all good qualities, the unsurpassed buddha field, and the perfection of the qualities of a buddha.

This is the twenty-ninth chapter, called "Knowing," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, the twenty-third volume.

Subhūti, furthermore, just as the bodhisattva, a great being, Ever-Weeping, now seeks the Perfection of Wisdom, so should it be sought, just as he sought it when he practiced the holy life in the presence of the Tathāgata, the arhat, the perfectly awakened buddha, who proclaimed the inexhaustible sound of the Dharma.

When the Blessed One had said this,

The venerable Subhūti then said to the Blessed One, "Blessed One, how did the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, search for that Perfection of Wisdom while he was seeking it?"

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Subhūti: "Subhūti, when the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, was seeking the Perfection of Wisdom, he did not exert himself for the sake of his body, he did not cling to his life, and he did not rest in gain, honor, or fame. He searched in this way.

"As he went searching for the Perfection of Wisdom, he came to a wilderness, and there a voice sounded from the sky: 'Son of good family, go to the east, and you will hear the Perfection of Wisdom. As you go, do not give rise to any thought of bodily fatigue. Do not give rise to any thought of sleep or drowsiness. Do not give rise to any thought of food, or of drink. Do not give rise to any thought of night, or of day. Do not give rise to any thought of cold, or of heat. Go in this way. Do not let your mind long for anything, inner or outer. Son of good family, go without looking to the left. Go without looking to the right, to the east, to the south, to the west, to the north, above, or below, and without looking to the intermediate directions either.

"'Son of good family, go in such a way that you do not stir from yourself, nor from the view of the perishable collection. Go in such a way that you do not stir from form, nor from feeling, perception, and formations, nor from consciousness. Whoever stirs from these is utterly lost. Lost from what? Lost from the qualities of a buddha. One who is lost from the qualities of a buddha moves in saṃsāra. One who moves in saṃsāra does not move in the Perfection of Wisdom, and so does not attain the Perfection of Wisdom.' This was the sound he heard."

When the voice had spoken in this way, the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, replied to it, "So I shall do. Why? Because I wish to bring light to all sentient beings, and I wish to accomplish all the qualities of a buddha."

When he had said this, the voice said to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, "Excellent, excellent, son of good family, Sadāprarudita!"

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, heard the voice again: "Son of good family, you should generate devotion toward all phenomena as empty, signless, and wishless, and you should search for the Perfection of Wisdom. You should abandon signs, abandon entities, and abandon the view of sentient beings. Son of good family, you should abandon bad companions. As for spiritual friends who teach that all phenomena are empty, signless, wishless, unarisen, unborn, unceasing, and without entity, you should rely on them, honor them, and serve them with respect. Son of good family, if you practice in this way, before long you will hear the Perfection of Wisdom, whether it is set down in a book or present in the body of a monk who is a Dharma teacher. Son of good family, toward the one from whom you hear this Perfection of Wisdom, you should generate the perception of him as your teacher, and you should remember the kindness done to you and feel gratitude for it."

"From whomever he heard this Perfection of Wisdom, that person is my spiritual friend. Because I have heard it, I will swiftly become irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. I will attend upon the Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, and I will be born in buddha-fields, never separated from the Tathāgatas. I will abandon the inopportune states, and I will obtain the conduct of the fully endowed leisure." Son of good family, you should fully understand these benefits, and you should cultivate the perception that the monk who teaches the Dharma is the Teacher.

Son of good family, you should not follow after the monk who teaches the Dharma with a mind that is bound up with worldly gain and honor. You should follow after him out of a desire for the Dharma and with reverence for the Dharma.

You should also understand the deeds of Māra. Son of good family, Māra the Evil One strives to lead bodhisattvas, great beings, to attend upon, to enjoy, and to indulge in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches. There are also some who are overpowered by that teacher of the Dharma and who, through skillful means, keep company with such things and attend upon them. Son of good family, you should not give rise to lack of faith in that monk who teaches the Dharma. Rather, you should give rise to this thought: "I do not know that skillful means. But this one knows skillful means well. By way of a manner of taming beings, and in order to take hold of the roots of virtue of beings, he relies upon these things, keeps company with them, and attends upon them. Bodhisattvas, great beings, have no attachment or obstruction toward anything."

At that very moment, son of good family, you yourself should examine individually the true nature of phenomena. Son of good family, what is the true nature of phenomena? It is this: no phenomenon is afflicted, and none is purified. Why is that? All phenomena are empty of intrinsic nature. All phenomena have no sentient being, no life, no living creature, no person, no individual. They are like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a mirage. Son of good family, if you thus contemplate the true nature of all phenomena and follow after the teacher of the Dharma, before long you will surely come forth into the Perfection of Wisdom.

Son of good family, be mindful also of the deeds of Māra. Son of good family, suppose that teachers of the Dharma show contempt for a son of good family who is seeking the Perfection of Wisdom, and do not give him their attention. Son of good family, you should not turn back because of that. Otherwise, you should follow after the monk who teaches the Dharma with a desire for the Dharma, with reverence for the Dharma, and without becoming discouraged. This too I have heard.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita ("Ever-Weeping"), took up this instruction from that voice and went to the east, to where he was bound. Before he had gone far, it occurred to him: "I did not ask the voice how far I should go." Thinking this, he wept and wailed in that very direction, grieving and lamenting as he sat there. Then it occurred to him: "In this very place I will pass the day and the night."

He resolved to spend two, three, four, five, or six days and nights, even seven days and nights, in that very place, and he thought: "Until I have heard the Perfection of Wisdom, I will not give any thought to bodily weariness. I will not give any thought to drowsiness and sleep. I will not give any thought to eating. I will not give any thought to drinking. I will not give any thought to night. I will not give any thought to day. I will not give any thought to cold. I will not give any thought to heat."

Subhūti, it is like this. Suppose the only son of some man were to die. That man would be filled with great suffering and distress, and apart from thinking of his grief for his only son, no other thought would arise in him. In just the same way, Subhūti, even as that bodhisattva, a great being, wept continually, no other thought arose in him except the thought, "When shall I hear the Perfection of Wisdom?"

Then, Subhūti, as that bodhisattva, a great being, sat weeping continually and grieving in this way, the form of a Tathāgata appeared before him and said, "Excellent!" And he said to him: "Son of good family, it is excellent, truly excellent, that you speak such words. Just as you now search, son of good family, so too the Tathāgatas of the past, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, searched for the Perfection of Wisdom when they were practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva. Therefore, son of good family, with this very diligence, this very joy, this very earnest striving, and this very longing, follow after it and go to the east. Son of good family, five hundred leagues from here there is a city called Fragrant, a city of the nature of the seven precious substances. It is encircled by seven tiers of walls, and surrounded by seven tiers of moats and seven rows of tāla trees. It measures twelve leagues in length and twelve leagues in breadth. It is prosperous and flourishing, comfortable, with good harvests, and filled with many people. Its rows of market halls are laid out in the middle as though painted in many colors; they are beautiful to look upon, delightful, level, and uniform. It is well kept by five hundred who dwell there free of envy, in places for people, for carriages, and for those who travel on foot. Around the city, for the sake of its low-lying ground, there is a ring of the nature of the seven precious substances. The pinnacles of those walls, of the nature of the seven precious substances, are made of gold from the Jambu River, lofty and well proportioned. From the tip of every pinnacle there grows a tree of the nature of the seven precious substances, bearing fruit of various shining jewels. From all the trees growing from the pinnacles, cords of the nature of jewels extend, so that the city is joined with all the trees of the second pinnacles. It is covered with nets of golden bells and small jingle-bells. When the wind strikes those nets of bells and jingle-bells, soft, melodious, and pleasing sounds arise. Just as when a skilled musician plays an ensemble of the five kinds of instruments, soft, melodious, and pleasing sounds arise, so too, when the wind strikes those nets of bells and jingle-bells, soft, melodious, and pleasing sounds arise, and by that sound those beings are delighted and live in joy."

All around that city there were moats, filled with water flowing along in harmony with its course. The water was neither too cold nor too warm, but perfectly full. On those very waters there were boats made of the seven precious substances, brilliant and lovely to behold, brought about by the ripening of the former karma of those beings. Beings would board them and delight in play and joy. All those waters were covered with blue lotuses (utpala), night lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses, and also with other flowers of great and excellent kinds, endowed with a fine fragrance. Among all the kinds of flowers found in the world system of the great trichiliocosm, there was none that was not there.

Within that city there were five hundred pleasure groves, every one of them made of the seven precious substances, brilliant and exceedingly lovely to behold. In each of those pleasure groves there were five hundred ponds, each measuring a full cry's distance across on every side. In all those ponds there grew blue lotuses, night lotuses, and white lotuses, made of the seven precious substances, brilliant and lovely to behold, and these covered the water. All those fine blue lotuses, night lotuses, and white lotuses were as wide across the water as the wheel of a chariot. There were fragrant blue ones, blue in color, displaying blue and appearing blue; yellow ones, yellow in color, displaying yellow and appearing yellow; red ones, red in color, displaying red and appearing red; and white ones, white in color, displaying white and appearing white. In all those ponds there were geese, ducks, cranes, kāraṇḍavas, and sārasas, calling out in their voices.

All those pleasure groves were without any sense of "mine" and without any possessiveness. For over a long time those beings had practiced the Perfection of Wisdom, had revered the way of the buddhas, and had rightly realized what they had heard and reflected on in accord with it. These groves were brought about by the ripening of the former karma of those very beings who had long been devoted to the profound Dharma.

Son of good family, at the crossroads in the middle of that city, Fragrant, there was a mansion belonging to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. It was made of the seven precious substances, measured a yojana all around, and was brilliant and lovely to behold. It was encircled by seven tiers of parapets and seven rows of palm trees. In that mansion, for the use, the near use, and the full enjoyment of the mansion, there were four pleasure groves, called Ever Joyful, Sorrowless, Free from Sorrow, and Of Many Flowers. In each of those groves there were eight ponds, named Excellent, Supreme Excellence, Joy, Supreme Joy, Bliss, Supreme Bliss, Certainty, and Unfalling. Moreover, one side of those ponds was of gold, a second side of silver, a third side of beryl, and a fourth side of crystal. The ground beneath was of carketana gems, strewn with golden sand. Each of those ponds had eight flights of steps, with treads adorned with precious substances of various kinds, each different from the others.

From among all those steps, golden trees of the Jambu River gold also grew. The waters of all those pools were covered with many kinds of flowers, blue lotuses, night lotuses, and white lotuses, and swans, cranes, kāraṇḍavas, and sarasas called out there. All around those pools, flowering trees of many different kinds grew, and as the wind stirred those flowering trees and the blossoms fell into the pools, the waters of all those pools were fragrant with the scent of sandalwood, and were possessed of color, scent, flavor, and touch.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, together with his retinue and with sixty-eight thousand women, delighted himself in the five qualities of desire, in full command of them, in play and in joy. And all the other beings, men and women, who lived in that city likewise delighted themselves constantly in the gardens and pools, in full command of the five qualities of desire, in play and in joy.

Yet at the same time, the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, while playing and rejoicing with his retinue, taught the Perfection of Wisdom there at the three times of day. The beings who lived in the city of Gandhavatī would gather at the crossroads in the middle of the city, where a seat was set up for the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. Its legs were of gold, of silver, of beryl, and of crystal. It was spread with cotton, covered with a fine woven cloth, and padded on top, with a Kāśi cloth laid over it, and a canopy was arranged above it at the distance of half a bowshot. Overhead, in the sky, an awning was stretched, adorned with pearls, and it seemed to the onlookers that it was truly well fixed in place. Through the ripening of their many kinds of good fortune, it stood firmly in place, held there together. All around that place, flowers of the five colors were scattered, strewn, and spread everywhere, and in whatever way one might wish, through pure aspiration for the Dharma and through the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata's reverence for the Dharma, that place was also thoroughly perfumed with many kinds of fragrances and incense.

There the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, sat and taught the Perfection of Wisdom. Son of good family, those beings thus revere the Dharma, rely on the teachings, and possess faith. Having generated faith and serene confidence, they listen to the Perfection of Wisdom in the presence of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. Among the gods and humans gathered there to listen, many hundreds of living beings, many thousands of living beings, many hundreds of thousands of living beings, some receive the transmission, some recite it by heart, some write it down, and some realize it through proper attention. All those beings are of a nature never to fall into error, and are irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Son of good family, go to the presence of that bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, and you will hear the Perfection of Wisdom from him. Son of good family, for a long time he has been your spiritual friend, one who has shown you unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, urged you to take hold of it, praised it, and made you rejoice in it. Son of good family, just as you have sought the Perfection of Wisdom in the past and now, so seek it thoroughly. Son of good family, by generating attention day and night without interruption, go, and

"You will hear the Perfection of Wisdom before long," he said. Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, hearing this, was delighted and elated, and overflowing with joy, gladness, and happiness. Just as a man struck by a poisoned arrow gives rise to no other thought except, "When shall I find a physician who can draw out this barb, who can free me from this suffering and release me from this pain?" so too the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, though he had been weeping, now gave attention to nothing at all except the thought, "Son of good family, if I hear that Perfection of Wisdom, and by hearing that Dharma I come to abandon my fixation on objects and my attention to them, then I will have truly seen it."

Then, as the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, remained in that very place, he heard the noble Dharma-teaching of the bodhisattva, the great being, explaining the Perfection of Wisdom. And having heard it, he generated the perception of non-abiding in all phenomena, and the following doors of meditative absorption became manifest to him: the meditative absorption called Seeing the Essential Nature of All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Non-Apprehension of the Essential Nature of All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Emerging Through Knowing the Essential Nature of All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Non-Difference of All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Seeing All Phenomena as Unchanging; the meditative absorption called Illuminating All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Freedom from Darkness in All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Dispelling the Ignorance of All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Thorough Clearing Away of All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Non-Apprehension of All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Scattering Flowers; the meditative absorption called Not Establishing Any Entity of Self in All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Utterly Abandoning Illusion; the meditative absorption called Accomplishing the Appearance of the Disk of a Mirror; the meditative absorption called Accomplishing the Speech of All Beings; the meditative absorption called Free of Dust; the meditative absorption called Delighting All Beings; the meditative absorption called Following Skill in the Speech of All Beings; the meditative absorption called Accomplishing Various Sounds, Words, and Letters; the meditative absorption called Free of Arrogance; the meditative absorption called Without Conventional Expression by Nature; the meditative absorption called Attaining Liberation Without Obstruction; the meditative absorption called Freedom from Dust; the meditative absorption called Names, Etymologies, and Letters; the meditative absorption called Viewing All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Free of Objects in All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called the Unobstructed Limit of All Phenomena; the meditative absorption called Equal to Space; the meditative absorption called Vajra-Like; the meditative absorption called Clearing Away the Dust of Form; the meditative absorption called Perfect Excellence; the meditative absorption called Attaining Victory; the meditative absorption called the Eye of Non-Regression; the meditative absorption called Certainty in the Dharmadhātu; the meditative absorption called Emerging from the Dharmadhātu; and the meditative absorption called Giving Relief.

the absorption called Proclaiming the Lion's Roar, the absorption called Overpowering All Beings, the absorption called Free from Dust, the absorption called Without Any Affliction, the absorption called Arrayed with Lotuses, the absorption called Cutting Through Stagnation, the absorption called Following All Essences, the absorption called Rising Above All Phenomena, the absorption called Having Attained the Superknowledges, the Powers, and the Fearlessnesses, the absorption called Penetrating All Phenomena, the absorption called the Seal of the Wealth of All Phenomena, the absorption called the Ocean of the Wealth of All Phenomena, the absorption called Seeing All Phenomena Without Distinction, the absorption called Completely Abandoning All Dense Obscurations of View, the absorption called Free from Darkness, the absorption called All Phenomena Free from Signs, the absorption called Liberated from All Clinging, the absorption called Free from All Laziness, the absorption called Illuminating the Profound Dharma, the absorption called Like Mount Meru, the absorption called Unassailable, the absorption called Dispelling the Circle of Māra, the absorption called Unattached to the Three Worlds, the absorption called Accomplishing Rays of Light, the absorption called Seeing the Tathāgatas, and the absorption called Seeing All the Tathāgatas.

Abiding in these absorptions, you will see, in the world systems of the ten directions, immeasurable and innumerable buddhas, blessed ones, teaching this very Perfection of Wisdom to bodhisattvas, great beings. Those Tathāgatas will say "Excellent!" and will console you, speaking these words: "Child of noble family, when I too, in former times, was practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, I sought this very Perfection of Wisdom just so. And in seeking it, I attained absorptions exactly like those you have attained. Having attained these absorptions, I came to realize and fully comprehend the Perfection of Wisdom, and I came to abide in the qualities of a buddha from which there is no turning back.

When I look at the essential nature and intrinsic nature of these absorptions, I do not truly perceive any phenomenon that is to be entered into in equipoise, or that is to be risen from, or that is to be practiced for awakening, or that is to be brought to complete manifest awakening as unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening.

Child of noble family, this is the Perfection of Wisdom: abiding in a state where one does nothing with any phenomenon, either with conceit or without conceit, I attained a body such as this, of golden hue. I attained the thirty-two marks of a great being, the eighty excellent minor marks, the radiance of a fathom's span, the wisdom of a buddha, the inconceivable and unsurpassed discernment of a buddha, the unsurpassed absorption of a buddha, and the perfection of all the qualities of the buddhas' Dharma. As for that perfection of qualities, if even the Tathāgatas are unable to fix its measure or to show its limit, what need is there to speak of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?"

Son of a good family, therefore you should give rise to the highest reverence for these very teachings, with earnest seeking and longing. Son of a good family, for one who seeks and longs, it is not difficult to find unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Son of a good family, you should give rise to deep reverence for your spiritual friend. You should hold him dear, and you should be devoted to him with perfect faith. A bodhisattva, a great being, who is embraced by a spiritual friend will swiftly and fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. So the Tathāgatas said.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, weeping, said to those Tathāgatas, "Who, then, is my spiritual friend?"

They said to him, "Son of a good family, for a long time the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, has brought you to maturity for unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening and has embraced you. He has trained you in the Perfection of Wisdom, in skillful means, and in the qualities of a buddha. Son of a good family, he is the spiritual friend who holds you. Be one who knows what has been done for you and feels gratitude for it. Take up what he instructs you, and do just as he has done.

Son of a good family, suppose that for one eon, or two eons, or three eons, or a hundred eons, or a thousand eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or even longer, you were to carry the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, on your head like a crown, and were to wait upon him with every comfort, and were to offer him all the forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangible things that exist in the great trichiliocosm world-system. Even so, son of a good family, you would not have repaid what he has done for you. Why is that? Son of a good family, through his power you have gained such meditative absorptions as these; through him you have heard the Perfection of Wisdom and skillful means, and have come to attain the Perfection of Wisdom."

So they spoke. Then those Tathāgatas, having made the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, sigh in longing, vanished from sight.

The son of a good family then arose from those meditative absorptions, and having arisen, he thought, "From where did those Tathāgatas come, and to where did those Tathāgatas go?" Not having seen those Tathāgatas, he was deeply distressed and unhappy.

Then he thought again, "The noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, has attained dhāraṇī. He possesses the five superknowledges. He has done his work in the presence of the buddhas of the past. He is my spiritual friend, who truly holds me, and for a long time he has worked for my benefit. I shall go into the presence of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, and when I have drawn near I shall ask him this very matter: from where did those Tathāgatas come, and to where did those Tathāgatas go?"

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, established in himself joy, faith, devotion, and reverence toward the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. Having done so, he thought, "With what kind of honoring offering should I go into the presence of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata? I am poor. What clothing or…

"Of precious substances, gold, jewels, pearls, beryl, conch, crystal, coral, silver, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, or pennants, I have nothing at all of the kind. If I were to go into the presence of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, in this way, I would be acting improperly, and no gladness or delight would arise in me." So he thought.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, possessed of such qualities, and with reverence and attentive regard for his teacher, went on, and in due course he arrived at another city. Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, went to the middle of that city, and having reached its center he thought, "I shall sell my own body, and with the price I shall make an honoring offering to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. For a long time my body has been sold in vain, wasted, exhausted, and spent. Through immeasurable cycles of existence, again and again, for the sake of desires and the causes of desire, I have undergone immeasurable sufferings of the hells. But it was never for the sake of such a Dharma, nor for the sake of honoring such a great being."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, sat down in the middle of the marketplace of the city, and proclaimed aloud and called out in a loud voice, "Who wants a man? Who wants a man? Who wishes to buy a man?"

Then Māra the Evil One thought, "This bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, desiring the Dharma, has sold himself in order to make an honoring offering to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. He will question him about the Perfection of Wisdom and about skill in means, asking how a bodhisattva, a great being, who practices the Perfection of Wisdom will quickly become fully perfected in unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening. Through this he will gain an ocean of learning. He will become unconquerable by Māra and by the gods of Māra's retinue. He will attain the perfection of all good qualities. There he will accomplish the benefit of many beings. And when he has fully and completely awakened to unsurpassed, perfect and complete awakening, he and others besides will pass beyond my domain. I shall therefore create an obstacle for him." So he thought.

Then Māra the Evil One so thoroughly veiled the minds of those brahmins and householders that they could not hear the voice of the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, saying, "Who wants a man? Who wants a man? Who wishes to buy a man?"

Then, when the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, could find no one to buy him, he went off to one side and wept, with tears streaming down, and said, "I wished to sell my body so as to make an honoring offering to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, yet I cannot even find a buyer for my body. Alas, I have gained a wretched lot!"

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), thought, "Is this bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, perfect in his superior intention of wholly giving up his own body for the sake of the Dharma, or is he not? I shall test this bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita." So he thought.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, magically transformed himself into the form of a young brahmin, and came to the place where the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, was.

He said to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, "Son of good family, why do you stand here dejected, tormented, and in tears?"

Sadāprarudita replied, "Young brahmin, I wish to sell my body, but I cannot find anyone to buy it."

Śakra, in the form of the young brahmin, said, "Son of good family, why do you wish to sell yourself?"

Sadāprarudita answered him, "Young brahmin, I have sold myself because I long for the Dharma. I wish to make offerings to the Dharma, and I also wish to honor and revere the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. But I could find no one to buy my body, and so I thought: Alas, my merit is small. I have offered my body for sale in this way, thinking to make offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom and to honor the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, and yet I cannot even find a buyer for my body."

Then the young brahmin said to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, "Son of good family, I have no use for a man. But I am preparing a sacrificial offering, and for it I need a human heart, blood, bones, and marrow. If you wish, sell them to me for a price."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, thought: "That I have found this young brahmin who will buy my heart, blood, bones, and marrow is the finest of all finds; I have found it well. For my body will bring to fulfillment the Perfection of Wisdom, skillful means, and the qualities of the buddhas." Thinking this, he became glad in mind, happy in mind, and filled with delight. He said to the young brahmin, "Young brahmin, from this body of mine I will give you whatever you wish."

The brahmin said to him, "Son of good family, I will give you whatever price you wish."

Sadāprarudita said to him, "Young brahmin, give me whatever you have in mind to give."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, took a sharp knife and pierced his right arm, so that the blood flowed out. He stripped the flesh from his right thigh and went to the foot of a wall in order to break the bone.

Now a merchant's daughter was sitting on the roof of her house. She saw the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, with much blood flowing, his thigh stripped of flesh, going to the foot of the wall to break the bone. She thought: "Why is this son of good family inflicting such suffering on himself? Let me go to him and ask."

So the merchant's daughter went to where the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, was. She said to him, "Son of good family, why do you inflict such suffering on yourself? What will you do with this blood, these bones, this marrow?"

Sadāprarudita said to her, "Young woman, I have sold my body to this young brahmin so that I may make offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom and honor the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata."

Then the merchant's daughter said to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, "Son of good family, you have sold even your heart, blood, bones, and marrow in this way, wishing to honor that person. What kind of merit, or what special excellence, will you gain from this?"

He said to the young woman, "Young woman, that son of good family is the one from whom I will learn the Perfection of Wisdom, and

She will teach skillful means, and if I train in them, I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening and become a support for all sentient beings. I shall also obtain a body of golden hue, the thirty-two marks of a great being and the eighty excellent minor marks, a halo of light one fathom wide, and boundless rays of light. I shall fully obtain great loving-kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity, the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of exact discernment, and the eighteen distinctive qualities of a buddha. I shall obtain the five higher cognitions, inconceivable; pure moral discipline, inconceivable; pure meditative absorption, inconceivable; and pure wisdom, inconceivable. I shall fully obtain the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and I shall awaken fully to the unsurpassed wisdom of a buddha, by which I shall also obtain the unsurpassed precious Dharma, which is shared out to all sentient beings. So she said.

Then the merchant's daughter said to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita: Son of good family, it is marvelous that you have proclaimed these vast and surpassing teachings in this way. Son of good family, if for the sake of even a single such teaching one would give up one's body for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, how much more would one do so for many! Since you have proclaimed these Dharma teachings, so vast and surpassing, I too wish for them and I am willing to bear what is needed. That being so, son of good family, whatever you need to honor the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, whether gold, jewels, pearls, beryl, silver, musāragalva, lohitaka, crystal, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, cloth, parasols, banners, bells, flags, or lamps, I shall give it to you, so do not cause yourself such suffering. I shall go with you to where the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, dwells, and together with you I shall generate roots of virtue in order to obtain such teachings.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), made the appearance of the young brahmin vanish, and in his own form sat before the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, and said: Son of good family, your steadfastness in such a resolve, and your seeking of such a Dharma, are excellent, excellent! In the past too, the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly complete buddhas, when they were practicing the conduct of bodhisattvas, inquired about the Perfection of Wisdom and skillful means, and having thoroughly obtained the precious Dharma, they awakened fully to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Son of good family, I have no need of your heart, blood, bones, or legs. I have come here to rouse you. Son of good family, ask for a boon. What boon shall I give you? So he said.

Sadāprarudita answered him: Śakra, grant me the unsurpassed qualities of a buddha. Śakra said: Son of good family, this is not within my power. This is the domain of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Ask for some other boon. Sadāprarudita said:

In this matter of completing my body, Śakra, lord of the gods, do not let your effort be slight. Lord of the gods, I myself will bless this body of mine with an act of truth. Lord of the gods, by that truth whereby the Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas have prophesied that I will not turn back from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and know that my higher resolve is unwavering, by that truth and by those words of truth, may my body become just as it was before.

Then, in an instant, in a moment, in the space of a breath, through the power of the buddhas and through the perfect purity of his higher resolve, the body of the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, stood just as it had been before, free of illness and free of harm.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, and Māra the Evil One as well, lost their boldness. No boldness arose in them to answer the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, and they vanished on the spot.

Then the merchant's daughter said this to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita: Noble son, come here. I will go to where my house is. I will take wealth from my parents, and I will give it to you, in order that I may seek the Dharma, that offerings may be made to the very Perfection of Wisdom, and that honor and reverence may be shown to the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, went together with that merchant's daughter to where her own house stood, and having arrived, he sat down by the door.

Then the merchant's daughter went into her own house and said this to her parents: Father, mother, please give me gold, silver, jewels, gems, garments, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, unguents, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, flags, and various musical instruments. And I ask that you also share with me these five hundred maidservants whom you gave me. I will go, together with the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, to make offerings in the presence of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. He will teach us the Dharma, and through him I too will obtain the qualities of the buddhas.

Then the girl's parents said this to her: Daughter, who is this one called the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, and where is he now? The girl said: Noble one, he is now sitting by the door of the cow pen. Noble one, with a higher resolve he has entered fully upon the path to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Wishing to free all sentient beings from the immeasurable sufferings of saṃsāra, he sold himself to seek the Dharma, wishing to make offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom and also to honor and revere the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. But he could not find anyone to buy his body, and because he found no one, he was in distress and unhappy, his mind joyless, and he stood there shedding tears.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, having transformed himself into the form of a young brahmin, said: Noble son, why are you distressed and unhappy, your mind joyless, shedding tears? He replied to him: I wish to sell myself, but I have not found anyone to buy me. Śakra, in the form of the young brahmin, said:

"Son of good family, why do you wish to sell your body?" I asked. Ever-Weeping replied, "I wish to make offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom, and to show reverence to the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. For my buddha-qualities depend on him, since I desire the Dharma."

Then Śakra, in the form of the brahmin youth, said, "Son of good family, I do not want you. But I am performing a sacrifice, and for it I need a human heart, blood, bone, and marrow."

Without a moment's hesitation that son of good family said, "I give them." Taking a sharp blade, he pierced his own arm and let the blood flow. He cut the flesh from his thigh and went to the foot of the wall to break the bone. He sat down to one side, thinking, "I will give the bone and the marrow."

I saw that son of good family drawing blood while I was on the roof of my house, and I thought, "Why is this man inflicting such torments on himself?" I went to where he was and said, "Son of good family, what will you do with this blood that you are drawing from your own body?"

He told me, "I am giving the blood, heart, bone, and marrow to this young brahmin. Why? Because I am poor, and I have no other wealth at all." I said to him, "What is wealth to you? What would you do with it?" He answered me, "I wish to make offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom, because I desire the Dharma, and to show reverence to the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata."

I then said to him, "Son of good family, what kind of virtue or special benefit will come to you from that?" He answered me, "He will speak of the inconceivable qualities of the buddhas, and he will teach the immeasurable qualities of the buddhas. Such qualities of the buddhas will arise from him."

When I heard of those inconceivable qualities of the buddhas, great joy and delight arose in me, and I thought, "This son of good family, out of his desire for the Dharma, takes no thought even of his own body. He is carrying out a difficult practice. How marvelous! If he gives up even his own body for the sake of the Dharma, then why should we, who have many vast possessions, not make offerings to the Dharma? Why should we not make aspirations toward such things?"

So I said to that son of good family, "Son of good family, do not torment yourself like this, in a way that takes your life. I will take much wealth from my parents for the reverence and honor to be shown to the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, and I will go with you to where the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, is. I too will make offerings to him. And as for what you have declared, namely those supreme buddha-qualities, I too will bring such qualities to completion."

Then, speaking to her parents, the young woman said, "Father and mother, please grant me that great store of wealth. I too will go with that son of good family and make offerings to the noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata."

Here ends the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Volume twenty-four.

Then the girl's father and mother said to her: "Noble child, if the hardships you have described are as you say, then those teachings are certainly beyond all conception, more excellent than anything in the whole world, and a source of happiness for all sentient beings. How wonderful! Noble child, if you take such delight in these hardships, we give you our permission. Daughter, let us too go with you to see the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, to pay homage to him, to attend and honor him, and to make offerings to him. Open the way for us to go."

Then the merchant's daughter, having prepared herself to make offerings to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, and to honor him, informed her parents and said: "Father and mother, do just as you have said. I will place no obstacle in the way of any virtuous course."

So the merchant's daughter made ready to make offerings to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, and to pay him honor. She adorned five hundred chariots, and the five hundred girls also adorned themselves. When they were adorned, they took flowers of many different colors and garments of many colors. They took incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, monastic robes, parasols, banners, bells, and pennants. They took many kinds of precious substances, and flowers fashioned of many kinds of precious substances. Her father and mother also took abundant food, both hard and soft, and, boarding a single chariot together with the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, they set out. The five hundred girls, seated in the five hundred chariots, surrounded them and went before them, and with her parents and a great retinue they went off toward the east, traveling on by stages.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, saw from far away the city of Gandhavatī, resplendent with the seven precious substances and lovely to behold. It was encircled by seven tiers of ramparts made of the seven precious substances, with seven stairways down to the moats, and was surrounded by seven moats and seven rows of tāla trees. In its breadth it measured twelve leagues in length and twelve leagues in width. It was prosperous, flourishing, and happy, with good harvests, and full of people and crowds. Its rows of market stalls were as if painted in many designs, lovely and exceedingly beautiful, level and even. Its paths for people, for carriages, and for those traveling on foot were well maintained by five hundred keepers, who lived free of jealousy.

At the crossroads in the middle of that city, he saw the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, seated on the Dharma throne, teaching the Dharma, surrounded and attended by many hundreds, many thousands, and many hundreds of thousands of followers. The moment he saw him, he attained a bliss like that of a monk who has entered the first meditative concentration with one-pointed attention. Seeing him, he thought: "Though I am sitting in this chariot, to go into the presence of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, in this way would not be fitting for me." And so he got down from the chariot.

Then, when she had descended from that carriage, the merchant's daughter and those five hundred young women descended from their carriages together with her. Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, surrounded by the five hundred young women led by the merchant's daughter, with them walking before him and bearing immeasurable arrays of offerings, went to where the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, was.

At that moment the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, had had a house of tiered storeys built for the Perfection of Wisdom. It was made of the seven precious substances, adorned with red sandalwood, and covered with a net of pearls. At its four corners precious jewels were set, and these served as lamps. Four incense burners made of silver were hung in the four directions, and in order to make offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom, pure black aloeswood was burned in them. In the middle of that tiered house four thrones made of the seven precious substances were set up, and on them were placed four precious caskets. Inside them was placed the Perfection of Wisdom, written in molten lapis lazuli on gold leaves, and the tiered house was adorned with many kinds of silk streamers of different sorts hanging down.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, together with the five hundred young women led by the merchant's daughter, saw that tiered house adorned with immeasurable arrays of offerings. There he also saw many thousands of gods. He saw Śakra, lord of the gods, scattering, scattering forth, and scattering abundantly over that tiered house divine mandārava flowers, divine sandalwood powder, divine gold powder, and divine silver powder. He also heard divine cymbals sounding.

Having seen and heard this, the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, said to Śakra, lord of the gods: Lord of the gods, why do you, together with many thousands of gods, scatter, scatter forth, and scatter abundantly over this precious tiered house divine mandārava flowers, divine sandalwood powder, divine gold powder, and divine silver powder? And why do these gods strike these divine cymbals in the sky?

When he had spoken thus, Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita: Son of good family, this Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the great beings, and the one who leads them forth. By training in her, the bodhisattvas, the great beings, follow after the perfection of all qualities, and they quickly attain all the qualities of a buddha and omniscience itself. Do you not know this?

When he had spoken thus, the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, said to Śakra, lord of the gods: Kauśika, where does the Perfection of Wisdom abide, she who is the mother of the bodhisattvas, the great beings, and the one who leads them forth?

Śakra said: Son of good family, she is inside this tiered house, written in molten lapis lazuli on gold leaves. The noble bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, has sealed her with seven layers of seals and placed her there. It is difficult for us to show her to you.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, together with the merchant's daughter and the others,

Together with the five hundred young women, they took up flowers, garlands, precious cloth, incense, perfumes, wreaths, unguents, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, pennants, and flowers made of gold and silver. The assembly that had come made offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom, and then, for the sake of honoring the noble Bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, they set aside further and separate offerings apart from these.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, together with the merchant's daughter and the five hundred young women, first made offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, unguents, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, pennants, sandalwood powder, flowers of gold and silver, and divine music. Then they went to where the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, was, and having arrived, for the sake of honoring the Dharma itself they scattered, strewed, and showered upon the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, unguents, powders, robes, parasols, banners, bells, pennants, sandalwood powder, and flowers of gold and silver. Divine cymbals and music also resounded.

Then those flowers became, above the head of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, a pavilion of heaped flowers. The flowers of gold and silver and the flowers of many colors remained in the sky like a celestial palace. His robes and precious garments likewise remained in the air like a mass of clouds made of many kinds of jewels.
