When the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, and the merchant's daughter with the five hundred young women saw such a miraculous display of supernatural power by the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, they felt joy, and they thought: How marvelous! This bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, has great miraculous power, great might, and great splendor. If this son of good family displays such miraculous manifestations even while still practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, what will it be like when he fully awakens into unsurpassed, perfect awakening?

Then the merchant's daughter and the five hundred young women, having conceived joy toward the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, and together with that whole assembly and with an exalted intention, generated the mind of unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and said: By this root of virtue, may we in a future time become Tathāgatas, arhats, perfectly awakened buddhas. While practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, may we also attain such qualities as the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, has attained. Just as we honor and revere the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, as our teacher, so may we honor and revere the Perfection of Wisdom as our teacher. And just as the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, teaches it rightly, so may we also teach it rightly to many beings.

May we too, just as this bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, is endowed with and has fully perfected the Perfection of Wisdom and skillful means, likewise be endowed with and fully perfect the Perfection of Wisdom and skillful means. So they said.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, and those five hundred young women, led by the merchant's daughter, made offerings to the Perfection of Wisdom and showed reverence to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata as well. They bowed with their heads at the feet of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, circumambulated him, joined their palms, and sat to one side.

Having sat to one side, the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, spoke these words to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata: "Son of good family, when I went to the wilderness seeking this Perfection of Wisdom, a voice said to me, 'Son of good family, go east, and you will hear the Perfection of Wisdom.' I heard that voice and the teaching it gave, and I set out toward the east. Then I thought: 'I am going on the strength of that voice, but in whose presence shall I listen to the Perfection of Wisdom and obtain it? I did not ask the voice that I heard, which told me to go.' Because of this I became unhappy and deeply distressed. I remained in that very place for seven days and nights. In such deep distress, no thought of food arose in me; rather, I attended to the Perfection of Wisdom alone, thinking, 'Where should I go? From whom shall I hear and obtain this Perfection of Wisdom? I did not ask the voice.' Then a form of a Tathāgata appeared before me, and he said, 'Son of good family, travel gradually from here for five hundred leagues. In the city called Gandhavatī you will see the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, teaching and expounding the Perfection of Wisdom.'

"Then I was filled with joy and with great delight, and, pervaded by that very great joy and delight, without moving from that place I heard you teaching the Perfection of Wisdom. When I heard this, many gateways of meditative absorption arose in me. When I was there, the buddhas, the Blessed Ones of the world systems of the ten directions, gave me relief and said, 'Excellent!' They said, 'Son of good family, excellent, excellent! These meditative absorptions of yours arise from the Perfection of Wisdom. Abiding in it, we too have fully perfected the qualities of a buddha.' Thus those Tathāgatas taught me well, caused me to grasp it rightly, praised me, and gladdened me completely, and then vanished.

"Then I too arose from that meditative absorption and thought: 'From where did those Tathāgatas come, and to where have those Tathāgatas gone?' Then I thought further: 'The bodhisattva, the great being, the noble Dharmodgata, has attained dhāraṇī and is endowed with the five superknowledges. He has served the Victors of the past, planted roots of virtue, and trained thoroughly in the Perfection of Wisdom and skillful means.'"

"Surely they will teach me, just as it is, from where those Tathāgatas came and to where those Tathāgatas went." Thinking this, I went to the east, to that place, exactly as the voice of the Tathāgata's form had instructed me. After I arrived, and from far off, I saw the noble one Dharmodgata teaching the Dharma. The moment I saw him, such bliss arose in me as arises for a monk who has entered the first meditative concentration and attends with one-pointed mind. Noble son, I ask you: from where did those Tathāgatas come, and to where did those Tathāgatas go? Noble son, so that I may not be separated from the sight of the Tathāgatas, please explain to me the coming and going of those Tathāgatas.

This is the chapter on Sadāprarudita, the thirtieth chapter of the noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

When he had spoken thus, the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, said this to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita.

Noble son, those Tathāgatas have not come from anywhere, nor have they gone anywhere, for they do not move from suchness. What is suchness is the Tathāgata. Noble son, in the unborn there is no coming or going; what is unborn is the Tathāgata. Noble son, in the true limit there is no knowing of coming or going; what is the true limit is the Tathāgata. Noble son, in emptiness there is no knowing of coming or going; what is emptiness is the Tathāgata. Noble son, in things just as they are there is no knowing of coming or going; what is things just as they are is the Tathāgata. Noble son, in freedom from attachment there is no knowing of coming or going; what is freedom from attachment is the Tathāgata. Noble son, in cessation there is no knowing of coming or going; what is cessation is the Tathāgata. Noble son, in the element of space there is no knowing of coming or going; what is the element of space is the Tathāgata.

Noble son, apart from these phenomena there is no other Tathāgata. Noble son, the suchness of these phenomena, the suchness of all phenomena, and the suchness of the Tathāgata are one suchness. Noble son, suchness cannot be made into two. Noble son, suchness is one; that is to say, because there is nothing there, it is beyond being counted as two or three.

Noble son, consider an example. Suppose that in the last month of autumn, in the hot autumn season, at the hour of midday, a man sees a mirage shimmering and thinks, "Here I will drink water." Wherever he sees water, he runs there. Noble son, what do you think? Did that water come from the great ocean in the east, or from the south, the west or the north? And where did that water go?

Sadāprarudita replied: Noble son, since there is no water in a mirage, how could there be any knowing of coming or going? Noble son, that man was scorched by the sun, childish by nature, and confused in his discernment; seeing the mirage, he took what was not water to be water. Yet in it, water by its own nature does not exist.

Dharmodgata said:

Son of good family, so it is, so it is. In just this way, son of good family, those who cling to the Tathāgata through form or sound imagine that the Tathāgata comes or goes. All those who imagine that the Tathāgata comes or goes are called childish by nature, of confused wisdom by nature. They are like that man who produced the perception of water where there was no water. And why is this so? Because the Tathāgata is not to be regarded as a body of form. The Tathāgata is the Dharma body. Son of good family, the nature of reality has no coming and no going. In just this way, son of good family, there is no coming or going for the Tathāgatas.

Son of good family, it is like this. Take the troops of elephants, or of horses, or of foot soldiers conjured by a magician. They neither come nor go. In just this way, son of good family, the Tathāgata neither comes nor goes.

Son of good family, it is like this. Suppose a man, fallen asleep, sees in a dream one Tathāgata, or two, or three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, or even more. Then he wakes, and does not see a single Tathāgata. What do you think, son of good family? Where did those Tathāgatas come from? Where did those Tathāgatas go?

Ever-Weeping said: Son of good family, in a dream no phenomenon is known to be truly established. A dream is false, and not real.

Dharmodgata said: Son of good family, so it is. The Blessed One has said that all phenomena are like a dream. Son of good family, those who do not know that the Tathāgata has taught all phenomena as like a dream, exactly as they are, cling to the Tathāgata as a body of name and a body of form. Because they thus do not know the nature of reality, they imagine that the Tathāgata comes and goes. All those childish ordinary beings who imagine that the Tathāgata comes and goes will wander, and keep wandering, through all these six destinies of saṃsāra. All of them are far from the Perfection of Wisdom. All of them are far from the qualities of the buddhas.

Son of good family, moreover, those who know that all phenomena are like a dream, and that the Tathāgata has taught that all phenomena are like a dream, exactly as they are, do not imagine any phenomenon to come, to go, to arise, or to cease. Those who do not imagine any phenomenon to come, to go, to arise, or to cease thoroughly know the nature of reality of the Tathāgata. Those who thoroughly know the nature of reality of the Tathāgata do not imagine that the Tathāgata comes or goes. Those who thoroughly know the nature of reality of the Tathāgata in this way draw near to unsurpassed, perfect awakening. That is, they practice the Perfection of Wisdom.

Such śrāvakas of the Blessed One eat the alms of the country meaningfully, and they are fields of offering for the world.

Son of good family, it is like this. The jewels in the great ocean do not come from the east, nor from the south, nor from the west, nor from the north, nor from the intermediate directions, nor from above or below.

They do not come from any of the ten directions, and yet, in dependence on the roots of virtue of sentient beings, precious jewels arise within the great ocean. Nor do they arise without a cause. They depend on causes, conditions, and a basis, and arise in dependence upon these. When those jewels cease, they likewise do not go to any world of the ten directions; yet when those conditions are present, the jewels become manifest, and when those conditions are absent, the jewels do not become manifest.

Son of good family, in just the same way the fully accomplished bodies of those Tathāgatas do not come from any world of the ten directions, nor do they go to any world of the ten directions. Nor are the bodies of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, without a cause. They are fully accomplished through former conduct, dependent on causes, dependent on conditions, and arisen from the ripening of former actions. That body does not exist in any world-system of the ten directions. Yet when the conditions are present, the body comes to be manifestly accomplished, and when those conditions are absent, the manifestly accomplished body does not appear.

Son of good family, take the example of the sound of a lute. It comes from nowhere, and when it ceases it goes nowhere and shifts nowhere. It arises in dependence on the assembly of causes and conditions, dependent on cause and dependent on condition. That is to say, it depends on the body of the lute, on the skin, on the strings, on the bridge, on the peg, on the frame, and on the effort of the person who plays it. In this way sound arises from that lute, dependent on cause and dependent on condition. Yet that sound did not come from the body of the lute, nor from the skin, nor from the strings, nor from the bridge, nor from the peg, nor from the frame, nor from the effort of the person who plays it. Nevertheless, from the gathering of all these together, it is designated as sound. And when that sound ceases, it goes nowhere.

Son of good family, in the same way the full accomplishment of the bodies of the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is dependent on cause and dependent on condition. It is accomplished through the application of many roots of virtue. It is not from a single cause, nor from a single condition, and the body of a buddha is not manifested by a single root of virtue. Yet it is not without a cause either. It arises from the gathering of many causes and conditions, and it does not come from anywhere. When the gathering of causes and conditions is absent, it does not go anywhere either. Son of good family, you should view the coming and going of those Tathāgatas in just this way.

Son of good family, you should also come to understand the nature of all phenomena in just this way. Son of good family, to the degree that you know the Tathāgata in this way, and know that all phenomena are without arising and without cessation, to that degree you will become certain of unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and you will certainly engage in the perfection of wisdom and in skillful means.

Then, as this teaching on the absence of coming and going of the Tathāgatas was being given, a great earthquake occurred. This entire great trichiliocosm world-system shook in eighteen great ways and in six modes. It trembled, trembled strongly, trembled completely and strongly. It shook, shook strongly, shook completely and strongly. It quaked, quaked strongly, quaked completely and strongly. It was agitated, agitated strongly, agitated completely and strongly.

It shook and shook thoroughly, shook completely and thoroughly; it trembled and trembled thoroughly, trembled completely and thoroughly; it rocked and rocked thoroughly, rocked completely and thoroughly; it was stirred and stirred thoroughly, stirred completely and thoroughly. It resounded and resounded thoroughly, resounded completely and thoroughly; it roared and roared thoroughly, roared completely and thoroughly. All the abodes of Māra were thrown into turmoil and their splendor was cast down.

Throughout the great trichiliocosm world-system, every grass, tree, shrub, herb, and forest bowed down separately toward the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. Out of season, flowers were scattered from the sky above, and great rains of flowers fell.

Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), and the Four Great Kings scattered, strewed, and showered divine sandalwood powder and divine flowers toward the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, and the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita. They spoke these words: "Well done, well done, son of good family! Through your power, today we too have heard a discourse arising from the ultimate, which runs counter to the whole world, to all beings who dwell on the level of the view of the perishable collection and are attached to all views."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, said this to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata: "Son of good family, what is the cause and what is the condition of this great earthquake that has occurred in the world?"

The bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, replied: "Son of good family, you asked about this teaching on the Tathāgatas neither coming nor going, and through my teaching it, eight thousand beings attained acceptance of the unborn nature of phenomena. Eighty billion beings generated the mind toward unsurpassed, perfect awakening. And for sixty-four thousand beings the Dharma eye, free of dust and free of stain, became perfectly pure."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, was filled with great joy and delight. He thought: "By my asking about the Perfection of Wisdom and this teaching that the Tathāgatas neither come nor go, so many beings have been benefited. I have gained a supremely excellent gain. Through this I have obtained the supreme root of virtue by which unsurpassed, perfect awakening is brought to completion, and so I have no further doubt about unsurpassed, perfect awakening. Without doubt I shall become a Tathāgata, an arhat, a perfectly awakened buddha."

Filled with that joy and delight, he rose into the sky to the height of seven palm trees and remained there at that height. And he thought: "Staying here in the sky, I shall pay homage to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata."

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, saw the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, rising up, and knowing his thought with his own mind, he gave him divine mandārava flowers. He said: "Son of good family, with these divine flowers, pay homage to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. Son of good family, I have taken you under my care in this. Son of good family, through your power, today I too have benefited many thousands of beings."

Son of good family, beings who rejoice as you rejoice for the sake of all sentient beings, and who bear such a great burden for immeasurable and uncountable eons, are rare indeed.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, took those mandārava flowers from Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), and scattered them over the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, strewing them again and again. Then he covered the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, with his own body, and said these words: Son of good family, from this day forth, in order to serve you and attend upon you, I offer you my body. Having offered his body, he sat before the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, with palms joined.

Then the merchant's daughter and the five hundred young women said this to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita: Son of good family, we too offer our bodies to you. By this root of virtue, may we attain those same qualities. Together with you, again and again, may we honor and revere the buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the bodhisattvas, and may we come to be close to them.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, said to the merchant's daughter and the five hundred young women: Young women, if you stand by me with a lofty intention, then give yourselves to me with a lofty intention, and in that case, young women, I will accept you. Those young women replied: With a lofty intention toward you, from the depths of our hearts we follow in accord with you. With a lofty intention toward you, we offer ourselves, to be used as you wish.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, adorned the merchant's daughter and the five hundred young women with every ornament, and adorned the five hundred chariots as well. He offered them all to the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, to serve and attend him, saying: Son of good family, I offer you these female attendants, and these five hundred chariots too, for your full enjoyment.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to that son of good family: Excellent! Son of good family, excellent! In this way, son of good family, bodhisattvas, great beings, should completely relinquish all their possessions. With such a mind of complete relinquishment, a bodhisattva, a great being, will swiftly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening. Thus, having made offerings to the teacher of the Dharma, you will be able to listen to the Perfection of Wisdom and skillful means. Son of good family, the former Tathāgatas, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, when they practiced the bodhisattva conduct, also relied on just such a way and just such relinquishment to accomplish unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening, and they too inquired about the Perfection of Wisdom and skillful means.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, in order to bring the root of virtue of the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, to fullness, accepted the merchant's daughter and the five hundred young women together with the five hundred chariots, and having accepted them, gave them back to the son of good family, Sadāprarudita.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, rose from his seat and entered his own house, and the sun set.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, thought: "I have come here out of a desire for the Dharma. For me to sit or to lie down would be improper. For the sake of attending the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, I will pass the time in the two postures of standing and walking, until he comes forth again to teach the Dharma."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, remained for seven years absorbed in a single samādhi. Abiding in thousands of bodhisattva samādhis, immeasurable and beyond counting, which arise from the Perfection of Wisdom and from skillful means, he lived in that state.

The bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, for his part, passed the seven years in the two postures, free of sleep and drowsiness. In those seven years no thought of desire arose in him, no thought of ill will arose, no thought of harming arose, and no wrong thought of craving for flavors arose. For otherwise, how could he have been present when the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, rose from his samādhi?

He thought: "Let us also prepare the Dharma seat on which that son of good family will sit to teach the Dharma, the Dharma seat of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata. And I will not sprinkle this ground with water. In the place where the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, will teach the Perfection of Wisdom and skillful means, I will spread a fine plaster, and I will lay out flowers of many kinds."

The five hundred young women, led by the merchant's daughter, likewise followed the example of the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, and passed the time in the two postures. In everything they did, they followed him.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita heard from the voices of the gods: "Now, in seven days, the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, will rise from this samādhi, take his seat in the middle of the city, and teach the Dharma."

When the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita heard that voice of the gods, he was delighted and glad, filled with great joy, and happiness and mental well-being arose in him. Together with the five hundred young women, led by the merchant's daughter, he swept that ground clean and arranged a Dharma seat, made of the seven precious substances.

Then each of those young women took off her own upper garment, and they spread those five hundred garments on the seat where the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, would sit to teach the Dharma. When the Dharma seat of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, had been prepared in this way, all those young women were delighted and glad, filled with great joy, and happiness and mental well-being arose in them.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita wished to sprinkle that place with water. But Māra the Evil One, wishing that the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, should find no water and so become displeased and distressed, unhappy in mind and changed in heart, so that his roots of virtue would be lost and that offering would be spoiled, made all the water that might have been sprinkled on that place vanish from sight. And though Sadāprarudita searched everywhere for water, he found none.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, thought: "I will pierce my own body and sprinkle this ground with my blood. Why? Because this ground is dusty, and dust rises from it; if it touched the body of the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, that would not be right. My body will certainly perish in any case, for it is subject to destruction. What is it good for? Through desire, and for the sake of desire, my body has been broken up for such useless purposes again and again, wandering in cyclic existence; many thousands of my bodies have been destroyed in such ways. But never was it destroyed in a place like this one, nor for the sake of taking up the Dharma. It was destroyed only for the sake of desire, and desire is a thing that perishes." So he reflected.

Having reflected in this way, the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, took a sharp weapon, pierced his body all over, and sprinkled all that ground with his own blood. Following the example of the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, the five hundred young women, the merchant's daughter and the others, all took sharp weapons as well, pierced their own bodies, and sprinkled all that ground with their own blood. Not one of them, neither the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, nor any of those young women, changed their mind in the least, so that Māra the Evil One could find no opening by which to obstruct their roots of virtue.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods (Indra), thought: "How wondrous that the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, has such a longing for the Dharma, such firmness in his commitment, such great armor of resolve, and such disregard for body, life, and possessions! He has entered upon this lofty intention: 'Having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, I will free all sentient beings from the boundless sufferings of cyclic existence.'"

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, blessed all that blood so that it became divine sandalwood water. The fragrance of that divine sandalwood water, supreme, vast, and inconceivable, filled that whole ground and its surroundings, to the full extent of five hundred leagues.

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family! Your diligence, inconceivable as it is, is excellent. Your longing for the Dharma and your search for the Dharma are also excellent. Son of good family, the Tathāgatas of the past, the arhats, the perfectly awakened buddhas, also accomplished unsurpassed, perfect awakening with just such lofty intention, just such diligence, and just such longing for the Dharma."

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, thought: "I have spread the Dharma seat for the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, and I have swept this ground well, and sprinkled it well. But with what flowers shall I scatter this ground? And where shall I find the flowers to scatter over the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, as he teaches the Dharma and sits upon the Dharma seat?"

Then Śakra, lord of the gods, said to the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita:

Son of good family, take these divine mandārava flowers, and scatter them in these places. Scatter them also over the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, who is seated on the Dharma throne teaching the Dharma. Having said this, he gave him a thousand loads of divine mandārava flowers.

Then the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, took those flowers. With some of them he scattered flowers over that place, and with others he scattered flowers over the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata.

Then, when seven years had passed, the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, rose from that absorption and came to the place where the Dharma seat was. He sat down upon the spread seat, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of followers, and gazing straight ahead he taught the Perfection of Wisdom.

Then, as soon as the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, saw the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, he attained a bliss like that of a monk who has entered the first meditative concentration and is attending to it with one-pointed mind.

This is how the bodhisattva, the great being Dharmodgata, taught the Perfection of Wisdom. Because all phenomena are equal, the Perfection of Wisdom is equal. Because all phenomena are secluded, the Perfection of Wisdom is secluded. Because all phenomena are unmoving, the Perfection of Wisdom is unmoving. Because all phenomena are without conceit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without conceit. Because all phenomena are without arrogance, the Perfection of Wisdom is without arrogance. Because all phenomena are of a single flavor, the Perfection of Wisdom is of a single flavor. Because all phenomena are without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without limit. Because all phenomena are unborn, the Perfection of Wisdom is unborn. Because all phenomena are unceasing, the Perfection of Wisdom is unceasing.

Because space is without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without limit. Because the ocean is without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without limit. Because Sumeru is varied, the Perfection of Wisdom is varied. Because space is without conceptual thought, the Perfection of Wisdom is without conceptual thought. Because form is without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without limit. In the same way, because feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without limit. Because the earth element is without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without limit. In the same way, because the water element, the fire element, and the wind element are without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without limit. Because the space element is without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without limit. Because the consciousness element is without limit, the Perfection of Wisdom is without limit.

Because the sameness of phenomena is like a vajra, the Perfection of Wisdom is sameness. Because all phenomena are unmixed, the Perfection of Wisdom is unmixed. Because all phenomena are without a basis for focus, the Perfection of Wisdom is without a basis for focus. Because the sameness of the destruction of all phenomena, the Perfection of Wisdom is the sameness of destruction. Because all phenomena are without action, the Perfection of Wisdom is without action.

Because all phenomena are inconceivable, the Perfection of Wisdom should be understood as inconceivable.

Then, as the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita sat there, the king of absorptions called "the equality of all phenomena" arose in him. He also obtained the absorption called "all phenomena are secluded"; the absorption called "all phenomena are unmoving"; the absorption called "all phenomena are free of conceit"; the absorption called "all phenomena are free of arrogance"; the absorption called "all phenomena are of a single taste"; the absorption called "all phenomena are boundless"; the absorption called "all phenomena are unborn"; the absorption called "all phenomena are unceasing"; the absorption called "boundless space"; the absorption called "boundless ocean"; the absorption called "the variegated Sumeru"; the absorption called "space free of conceptualization"; the absorption called "boundless form"; and likewise the absorptions called "boundless feeling," "boundless perception," "boundless formations," and "boundless consciousness"; the absorption called "the boundless earth element"; and likewise the absorptions called "the boundless water element," "the boundless fire element," and "the boundless wind element"; the absorption called "the boundless space element"; the absorption called "the boundless consciousness element"; the absorption called "vajra-like"; the absorption called "all phenomena are unmixed"; the absorption called "all phenomena are without a basis of focus"; the absorption called "the equality of the destruction of all phenomena"; the absorption called "all phenomena are without action"; and the absorption called "all phenomena are inconceivable." Thus the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, attained six hundred thousand gateways of absorption of this kind and others like them.

This is the thirty-first chapter, called "Dharmodgata," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Subhūti, immediately after the bodhisattva, the great being Sadāprarudita, had attained these six hundred thousand gateways of absorption, he saw, in the east, south, west and north, in the intermediate directions, below and above, in all ten directions, in as many great trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā, as many buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā. Each was surrounded by an assembly of monks, with a company of bodhisattvas before him, and each was teaching this Perfection of Wisdom in exactly this manner, with exactly these names and these letters. It was just as I now, in this great trichiliocosm world-system, teach the Dharma surrounded by an assembly of monks, with a company of bodhisattvas before me, and teach this Perfection of Wisdom in exactly this manner, with exactly these names and these letters.

He became one of inconceivably vast learning, with learning as deep as the ocean. In every place where he was born, he was never separated from the buddhas. In every birth, he was born in those very places where buddhas, Blessed Ones, become manifest, and even in dreams he was never parted from the buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

Through this he will have abandoned all the unfavorable conditions and will have accomplished the perfect leisure and endowment.

Then the Blessed One said to the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, through this explanation too you should understand that this Perfection of Wisdom brings about the omniscient wisdom of bodhisattvas, great beings. Therefore, Ānanda, bodhisattvas, great beings, who wish to attain omniscient wisdom should practice this Perfection of Wisdom. They should listen to this Perfection of Wisdom, take it up, hold it, read it, thoroughly comprehend it, recite it, teach it, explain it in detail, give the transmission of it, memorize it, and write it down. By the blessing of the Tathāgata, they should write it out well, with clear and perfectly clear letters, on great scrolls. They should honor it, revere it, regard it as their teacher, make offerings to it, venerate it, make images of it, and serve it, with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, music, clothing, parasols, banners, bells, and flags, and with rows of lamps all around, and with many kinds of offerings. Ānanda, this is my instruction.

Why is that? Because from this Perfection of Wisdom, omniscient wisdom becomes fully perfected.

Ānanda, what do you think? Is the Tathāgata your teacher?"

Ānanda replied: "Blessed One, he is my teacher. Sugata, he is my teacher."

When he had said this, the Blessed One spoke to the venerable Ānanda in this way: "Ānanda, you have attended your teacher the Tathāgata with bodily action that is loving and pleasing, with speech that is loving and pleasing, and with mind that is loving and pleasing. Therefore, Ānanda, just as you now show joy, devotion, faith, and reverence toward this body of mine, which remains here, living and sustained, so, Ānanda, after I have passed away, do the same toward this Perfection of Wisdom. So that this Perfection of Wisdom may not disappear, and so that you may not become the last of such persons, Ānanda, I entrust it to you, a second time and a third time; I entrust it to you completely and repeatedly.

Ānanda, as long as this Perfection of Wisdom is practiced in the world, for so long you should know that the Tathāgata is present. Ānanda, for so long you should know that the Tathāgata is teaching the Dharma.

Ānanda, those beings who listen to this Perfection of Wisdom, take it up, hold it, read it, thoroughly comprehend it, recite it, teach it, explain it in detail, give the transmission of it, memorize it, and write it down in letters, and who honor it, revere it, regard it as their teacher, make offerings to it, venerate it, make images of it, and serve it, with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, clothing, parasols, banners, bells, and flags, and with rows of lamps all around, and with many kinds of offerings, you should know that such beings will never be separated from seeing the buddhas, from hearing the sacred Dharma, or from serving the Saṅgha. Ānanda, you should know that those beings dwell in the presence of the Tathāgata."

The Blessed One was pleased, and when he had spoken in this way,

Then the bodhisattvas, the great beings, headed by Maitreya, together with the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Ānanda, Śakra, lord of the gods, and the whole world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had spoken.

This concludes the thirty-second chapter, called "The Entrusting," from the Noble Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, the Mother of the Blessed Ones, is complete.

It was translated, revised, and finalized by the Indian preceptor Śākyasena, Jñānasiddhi, and the great editor-translator, the venerable Dharmatāśīla, and others. Later, by command of the sacred sovereign of Tibet, the glorious divine king Tashi Lhadé Tsen, the Indian preceptor Subhāṣita and the translator, the monk Rinchen Zangpo, translated it again in accordance with the commentary. Later still, the Indian preceptor, the great paṇḍita Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna, and the great editor-translator, the monk Rinchen Zangpo, corrected and revised it against the commentary of the Central Land, and finalized it. Afterwards, at Nyethang Nemoché in Kyi Mé, the great paṇḍita Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna and the translator Drom Gyalwé Jungné, while expounding the Eight Thousand Lines, finalized a major revision. Later, at Rasgreng Monastery, the translator Drom Gyalwé Jungné finalized it twice, checking it against three Indian sūtra manuscripts. Afterwards that same translator wrote an exposition and also finalized the minor details. At a still later time, the great translator, the Śākya monk Lodan Sherab, gathered many Kashmiri manuscripts and many manuscripts from the Central Land, and finalized it.

Here ends the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines.

Translator's notes

The phrase rendered "of noble lineage, great elephants" translates the stock epithet "ཅང་ཤེས་པ། གླང་པོ་ཆེན་པོ", usually understood as "well-bred, noble, great elephants." This is a traditional image for arhats. The phrase "sons of good family" renders the standard "རིགས་ཀྱི་བུ". The final sentence ("I do not truly see…") is the opening of Subhūti's famous inquiry, which leads into the teaching on the emptiness of the bodhisattva; "as an actual phenomenon" renders the sense of "ཡང་དག་པར་རྗེས་སུ་མ་མཐོང" ("do not correctly perceive after investigation"). The Tibetan text uses "ཤཱ་རིའི་བུ" for Śāriputra, which I have given in Sanskrit form per house style. The Tibetan has Śāriputra's challenge and Subhūti's reply in a compact form; I have kept the sense that Subhūti turns the question back on Śāriputra, since neither existence nor non-existence can be found in no-mind. The phrase "irreversible from unsurpassed, perfect, complete awakening" translates the Tibetan as it stands, where the verb "to be examined, to be recognized" governs the bodhisattva's irreversibility. Subhūti's epithet in Śāriputra's praise renders "abiding in freedom from affliction," the Tibetan form of the arana-vihārin tradition. The Tibetan "འགོང་" is rendered "stiff" following the standard stock series (stiffening, sinking, anxiety, fear). "གློ་བ་ལ་གཅགས" is idiomatic, literally "stuck in the lungs/heart"; I render it as a hindrance weighing upon the heart. In the continuity text, "the stage of the hearers" parallels the "stage of the solitary buddhas" here. The phrase "ཀུན་ཏུ་རྒྱུ་ཕྲེང་བ་ཅན" is rendered "the one who wanders in the cycle of existence." It most likely stands for a Sanskrit term meaning a wanderer or one who moves through saṃsāra, and some lineages read it as a proper epithet. It is rendered consistently, but its exact sense is not fully settled. The phrase "ཡངས་པ་མདུན་དུ་བགྱིས་པ་ཚད་མེད་པར་ངེས་བ" is syntactically difficult. I have taken it to mean "vast, pioneered by the immeasurable, definitive," but other readings are possible. The phrase "ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཉིད་ལ་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ" is rendered "emerge into omniscience" in the sense of definitive emergence (niryāṇa). The sentence "ཅི་ཆོས་གང་མེད་པ་དང་མི་དམིགས་པ་དེ་..." is read as a self-posed question in the bodhisattva's reflection, taking the absence of any phenomenon and non-apprehension as a candidate definition of the perfection of wisdom. The terms "ངོ་བོ་ཉིད" and "མཚན་ཉིད" are rendered "essential nature" and "defining characteristic" respectively, following the house glossary. The Tibetan text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of this passage, so the final sentence is left open, awaiting its conclusion in the next passage. The repeated formula "practices in signs" renders "mtshan ma la spyod," with "sign" for nimitta, the conceptual mark by which things are grasped; "fixation on an object" renders "dmigs pa" (ālambana/upalambha). The phrase "definitive emergence" renders "nges par 'byung ba," the sense being that phenomena have no real going-forth or release because they are unborn. The Tibetan "ཡངས་པ་མདུན་དུ་བྱས་པ་ཚང་མེད་པར་ངེས་པ" is obscure and may be a corrupted or idiosyncratic rendering of a Sanskrit phrase; my rendering is tentative. The phrase "the Vast One placed before it" is a literal reading. The sentence about "for one such as that, there is not, in any way... anything at all" is also cryptic in the Tibetan, and I have rendered it close to the literal wording. The phrase "does not know and does not truly know" is rendered literally; in context Subhūti's point is that, since the absorption has no inherent existence, there is nothing to be known. The phrase "ཡང་དག་པར་ཡོད་དེ་དེ་ལྟར་མེད་པ" is rendered "truly exist just as they do not exist," following the evident paradox of the Perfection of Wisdom idiom: their reality is precisely their lack of the existence imputed to them. The phrase "གཞིས་དམིགས་པ་ལ་གནས་ནས" is somewhat obscure in the received text; I have rendered it as resting on the basis of fixation, in the focusing of the mind (apprehending a supposed object), but the grammar may be corrupt. The passage ends mid-sentence, with the Blessed One's reply to follow in the next passage. The final sentence is cut off at the passage boundary and continues in what follows. The phrase "the Perfection of Wisdom" in Subhūti's reply is rendered as in the house glossary. "Sense faculties" renders དབང་པོ; the "six" faculties are the standard enumeration of the five physical faculties plus the mental faculty. The sentence at the start, "the faults of Māra should be recognized in this way," follows directly on the preceding question about the virtuous spiritual friends. The Tibetan gives the speakers' teaching in a compressed form, and I have read "those who speak in this way" as the antecedent of "these" in the final sentence of the first paragraph. The closing lines of Subhūti's statement are terse and slightly elliptical in this translation tradition. I have rendered "not seized" in the sense of non-appropriation, in line with the sense that the mind is not grasped as a real entity. In the Tibetan, Subhūti's reply to Śāriputra is somewhat elliptical; I have followed the sense that Subhūti answers Śāriputra's question with a counter-question about whether mindlessness can be found as either existing or nonexistent. Pūrṇa's name appears in the text as "Gaṅ-po," son of Maitrāyaṇī, a standard Tibetan rendering of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. The Tibetan gang po byams ma'i bu is the elder Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra (Skt. Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra), rendered accordingly. In the phrase "armor that is no armor," the Tibetan go cha med pa is rendered as the doctrinal point that the armor of vowed aspiration has no real basis, since neither omniscience nor the beings to be liberated are truly produced. The Tibetan text as given ends mid-argument, after the illusory person's form and its suchness; the parallel statements for the other aggregates' suchnesses would follow in the next passage. Subhūti's final speech ends with the remark that no coming, going, or abiding is seen in the Vehicle. The phrase rendered "overpowering the world" follows the Tibetan "zil gyis mnan nas," though the verb "rjod" ("is spoken of") sits oddly in the received text. The "armor that is without armor" is the standard paradox of the bodhisattva's armor in the Perfection of Wisdom literature. The Tibetan gang bo is rendered Pūrṇa (Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra), following the standard identification of this interlocutor in the Prajñāpāramitā literature. The phrase "that name too is not actually established" and the following simile of the self is a compressed passage; I have kept the rhetorical sense that names, like the notion of "I," are used conventionally without any established referent. The phrase translated "is not fully realized" (ཉེ་བར་མ་རྟོགས) follows the sense of the Sanskrit upalabdhi-type negation, "not apprehended," and is paired deliberately with "not observed." The passage breaks off mid-sentence, as the Tibetan does; the thought continues with consciousness in the following passage. The Tibetan verb ཉེ་བར་རྟོག་པ (upalakṣ-/upaparīkṣ-type contemplation) is rendered "closely contemplate," with the paired negations "closely conceive" and "closely grasp" following the parallel verbs in the text. The phrase "is not a phenomenon" in the opening lines reflects the text's insistence that even non-establishment is not a reified entity. The Tibetan text includes a colophon-like marker, the end of the first volume (bampo) of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines and the start of the second. I omitted it so the narration flows without interruption. The Tibetan opens mid-statement with the object "consciousness," continuing the preceding sentence's pattern about form, feeling, perception and formations. The pattern is completed here for consciousness. The final clause on "even a little harmful intent" renders the Tibetan chung ngu na, which can also be read as "even in the smallest degree." The final exchange is deliberately paradoxical, and the Tibetan phrase "ཐོབ་པ" (attainment) is used both as a noun and verb; I have rendered it as "attained" for readability. The passage ends mid-dialogue, with Subhūti's counter-question. In the first paragraph, "the perception of hardship" renders དཀའ་བའི་འདུ་ཤེས, meaning the sense of difficulty or arduousness in the bodhisattva's task, which the realization of non-apprehension removes. The opening sentence is the tail of Subhūti's rejoinder in the preceding passage. The Tibetan "ཆོས་མ་སྐྱེས་པ་ཉིད་ཡིན" is syntactically awkward, and I have rendered it as a rhetorical question, matching the preceding line. The sentences about non-arising being "disputed" and "appearing distinctly" (རྗོད་པ, སོ་སོར་སྣང་བ) are terse and somewhat obscure in this translation. Subhūti's point seems to be that non-arising is the very topic of debate, yet is evident as suchness, and the sense is preserved with some uncertainty. The final exchange is a deliberate paradox: attention (manaskāra) and abiding in the Perfection of Wisdom are mutually exclusive in the sense that wisdom abides in nothing, which also means it does not rest even on an act of attention. The opening of this passage continues Subhūti's reply in the dialogue; the Tibetan addresses Śāriputra as "Venerable Subhūti" only in the preceding passage's rendering, so here I have taken the speaker in the first sentence to be Subhūti addressing Śāriputra, which fits the following sentence "Subhūti said this to Śāriputra" as a resumed speech. If the first sentence is instead Śāriputra's own objection addressed to Subhūti, the attribution of the opening quotation would reverse. The phrase "even you are open to criticism" is a literal rendering of the Tibetan; the commentarial point is that Śāriputra's own statement, taken at face value, also lacks an inherently existing referent, which Subhūti then clarifies through the series of parallels between sentient beings and attention. "The real as it is" renders the Tibetan for what is not accurately as it is, in the sense of deluded, mistaken apprehension. "The certainty of what is right" refers to the fixed course of the śrāvaka, whom Subhūti declares to be without the opportunity of generating the awakening mind in that state. The first sentence is elliptical: "they" are those who have entered into the certainty of what is right (the fixed ones named in the preceding passage), who have, in the tradition's reading, set a boundary to saṃsāra's stream by their own attainment, so that they no longer have the disposition to generate the mind of awakening. I have rendered it as the text has it, without adding explanation in the body. The phrase "the coming together of eye, form, and consciousness" glosses the technical term for contact (sparśa), literally "the meeting," added for the listener's clarity. Subhūti's remark that he will "repay the kindness" echoes the Buddha's former practice and the hearers' role in instructing others, per the standard reading of this passage. The Tibetan གནས་པར་མི་བྱ is rendered consistently as "should not abide," continuing the preceding passage, and the "should not abide in the thought" constructions reflect the ཞེས་ quotative. The phrase "distinguished by the unconditioned" follows the standard Vajracchedikā-type formulation (asaṃskṛtaprabhāvita), in which noble ones are differentiated by the unconditioned. "Worthy recipient of offerings" renders སྦྱིན་པའི་གནས, literally "a basis for giving" (Skt. dakṣiṇīya). The sentences about non-abiding ("does not abide in disagreement, yet is not one who fails to abide in agreement," translating མི་འཐུན་པར་གནས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཞིང་མི་འཐུན་པར་མི་གནས་པ་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་པ) are difficult, and the Tibetan itself appears awkward. The rendering gives the likely sense, that the Buddha's abiding is neither a fixed standpoint nor a mere absence of one. The Tibetan text repeats the earlier thought about the Buddha's passing into nirvāṇa with slight variation, and I have kept that parallel structure. The passage ends mid-sentence, continuing the list of the noble ones; I have left it open to join the next passage. In the first sentence, the gods' "cannot be understood" is the sense of ཤེས་པར་མི་རུང་. The phrase ཆོས་ཉན་པ་རང་བཞིན་ཅི་ལྟ་བུ་ is rendered as "what kind of nature should we look for in those who listen to the Dharma," following the Tibetan's own wording rather than smoothing it. The odd syntax of the Tibetan in the sentence "those who listen to the Dharma from me should be sought among beings like illusions" has been kept close to its literal sense. The Tibetan names Ānanda as speaker of the answer about who will uphold the teaching, though the Sanskrit tradition varies on this attribution; I follow the Tibetan. "Pūrṇa son of Maitrāyaṇī" and "Mahākauṣṭhila" render the Tibetan epithets for Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra and Mahākauṣṭhila. "Mahākāśyapa" renders Tibetan 'od srung chen po. Kauśika is a standard epithet of Śakra (Indra), so the vocative is left in Sanskrit. The phrase "yet one who does not train in these stages" renders the Tibetan "these grounds" (sa), referring to the stages of the hearers and solitary buddhas just listed. The Tibetan "ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བ" in the final line is rendered "emerge into" (literally "definitely come forth"), following the sense of definite emergence into omniscience. Śakra is addressed in the Tibetan as Kauśika, one of his common names, and he is introduced as lord of the gods; I have glossed this on first use. The Tibetan puts a question in Śāriputra's mouth where the preceding English passage ended with Subhūti's affirmation; I have rendered it as a question and Subhūti's reply as the confirming answer, following the Tibetan. The word "blessing" renders byin gyi rlabs (adhiṣṭhāna), here understood as the buddha's empowering support of the teaching. The passage ends mid-argument, with the same reasoning to be applied to the other aggregates in what follows. The Tibetan has three near-synonymous terms for "immeasurable" and "limitless": tshad ma med pa, tshad med pa, and mtha' yas pa. I rendered them as immeasurable, limitless, and unending, in that order, to keep the three distinct for the listener. In the first exchange, the Tibetan has Śakra's final epithet as mtha' yas pa, which I rendered "limitless" there and "unending" for the later repetitions only in the sense of keeping the series consistent. If a different pairing is preferred, adjust uniformly throughout. The term dmigs pa is rendered "object of focus," its standard meaning of an apprehended or observed object. The sentence beginning "Kauśika, one does not become fixated" translates a phrase meaning that one does not cling to these as inherently existent designations. The Tibetan "mu med" (without limit) is rendered "without limit." The phrase "bgrang ba dang mi ldan pa'am bgrang ba mang pos" is difficult; I have taken it as "beyond any reckoning, or reckoned as numberless." Subhūti's "yongs su brtan par byas pa" (and the later "yongs su bstan par byas pa") is rendered "established," following the Tibetan's apparent sense of a sentient being being definitively posited as an entity. The Tibetan text here is slightly disordered in places. "Mar me mdzad" is rendered Dīpaṃkara; the city called "Mar me can" is rendered Dīpavatī, following the Sanskrit tradition. "Lords of beings" renders skye dgu'i bdag po, which may be understood as Prajāpati. The final Tibetan sentence in the first paragraph before the gods' declaration is slightly elliptical; I have rendered its sense. The "gods of Lesser Virtue" renders dge chung (Parīttaśubha); "Akaniṣṭha" renders 'og min. The opening sentence is difficult: the Tibetan reads literally that the person "will not die without having abandoned yang yang ba" (a rare or possibly corrupt expression). I have rendered it as faults of body and speech following the likely sense of the parallel Sanskrit tradition, which speaks of freedom from untimely death; the exact reading is uncertain.

The phrase translated "Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world-system" renders the Tibetan "mi mjed kyi bdag po," the standard epithet of Mahābrahmā. Kauśika is a common epithet of Śakra (Indra). The plant name rtsi ma ghi is left in transliteration because its identification is uncertain; the text describes only an antidote plant that neutralizes poison. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at "and all the bodhisattvas as well," continuing in the next section. Brahmā is described by the Tibetan epithet "lord of the unendurable (world)," rendered as lord of this world (Sahāpati). The Tibetan sentence about entering battle is syntactically loose, with several verbs listed in sequence. I have rendered it in the sense of the parallel Sanskrit tradition, in which the devotee is protected anywhere in the battlefield. The verb string translated "holds, bears in mind, reads, thoroughly understands, recites, teaches, explains, expounds, and memorizes" follows the standard Prajñāpāramitā formula and is kept uniform throughout. The Tibetan "ཁེངས་པ" is rendered as "arrogance." The Tibetan rig sngags is rendered "knowledge-mantra (vidyā)," following the usual sense of "spell of knowledge." The phrase "tshad med pa" and "tshad ma med pa" in the second and third epithets are rendered "immeasurable" and "boundless" to keep them distinct. The final sentence's three verbal tenses (past, present, future awakening) follow the Tibetan sequence closely. The phrase "ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་བདག་གི་དངོས་པོ་མངོན་པར་གྲུབ་པ" is awkward in the Tibetan; I have rendered it literally as "the realization of the very substance of omniscience." The Sanskrit parallel likely reads something like "the attainment of the self-nature of omniscience," and the sense is that omniscience itself is the fruit being asked about. The final line, "The Blessed One said," leads into the next passage, which is not included here. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the Tibetan does; Śakra's statement continues in the next passage. The word for "body" (sku) occurs in the sequence "body of the Buddha, body of the Dharma, body of the Saṅgha"; I rendered it as "body" in these three, understanding it as the Jewels being made manifest, rather than as the formal trikāya. In the passage on offering after parinirvāṇa, "relics" is supplied from the sense of "those bodies" (sku de dag). The passage breaks off mid-sentence, so the translation ends with an ellipsis; the sentence presumably continues in the following passage. The opening question, addressed to Śakra, is somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan; it has been rendered as the Blessed One's rhetorical challenge, with the Blessed One then turning to examine Śakra's own understanding. In the final paragraph the grammatical subject is compressed in the Tibetan; "those buddhas" has been supplied from the sense of those who have awakened fully. The passage continues a sentence begun in the prior passage, so the opening "and cause them to hold it" completes the thought "those buddhas teach this Perfection of Wisdom to others, give them prophecy, and lead them..." The sequence of verbs (hold, read, comprehend, recite, teach, explain, give transmission, memorize) is rendered consistently in both the causative and the imperative forms. The phrase "perhaps only one or two" renders a conditional construction implying rarity. The final line introduces Śakra's reply, which continues in the next passage. The passage breaks off mid-sentence, as the source does; the final sentence is left open to be completed in the following passage. The phrase "never separated from this approach" renders a slightly obscure Tibetan phrase (tshul dang ma bral ba). The Tibetan repeats the whole preceding sequence as the same formula recurs, so the repetition in the translation is faithful to the text. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as the Tibetan does; the comparison continues in the following passage. The phrase "stūpas ... containing the relics of the Tathāgatas" renders the Tibetan literally as "having the essence of the relics." The rendering "thousandfold world system" for the Tibetan "stong spyi phud" is a reasonable choice for the first of the three-thousandfold world-system series, though the term is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan. The Tibetan text ends mid-sentence, as the passage is cut at "having generated the mind of awakening"; the sentence continues in the next passage. The word rendered "adorns it with fine decoration" translates a term (rimor byed) whose exact nuance, "paint, decorate, or depict," is somewhat open. I kept the same rendering as in the preceding passage for continuity. The phrase "Not departing from the proper way" renders tshul dang ma bral ba, which could also be read as "not lacking the proper method." The "twofold thousandfold" system is the middle chiliocosm of the standard cosmology (the thousand-cubed, dvisāhasra madhyama lokadhātu), left in the text's own wording. The Tibetan text breaks off at the end with a conditional clause, "if he does so," and no concluding statement of merit; the translation reproduces this, since the passage ends mid-sentence. The phrase translated "in a way that is not divorced from the proper manner" (ཚུལ་དང་མ་བྲལ་བས) is a compressed, somewhat obscure construction; the rendering follows the sense of acting in accord with the proper method. The variant spellings rjod par byed / rjed par byed in the source are treated as the same verb, rendered "making offerings to it," in keeping with the surrounding list. The final sentence breaks off at the end of the Tibetan passage, as it did in the prior passage; its remaining clauses of reverence continue in the next section. I rendered the opening "Let that stand" for ལྟ་ཞོག, which marks the first scenario as a baseline set aside before the greater comparison. The phrase "the thought, 'May the lineage of the buddhas not be cut off'" follows the Tibetan's quoted wish. The phrase "it is the one who does so... " serves to carry the long chain of participles toward its eventual predicate, which falls in the next passage. The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing the preceding clause ("if such a person honors it, reveres it..."), which I have rendered to join seamlessly with the continuity text. The six-fold honorific series (བཀུར་སྟིར་ etc.) is rendered consistently as honors, reveres, esteems, makes offerings, depicts in paintings, and serves with respect; the sense of རྗེད་པར་བྱེད་ (esteem, as in treating as one's gain or honored possession) and རི་མོར་བྱེད་ (depict/paint) follows the standard Prajñāpāramitā usage. The phrase ཡིད་ཀྱིས་རྫས་སུ་རྟོག་པ is rendered as contemplating it in the mind as a real object, which is a literal reading of a somewhat opaque phrase. Śakra is glossed as lord of the gods in the narration, with his name Kauśika used by the Buddha. The phrase beginning "that person works so that the sacred Dharma may endure" and the clause about benefiting bodhisattvas "through the Dharma not being separated from its proper manner of presentation" (tshul dang ma bral ba) is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan; the rendering follows the evident sense. The numerical sequence of fractions includes the unusual term "khrag khrig" (a very large number), here rendered as "a vast multiple of ten million." The first sentence picks up directly from the preceding passage, so "that person" there refers to the one who sets the Perfection of Wisdom down in a book and makes offerings. The Tibetan uses the name Kauśika (an epithet of Śakra) where the continuity passage used "Friend"; I kept Kauśika here as it is the name in the text. The term rigs sngags (vidyā, here "spell of knowledge") means a mantra-like formula of knowledge; "spell of knowledge" preserves both senses. The pairing "equal to the unequaled" renders the standard formula asamasama. Two small points. The Tibetan reads "the great thousand of the three thousand" for the world system, which I have rendered literally. The phrase "what accords with the cause of the Perfection of Wisdom" translates a compound that could also be read as "a continuity of causes in keeping with the Perfection of Wisdom"; I kept the simpler reading. The sentence at the end is left open because the passage breaks off mid-sentence in the source. The line "the fourth section of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines" is a colophon marking the end of the fourth volume and is kept as a narrated divider. The Tibetan "ཁ་ཏོན" is rendered "recite" or "memorize" according to context. "Kauśika" is Śakra's own epithet and is kept in the address. The passage ends mid-episode, at Śakra's resolve to prevent the non-Buddhists from approaching. Two renderings are uncertain. The phrase "so that their eyes may not be set at ease" is a literal rendering of a difficult Tibetan clause about Māra's motive, probably meaning that he intends to unsettle or disturb the assembly. The two Tibetan royal names, rendered here as Bimbisāra and Prasenajit, are given in the text as "King Rūpacan-snying-po" and "King Gsal-rgyal," that is, Bimbisāra (Gzugs-can snying-po) and Prasenajit (Gsal-rgyal), the standard Tibetan equivalents. The passage opens mid-thought, continuing Śakra's reflection from the preceding passage, so it begins with the closing quotation mark. "Sons of the gods" renders lha'i bu (devaputra); "the gods of Māra's host" renders bdud kyi ris kyi lha. The simile of the ocean and its jewels is rendered closely. Kauśika is a standard epithet of Śakra (Indra) and is used here in direct address by the Buddha. The Tibetan has the opening lines of Ānanda's speech without an explicit marker, so I rendered them as a continuation of his words. The Tibetan "བསྔོས" is rendered "dedicated," in keeping with the standard sense of dedication to omniscience. In the line about the seeds, the Tibetan "ཚོགས་པ་དང་ཕྲད་ན" is rendered as meeting "the right gathering of conditions," which is the sense the context supports. The first sentence concludes the discourse of the preceding passage; I have rendered it as the closing line of the Buddha's words to Ānanda. In the final sentence, the Tibetan lists "ask about" (འདྲི་བ) among Śakra's list of practices, which does not appear in the Buddha's earlier list; I have kept it as it stands. The closing phrase "ལྟ་སྨོས་ཀྱང་ཅི་འཚལ" is rendered as a rhetorical "what need is there to speak of" the greater case. The passage breaks off mid-sentence in the source, so the final sentence is left open, as in the Tibetan. The phrase rendered "nor will that person be possessed of dread, either of others or of self, or of any thorough fear" follows the Tibetan literally; the Sanskrit parallel may read differently, but the sense is clear. The "Four Great Kings" are the guardian deities of the four directions, the lowest heaven of the desire realm. The Tibetan has no explicit mention of the Four Great Kings in this passage, but the first paragraph continues the previous sentence about the gods of that class. In the second paragraph, "Thirty-Three" is the standard class of gods ruled by Śakra (Indra). The Tibetan text breaks off after the Nirmāṇarati paragraph, in the middle of the sequence of verbs. In one instance the source reads "expound" where its parallels read "bear in mind"; I followed the pattern of the surrounding repetitions, which is probably a scribal variation. The passage breaks off mid-sentence, as the thought to be generated continues in the next passage. The list of form-realm gods is rendered by the conventional names of the Sanskrit divine classes (Brahmapāriṣadya, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, Śubhakṛtsna, Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Asaṃjñisattva, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana), while the Tibetan list here is abbreviated and somewhat irregular. The sentence about the gods who stand before Brahmā is an abbreviation instruction in the Tibetan, so it is rendered as such. The opening imperatives (look upon, pay homage, and so on) are addressed in the Tibetan as direct commands, apparently from the beings being instructed to attend to the volume. I have kept them as imperatives, continuing the thought from the previous passage. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end, as in the source. The Tibetan list of beings here uses "ལྟོ་འཕྱེ་ཆེན་པོ" for mahoragas ("great belly-crawlers") and "མི་འམ་ཅི" for kinnaras, as in the preceding passage. The Tibetan "གཟི་བརྗིད་ཆེ་བ" ("greatly majestic") appears to be a descriptive epithet applied to these beings, and I have rendered it literally. The Tibetan has "gods and nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans"; the corrupt-looking "ཅི" in "མི་འམ་ཅི" is the standard Tibetan rendering of kinnara (literally "is he human?"), and ལྟོ་འཕྱེ་ཆེན་པོ is mahoraga. The phrase "the Dharma's way, place" (chos kyi tshul gyi gnas) is rendered literally; it likely refers to the site where this Dharma teaching is held or kept. In the awakening-factors line, "the factors that lead to awakening" renders the standard bodhipākṣika dharmas. The passage ends mid-sentence in the Tibetan, as the text breaks off after "keeps it or sets it in place." Terms such as "so-and-so" render the placeholder names in the Tibetan (gag ge mo zhig, che ge mo), which are formulaic stand-ins for unspecified directions and a buddha's name. The repeated masculine pronoun follows the Tibetan phrasing "son or daughter of good family," used for both. The phrase "lightness and spaciousness" renders the repeated expression for bodily ease and expansiveness, which is slightly obscure in this transmission. "Moistened by the mental engagement" is a literal rendering of a stock simile for the nourishing effect of samādhi. The Tibetan phrase "བྱུར་བུར" (translated "as thick as a mass of clustered grains") is a difficult and probably corrupt or idiosyncratic expression, and my rendering follows the parallel context of the Eight Thousand Line text. The phrase "ཡང་དག་པའི་མཐས་རབ་ཏུ་ཕྱེ་བར་བལྟ" ("distinguished by the ultimate limit") corresponds to the Sanskrit idea of the Dharma body as the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi), the basis of the Tathāgata's true body. The passage ends mid-sentence in the Tibetan, which I have rendered as it stands. The seat passage: the Tibetan says "gods of the Dharma hall" (chos bzang lha'i mdun sa), which renders Sudharmā, the assembly hall of the gods; the speaker is Śakra (Indra), whose seat in that hall is honored even in his absence. The phrase "thoroughly pervaded" renders yongs su bsgos pa, literally "thoroughly imbued" or "perfumed," in the sense of being permeated by the Perfection of Wisdom. The sentence about the Perfection of Wisdom being "renowned as powerful and become the cause and condition" is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan; I have kept its sense without expanding it. The passage opens by completing Subhūti's statement, then marks the section break with its colophon, which I have kept as a closing line. In the colophon, the fifth bam po, the Tibetan text of the passage does not state the continuation of Śakra's reply; it is left unfinished here, as in the source. The humors are rendered as wind, bile and phlegm, the three standard Indian humors, with the "combined disorder" being the sannipāta, in which all three are disturbed together. The passage addresses "Noble Ānanda" at the start, so Śakra's reply to Ānanda runs into his address to the Blessed One without a marked break; I have marked the shift for the listener. The long numerical series (hundredth, thousandth, up to the final term) follows the Tibetan's escalating enumeration, whose last terms are inexact. "Bubbling mass" renders བྱུར་བུར་, understood as "filled to the brim and overflowing." Śakra and Kauśika are the same figure; the text uses both Tibetan renderings of his epithets (Indra, lord of the gods), and I have kept them as Śakra and Kauśika. The phrase rendered "in the nature of reality" translates "as dharmatā," that is, seeing the buddhas through the nature of reality rather than through their physical forms. The final sentence's six items, ending with "discerning of phenomena," stand for the sixth perfection, wisdom itself, whose precedence is the point being made. The passage breaks off mid-sentence in the Tibetan, since Śakra's description of the devotee continues beyond it; I have closed it with a full stop for narration, though the sentence is grammatically incomplete in the original. The phrase "keeps it or sets it in place" renders འཆང་ངམ་འཇོག་པ, which may mean keeping the text in one's possession or enshrining it. In the opening, the lesser quoted phrase "settles" is not an issue; the shadow analogy is the standard Eight Thousand Lines image for the non-difference of the perfections when unified through wisdom and dedicated to omniscience. The phrase about exhausting the aggregates and the analysis of the true limit is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan, and I have rendered it as literally as possible. The parallel "through X, to one with X" clauses describing the bodhisattva recipient follow the Tibetan's repeated instrumental structure. The passage ends mid-argument, as the Tibetan does, so the comparison of merit for the higher world systems is completed in the next passage. The Tibetan is somewhat corrupt or repetitive in places, notably the clause on "even if only in a small measure" (ཆུང་ངུ་ན), which I have rendered tentatively. The phrase rendered "the unsurpassed discerning of the true limit" (ཡང་དག་པའི་མཐའ་རབ་ཏུ་འབྱེད་པ) is obscure. The passage breaks off mid-quotation at its end, as in the Tibetan source, so the final speech is left unfinished. The clause beginning "having become fully awakened, you will bring to discipline..." is syntactically compressed and slightly irregular in the Tibetan, probably reflecting a Sanskrit idiom about the "true limit" (bhūtakoṭi); I have kept the rendering close to the wording. The "small thousand," "middling second thousand," and "great thousand of thousands" are the standard nested world-system counts: one thousand worlds, one million worlds, and one billion worlds. The final sentence of the Tibetan repeats the opening of this passage, as the framing quotation closes. The Tibetan breaks off mid-sentence at the end, so the final sentence is left open ("and so on") rather than completed. The phrase "exhaustion of the aggregates" and "true limit" (yang dag pa'i mtha', bhūtakoṭi) is rendered according to its sense in the Perfection of Wisdom literature, where the true limit is the ultimate reality in which the bodhisattva does not abide. The repeated passage in the opening paragraph reproduces the Tibetan's own repetition of the preceding speech, now framed as the speaker's own words of vow. The long middle sentence about the recipient is syntactically elliptical in the Tibetan, with a chain of instrumental phrases (faith through faith, and so on) and a series of verbs (teaching, establishing, praising, gladdening). I have rendered it as one continuous sentence to preserve the structure. "Exhaustion of the aggregates" and "true limit" (yang dag pa'i mtha', bhūtakoṭi) follow the Tibetan; the phrasing is somewhat condensed. The lines about writing and reading with "only" effort render the Tibetan's difficult clause with some interpretive smoothing. The passage on the semblance of the Perfection of Wisdom is doctrinally delicate. The Tibetan text seems internally troubled: the first and second descriptions of how the false teachers speak appear nearly identical. The sense is probably that the false teaching treats impermanence as an eternalist-style discernment of destruction, whereas the true view does not see the destruction of form as the impermanence of form. I have rendered the Tibetan as it stands, without smoothing. The sentence "Thereby be ruined" renders ཆུད་ཟོས་པར་གྱུར, literally "become wasted." The opening of this passage continues from the preceding one, so the "previous" son or daughter refers to the earlier person who writes and gives the text to others. The phrase rendered "the utter exhaustion of the aggregates, the unsurpassable, that is, in the discernment of the ultimate limit" is syntactically awkward in the Tibetan. It is a standard but difficult formula, and "ultimate limit" renders yang dag pa'i mtha' (Skt. bhūtakoṭi). The Tibetan text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of this passage, as the continuation falls in the next section. Since the reading is clearly corrupt or elliptical at "ཕུང་པོ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཟད་པ", my rendering is provisional there. The verbal chain "writes... gives" follows the Tibetan's linked instrumental and locative clauses; the sense is that the Perfection of Wisdom is given, with the appropriate qualities, to a worthy recipient. The wording "the awakening mind by means of the awakening mind" renders a Tibetan idiom of repeated instrumental and dative constructions, in which each quality is the means by which the bodhisattva possesses it. The phrase about the aggregates being "completely exhausted, unsurpassed, which is to say within the discernment of the true limit" is syntactically awkward in the Tibetan, and my rendering follows the text as given. The passage ends mid-sentence, as the Tibetan does. The passage begins mid-sentence, continuing the prior passage's subject, a person who gives this Perfection of Wisdom to a worthy bodhisattva. I have kept "he" for the bodhisattva being addressed. The phrase "the true limit" renders the Tibetan term for the ultimate boundary of reality (Skt. bhūtakoṭi). The clause on exhausting the aggregates is compressed in the Tibetan, and I have rendered it as literally as sense allows. Kauśika is a standard address for Śakra. The Tibetan names the once-returner's fruit throughout, a slight departure from the usual Sanskrit sequence, but I follow the text as given. The clause rendered "the supreme exhaustion of the aggregates, that is, the discernment of the ultimate limit" is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan, and the phrase "ཕུང་པོ་ཡང་དག་པར་ཟད་པ" is difficult. I have followed the reading in which the bodhisattva leads beings to the complete exhaustion of the aggregates, understood as the realization of the true limit (bhūtakoṭi). The three terms rendered "by words, by designations, by detailed indications, and by following expositions" (tshig, mtshon, rnam par mtshon, rjes su mtshon) are close synonyms for modes of explaining. The section colophon "Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines, sixth section" appears in the middle of the text and is retained as a structural marker. The Tibetan restates the full passage on the non-returner, with the final clause truncated at the end. The opening sentence is difficult. The phrase "exhaustion of the aggregates" together with "the limit of reality" (yang dag pa'i mtha', Skt. bhūtakoṭi) is rendered literally. The syntax of "bring to maturity" for mngon par 'dul bar byed is a considered choice. The Tibetan text has some scribal irregularities, for example "mi 'oṅ pa'i" in one place, which I have read as the non-returner. The final sentence breaks off and continues beyond this passage, so the grammatical completion is not given here. "The small chiliocosm" and the other chiliocosm terms are my interpretive glosses on the Tibetan numerical names. The passage repeats itself: the opening lines duplicate the end of the preceding passage, so the repetition is retained as in the Tibetan. The clause on the realms of sentient beings, the exhaustion of the aggregates, and the true limit is syntactically obscure in the Tibetan and probably reflects a difficult Sanskrit original. I have given a literal rendering of the construction rather than smoothing it into a more confident doctrinal claim. The sentence beginning "Kauśika, even so... Namely, one who writes out..." breaks off at the end of the passage and continues in the next section. In the opening, the Tibetan has the speaker address a single "you," then closes with the narrator's remark that he increases joy. I kept this as given. The "small thousand, second thousand, third thousand" sequence refers to the standard cosmological hierarchy culminating in the great trichiliocosm. The passage repeats a formula, first with the arhat and then with the pratyekabuddha as the result discerned. The sentence about bringing beings to maturity is rendered in the same way in both occurrences, though the Tibetan in the first occurrence reads "purifying" (sbyong) and in the repetition "conducting" (spyod) the person's mind; I have followed the sense of purification in both. The phrase "exhaustion of the aggregates... the true limit" is a compressed and somewhat obscure formula, and I have kept it close to the Tibetan. The final sentence is left open in the Tibetan, as the passage ends mid-sentence and the sense continues beyond this section. The phrase "to a bodhisattva who has generated the awakening mind" follows the Tibetan syntax, which is dense and repetitive. The tiered world-system terms are rendered literally: the small thousand, middling twofold thousand, and great threefold thousand. The Tibetan passage ends abruptly with a set-aside formula ("let alone...") whose main clause lies in the following passage, so the sentence is left open. In the second paragraph, the phrase about taming beings "within the unsurpassable exhaustion of the aggregates... distinguished in the true limit" is syntactically dense and likely corrupt or elliptical in the Tibetan; I have rendered it as literally as sense allows.
