In the final paragraph, the opening "Kauschika" is a slip for Kauśika, the epithet of Śakra (Indra), the interlocutor in this sūtra. The Tibetan phrase for the first world system reads stong spyi phud, literally something like "the chief or topmost of the thousand," corresponding to the "small chiliocosm" (one thousand worlds); the second, "middle" thousand and the third, "great thousand of thousands," complete the standard threefold cosmology (the three-thousand great-thousand world system). The opening line of the passage as given reads "all the beings" with the thousand-world system implicit; I rendered it as the first of the series for clarity. The earlier continuity text uses "Kauschika" once; I have normalized to Kauśika throughout, in line with the rest of the continuity. The passage breaks off mid-argument: the main clause stating the comparison of merit is not yet given, and the repeated "set aside the merit" clauses build toward it. The opening sentence is syntactically elliptical in the Tibetan, and I have rendered it as a continuation of the preceding hypothetical, adding "suppose" for clarity. The terms for the nested world systems (the small, middling, and great thousand realms) follow the standard Prajñāpāramitā cosmological scheme, and the Tibetan phrasing is rendered closely rather than normalized. The sentence "the lord of the gods... Sugata" renders བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པ as Sugata, a Buddha epithet in Śakra's address. The phrase translated "make that offering bring great fruit and great reward" renders the Tibetan literally as making the doing of their work bear great fruit and great reward for the donors. The sense is that alms-givers' gifts become greatly fruitful, as in the standard formula. The word "nature" in "such is the very nature" renders the Tibetan "de lta bu nyid," meaning "exactly thus." The opening phrase about Gaṅgā-sand-many world systems is rendered from the Tibetan as given, though the preceding English summary lacked it. The passage ends mid-sentence in the Tibetan, with "that is to say" (te), so the list of what is rejoiced in continues in the following passage. The opening lines complete the answer to Subhūti's "And why is that?" from the preceding passage. The chapter colophon ("the fifth chapter") is rendered as it stands, though it is a textual marker rather than part of the spoken discourse. The phrase "that which equals the unequaled" renders the Tibetan literally, following the Sanskrit sense of a term that equals what has no equal. The passage is one long sentence, a continuation of the bodhisattva's rejoicing, so I have supplied the repeated phrase "rejoices in" to keep it intelligible when heard aloud. The Tibetan lists the roots of virtue in a series ending with "and" clauses.

The Tibetan says "sounding" the conch twice in the same way (dung 'bud pa and dung sgrogs pa). I rendered them as "blowing" and "proclaiming" to preserve the distinction.

"Bases of meritorious action" renders bsod nams bya ba'i dngos po (Skt. puṇyakriyāvastu), the standard threefold category of giving, discipline, and meditation. The list of beings, which in this tradition continues the eight classes of nonhuman beings, renders དྲི་ཟ as gandharva, ནམ་མཁའ་ལྡིང་ as garuḍa, མི་འམ་ཅི་ as kinnara, and ལྟོ་འཕྱེ་ཆེན་པོ as mahoraga. The Tibetan text breaks off mid-question at the end of this passage, so the final sentence is left as a question, as in the source. The "bases" (dngos po) in Subhūti's reply carry the sense of "real entities" or "substrata," which is why I give "no real basis" where the passage speaks of attachment. The passage opens with the tail of the preceding sentence, which is joined here to the continuity text's closing question. The Tibetan "chapter-end" line (the seventh volume of the Eight Thousand Line Perfection of Wisdom) falls in the middle of the discourse, so it is kept as a plain colophon sentence. The final sentence breaks off where the next section begins and is rendered as it stands. The long list of the buddhas' qualities follows the standard arhat formula, adapted to describe the buddhas. "Cut off the path, cut off the entering" renders the Tibetan literally; the sense is that the avenues of rebirth are severed. The eight classes of beings (gods through non-humans) are given with their usual Sanskrit identities: gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas. The passage ends with Subhūti's question, so the text breaks mid-exchange, and Maitreya's reply begins in the next passage. The passage breaks off mid-sentence, with its list of roots of virtue to be continued in the following passage. The clause about the Buddhas whose "paths are cut off" is difficult, and I have rendered it literally. In the "exhausted" sentence the Tibetan is terse, and "devoid of any basis" is my interpretive rendering of bral ba. The phrase "form the perception of mind" renders sems su 'du shes pa, meaning to conceive of it as a really existing mind. The passage breaks off mid-sentence in the Tibetan, as the main verb belongs to the continuation, so the final sentence is left open. The phrase "cut off the path, cut off entry, cut off conceptual elaboration" is rendered literally. It most likely refers to the Buddhas having severed the paths and entrances of saṃsāric rebirth and elaboration. I have supplied "considers" as the governing verb for the closing sentence from context, since the Tibetan has not yet reached it; this may change when the next passage supplies the actual verb. "Hearers" here is the Tibetan nyan thos, rendered per the house glossary as hearer (śrāvaka). The passage begins in the middle of a long sentence from the previous section, so the opening "from then until" continues the earlier span from the first generation of the mind of awakening. The translation of the Tibetan honorific question as "Venerable Subhūti may ask" is a supplied connective; the Tibetan simply poses the question ("how...?") in the flow of the text, and the speaker's address to Subhūti is implicit from the preceding passage. The passage breaks off mid-sentence, as the Tibetan continues the list of roots of virtue to be dedicated. The phrase "I" in the third nature-of-reality clause (ང་ཡིན) is probably a scribal error for "that" (དེ་ཡིན), and is rendered as "just this." The phrase rendered "cut off the path, cut off entry..." follows the Tibetan literally, referring to the cutting off of the paths of rebirth. The Tibetan text is somewhat elliptical and the speaker changes without marking. I have supplied the exchange between Subhūti and the Blessed One (the question beginning "How does a bodhisattva..." and the answer beginning "Suppose the one who dedicates...") to keep the passage intelligible aloud. The Tibetan reads as continuous prose. "Volitional formation of merit" renders bsod nams mngon par 'du byed pa (puṇyābhisaṃskāra). The list of eight classes of beings has been normalized with standard Sanskrit names (gandharva, garuḍa, kinnara, mahoraga) for the Tibetan dri za, nam mkha' lding, mi 'am ci, and lto 'phye chen po. The final sentence breaks off mid-argument, as the passage ends there; I have rendered it as it stands. The opening clause is difficult: it reads literally "if he does not know even thus, 'all conditioning factors are secluded and peaceful,'" which I have taken as the Perfection-of-Wisdom-style paradox that such unknowing is itself wisdom, since there is no one to apprehend the seclusion. In "do not say so," the Tibetan imperative is addressed to the objector. I rendered "mtshan ma" as "sign" and "dmigs pa" as "object of focus" or "fixation" according to context. The passage breaks off mid-argument, with the reply to "Why is this so?" falling in the next passage. The long sequence of tenses (past, future, present) in the instruction is rendered in compressed form, following the Tibetan's repeated triple structure. "Aggregate" here renders phung po in the sense of the five "aggregates of the Dharma" (moral discipline, absorption, wisdom, liberation, and the vision of liberation), not the five skandhas of the person. The opening sentence follows on the preceding passage's question, "Why is this so?" The poison is the perception of an object, which makes a dedication through signs like a poisoned meal. In the verb "to take up" (yongs su gzung ba), I have rendered the sense of embracing or holding the roots of virtue so that they are well secured. The phrase rendered "not belonging to" the realms and times means "not included in" (Skt. asaṃgṛhīta or aparyāpanna): the dedicated virtue, like the act of dedicating, transcends the three realms and three times. In the final sentence I took mngon par chags shing mtshan mar byed pa as "becomes attached and makes a sign," which is the opposite of the signless dedication taught above. The passage breaks off mid-sentence, since the source text ends there with "and" (དང་), and the rendering follows it. The phrase "equal to the unequaled" translates a standard Prajñāpāramitā formula (མི་མཉམ་པ་དང་མཉམ་པ) whose literal sense is "equal to the unequal"; it is conventionally rendered as above. The passage breaks off mid-sentence, as the source does. The list of requisites (robes, alms food, and so on) continues in the next passage. The Tibetan repeatedly pairs the phrase "set aside the merit" with the supposition that precedes it; I have kept this rhythm of supposition and setting aside, since it is the structure of the sūtra's argument. The five higher knowledges are the standard abhijñās (divine eye, divine ear, knowing others' minds, recollection of past lives, and miraculous powers). The phrase "perception that apprehends an object" renders dmigs pa'i 'du shes, the perception that grasps at a referent and thus remains bound to dualistic reference; its contrast is the non-referential dedication "of the dharmadhātu." The final phrase about the earlier generosity ("comes to be counted as great only in the sense of a reckonable number") renders a terse and slightly corrupt-looking Tibetan sentence; the sense given follows the argument of the passage. The long numerical series is rendered as it stands, with its repetitive compounds reflecting the Tibetan. The final sentence breaks off mid-construction in the Tibetan, since the passage ends on "having aroused the awakening mind." The sense clearly continues into the next passage, so the English leaves it open. The names of the heavens follow standard equivalents: Heaven Without Combat is Yāma, Joyful Heaven is Tuṣita, and the final five are the Pure Abodes (Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Akaniṣṭha). "Dharmadhātu" in the gods' praise is kept as in the Tibetan, which qualifies the dedication. Gloss: the Thirty-Three is the heaven ruled by Indra. The passage opens mid-sentence, continuing the preceding comparison, so I rendered it as a series of "suppose that" clauses to keep the conditional structure audible. The volume colophon in the middle belongs to the sūtra's text division and is retained as spoken. The passage ends mid-sentence, as the quotation of the Buddha's words by Subhūti continues in the next passage. The long series of numerical fractions is rendered approximately; the terms involving "khrag khrig" (an immense number) are given as "billionth" for narration. Subhūti's opening speech is rendered as a direct continuation of the question begun in the preceding passage. The repeated phrase "as liberation is, so is..." renders the Tibetan "rnam par grol ba ci lta ba de bzhin du," which equates each factor with the nature of liberation, that is, with its emptiness and unborn nature. I rendered it literally to keep that doctrinal force. The passage ends mid-sentence in the Tibetan, since the clause continues into the next passage; I have left the sentence open to match. The comparison is a long hypothetical whose main clause ("the merit of the bodhisattva who rejoices in this way is far greater") comes later, so the "suppose" clauses stay unresolved here. "Perception of objective support" renders dmigs pa'i 'du shes (Skt. upalambha-saṃjñā), meaning giving and discipline that still grasp at the three spheres of giver, recipient, and gift; the parenthetical gloss gives this in plain terms. The Tibetan opening is a continuation of the preceding sentence, so the passage begins mid-sentence as a list of what the bodhisattva rejoices in. The sentence about patience is elliptical and repetitive in the Tibetan, with the abbreviation marker "from... up to"; I have rendered it in a way that smooths the repetition while preserving its sense. The inconsistency of the "pride" (ང་རྒྱལ) qualification is as in the source: patience practiced with pride and objective support is the flawed kind being contrasted with the wisdom-embraced rejoicing. The passage breaks off in mid-sentence, as is the case in the Tibetan text at this point, and the sentence continues in the following section. In the second paragraph I read the very large fractions as a series ascending toward ten-millionths. The final fraction in the Tibetan is awkward, and I rendered it literally as given. The phrase "a perception of objective support" renders the Tibetan idiom of apprehending an object, as in the preceding passage, to keep terminology consistent. The sentence about bodhisattvas "leaving aside" patience is a rhetorical setup, to be completed by the matching comparison in the next section. The opening phrase begins mid-sentence, continuing the list of aggregates from the preceding passage, so I rendered it as a continuation ("And also..."). The Tibetan text is somewhat repetitive, as is typical of the Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines. The epithets of the rejoicing (dam pa, gtso bo, rab, mchog rab, gya nom pa, and so on) are a conventional list, and some members are difficult to distinguish precisely; I have followed the standard sense of excellence and incomparability. The phrase "comparable only to the incomparable" renders a deliberately paradoxical pair (mi mnyam pa and mnyam pa) with "utterly without peer," following the sūtra's rhetorical intent. The sentence "Let that be as it may" renders the idiom lta zhog, meaning "never mind that case," since the sūtra proceeds to a still greater scenario. The honorific series at the opening reflects the standard Perfection of Wisdom litany. The renderings "without superior" and "higher even than the highest" follow the Tibetan sequence. The final numerical sequence uses the Tibetan's compounded counting terms, and I have rendered the largest as a hundred-thousand-times-a-billionth part to convey the escalating scale rather than a precise figure. The phrase "rejoicing that accompanies" the merit follows the technical phrasing of the sūtra. The five eyes are the physical eye, divine eye, wisdom eye, Dharma eye, and buddha eye. The passage breaks off mid-sentence at the end; the sentence continues in the next section. In the first part, "own-characteristic" renders the Tibetan literally. The phrase "the habitual tendencies of the cognitive obscurations" follows the Tibetan, which pairs the afflictions with the imprints of the cognitive obscuration. "Dedicates to omniscience" follows the Tibetan; "caught up in objectifying" renders "those with a referent," meaning bodhisattvas who still apprehend objects. The verb གཏོད་པ (gtod pa) is rendered as "destroy," following the sense of the Sanskrit underlying this section (likely a form of "to crush/injure"), but the sense could be "to harm" or "to injure." The final line of the Blessed One's reply, "it destroys in the way that it does not destroy," is the paradoxical sense of the Tibetan; the point is that the Perfection of Wisdom neither objectifies nor harms phenomena, since they are by nature unfindable. The opening sentence is a continuation of the preceding passage, in which Śāriputra enumerates the merit of the other perfections as overpowered by the merit of meditative concentration; the phrase "on this basis" renders གཞི་འདི་ལས, and the logic is that the question concerns what outshines even these. The opening sentence is Śakra's continuing speech, following the preceding "Śakra said:". The verb pair "distant" and "gather / amass" (རིང་དུ་བྱེད, གསོག་ཏུ་བྱེད, གསོབ་ཏུ་བྱེད) is rendered literally; the Tibetan is terse and the idea is that conceiving of the perfection as an object to be accumulated alienates one from it. Likewise "fully illumined" renders ཡོངས་སུ་གསལ་བར་བྱས་པ, and the second "gathering" pair (སྡུད་པ, གཡེངས་པ) is rendered as "gather together" and "scatter." The phrase "this very focusing upon beings becomes for him a great object of fixation" takes དམིགས་པ as "object of focus/fixation," in the sense of objectifying. The sentence about "beings accomplish the powers perfectly" follows the Tibetan as given; the parallel logic (beings, therefore the Tathāgata's powers) is abrupt in the text itself. The phrase "in a single-minded way" renders གཅིག་ཏུ, with ཚུལ་བསྲུངས་ taken as keeping discipline, in line with the Tibetan's own wording. The Tibetan "ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ" is rendered "venerable." The final question breaks off at the passage boundary and may be continued in the next section. The Tibetan opens mid-question with no explicit speaker; it continues Subhūti's question from the preceding passage, so I have rendered it as the content of that question. The term "grounds" renders rnam grangs, which here carries the sense of a basis or mode of explanation; "the faculties differ in degree" renders dbang po'i rim pa, literally a gradation of faculties. The phrase "deprived of the Dharma" renders chos kyis phongs pa, the standard expression for the karma of rejecting the Dharma. The very large number terms near the end (bye ba khrag khrig, etc.) follow the Tibetan's escalating numerical series; I have rendered them in a smooth progression, with the final term given as "hundreds of thousands of millions," since the Tibetan's last unit is a transliterated Sanskrit-style number of uncertain exact value. The phrase "beginners who are by nature without the fortune for it" renders the Tibetan's qualification of these persons as lacking the destiny or capacity for the Dharma. Near the end, the Tibetan has a statement that the Blessed One "showed" the body-size of such a person, which Śāriputra says here as a closing remark. The sentence is abrupt, probably because it leads into the next passage, where the size is described, so I have kept it as written. The phrase rendered "rejecters of the Dharma" corresponds to the standard Sanskrit notion of dharma-pratikṣepa, the rejection of the Dharma. The text is evidently corrupt or compressed in places. The opening phrase translated "leave aside the measure" (ལྟ་ཞོག་ཤིག) is rendered according to the sense the argument requires, since the Buddha refuses to state the measure. The phrase "the manifold suffering that is spoken of" is also condensed in the Tibetan. In the description of the foolish people, the verb "go forth" (rab tu 'byung) is kept literally, and the point is that they are ordained within the well-taught teaching, which makes their rejection of the Perfection of Wisdom more grave. The repeated word "cast back" renders the verb "to throw back" (phyir bcil), used here in the sense of rejection and repudiation. The Tibetan here uses the verb ཕྱིར་བཅིལ་ / ཕྱིར་གཞིལ་ / ཕྱིར་འཇིལ་ in variant spellings; I have rendered all consistently as "cast back" or "reject," following the preceding passage. The phrase "former extreme" and "later extreme" renders the past and future limits (Skt. pūrvānta, aparānta); "present arising" renders ད་ལྟར་བྱུང་བ. The passage runs across a chapter boundary and a colophon, which are retained as in the source. The recurring phrase "ཐ་མི་དད་ཅིང་མཆད་པ" is rendered "not different, and not divided"; the final verb is a corrupt or unusual reading, probably standing for "not separate, not cut apart," and the rendering follows the evident sense. The passage ends mid-exchange with Śāriputra's next statement, which continues in the following passage. The Tibetan rendering ཐོབ་པ་མ་མཆིས་པ་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་མ་མཆིས་པ is taken as "no attainment and no realization." The repeated phrase ཤིན་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ is rendered "utter purity." The passage ends with a quotation introduction, as in the source, so the final line is left open to continue in the next passage. The terms མ་འཚལ་ and ཤེས་ in the sequence on grasping and knowing are rendered "grasp" and "know" respectively, following the sense of the Tibetan as it stands. The opening Tibetan reads མུ་མ་མཆིས་པ ("without end/limit," Skt. likely ananta or aparyanta), where the preceding English passage rendered "pure"; the text as given differs, so I rendered literally. The final sentence breaks off mid-thought, as the passage does, so I left it unfinished to match the source. The sense of Subhūti's dedication remark is that dedicating "the first thought" as a grasped object is itself attachment, since the intrinsic nature of mind cannot be dedicated. The passage turns on the Tibetan wordplay of rang bzhin (intrinsic nature) and rang bzhin med pa (without intrinsic nature), together with mtshan nyid med pa and mtshan nyid gcig pa (no characteristic and single characteristic). I have kept the paradoxical sense as written. The word mtshan ma ("sign") is rendered consistently as "sign," in the sense of a conceptually fixed mark or reference point, which is what the Buddha identifies as the root of attachment here. The sentence "rang bzhin gang yin pa de ni rang bzhin med pa" is terse; I read it as the Prajñāpāramitā idiom that the only intrinsic nature of phenomena is their lack of intrinsic nature. The Tibetan "ཆགས་པའི་མཐའ" is rendered "extremes of attachment," following the Tibetan as it stands. The phrase "ཆགས་པ་དང་བཅས་པ་ཉིད་དང་ཆགས་པ་མ་མཆིས་པ་ཉིད" is taken as "being with attachment and being without attachment," and Subhūti's exclamation is rendered closely to the Tibetan, which is somewhat compressed. The final sentence about the Great Kings, Śakras, and Brahmās is syntactically dense in the Tibetan; I have read the main verb as "came to know" (ཤེས་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ), governing all three clauses. The chapter's Tibetan title here is "Purification" (རྣམ་པར་དག་པ), as given in the colophon. The Tibetan "bya ca smra ba" in the phrase about space and the echo is rendered here as "echo" (the Tibetan is likely "brag ca" meaning echo). The sentence "Blessed One, how wonderful" renders an exclamation of wonder (e ma'o). The passage's last sentence is cut off mid-speech by the piece boundary, so the next piece will carry Subhūti's words. The phrase "does not truly understand" in the passage on the bodhisattva follows the Tibetan literally. The sentence is elliptical and could be read as "even though the bodhisattva does not truly know it, he practices"; the sense is that the practitioner does not apprehend the perfection as an object. The Tibetan text for "writes down" is "yi ger 'dri ba." The sentence beginning "Subhūti, many obstacles will arise" mentions the practices in order; the verb for writing appears only there. The phrase "perfection of what is not to be forgotten" renders a term whose exact sense is slightly uncertain in the Tibetan (literally something like "not lost" or "not wasted"). The Tibetan "mi 'phrogs pa" at the end is rendered "what cannot be seized." Several lines in this litany are paradoxical by design: "impermanence" and "suffering" here are presented as perfections because uncompounded phenomena and space-like equality are ultimately beyond the ordinary senses of those words. Likewise "the perfection that has nothing to be tamed" (འདུལ་བ་མེད་པ) follows the sense that, with no real past, future, or present, nothing remains to be disciplined. "Unmistaken" is read as qualifying suchness (ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པ). The two statements about "not apprehended" (mi dmigs pa) and "no apprehending" follow the standard Prajñāpāramitā idiom. "The self-arisen" renders rang byung and is probably Svayambhū-related wording, kept literal. The "fully discriminating knowledges" is the pratisaṃvid set. The final sentence of the piece breaks off mid-statement, and the next piece completes it. The word rendered "he" for the bodhisattva is a stylistic choice for the generic subject. The words rendered "engage in yogic practice" translate the verb "rnal 'byor du byed pa," meaning to devote oneself to practice. The piece ends mid-sentence, as the cut falls there; the sentence continues in the next piece. In the Tibetan the second paragraph's wording ("does not practice... thus does not abide") is a deliberate mirror of the first and has been kept as written. The words "Should it be taught" render a respectful Tibetan construction that is an implied question in context. The passage ends mid-question ("Why is that?"), and the answer follows in the next piece. The phrase "Even though ... face to face" renders "mngon sum du ni lung ma bstan pa", which I take as "not directly prophesied". The man in the first simile gives no thought to bandits (chom po), the dangers of the wilderness. The opening clause continues a sentence begun in the preceding piece, so the subject (the bodhisattvas, great beings, just described) is supplied by that context. The Tibetan "mi rtog" is rendered as "has no conceptual thought," following the ordinary sense of rtog pa as conceptualization. "Spyad par gyur pa" is rendered "one who has practiced," a title that the passage itself explains. The phrase "ཡི་དམ་མ་ཉམས་པའི" is rendered "who have not lost their commitment"; yi dam here has the sense of a resolve or pledge, not a tutelary deity. "Mastered" renders ཀུན་ཆུབ་པར་བྱེད་པ, literally "thoroughly comprehends." The sentence about requests to be written is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan; it is taken as a future conditional request for the text to be copied. "Vartani" (བར་ཏ་ནི, also written བར་ཏ་ནི་) is reconstructed tentatively from the Tibetan transliteration; the region is not securely identified. The phrase about the Dharma and Vinaya having reached "their essence and their last remnant" renders a difficult Tibetan expression (སྙིང་པོ་སར་བ་ཐོབ་པ) and is a best reading of it. The sentence on the sūtras appearing in the south, Vartani, and the north continues in the following piece. The passage ends mid-sentence, with the construction continuing in the next piece. The final sentence is rendered as a dangling clause to preserve this. The long numerical series of beings is rendered with approximate standard multiples; the Tibetan repeats the series as "many" of each unit, and the exact word-for-word values of the largest terms are conventional. The opening clause, which continues a sentence begun in the preceding piece, reads literally "from whom (the Tathāgatas) this Perfection of Wisdom will be heard extensively." I have taken it as a locative of the buddha fields, to link it with the following sentence. The grammar of the intermediate passage on bodhisattvas who "seek and find" is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan, and I have kept the structure faithfully rather than smoothing it. The sequence of large numbers (hundreds, thousands, hundreds of thousands, and so on) follows the Tibetan literally, with the final term, khrag khrig, rendered as "billions" in line with the standard Prajñāpāramitā enumeration. The phrase "ཡི་གེར་འདྲི་བ" is rendered "inquisitive about the letters," meaning an excessive preoccupation with the written form; the sense is somewhat compressed and uncertain. The lines between the end of the tenth chapter and the beginning of the eleventh volume are colophon material and have been translated as they appear. The first sentence of the passage, "ཕན་ཚུན་དང་ལྡན་པས" with "རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ", is awkward in the Tibetan. I have rendered it as distraction through mutual awareness of one another, which is a tentative reading. The clause "གང་དུ་དེ་དག་གིས་སླར་རྣལ་འབྱོར་ཉིད་དུ་བྱ་བར་འགྱུར་བ" is also obscure; I have followed the sense that wherever they must again take up practice, they will be held in saṃsāra for as many eons as their thoughts. The piece ends mid-sentence ("wherever the bodhisattva vehicle has not been taught"); the next piece completes it. In the elephant simile, "judged it to be like whatever he felt of it" renders the Tibetan "he judged it to be wherever there was light," which is awkward in the source; the sense is that he mistakes a part touched in the dark for the whole elephant. Rendered "Vaijayanta palace" for རྣམ་པར་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཁང་པ (Skt. vaijayanta, Indra's palace). The "fortress ruler" (མཁར་གྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ) is a local or petty king, as the comparison continues in the next piece. The passage ends mid-sentence, as the piece is cut there. The piece ends mid-sentence, as it was cut there; the sentence continues in the next piece. In the Tibetan, the sentence "Subhūti, this too should be understood as the work of māra" translates literally; the later phrase about being "truly accomplished" renders a difficult clause, and it may also be read as "it is hard for bodhisattvas to be perfectly achieved." Viśikhā (bi shi khā) and Śivika (shi bi ka) are transliterated in the Tibetan and are reconstructed here. The Sanskrit tradition for this passage may differ; Viśikhā may mean a street or lane. The word translated "predators" (la gcan) is a rare term, and "those who instruct in everything" (kun tu ston pa) is rendered literally. The line about a priceless jewel versus a jewel of small value follows the standard sense of the passage. The phrase "ལག་ཅན་གྱི་ཆོ་ལོ་ལྟ་བ" is obscure; I have rendered it as the spectacle of entertainers' performances, which is a tentative reading. "བདག་ལ་བར་ཆད་བྱེད་པར" in the gains passage is probably a slip for "བདག་ལ" or similar, and I have read it as the gains becoming an obstacle to him. The sentence breaks off at the end of the piece and continues in the next. The phrase ཆོས་ཀྱི་བར་ཆད་དུ་གྱུར་པས is rendered "has become an obstacle to the Dharma." The final sentence is somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan, and I have kept its sense without adding explanation. The repeated "lack of harmony" renders ཚོགས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བ, literally "separated from the assembly" or "without the gathering of conditions," in the sense that the necessary conditions for teaching and hearing fail to come together. The phrase "not provided with a gathering" renders the Tibetan literally, and the nuance of "gathering" (tshogs pa, probably meaning a harmonious assembly or the coming together of favorable conditions) is uncertain. The quotation attributed to the Blessed One about rebirth ("not even as brief as a fingersnap") is an uncertain rendering of a difficult, apparently corrupt phrase in the Tibetan. The last clause of the speaker's address, about meeting ruin and suffering again, is also somewhat obscure in the Tibetan. The opening clause continues a sentence begun in the previous piece, where a person is distracted by thoughts of household business. The Tibetan for "newly set out" and the repeated phrase about being "made to doubt" are rendered closely. The sentence beginning "Rather, only what is included within my sūtras" is a Māra-quoted claim; the Tibetan is somewhat elliptical here, and the sense given is the standard reading of the Prajñāpāramitā text. The final clause of the text just before this piece is completed here by the opening sentence, whose subject is the newly set out, weak-minded bodhisattvas who fall into doubt. The phrase "realizing the true limit" renders the Tibetan for Skt. bhūtakoṭi, the Māra-figure's claim being that the bodhisattva will fall into the śrāvaka's cessation. "Vehicle" here is the Great Vehicle. The passage runs from the end of chapter 11 into the beginning of chapter 12, with the colophon and volume heading rendered as they stand. The opening "dgra" in the Tibetan appears to be a damaged or unusual reading (possibly "they" with a corrupt particle); I took the sense as "in that way." In the mother simile the humoral and affliction terms are rendered conventionally. The word translated here as "indestructible" (mi 'jig) plays on 'jig rten, "world," which the tradition glosses as that which is perishable (the Sanskrit loka). The passage says the aggregates are called the world because their emptiness cannot be destroyed. The phrase "without any real entity" renders dngos po med pa, the absence of any substantial thing in sentient beings. The passage turns on a series of paired terms for states of mind: contracted (bsdus pa, Skt. saṃkṣipta), distracted (gyengs pa, Skt. vikṣipta), and afflicted (kun nas nyon mongs par gyur pa, Skt. saṃkliṣṭa). The sentence "that contracted mind, together with its contraction, is exhausted" is rendered literally. The Tibetan "de bsdus pa dang bcas pa" is somewhat elliptical, and the sense follows the usual Perfection of Wisdom point that exhaustion and its inexhaustibility are not different. The piece ends with a question whose answer begins in the next piece. Both the verb "to be afflicted" and the noun "affliction" here render the same Tibetan root (nyon mongs), so the opening sentence is deliberately repetitive; "defilement" in the final section renders zag pa (āsrava), which is distinct from affliction. The passage is part of the long Perfection of Wisdom enumeration of the Tathāgata's knowledge of minds, and each section follows the same question-and-answer pattern. The phrase "dngos po med par gzol ba lhun gyis grub pa" is rendered closely as "inclined toward the absence of real entities, and this is spontaneously accomplished"; the syntax of the original is terse and the sense is somewhat compressed. In the sentence about freedom from attachment, the Tibetan has "the freedom (bral ba) of the mind is not the mind's being with attachment"; I have kept this literal reading. The sentence "the freedom of the mind is not a state of having aversion" follows the Tibetan literally. In the aversion passage the final line as transmitted reads "freed from aversion" where the parallel would suggest "that has aversion"; I have kept the logic of the parallel with the delusion passage. The last sentence is the start of a new series (on the "expansive" or "vast" mind), which continues in the next piece. The terms for "vast" (rgya chen po) and "exalted" (sems chen po, literally "great mind") correspond to the standard sequence of mind-types in the Perfection of Wisdom. The Tibetan text itself says "became exalted" (chen por gyur pa); "exalted" is used here for readability. The sentence "because minds are never separated from their nature" renders a somewhat compressed Tibetan clause, "sems rnams bral ba med pa'i phyir", and the sense given follows the context of non-separation. The final sentence of the piece contains the question but no stated answer in the Tibetan; the passage ends there and the answer is not supplied in this piece, so I have rendered it as it stands without adding anything. "The three eyes" (spyan gsum) is rendered literally; the sense of the phrase "or all of them" is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan. The terms sems bla na yod pa and sems bla na med pa (literally "having something higher" and "having nothing higher") are rendered "surpassable" and "unsurpassable," following the standard Prajñāpāramitā usage (Skt. sauttara and anuttara citta). The passage contains a duplicated sentence on the surpassable mind, as in the Tibetan. "Concentrated" and "unconcentrated" render the terms for being placed or not placed in meditative equipoise (samāhita and asamāhita). The terms ཕྱེ་བ and བཙུམས་པ, "open" and "closed," are rendered literally. The Tibetan is somewhat ambiguous, and this passage seems to correspond to the Sanskrit sequence of "contracted" and "distracted" (saṃkṣipta, vikṣipta) minds. The literal rendering has been kept, and the sequel continues the list through the aggregates. The phrase "open mind" and "closed mind" renders phye ba and btsum pa, literally "opened" and "closed"; in this sūtra it refers to minds that are expansive or distracted versus contracted. The sense is rendered in the standard way. The passage restates the traditional fourfold undetermined questions, concerning the Tathāgata after death and the self and world being permanent or having an end, as views that rest upon the aggregates. The colophon-like line between the passage's two halves marks the division between fascicles twelve and thirteen in the Tibetan text and is rendered as a transition. The first sentence ("have no end") departs from the preceding context, which reads "with an end." This is evidently the second of the four standard positions, and I follow the text as given. "Open and closed minds" renders a pair meaning distracted or expansive and contracted or withdrawn states of mind (Skt. vikṣipta and saṃkṣipta). The phrase "designates, within suchness" follows the Tibetan literally; it expresses that the Tathāgata applies these labels to a single suchness. The passage ends mid-sentence, as the piece is cut here; the sense continues in the next piece. The phrase "paint it in images" renders a verb of depicting or portraying, and may be read as making representations of the Dharma. The phrase "knows what has been done for him and feels gratitude for it" renders the standard idiom for gratitude (Skt. kṛtajña, kṛtavedin), with the Tibetan taking "what has been done" as the benefit received. "Not constructed by any conditioning activity" renders the Tibetan for "not fully constructed" (Skt. anabhisaṃskṛta). The chapter title in the Tibetan is "Truly Showing the World" (jig rten yang dag par ston pa). The final lines of the passage lead directly into the Buddha's next explanation, which falls in the following piece. The last phrase of the Buddha's reply, "a deed equal to the unequaled" (mi mnyam pa dang mnyam pa), could also be read as "unequal and equal", but I have followed the parallel sense of "equal to the unequaled." The term rang byung (self-arisen) is rendered as "self-arisen nature," following the standard sense of svayambhū in this sūtra's list of buddha-qualities. The phrase "unequal and equal" renders mi mnyam pa dang mnyam pa, the sūtra's paradoxical formulation (asamasama); the sense is "peerless, equal only to the unequalled." The final sentence continues into the next piece. The phrase "the Dharma that has become consciousness" renders a difficult clause (rnam par shes par gyur pa'i chos); the sense may be a designation of what has become known or cognized. The word rendered "equality" and "comparison" (mnyam pa, snyom pa) is used in a deliberately plural sense in this passage, and the repeated "unequal and equal" is a paradox of the text, not a scribal error. The tshad ma here means "measure," not "valid cognition." The phrase rang byang chub, "self-arisen awakening," is rendered literally here. Context suggests the awakening of the solitary buddhas. The sūtra's earlier phrase "this very Fortunate Eon" refers to the Bhadrakalpa, the present eon. The final colophon line is rendered as part of the text, since it appears in the Tibetan. The phrase "stage of those who follow through faith" renders the Tibetan "dad pa'i rjes su 'brang ba'i sa" (Skt. śraddhānusārin-bhūmi). Subhūti's reply in the first line answers the Blessed One's closing question in the preceding piece. The piece breaks off mid-sentence; the following piece continues the thought. The phrase "takes delight just in looking at it" renders a difficult expression (བལྟ་བ་དང་མཉམ་པ་ལ), which I took as "delight upon merely seeing it." The sense of "ཐོགས་པ" in "taken up in his body" is uncertain; I took it as bodily retention or memorization, parallel with the written book. The passage contains a volume colophon ("the fourteenth volume") in the middle of the text, which I have rendered as it stands. The sentences about the bodhisattva's loss of "his own great aim" and "the great aim of others" follow the Tibetan's own repetitive phrasing. The passage ends mid-sentence, since the sentence is completed in the next piece. The list of qualities is a series of near-synonyms (dad pa, bzod pa, sred pa, 'dun pa, etc.). The renderings follow the sense of the standard sequence, and several terms, such as sred pa ("longing"), are positive here, not the afflictive "craving." Ma 'bral bar gyur pa and the "embraced" (yongs su bzung) construction are kept literal for doctrinal clarity. The passage includes the colophon of the fourteenth chapter, rendered as it stands in the source, followed by the opening of the next chapter. The Tibetan for the aged man's illness lists wind, bile, phlegm and their combination, the standard humoral categories of Tibetan medicine. The lines before this passage speak of a bodhisattva who does have the Perfection of Wisdom, so the opening of this piece begins the contrasting case and refers back to such a bodhisattva. The sentence about not taking pride in awakening "as form" and so on is repeated in the Tibetan, once after the instruction on generosity and once after the other perfections, and is rendered as it stands. The Tibetan has a minor irregularity in the first occurrence, "awakening as form" without the particle that appears in the second; the sense is the same. The Tibetan sequence of epithets here (protector, refuge, resting place, ally) corresponds to the Sanskrit series trāṇa, śaraṇa, parāyaṇa, and so on. I have rendered the Tibetan gnas as "resting place." The terms for engagement and connection (sbyor ba and 'brel ba) are rendered "engagement" and "connection" consistently, and the Tibetan itself shows slight variation in the repeated formulas, which I have followed as written. The phrase "become a protector for the world" is my rendering of the Tibetan "dpung gnyen," a literal "ally" or "support"; the Sanskrit probably corresponds to "trāṇa" or a similar term. The Tibetan ཆད་པ in the island passage is rendered "cut off," in the sense of the complete severance of limits, not as nihilist annihilation. The Tibetan has three related phrases: "light of the world" ('jig rten gyi snang ba), "guide of the world" ('jig rten gyi yongs su 'dren pa), and "support of the world" ('jig rten gyi rten). I rendered the middle one as "guide" in keeping with the verb 'dren pa. The term rendered "non-occurrence" is 'byung ba med pa; "non-fabrication" renders mngon par 'du mi byed pa. The phrase "arisen from the Vinaya" renders འདུལ་བ་ལས་བྱུང་བ, which could also be read as "arisen from taming" or "from discipline" in a general sense. The rendering "the unextractable" for དབྱུང་དུ་མེད་པ is literal. The Sanskrit probably has an equivalent of "without removal" or "inexpressible," and the sense is uncertain. "Boundless" renders མུ་མེད་པ, literally "without limit." Most of the sūtra's honorific and humble verb forms are rendered in plain English. In the sentence beginning "Subhūti, what purpose do you see," the text reads sangs rgyas kyis nyid la re bar bya'o. I render it "should hope for buddhahood itself," taking the sentence as the Buddha's contrast with the stages of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. The term rendered "mental continuum" (rgyud) is also "continuum" in the Blessed One's replies; it carries the sense of a stream of mind directed toward its aim. The repeated "rnam par shes pa" appears twice in the list of negations (once as consciousness among the aggregates, once after wisdom); I kept both as in the Tibetan. The passage ends mid-sentence in the source, continuing in the next piece. The Tibetan "mi mjed kyi bdag po" is the standard rendering of Sahāṃpati, Brahmā, lord of the Sahā world; I supplied "Sahā world" for the listener's benefit. The final sentence, with its triple negation of anyone ever awakening, is rendered closely; it expresses that awakening is ultimately without any awakener or awakened. The Tibetan renders Brahmā as "lord of the unendurable (world)," which corresponds to Sahāṃpati, lord of the Sahā world. The phrase "Dharma that I have fully awakened to" is spoken by the Buddha. The chapter title and colophon are translated as they stand in the source, and the next volume begins at the break. The phrase "gang gi yang de bzhin nyid ma yin pa" is read as "not the suchness of anything" in the first sentences, and "gang du yang... gang las kyang... gang gi yang" as "located in, arising from, belonging to anything" in the nondual passage; the sense is that suchness is not a property of a distinct thing. "Manifested" renders "mngon par sprul pa" (abhinirmita). The passage is the Perfection of Wisdom's teaching that suchness is non-dual and untouched by time; the phrase "born after the Tathāgata" renders the Tibetan "following along with" (rjes su skye ba), which plays on the Tathāgata's own name, "thus-gone." The speaker of the sentence beginning "Blessed One" is presumably a participant addressing the Buddha; the source does not name him, so I have not supplied a name. The opening sentence is very compressed and its syntax is ambiguous; I have rendered it as literally as clarity allows. The passage breaks off at the end of the bird simile, and the application of the simile to the bodhisattvas follows in the next piece. The Tibetan "mi mjed kyi bdag po" is rendered as "lord of the Sahā world" (Sahāṃpati), the standard epithet of Brahmā, and glossed on first use. The passage on "hearing the sound 'emptiness'" is rendered literally, in line with the traditional reading that clinging to the word as a sign is itself the error. The Tibetan "mi mjed kyi bdag po" is rendered "lord of the world of endurance" (Skt. Sahāṃpati), the usual epithet of Brahmā. In the Tibetan, "yang dag pa ma yin pa" ("not truly real") renders a Sanskrit term often translated "unreal" or "not actual." Here it is read as saying that awakening has no real, substantial existence that could be found, which is the basis of its being hard to come by. The expression "ཕྱིར་ལྡོག" is rendered "turn back," and "ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ" as "irreversible" (Skt. avaivartika). The Tibetan "འབྱུང་བར་སླར་ཟིན" ("truly something that could come about") is rendered as a conditional of real arising; the sense is that if awakening were an actual, inherently existing thing, irreversibility would be universal. This piece ends mid-exchange; Śāriputra's reply, and the parallel question about the other four aggregates, follow in the next piece. The Tibetan text has the small variant spelling of "feeling" (ཚོར་པ) in a couple of places, rendered uniformly as "feeling." Subhūti's long question about "abiding in the manner of not abiding" and "the phenomenon that has become suchness" is dense. I have kept its sequence of clauses as they stand in the Tibetan. "The three kinds of persons belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas" is a literal rendering of the Tibetan; the sense is the three vehicles, which Śāriputra then reduces to one. Pūrṇa, son of Maitrāyaṇī, is the standard identification of the Tibetan "Byams ma'i bu Gang po." The phrase "bden pa nyid dang gnas pa nyid" is rendered "true reality and the abiding nature." The word "ཐོ་འཚམ་པ" is rendered "enmity" in the sense of hostility or ill will; the exact nuance is slightly uncertain. The repeated "by the power of the Tathāgata" follows the standard Prajñāpāramitā formula. The phrase "from the truths up to the bodhisattva's entry into the state beyond fault" is a compressed abbreviation in the Tibetan (bden pa nas ... bar), standing for a longer list of items. I have rendered it as it stands, without supplying the omitted list. The Tibetan text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of this piece. The words of Māra's speech, "have been born in these eight great hells," are left open for the next piece to complete, and the closing quotation mark is deliberately omitted.

The Tibetan "ཤིག་མེད་པར་འགྱུར" is rendered "do not wear out," and "ཡོན་པོ་མེད་པ" as "without pretense," following the usual sense of these stock phrases. The phrase "will not be placed in the keeping of others" renders a idiom (gzhan gyi dring la mi 'jog pa) whose sense is that he will not be left or handed over to the guidance of another. The volume colophon is included as it stands in the source, followed by the opening of the next volume. The opening "mother" (ma) is a vocative address by the speaker, the disguised Māra, in a scene begun in the preceding piece; I kept it as a plain vocative. "Defilements exhausted" renders the standard epithet of arhats (zag pa zad pa), and "nature of reality" renders chos nyid. Otherwise none. The long list of epithets for "persons" (purusha-epithets) is rendered fairly literally. Terms such as "best of the herd" (ཁྱུ་མཆོག) and "turn the reins of those to be trained" (གདུལ་བྱའི་ཁ་ལོ་སྒྱུར་བ) are standard Perfection of Wisdom idioms. The sentence about "the supreme of bliss" is rendered closely to the Tibetan; the syntax is compressed in the source. The sentence "Rather, they dwell..." renders a clause beginning gzhan du na, which I have read as a contrast with the preceding list. The fused final lines of the source appear to repeat the earlier phrase "do not dwell in strenuous application" for talk about quarrels, as in the Tibetan. The terms sbyor ba and rjes su sbyor ba are rendered "practice" and "continued practice." The Tibetan "lus srul po" is rendered "crawling ghouls," following the usual gloss for this class of spirits. The piece ends mid-sentence; the thought continues in the next piece. The "deed of immediate retribution" (mtshams med pa) is one of the five heinous deeds that bring immediate karmic result. The passage's opening clauses are cut at the start of the piece, so the first sentence continues from the preceding context. The phrase "unplundered" renders mi 'phrogs pa, meaning that the mind cannot be seized or carried off by Māra. The final sentence ends the piece in mid-sentence; the verb "sbyod de" ("would still go on practicing") is awkward, and the sense is likely completed in the next piece. The renderings "set forth" and "go on practicing" are tentative. The phrase "he has no regret" renders nem nur, which can also mean "remorse" or "worry." The passage has no cut mid-sentence of consequence, but it ends mid-simile; the sentence about the woman, held by another, continues in the next piece. The rendering of "skillful means" (thabs zhib mo, "subtle method") follows Subhūti's wonder at the Buddha's teaching of turning away from the aggregates while still showing nirvāṇa. The terms "unconditioned" (mngon par 'du mi byed pa) and "wishless" (smon pa med pa) follow the standard Prajñāpāramitā lists. The passage breaks off in mid-sentence, as the source does. The Tibetan "gdugs" in "gdugs 'das kyi bar du" appears to be a corruption of "nyi ma" (day), so I rendered it as "until the day has passed." The first sentence's opening lines depend on the preceding context of a man tied to a woman who belongs to another. The sentence "this manifest composing is conceptual construction" renders mngon par 'dus byas pa and rnam par rtog pa. The final four phrases are rendered literally: ston pa as "something shown," gsog as "accumulated," gso ba as "nourished," snying po med pa as "without essence." The rendering of ston pa, however, is not fully certain. Where the text says "the establishing of the teaching" (bstan pa mngon par bsgrub pa), the sense is uncertain: it could also mean "the accomplishing of what is taught." The Tibetan's "synonym" (tshig bla dwags) is rendered as "synonym" throughout. "Wishless" renders smon pa med pa (Skt. apraṇihita). The piece ends mid-sentence, where the sentence continues in the next piece. In the first Subhūti passage, the phrase "as I understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said" renders the Tibetan literally; the sense is that Subhūti affirms the Buddha's teaching in his own understanding. The Tibetan alternates between "he" and "that one" for the bodhisattva; I have kept "he" throughout. The phrase "just as awakening truly is" renders the Tibetan formula that dedication is made in accord with the actual nature of awakening, that is, without reifying it. The passage has a sectional colophon (the end of the eighteenth chapter and of the seventeenth volume) followed by the opening of the next chapter's discussion. I translated the colophon as it stands, since it is in the Tibetan. In the final sentence the Tibetan is slightly elliptical ("it is not by those arisings of the mind, nor by anything other than those"); I have filled out the sense in line with the preceding sentences. The text is cut mid-sentence at the end of this piece; the sense is complete as translated. The phrase at the end of the Blessed One's question about suchness abiding "not permanently fixed" renders ཐེར་ཟུག་མ་ཡིན་པ, "not permanent, not fixed"; the sense in context is that suchness, though said to "abide," is not an abiding entity. The opening line is the end of a sentence begun in the preceding piece, and the final sentence of the preceding piece continues into it. Piece ends mid-sentence with Subhūti beginning his reply; the answer follows in the next piece. The phrase "ཀུན་ཏུ་སྤྱོད་པ" is rendered "engagements/engaging" in the Subhūti reply; its sense is somewhat compressed in the Tibetan. "རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པ" is rendered "without conceptual distinction." The last sentence of the passage (the Tibetan breaks off at "if he is present") is cut where the piece ends; the following piece continues the answer, in which Subhūti directs Śāriputra to ask Maitreya. I have rendered it as given. "Perception that exhaustion" in the Buddha question follows the Tibetan "zad pa'i 'du shes" as written, though the reading may be a variant of "perception of killing" in other witnesses. Maitreya's epithet "Invincible One" renders the Tibetan "mi pham pa," here in the form ma pham pa, a standard epithet of Maitreya (Ajita). The passage ends mid-sentence with the Blessed One's speech, which continues in the next piece. The expression "ཐམས་ཅད་ནས་ཐམས་ཅད་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དུ་ཐམས་ཅད" is a standard Prajñāpāramitā intensive negation and is rendered with the repeated "never, in any way, anywhere." The Tibetan "ཆོས་འདི་" is taken as the Dharma (the practice or phenomenon in question) being prophesied, as the sense of the passage is that the bodhisattva does not cling to the idea of such a prophecy. The passage ends mid-speech; Ānanda's question about the cause of the smile continues in the next piece. The woman is called Gaṅgādevī (the river goddess Gaṅgā), which I have rendered as "goddess Gaṅgā." Ānanda addresses the Buddha in the opening sentence, asking why the Buddha smiled; the piece begins in mid-speech. Akṣobhya's field Abhirati is rendered by its Sanskrit name with a gloss. The final sentence continues into the next piece. The Tibetan has a lacuna-like elision in the Buddha's speech where Dīpaṃkara's scattering is described; I followed the Tibetan wording, including the "five stalks of lotus" (utpala), which is a standard detail of the Dīpaṃkara story. In the Tibetan, the buddha's name, Golden Flower, is rendered into Sanskrit as Suvarṇapuṣpa, and the goddess's name, the River Ganges goddess, as Gaṅgādevī. "Sister" is the Buddha's own mode of address for her. Following the Tibetan, I translated "ཡང་དག་པའི་མཐའ" as "true limit," matching the term already used earlier, and "ཡང་དག་པའི་མཐའ་དམ་པ" as "that true limit." The phrase "མཆོག་གིས་ཉེ་བར་འབྲེལ་བར་བྱེད་པ" is rendered "unites himself with them through the supreme of loving-kindness." The sentence "སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ལ་གནས་པས་གནས་ཤིང་" is rendered "abides by abiding in emptiness." The Tibetan has the colophon, "the eighteenth volume," and the first line of the next volume inside the passage. I translated the colophon as it stands, though it may be dropped for narration. The final clause "he should set his mind thus" is cut off at the end of the piece and continues in the next. The passage is cut off mid-sentence and continues in the next piece. In the third paragraph the Tibetan has "concentration of the door of liberation of emptiness" (the first of the three doors), matching the pattern of the paragraph; I have kept it as written, although the corresponding section of the sequence might be expected to treat another door. The phrase "རིལ་པོར་འདུ་ཤེས་པ" is rendered "perception of wholes" in the sense of apprehending things as unanalyzed, solid totalities. The sentence about "not falling into non-conditioning" is as the text has it; the commentarial reading is that the bodhisattva does not fall into the extreme of cessation. The opening wish is addressed in the first person as the bodhisattva's own thought, continuing from the preceding piece. Following the standard Perfection of Wisdom usage, the repeated phrase translated "bring into direct experience" renders a verb meaning to actualize, make manifest, or realize before oneself, and the context concerns not "realizing" the three doors of liberation prematurely in a way that abandons beings. The word "ground" for the final stage-related terms (ས) is used in the sense of the bodhisattva grounds; "stage" is a possible alternative. The phrase rendered "light fills a fathom's breadth" follows the Tibetan "od 'dom gang bar"; the passage elsewhere describes the body's radiance of a fathom, and the syntax here is compressed. The "billions" (khrag khrig) is a very large number in the Indian numerical series; the exact value is unspecified. The sentence about "karma that accords with rising up in this very life" (mthong ba'i chos la 'byung bar 'gyur ba dang rjes su mthun pa) is difficult and may be corrupt or elliptical; the rendering here follows the Tibetan literally. The "remainder" (lhag ma dang bcas pa) suggests a karmic result that persists beyond the immediate ripening. The passage contains a chapter colophon in the Tibetan itself, "Practice in Skillful Means," as the twentieth chapter, followed by the opening of the next chapter. The repeated verbs of departing and not departing follow the Tibetan. The final line of the passage is an incomplete sentence (the question "Why is that?") whose answer begins the next piece. The passage continues mid-sentence into the next piece, where the list of names goes on. "Non-human" renders mi ma yin pa, a spirit, as in the preceding context. The Tibetan says "through the blessing of that truth" (bden pa'i byin gyi rlabs); I kept it literal. The sentence at the end is cut off at the piece boundary and continues in the next piece. The list of ascetic practices follows the standard dhūtaṅga categories as rendered by the Tibetan; a few terms are rendered by sense, for example the one who keeps to the seat as laid out and the one who wears felt. The piece ends mid-sentence; the sense continues in the following passage. The phrase "those of Māra's following" renders a Tibetan expression of somewhat uncertain wording (bdud kyi ris kyi lta dag), taken here as a reference to Māra's retinue. The passage speaks of the "four root downfalls" and the "five acts of immediate retribution" without listing them; they are the standard pārājikas of the Vinaya and the five ānantarya crimes. The "naming" (mtshan bstan / ming bstan) refers to declaring or predicting a bodhisattva's name; I have kept the text's sense that the contempt arises on the occasion of such naming. The terms gdol pa, sun 'byin pa, gzugs brnyan, bcos bu, and sre dar are rendered by context as "outcaste," "refuter," "reflection," "counterfeit," and "sprout gone to waste." The last, sre dar, is the least certain; it may also be read as "blighted sprout" or "weed." The phrase "a quality of seclusion that has gone astray" renders a difficult clause, literally "through the quality of seclusion, a work of Māra"; I have taken it as a warning about misdirected solitude. The remark about overcoming others "through their own direct knowledge" is also compressed in the Tibetan and is rendered closely. The Tibetan has "dpung gnyen" for "ally"; this probably renders a Sanskrit term for a supporting companion or defender. The sequence of epithets is formulaic. In the sentence about the wisdom "that is unequal and equal," the Tibetan reads mi mnyam pa dang mnyam pa'i ye shes, translated literally. The phrase "go without relying on others" renders a stock expression whose literal sense is "not placing the neck (burden) on another," meaning independence from others' guidance. "Secluded" renders dben pa (Skt. viveka), which can also mean "solitary" or "isolated." The final sentence of the passage lists four states of the fully awakened: buddhahood, Tathāgata-hood, self-arisen-ness (rang 'byung), and omniscience. I have rendered rang 'byung nyid as "the state of the self-arisen one," following the Sanskrit svayambhū. The sentence "it is just as there is no grasping and no clinging that one does not know grasping at 'I' and 'mine' at all" renders a compressed Tibetan clause literally; it means that in the absence of grasping, "I" and "mine" are not known as real. Where the Tibetan has the negated verb "practice in form" (gzugs la mi spyod), I have kept the literal "does not practice in form," as in the Perfection of Wisdom idiom. The first sentence is a continuation from the previous piece, where Subhūti is speaking; I have kept it in his voice without a label. The Tibetan shows variant spellings (for example "rang byung" and "rang 'byung" for the self-arisen state); both are rendered the same. The final sentences about the Tathāgata's incomparability are given as a reason for the preceding statement about loving-kindness, following the repeated "why is that" structure. The piece begins mid-simile, after the man has lost his jewel. The sentence about the bodhisattva who has "fallen away" from the Perfection of Wisdom is compressed in the Tibetan; I have kept its parallel with the man who has lost the jewel and still perceives it as precious. The Tibetan "ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ" is rendered "attention" (Skt. manasikāra) throughout. The passage ends mid-exchange with the Blessed One about to speak, as the cut falls there. In the Tibetan, the question "does X practice the Perfection of Wisdom" uses the same verb throughout, and I kept it uniform. The last question of the Buddha is rendered with its tense series (has arisen, is arising, will arise, and so on) as the Tibetan lists them. The phrase "caravan leader" renders the epithet "great leader of the caravan" (dped dpon chen po), the Buddha as guide of beings. In the last sentence the Tibetan reads "ngan ngon gyi dge ba'i rtsa ba," rendered "inferior root of virtue"; the line is the beginning of a statement continued in the next piece, where the Blessed One's confirmation completes it. The Tibetan has the passage on the bowls with the odd phrase "do not be slow" rendered here from "la gor slobs shig"; the sense of urging haste is clear from context. The four alms bowls are the bowls offered by the Four Great Kings to the Buddha at his awakening, a well-known episode. The volume and chapter headings are translated as they stand in the text. The passage ends mid-thought; the next piece continues the thought of the bodhisattva who believes he has found a companion who fulfills his wishes. "Spu zing" is rendered literally as "struck with terror" (lit. causing the hair to stand on end), following the earlier usage in this text. The final quoted sentence is cut off at the end of the piece and continues in the next piece; I have left it open as in the Tibetan. "Put on the armor" renders the idiom of donning the armor of bodhisattva practice, here meaning to undergo the long course of practice again for as many eons as the thoughts of awakening. The opening line continues a speech begun in the previous piece, where the bodhisattva reflects in the first person. The phrase "swiftly awaken" translates the standard formula for complete buddhahood. "Training in exhaustion" (zad pa) is left literal; the next piece elaborates it as the exhaustion of phenomena. The "caste of bamboo workers" renders the Tibetan "bya ba'i rigs," a standard rendering of a low-caste occupational group; the exact Sanskrit referent is uncertain. "Realm of the deathless" renders the "nectar" (amṛta) realm, a common figure for nirvāṇa. The terms for the faults in the list of nine are rendered by the most natural senses: crookedness (ཐ་བ), doubt, envy, miserliness, immoral conduct, malice, laziness, distraction, and confused wisdom. The phrase "practice in accordance with suchness" renders a clause whose exact sense is slightly uncertain, but it is not significantly in doubt. The piece ends mid-sentence with a simile whose content follows in the next passage. The sixty-two views are the standard list of wrong views, here said to be contained within the view of the perishable aggregates (satkāyadṛṣṭi). The Tibetan "ཁྱུ་མཆོག" ("supreme leader of the herd") is rendered literally; it corresponds to the Sanskrit image of the bull or leader of the herd as an epithet of a buddha. The text ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the middle of the colophon and begins a new volume and chapter with Śakra's thought. The phrase "the excellences of the śrāvakas" renders phun sum tshogs pa, meaning accomplishments or perfections. The passage on "those who need no further training" refers to arhats; the sense is that the bodhisattva does not train in the thought of dwelling in such excellences. The phrase "those excellent beings" at the start follows the Tibetan "sems can dam pa," which refers back to the preceding statement about beings who will fully awaken. The sentence "wishing for the sake of great compassion" is rendered as the Tibetan stands; the sense is that such bodhisattvas are moved by great compassion. The phrase "bound to only one more birth" renders the traditional category of a bodhisattva who is one birth away from buddhahood. The sentence "should be known as blessed, that is, possessed, by Māra" renders a phrase that literally says "empowered by Māra" (the Tibetan uses the word for blessing or empowerment in a negative sense, meaning they are under Māra's influence). The text breaks off at the end with Śakra about to speak; his words belong to the next piece. The phrase "the fourth great continent" is as in the Tibetan, continuing an enumeration of world-systems begun earlier. The passage ends mid-exchange, with Subhūti's reply beginning in the next piece. The Tibetan "bskyed pa" in "sems bskyed pa" is rendered "generation of the awakening mind," following the context. The final sentence is syntactically compressed in the Tibetan; I have kept the sense that not realizing the profound meaning at the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha stage, while practicing in it, is the difficult deed. The qualifier "the Perfection of Wisdom, utterly secluded" renders shin tu dben pa, which can also be read as "utterly isolated" or "empty." The Tibetan ends with the introduction to Subhūti's reply. The reply itself, that practicing the Perfection of Wisdom is practicing in what is not the essence, appears in the following passage. The statement that bodhisattvas who do not directly realize the true limit "are not doing what is difficult" is taken as Subhūti's deliberate reframing: the truly difficult thing is vowing to liberate beings who ultimately do not exist. The Tibetan lists of Brahmā-realm gods give the standard Tibetan names of the Sanskrit heavens, rendered here by their usual English equivalents. "Priests of Brahmā" renders the god named "Facing Brahmā" (Brahmapurohita). The names of the Brahmā-world gods are given in the usual English forms of the Tibetan; the identifications are not fully certain in every case. "Prajāpati" renders the Tibetan "Lord of Beings" (skye dgu'i bdag po) and "Īśāna" renders dbang ldan, as in the glossary. The phrase "gnas pa'i gnas pa" in the gods' speech is rendered as "abiding of the Perfection of Wisdom," following the repeated "gnas" and "abide" structure; the wording is slightly redundant in the Tibetan. The words "ldongs pa" are rendered "blind," with "light" for "snang ba," in keeping with the stock series of epithets. Ratnaketu and Śikhin render the Tibetan names "Jewel Crest" and "Topknot-bearer"; these are the standard Sanskrit equivalents of the bodhisattva names in this sūtra. The final question, "And who are they?", leads directly into the next piece. "Qualities of inherent nature" renders a somewhat awkward Tibetan phrase and is kept close to the source. Ratnaketu (རིན་པོ་ཆེའི་ཏོག) is a standard Prajñāpāramitā reference to the tathāgata of that name. The text reads as a bodhisattva "Ratnaketu", but the Tibetan matches the preceding "Tathāgata" pattern, so this is likely a Tathāgata. I have kept it as the Tibetan states. Near the end, the final clause before the Tathāgata exception, "whatever is not that," is a slightly awkward Tibetan phrase; I have kept it as it stands. In the passage on comparison, I read the series of numerical fractions as the standard ascending sequence of the Perfection of Wisdom sūtras; one large term in it is rendered by approximation, and I have not fixed its exact numerical value. Because Subhūti is first named without his full honorific here, "Subhūti" in the opening line follows the earlier established name.

In the translation body, one spelling slipped: "Kauschika" in the seventh paragraph should read "Kauśika" throughout. The passage runs from the end of chapter 27 into the beginning of the twenty-second section. The Tibetan makes the six hundred thousand monks (dge slong brgya phrag drug cu) a large number. Their name in the future, Spread of Flowers, is rendered from the Tibetan me tog bkram pa. The text breaks off mid-sentence in the following piece, which continues with the equality of their lifespans. The long list of verbs for holding, reading, teaching and memorizing the sūtra is repeated in the Tibetan with small variations, and is rendered here accordingly. The phrase "at the least in writing" translates the Tibetan "ཆུང་ངུ་ན་ཡི་གེར", which I understand as "even if only by writing it down." In the Tibetan, "the Victors" in the opening paragraph stands for the buddhas of the past. The instructions in the closing sentences are imperatives addressed to Ānanda, by the Blessed One, who is understood to be the speaker throughout. The next piece continues the same series of injunctions. The Tibetan breaks off mid-sentence at the end ("...and asks about it,"); the sentence continues in the next piece, so I have left it open. The phrase "this is my final instruction" renders ངའི་རྗེས་སུ་བསྟན་པ, which could also be read as "my subsequent teaching." The final run of numerals for eons is rendered with approximate values, as the Tibetan numerals there are idiomatic. The opening sentence continues from the previous piece, so "it" refers to the Perfection of Wisdom there. In the Tibetan, "mi zad pa" modifies the treasury of the Dharma, and I have kept it so. The source has a few minor orthographic slips, such as "gdon" for "'don" and "byung par gyur pa" for "byung bar gyur pa"; I read them as the intended standard forms. The terms for short durations (nyi ma, snga dro, chu tshod, yud tsam, thang cig, skad cig) are rendered as day, morning, hour, brief while, moment, instant, a descending scale; the exact units are approximate. The phrase "the work of a śrāvaka" translates the Tibetan idiom of fulfilling a śrāvaka's task. The Tibetan uses "dgos pa byed nus pa" for "capacity to perform a function"; I read it as the ability to accomplish a purpose. The listing of arhat qualities follows the standard formula. In the first paragraph, "think upon" renders "sems pa", meaning those who reflect on or contemplate such roots of virtue. The phrase "equal to the unequal" renders the Tibetan literally (mi mnyam pa dang mnyam pa), the standard epithet "equal to the unequalled." "Unfathomable" renders gzhal du med pa, which can also be rendered "immeasurable"; I used "unfathomable" to avoid repeating the word. The statement about the present buddha ("the present Tathāgata") follows the Tibetan literally; it likely refers to the Buddha himself, who is speaking. In the chain of dependent origination, the Tibetan lists "feeling" a second time after "contact," as in the standard twelve links, so I have kept the repetition. The sentence "this attention and this skillful means" refers back to the practice of viewing dependent origination through inexhaustibility; the Tibetan "ཡིད་ལ་བྱེད་པ" is rendered as "attention" (Skt. manasikāra). The final sentence is cut off by the piece boundary; it continues into the list of dependent-origination links in the next piece. The passage ends in mid-sentence ("brings to completion the cultivation of all skillful means"), which is a cut between pieces, not damage in the source. Māra is written in the plural ("Māras the Evil One") where the text asks about many Māras, following the text's own usage. The phrase ན་སེ་གོལ་གཏོགས་པ is rendered as a "snap of the fingers," following the common sense of the idiom. The phrase rendered "fortunate-lacking condition" (སྐལ་པ་མེད་པ) is uncertain in this context; it may refer to an unfavorable birth lacking opportunity for the Dharma. Gandhahastin renders the Tibetan "spos kyi glang po" (literally "Incense Elephant"). The line about the arhat is taken to mean that all phenomena are pure by nature, as a noble arhat is pure. The phrase on laying down the burden follows the standard image of the arhat who has put down the burden. "Definitively distinguished" is a literal reading of "nges par 'byed pa." The phrase rendered "Brahmā-like" translates the Tibetan ཚངས་པར་གྱུར་བ, literally "having become Brahmā" or "become holy"; I read it as a figurative expression of the purity and peacefulness of all phenomena. The phrase "like medicine" follows the Tibetan literally. The word སྨོན་པ་མེད་པ is rendered "wishless" in the triad of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and "without wishes" in the later parallel line. The Tibetan "mu med pa" (without limit, boundless) is used throughout; I rendered it as "without limit" or "the limitless." In the lion's-roar sentence the Tibetan is elliptical, and I kept it close to the source. The last line ends the piece, and the continuation for feeling and the other aggregates follows in the next piece. The phrase ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་མུ་མེད་པ is rendered "boundless absorption" and མུ་མེད་པ elsewhere as "boundless." The statement that form "extends to the virtuous, the non-virtuous, and the unapprehendable" is a literal rendering of a terse phrase. The final clause about abandoning "all beings" is taken as the Tibetan states it, meaning giving up clinging to beings as objects of attachment. The opening of the next chapter names the bodhisattva Sadāprarudita (Ever-Weeping) in a sentence that continues into the next piece. Sadāprarudita is the standard Sanskrit name for "Ever-Weeping" (rtag tu ngu), the bodhisattva's name in this chapter; I used the Sanskrit as a proper name. The Tibetan text has a few irregular spellings (for example "rtag tu ngu sngon" and "rtag tu ngus") that I took as the same name. "The view of the perishable collection" renders 'jig tshogs (satkāyadṛṣṭi), and the clause about not stirring from it is as in the Tibetan. The ending is unusual: "pass a day and a night" follows the Tibetan. The name Sadāprarudita (Tibetan rtag tu ngu) is not spelled out in this piece, since the Tibetan gives only the epithet "ever weeping" (rtag tu ngus); I used the standard Sanskrit name, as the Tibetan renders it. In the quotation of the voice's instruction, I have taken the opening lines as the bodhisattva's resolve and the rest as the instruction continuing. The phrase about the "low-lying ground" and the ring of precious substances around the city is obscure in the Tibetan; I have kept it literal. Likewise "five hundred who dwell there free of envy" omits a head noun in the Tibetan, and I have not supplied one. The passage is a piece cut from within a longer description. The names of the groves and ponds are rendered literally, as they appear to be descriptive names, not standard Indian proper names. "A cry's distance" renders a unit of measure (krośa, the distance a shout carries). The mansion's owner is Dharmodgata (Tibetan chos 'phags, "Noble Dharma"), identified by the standard name of the teacher in this chapter; the city is Gandhavatī, here rendered "Fragrant." The piece ends mid-sentence ("go, and"); the next piece completes it. The Tibetan names the bodhisattva Chos 'phags, rendered Dharmodgata (the usual Sanskrit name, Dharmodgata). The city is Spos ldan, rendered Gandhavatī; it appears only in the text itself as "the city" before this passage, so I gave the Sanskrit name where the Tibetan has it. The Tibetan "rgyang grags phyed" in the canopy passage is rendered "half a bowshot," a standard measure; the exact sense of the passage describing the awning and its being "well fixed" is slightly obscure in the source, and I have given the plainest reading. The name of the bodhisattva (ཏུ་ངུས, "Always Weeping") is rendered Sadāprarudita, the standard Sanskrit. The names of the meditative absorptions are rendered literally from the Tibetan; the Sanskrit titles of many are not securely reconstructable. The sentence beginning "Son of good family, if I hear…" is somewhat elliptical in the Tibetan; I have rendered it as Sadāprarudita's own thought. The passage ends mid-sentence, as the piece is cut there; the sense continues in the next piece (what clothing or other gift he might offer to honor Dharmodgata). The Tibetan names Sadāprarudita as བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་རྟག་ཏུ་ངུ ("Ever-Weeping") and Dharmodgata as ཆོས་འཕགས; I used the standard Sanskrit names. The Tibetan lists offerings in a long series; I have rendered ཕྱེ་མ as powders and བ་དན་ as pennants, and kept the list in plain flowing form. The sentence "for a long time my body has been sold in vain, wasted" follows the Tibetan literally; the sense is that his bodies in past lives were repeatedly spent on worthless ends. The passage ends mid-sentence, as the piece is cut there; the sentence continues in the next piece. The text calls the one being addressed in the opening line "he"; I took this as Śakra, since the preceding context has him approach in the form of a young brahmin. The Tibetan for the sacrificial rite uses "mchod sbyin"; I rendered it as a sacrificial offering. The first sentence continues the preceding speech of the merchant's daughter, who is describing the benefits of training under the teacher (Dharmodgata). I rendered the verbs as the speaker's own aspiration, as the Tibetan context suggests. The names for the offerings (musāragalva, lohitaka) are left in Sanskrit. The phrase about sharing out the Dharma to all beings follows the Tibetan. The passage is a nested report. The young woman, a householder's daughter, narrates to her parents what she saw and said, and the opening line is her own question to Ever-Weeping as quoted within her speech. Her speech continues to the end, where she addresses her parents and asks for their wealth. The final colophon line is rendered as it stands. Śakra's speech is a test: he wants no actual sacrifice but is probing Ever-Weeping's resolve, so his demand for a human heart, blood, bone, and marrow is rendered literally. The piece breaks off mid-sentence, as the source does; the sentence continues in the next piece. "Seven layers of seals" renders the Tibetan literally (rgya rim bdun). "Tiered house" renders khang pa brtsegs pa, a multi-storeyed pavilion. Following the standard rendering of this passage, "things just as they are" renders ཅི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན (Skt. yathāvat), distinct from suchness (de bzhin nyid). The piece ends mid-exchange with Dharmodgata's reply; the Tibetan then continues in the next piece. The final sentence about the great ocean's jewels continues in the next piece, where Dharmodgata completes the simile. The sentence about the śrāvakas eating alms meaningfully is rendered as the Tibetan stands; its link to the surrounding argument is elliptical in the source. The lute is rendered from pi bang (Skt. vīṇā). The names of its parts, such as the bridge, the peg, and the frame, follow the usual sense of the terms, though the exact identification of some parts is uncertain. The "eighteen great ways and six modes" is the standard formula for earthquakes in the sūtras. Here the Tibetan lists only four of the six modes in this piece. The remaining two follow in the next piece. The repeated verbs of the earthquake (the shaking, trembling, rocking, resounding) are a standard sūtra formula for the six kinds of quake; I rendered each pair literally rather than collapsing them. In the final lines, the Tibetan is cut off mid-sentence where the piece ends; the sense is completed by the next piece. The phrase "eighty billion" renders ཁྲག་ཁྲིག་ཕྲག་བརྒྱད་ཅུ, a very large number in the text's counting. Uncertain: "ཆག་ཆག་གདབ" is rendered "sprinkle with water" because the text itself links it to ཆུ (water). The clause on destruction (རྣམ་པར་འཇིག་པ་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད) is rendered literally as it appears.
